  shipped `createExoSchema` at 2.05. **Two of the ladder's steps may be quoted and the rest may not.**
  Quotable: `+number` → `+builder` is **+1.15 µs**, and `+builder` → `+checks` is **+0.80 µs** —
  **the builder costs more than the refusals do**, which is the opposite of the order the core
  section below assumed when it called the refusals the 2026-08-22 production cost. Not quotable:
  `literal` → `+number` lands at 0.10 µs, exactly this run's resolution floor, and the run refuses
  it by name; `PAGE-US/literal` is refused outright as quantisation. **And the top rung is void**:
  `createExoSchema` 2.05 came in *under* `+checks` 2.20, so the last step is negative and prices nothing —
  the shipped call measured cheaper than the local replica of what it contains.
  The refusals' own cost, per `el()`, read off the `perElement` column of the two censuses in that
  same recording: `APP-US` `+checks` 275 ns − `+builder` 175 = **100 ns per `el()`**; `PAGE-US`
  315.4 − 176.9 = **138.5 ns per `el()`**. That is a cost per call and this page will not turn it
  into a share of anything. **The axis refuses to pick between two estimates of it**: the ladder
  subtraction and the transcribed check bodies in `checks·parts` (0.55 µs) disagree by 0.25 µs over
  the region, more than the run's resolution floor, and the recording says to read both before
  quoting either. `SPEC-US` adds the one cold path: `spec·warm` 0.75 µs against `spec·cold` 3.95
  over eight names, which the axis prints as **+400 ns for a first-ever attribute name** over a
  memoised one.
  **The composition, and it needs no run to state**: write the schema literal by hand and skip the
  builder. It is the `literal` / `+number` rung, it is copyable, and the recording already says
  what it saves. It is listed here rather than in the strategy column because it is the floor, not
  a different composition of the shipped path.

`clone-threshold` is the sixth axis with a floor, and it needs no strategy row: its **default** is
the row that beats the floor.

## The situations nothing measures

Ordered by how often a real application does the thing. This is the part of the check that does
not come out of the axis list — it comes from what the packages ship.

**First, the state between the two.** A situation can have an axis built for it and still have no
number, and this page will not file that as either "covered" or "nothing measures it".

- **A user types into a form** — *an axis exists and has produced nothing.* `@exodra/forms` ships
  `readExoControlValue`, `readExoControlValues` and `writeExoChoice` for every control, and until 2026-08-22 no axis in
  the map loaded the package. `keystroke-floor` now does: one keystroke in one field of a
  fifty-field form, with `floor·per-el` and `floor·root` as hand-written listener programs,
  `exodra·deleg` for the delegated pack and `exodra·free` for the same field left uncontrolled —
  so the write-back that makes a field controlled (`el.value = next`, put back over the string the
  browser already wrote) gets a price of its own. **There is no recording.** The axis's markup gate
  fired on its first run and refused to time programs whose markup differed, and nothing has been
  recorded since. Until it runs, the most common interaction a web application has still has no
  number — it now has a program waiting to produce one, which is a different sentence.

**And then the situations with neither.**

1. **The user navigates to another page.** `@exodra/router` ships — matching, guards, lazy
   branches, catch-all — and **no axis loads it either**. A `router-navigate` axis is the missing
   instrument. Every list axis measures a list
   changing; nothing measures a whole page being replaced by another.
2. **A list is refetched.** Fresh objects, same ids. `axes/list/reconcile.tsx:103` says in as many words that
   it hands out **one object per id for the life of the process**, and every other list axis does
   the same. Identity reconcile is the engine's central bet, and its adversarial case — the data
   layer handing back new object identities for unchanged rows — is measured **nowhere**. The
   pack that exists for exactly this, `EXO_KEYED_LIST_VOCABULARY` in `@exodra/list-reconcile`,
   appears in no axis.
3. **A click on a page with a thousand handlers.** The delegated pack has two appearances and
   neither prices a dispatch. On `toggle` it is `exodraDelegated`, on an axis whose timed region is
   a rebuild — so the pack is priced by what it costs to *install*. That install now has a floor
   beside it: `toggle.with-floor` puts `exodraDelegated` at 5.5 ms against `floor·rebuild·owned`
   5.3, same contract, one root listener against 200 handlers, and the 0.2 ms between them is
   inside what that run can resolve. `keystroke-floor` is the axis that would time a dispatch, and
   it has produced nothing. `event-dispatch` is still booked as a missing axis worth six decisions.
4. **Deeply nested markup.** Every DOM axis runs the 80-card app (three to four levels) or a flat
   list of 200 / 300 / 1000 rows. Depth is swept only by `context-cost`, for the context climb,
   and by `teardown-floor`'s single `scale·deep4` row. No axis mounts, updates or tears down a
   deep tree as its subject.
5. **An attribute-heavy update.** `reactive-update` and `update-floor`'s two text transitions
   write text. Classes, styles, boolean properties and namespaced attributes have parity *tests*
   and no measurement; `attribute-write-memo` is booked as a missing axis.
6. **A hydrated page that then updates.** `hydrate-floor` proves a port is live with one bubbling
   click, and stops there. What the first update after hydration costs — the case every server-
   rendered application reaches within a second — is measured by nothing.
7. **A server render that provides context.** `ssr-floor` renders one 5-port component with a
   **stateless** wire, and the five apps in `packages/benchmarks/ssr/apps` use no
   `provide` anywhere. The documented way a page reaches the request is a context token,
   and that path has no number. The same gap covers document assembly: `@exodra/ssr` builds the
   document around the instance markup `ssr-floor` measures, and no axis includes it.
8. **A component that unmounts and remounts.** `toggle` hides and shows a block of a live app —
   and since 2026-08-22 it does so against a floor per contract — but nothing swaps a component
   boundary the way a route change does. `component-split` measures many-small against few-large at
   exactly one size and one shape, and has no recording on disk.
9. **SVG.** No axis renders any. There is a test file and no measurement.
10. **A backend other than `@exodra/dom`.** `@exodra/term` is a shipped backend that runs the
    README's components, and no axis loads it. The one axis that ever ran a second backend beside
    the DOM one, `dom-vs-stage0-phases`, went with the backend it measured, so nothing in the map
    now prices the schema core anywhere but in a browser.
11. **Memory over a session.** Two axes print a heap column; `retained-size` is booked as a
    missing axis. Nothing measures what a long-lived page retains.

**One situation from the original list turned out to be covered**, and it is worth saying so
rather than padding the list with it: *teardown of a page that never updated* is precisely
`teardown-floor`'s `SINGLE` family — the 80-card app is mounted, torn down, and the teardown is
gated by a bubbling click on all 80 toggles that must move nothing.

## Where a no-floor axis's floor actually lives

Four of the five comparison axes with no floor participant do have one — on `update-floor`, which
took its five transitions from them by name. The work-list this implies is not "build five floors"
but "quote the one that exists":

| axis with no floor | its floor | contract the pair must share |
|---|---|---|
| `reactive-update` | `update-floor` / `TEXT-ONE`, `TEXT-SWEEP` | `told` vs `derive`, and `floor·bound` for the dispatch |
| `reconcile` | `update-floor` / `REORDER` | `floor·told` and `floor·diff` are two defensible answers |
| `list-update` | `update-floor` / `GROW-SHRINK` | the derive floor **loses** here; use `floor·told` |
| `app-update`, `exodra-app-update` | `update-floor` / `WIDE` | `WIDE`'s renderer row is a re-declaration with hoisted state |
| `initial-render`, `exodra-initial-render` | `mount-floor` | same app, byte-identical output |

**`virtual-list` and `component-split` have no floor on any axis** — and neither has a recording on
disk either, so nothing about them can be quoted at all. `props-vs-ports` was a third of this kind
and is no longer in the suite: it had no floor, both of its participants were the same renderer, and
one grid step of its `ms/mount` was 25 ns per port fill, so it could not resolve the difference it
existed to price. **A situation with no floor and no number is unmeasured, and striking an axis that
cannot resolve does not make it more unmeasured than it already was** — what it removes is a row in
this table implying otherwise. The question it stood for — what it costs a parent to hand a nested
child one object — is still unmeasured, and would need a different shape to answer: a timed region
containing only the fills, against pre-built instances, with a straight-line participant writing the
same values into the same nodes as its floor.

**`toggle` was the fourth, and it is the one that got fixed.** It was the sharpest of the four
because it is the only recorded axis where the default `exodra` row sits behind `solid`, and the
newer recording says so too: `toggle.with-floor` has `exodra` at 6.2 ms and `solid` at 5.9, where
`initial-render`, `app-update`, `list-update`, `reconcile` and `reactive-update` all put `exodra`
ahead of it. (`toggle.base1` had the same two at 10.2 and 9.2; the runs are not comparable to each
other and the ordering is what carries across.) Its expensive half is destruction. Both halves of
its 200-panel block now have a floor **on the axis itself** — `floor·rebuild·owned` for the half
that rebuilds, `floor·kept·owned` for the half that keeps — which is why `toggle` has moved out of
this section and into both columns of [The arithmetic](#the-arithmetic). `teardown-floor` still
measures a different app, and is still not that floor.

## What is unmeasured in `@exodra/core`

The list above is read off the packages. This section is the same check read off **one** package,
the one every other package and every axis sits on top of. It was written the same way: from
`packages/core/src`, the axis sources under `packages/benchmarks/src/benchmarks`, `harness.ts`,
and the JSON in `packages/benchmarks/measurements/`. **Nothing was run to write it.**

One rule decides every "is it covered?" below, and it is the rule this page exists to enforce. A
core symbol named in a benchmark file's **comment**, or **imported** and used only to build a
fixture before the clock starts, is **not covered**. Coverage means the call happens between
`harness.ts:347`'s `performance.now()` and `:349`'s.

### The seven areas

| area | in a timed region? | floor? | strategy row? | the situation, in a user's words |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `@exodra/list-reconcile` | **yes, through `reconcileExoOrder` only** — called from a transition over `c.childList(port)`; it calls the package-internal `getExoSequence` on a middle whose survivors changed order. The REORDER rungs that called the subsequence and the placement pass BY HAND, `floor·seq` and `floor·place`, are struck (`packages/benchmarks/src/benchmarks/axes/floors/update-floor.ts:228-243`), and the placement pass itself is deleted. No backend reaches the package: `.dependency-cruiser.cjs`'s `backends-do-not-know-the-reconciler` keeps it so | **yes** — `update-floor` / `REORDER` / `floor·told` | **yes** — `exodraOps` on `GROW-SHRINK`, `exodra·children` on `REORDER` | a list is reordered, grows, shrinks |
| `attr/` | **no** — not one symbol is named in any axis, and the plan compilers that call them run in `prepare()` or in warm-up | **no**, and only half of it can have one | **no** | an update writes `class`, `style`, `checked`, `aria-*` — not text |
| `events/` | **yes** — `assertExoEventPort` is, on `toggle`, and `op-click-floor` and `keystroke-floor` both fill a real event port and then drive it. `TExoEventHandler` is a type and emits nothing: what a timed region reaches is the backend's slot setter and its one `handler.call` | **yes** — `op-click-floor` and `keystroke-floor` each carry hand-written listener programs with no framework in them (`floor·per-el`, `floor·root`) | **yes** — `op-click-floor`'s `exodra·closure` / `exodra·op` / `exodra·op·deleg`, `keystroke-floor`'s `exodra·deleg` / `exodra·free` | a button is clicked and a value changes |
| `context/` | **yes** — `exoContextFrame` and `readExoContext` both, on `context-cost` | **for the provide, yes** (`push` is the floor its own header names); **for the read, no** | **no** — this page books "hoist the read" as a GUESS | a component reads a value an ancestor provided |
| `runtime/` | **no** — `grep 'exoRuntime('` over all of `packages/benchmarks` returns nothing outside `dist/` | **no** | **no**, and this is the sharpest absence: plugins are the design's stated point | a user adds a plugin, or swaps one |
| root, the schema | **yes, since 2026-08-22** — `schema-build`'s timed region *is* `createExoSchema` (`APP-US/createExoSchema` 2.05 µs, `PAGE-US/createExoSchema` 19.0), with `numberPorts` isolated as its own rung (`+number`). Everywhere else it is still **no**: `createExoSchema`/`createExoMachineBuilder` sit outside every clock on all 24 other axes. `createExoStatic` and `exoOne` are timed by nothing. `ssr-floor`'s struck `+stack` rung timed a depth-indexed instance pool that `@exodra/core` no longer ships; `wire-exo-instance.ts` keeps its own inline `plan.depth++`/`plan.depth--` and never had a pool to reach | **yes for the builder** — `literal`, `+number`: hand-written schema literals, census-checked against the shape actually built | **no** | the program starts and every component's shape is declared |
| root, the refusals | **yes, since 2026-08-22** — `schema-build`'s `+checks` rung and its `checks·parts` cross-check | **not definable** — a refusal fires or it does not | **no** | the same module load, now paying ten checks per builder call |

### `@exodra/list-reconcile` — measured, and the run resolved less than it looks

These five modules are not in `@exodra/core`: they call `insertBefore` and `removeChild`,
which a base shared with the server renderer and `@exodra/term` may not, so they are their own
package.

`update-floor.shuffled`, section `REORDER`, in µs: `floor·told` 18.4896, `floor·record` 21.875,
`floor·seq` 21.875, `floor·place` 28.3854, `floor·registry` 31.7708, `exodra·children` 29.6875,
`exodra` 33.8542. `floor·seq` swaps the hand-written `markKeepers` over `Int32Array`s for the
shipped `getExoSequence` over a `number[]`; `floor·place` then swapped the hand-written walk for
the shipped placement pass, which has since been deleted with its rung.

**Judgement: `floor·seq` and `floor·record` are equal to the digit, so that run resolved no
difference between the shipped sequence and the hand-written one.** Read it as a null, not as a
proven tie — this page's own rule about `update-floor.published` and `update-floor.shuffled`
disagreeing applies here too.

### `events/` — a shared handler has an axis of its own

`axes/list/toggle.tsx:1785` is a real `c.on(...)`, and it is what carries `toggle`'s timed region
into the `on` door — `packages/dom/src/dom/EXO_DOM_NODE_VOCABULARY.ts:155-163`, which reads
`port.index` and hands the element, the port's write data, the handler and the subject to
`schema.events.attach`.

**There is no runtime port check on that path, and there used to be a sentence here claiming one.**
`on` tests nothing: what keeps a non-event port out of it is the TYPE on the door plus the cursor
that minted the port as an event port in the first place
(`packages/core/src/schema/cursor/ExoAssertingSchemaCursor.ts:188-196`). A reader who came here looking
for the refusal would have found a function name that no longer exists in the tree.

It is **no longer the suite's only `c.on`** — `^\s*c\.on\(` also hits
`axes/mechanism/handler-count.ts`, `axes/mechanism/machine-vs-cells.ts`,
`axes/floors/op-click-floor.ts` and `axes/floors/keystroke-floor.ts`, and whether each of those
sits inside a timed region is not re-checked here.

**The dispatch hole is what `op-click-floor` was written for.** Its question, in the words of its
own header: *how much room is there below a shared handler — one module-level function plus a
per-position subject — at serving one interaction on one row of a list, and what does the delegated
strategy cost against the direct one?* Its timed region is a bubbling `dispatchEvent` on a real
button (`op-click-floor.ts:783`), not a rebuild, with the handlers installed outside that clock —
mounting is the axis's other phase and has its own table. `driver` times the instrument alone — the
`MouseEvent` and the dispatch with no handler at the end — so a handler's own share is a difference
against it. `floor·per-el` and `floor·root` are
the two hand-written programs with no framework in them, one listener per row and one listener on
the container, with `floor·per-el·twin` as the resolution null. The three framework rows vary one
thing each: `exodra·closure` is one closure per row on the direct pack, `exodra·op` is one shared
function plus 200 subjects on the same pack, and `exodra·op·deleg` is that same handler and those
same subjects under `createExoDelegatedEvents(['click'])`. So the first pair isolates the handler form
and the second isolates the pack. It prints two tables, because what a shared handler changes is
split: at mount it is one function object for the process instead of one per row, and per dispatch
it is one keyed load on the subject where a closure reads its own context.

`keystroke-floor` asks the same question of a keystroke, and it is the axis whose own header booked
this pair as missing: its `exodra·deleg` changes the pack and the handler form together, so it
cannot separate "one function for every row" from "one root listener instead of fifty".

### `context/` — the one core area with real coverage

`context-cost.b4`, in nanoseconds. Group B: `push` 1.5625, `provide·marked` 5.4687,
`provide·nomark` 7.8125 — and the axis's header calls `push` "the irreducible part of a provide on
ANY backend, server included", which is a floor claim about core's own function. Group C:
`inject·1` 1.6667, `inject·2` 2.6667, `inject·8` 7.6667, `inject·miss8` 7.6667, against the
resolution null `inject·1·twin` 1.6667. So a **context chain read at depth is swept**, and the
slope is a real per-link number.

**Judgement: group C still has no floor, and now nothing in the axis does.** `inject·1·twin` is a
null, not a floor. The floor group C lacks is a straight-line walk over the same three-field links
with the token compare removed. It used to stand beside a group that HAD one — group A's
`parent·dN`, a bare `parentNode` walk under the DOM climb — but that group and group D (the
cross-mount seam) were removed with the DOM context walk itself, so `context-cost` now carries no
floor participant of any kind and says so in its own header and ANSWER line. The numbers quoted
above for `inject·*` are still live; any figure from `climb·*`, `local·*`, `parent·*`,
`provide·marked`, `provide·nomark` or `mount·*` in `measurements/context-cost.b4.json` prices an
operation that no longer exists.

### root, the schema — the claim held on three independent readings, and then an axis was built

**Read this section as the state of the other 25 axes.** On 2026-08-22 `schema-build` was
registered and recorded, and its timed region is schema construction itself, so the sentence "no
axis in the suite constructs a schema inside a timed region" is no longer true of the map as a
whole. It remains true of every axis that measures rendering, and that is what the three readings
below establish.

Every `createExoSchema` / `createExoMachineBuilder` call in those axes is outside every clock:

- **Module scope**, most of them: `apps/exodra/exodra.tsx:57,105,261,290`; `ssr-floor.ts:817,840,870,909`;
  `axes/phases/clone-threshold.tsx:149,177,205,239,286,372`;
  `axes/app/component-split.tsx:242`. (`props-vs-ports.ts` stood in this list and its axis has been struck.
  `context-cost` used to stand in it and no longer belongs to it:
  it declares no `createExoMachineBuilder` and no `createExoSchema` at all — it times `exoContextFrame` and
  `readExoContext` over a chain it builds by hand.)
- **Setup functions**, the rest: `axes/floors/update-floor.ts:1048,1413,2127` all sit inside a
  `mount*()` whose own comment at `:1042` says "It is setup, never timed."
- **The harness forbids the residue.** `harness.ts:346-349` builds every scenario through `prep()`
  before `t0` and times only `measure()`; `:557` then throws away ten warm-up rounds before the
  first recorded sample. So even a first-mount plan compile cannot land in a median.

`createExoStatic` and `exoOne` appear in no benchmark file at all. `numberPorts` is internal to
`createExoSchema` and is reached only through it.

**`schema-build` is no longer an unlit path, and anything in this repository that still calls it one
is stale.** It used to be true that every axis in the suite starts *after* the schema exists. The
path was lit on 2026-08-22: `schema-build.published`, 15 rows
across three censuses, 4 refusals. What that recording says — including which of its steps may not
be quoted, and the top rung that came out **void** — is in
[Floor, no strategy](#floor-no-strategy--and-a-named-guess-for-each) above, and the headline is
that the **builder** costs more than the refusals do (+1.15 µs against +0.80 on `APP-US`), which
inverts what the next section assumed.

One recorded rung prices a mechanism that no longer exists anywhere. `ssr-floor.published` CENSUS
puts `+try` at 0.2075 ms and `+stack` — the rung that bracketed each instance with a depth-indexed
pool — at 0.2175, with `exodra` at 0.2450 and the hand-written `floor` at 0.0575. **The rung is
struck and the recording is kept**: the pool it priced has been deleted from `@exodra/core`, and no
backend pools anything, so those two figures rank nothing a render path runs today.

### root, the refusals — a production build now runs ten of them, and one axis now prices them

The move is visible in the sources, and it is now enforced rather than described. Every refusal in
this package puts `typeof process !== 'undefined' && process.env.NODE_ENV !== 'production'`
**inside `throw new Error(…)`**, with the explanation on the development side and a short code on
the production side, so a bundler folds the explanation away and the condition survives.
`packages/core/src/tests/errorCodeRegistry.test.ts` is what holds that shape: it fails on a
refusal that ships prose, on a code with no registry row, and on a row with no page section.

The several-roots check has the same shape —
`packages/core/src/schema/markup/asserts/assertExoOneRoot.ts:2-19`: its `if` survives a production
build, and the production side of the message is the code `EXO0105` with the root count (`:17`).

What that costs per builder call, read off `ExoSchemaBuilder.ts`:

| call | refusals a production build runs |
|---|---|
| `el(tag, attrs)` | `assertExoLegalTagName` (`:66`), `assertExoNoElementInRawText` (`:67`), `assertExoLegalAttrName` **once per static attribute** (`:71`) |
| `port(name)` | `assertExoLegalAttrName` (`:89`), `assertExoUniqueAttr` (`:90`), `assertExoServablePropertyPort` (`:91`) |
| `text(value)` | `assertExoIntactRawTextBoundary` (`:83`) |
| `textPort()` | `assertExoNoTextPortInRawText` (`:110`) |
| `childrenPort()` | `assertExoSoleChildRawTextPort` (`:118`) |

`assertExoUniqueAttr` is the one with a shape rather than a constant: it scans `node.attrs` and
`node.attrPorts` and calls `exoAttribute` on every entry
(`packages/core/src/attr/asserts/assertExoUniqueAttr.ts:11,16`), so
declaring the *n*th port on an element is O(n). **`schema-build` now measures the aggregate of this
and refuses to resolve it into parts.** `schema-build.published` prices the whole set added at once
— `APP-US` `+builder` 1.40 µs → `+checks` 2.20, a step of **+0.80 µs** over the app's four schemas,
or **100 ns per `el()`** by that census's `perElement` column and **138.5 ns per `el()`** by
`PAGE-US`'s — and then refuses to pick between that estimate and the 0.55 µs the transcribed check
bodies (`checks·parts`) cost, because the two disagree by 0.25 µs, more than the run's resolution
floor. Nothing prices `assertExoUniqueAttr`'s O(n) shape separately, and the axis has no rung that
varies *n*.

One of the two `@exodra/core` files that decide what a *name* becomes is now timed as well:
`exoAttribute`'s memo is the subject of `SPEC-US`, where `spec·warm` 0.75 µs against
`spec·cold` 3.95 over eight names is printed by the axis as **+400 ns for a first-ever attribute
name**. `exoDomPropertyKind` is still reached only from here and from the plan compilers, all of
which run before every clock.

**A refusal has no floor, and that is a real answer rather than a missing one.** It either fires or
it does not; the only measurable question is what it costs on the happy path, which is a ladder
(the shape `child-mark` and `ssr-floor`'s CENSUS already use), not a floor comparison. The suite
already contains the proof that such a ladder resolves: `ssr-floor.published` puts `CENSUS/floor`
at 0.0575 ms and `CENSUS/esc` — the identical program with `escapeExoText` and
`escapeExoAttributeValue` on all four dynamic values — at 0.1125, against the null `CENSUS/esc·twin`
at 0.1125.

### The core situations nothing measures, most common first

Ordered by how often a running program reaches the code, not by how interesting the gap is. "Floor
definable?" asks whether a straight-line program doing the same job can be written at all.

| # | the situation | what would have to be built | floor definable? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | ~~**A button is clicked and a shared handler runs.**~~ **BUILT** — `op-click-floor` is that axis: the timed region is a bubbling `dispatchEvent` with the handlers installed outside it, and a closure, a shared handler on the direct pack and the same shared handler under `createExoDelegatedEvents(['click'])` are three separate rows against two hand-written floors | nothing further until it runs — no file for it exists in `packages/benchmarks/measurements/` | **yes** — `el.onclick = () => { row.closed = true }`, straight-line, same observable effect |
| 2 | **An update writes something that is not text.** class, style, a boolean property, a namespaced attribute | an `attribute-write-memo` axis, with `exoAttribute`'s memo hit and miss as separate rungs | **yes** — a direct `setAttribute` / property store per write |
| 3 | ~~**The program starts and every schema is declared.**~~ **BUILT AND RECORDED, 2026-08-22** — `schema-build.published`, three censuses, 15 rows, 4 refusals. It is a ladder over the app's four schemas and a 65-element page: literals, `+number`, `+builder`, `+checks`, shipped `createExoSchema`, plus `checks·parts` as a second estimate and `SPEC-US` for the name memo | nothing further, except the two things the run itself asks for: a larger batch, since it refused `PAGE-US/literal` and every ladder step under its 0.100 µs resolution floor, and a rung that varies *n* for `assertExoUniqueAttr`'s O(n) | **yes for the builder** (hand-written schema literals, and they are the `literal` rung); **no for the refusals** |
| 4 | **A backend is composed with N plugins, then called through.** `new ExoDomBackend(...plugins)`, `composeExoPlugins` | two regions: composition at N = 0/1/4/16, and a call through a merged method against a direct call to the same implementation. **Built:** `plugin-compose` measures exactly these two moments; the rows it replaced on 2026-08-29 measured the deleted named-slot runtime and are void | **yes** — the direct call is the floor for the call; composition's floor is the object literal it replaces |
| 5 | **A context read at depth, aggregated over a mount.** partially covered: `inject·1..8` is swept, the per-mount total and the floor are not | one floor row in group C (the same chain walk with the token compare removed) and one mount-scale row (M consumers × depth D) | **yes** |
| 6 | ~~**Two backends place the same rows.**~~ **VOID** — the node-anchored placement pass this compared against `reconcileExoOrder` is deleted; every backend places through the `childList` door | nothing | — |
| 7 | **A child is placed by `exoOne` or `createExoStatic`.** the two non-list child primitives | rungs on an existing mount axis, since both are per-instance and not per-row | **yes** |
| 8 | **A row leaves a list and its subscriptions end.** a `childList` `remove` and a teardown of the whole region | a teardown-side list axis | **yes** — `teardown-floor`'s contracts already define what "the same job" means |

**Judgement on the ordering.** 1 and 2 are things a page does continuously; 3 and 4 are once per
process but sit on the critical path to first paint, and 3 became a production cost on 2026-08-22
rather than a development one. **3 is also the one that has since been measured, and it moved the
argument**: the reason it was ranked here was the refusals, and the recording puts the builder
above them (+1.15 µs against +0.80 on `APP-US`). The ordering stands; the cause named for it does
not. 6, 7 and 8 are last because a real program reaches 6 and 8 **zero times today** — no caller
exists.



- **Firm.** The axis list, the participant rows and every median quoted: read from
  `run-one-axis.js`, from the axis sources, and from the JSON in
  `packages/benchmarks/measurements/`. The count of 25 is a count of the keys in `AXES`.
- **Firm.** Which axes have a recording and which do not: it is the file list of
  `packages/benchmarks/measurements/` against the keys of `AXES`, and the six with none are named
  in [The arithmetic](#the-arithmetic).
- **Firm.** The absences. `@exodra/router` and `EXO_KEYED_LIST_VOCABULARY` are matched by
  nothing under `packages/benchmarks/src`, and `mount-floor` mentions node recycling only to say
  its floor refuses to do it — which nothing in `@exodra/dom` does. `@exodra/forms` left that list on 2026-08-22 and entered the "built, unrun" one:
  `keystroke-floor.ts` imports it, and no recording exists.
- **Judgement.** The floor/no-floor verdict on `mount-phases`, `child-mark`, `teardown-phases` and
  `bank-vs-clone` — the last of which has since been **deleted with the node bank**, so the counts
  in this bullet are the counts as they stood when it was written and nobody has recomputed them.
  Each of those has a hand-written base rung, and each rung produces something
  *other* than the measured subject's output — a tree with no wiring, a clone with no mark, a
  cleared region. Read strictly ("same output"), they are not floors; read loosely, three of them
  are. The strict reading is used throughout, and it is why the count is 6 and not 9.
- **Judgement.** Calling `exodraOimdb`, `exodraMono` and `ports` strategy rows.
  Each is a composition a user could write, and none of them was put in its axis to close a gap to
  a floor — there is no floor in those axes to close.
- **Guess, and labelled as one in the text.** All four proposed strategy rows in
  [Floor, no strategy](#floor-no-strategy--and-a-named-guess-for-each). Nothing here was measured.
- **Not checked.** Whether any of the eleven uncovered situations would come out well or badly, or
  what `keystroke-floor` will print when it runs. This page says only that nothing measures them.

And for [What is unmeasured in `@exodra/core`](#what-is-unmeasured-in-exodracore):

- **Firm.** Every call-site line number, every "appears only in a comment", and the guard shape of
  all eleven `NODE_ENV` sites in `@exodra/core` — grepped over `packages/core/src` and
  `packages/*/src`, `dist/` and `node_modules/` excluded. Every median: read from
  `update-floor.shuffled.json`, `context-cost.b4.json` and `ssr-floor.published.json`.
- **Firm.** That no axis **that measures rendering** constructs a schema inside a timed region. It
  rests on three independent facts, not one — module-scope declaration, the `mount*()` setup
  comment, and `harness.ts`'s untimed `prep()` plus ten discarded warm-up rounds — and any one of
  them alone would settle it. `schema-build` is the axis for which the opposite is true by
  construction, and it measures no rendering.
- **Firm.** That `op-click-floor`'s timed region is a real dispatch: `op-click-floor.ts:783`
  constructs a bubbling `MouseEvent` and calls `dispatchEvent` on a button.
- **Judgement.** Reading `floor·seq` = `floor·record` = 21.875 µs as a null rather than as a
  measured tie, and calling group C floorless while counting group B's `push` as a floor.
- **Judgement.** The ordering of the eight situations, and the claim that a refusal has no floor.
- **Not checked.** What any of the eight would cost. Not one of them was run, and no figure in that
  section is an estimate of a thing nobody measured — every number quoted there is a recorded row.


==============================================================================
# Security

Exodra renders untrusted data in two places — as element content and as attribute
values — and serialises server state into a `<script>` element. This page states
exactly what the framework guarantees at each of those points, what it explicitly
does **not** do, and where the executable proof lives.

:::note One pair of escapers
Text and attribute values go through `escapeExoText` and `escapeExoAttributeValue`
from `@exodra/core` — the **same** two functions on the server and in the DOM
compiler, because hydration rests on the two producing the same bytes. A copy
made "for the DOM side" would not be a duplicate helper; it would be the end of
hydration.
:::

The guarantees are mapped to published references rather than to our own
categories, so you can audit them against something that is not us:

- **[OWASP ASVS](https://owasp.org/www-project-application-security-verification-standard/)**,
  chapter *Validation, Sanitization and Encoding*, section **V5.3 Output Encoding
  and Injection Prevention**. The two requirements that apply to a rendering
  library are that output encoding matches the interpreter and context, and that
  context-aware escaping protects against reflected, stored and DOM-based XSS. We
  cite the section rather than individual requirement numbers on purpose: ASVS 5.0
  renumbered the chapters, and a pinned number would rot.
- **CWE** identifiers for naming each weakness precisely.
- Payloads from the **OWASP XSS Filter Evasion Cheat Sheet** and the **html5sec**
  corpus.

There is no official conformance suite for XSS encoding — no W3C or IETF document
defines one — so those corpora are the de-facto standard, and they are what every
framework tests against.

## What is covered

| Reference | Context | Exodra's guarantee | Tests |
|---|---|---|---|
| ASVS V5.3 · CWE-79, CWE-80 | Untrusted data in element content | `&`, `<`, `>`, `"` are escaped before any text reaches the output. Pre-escaped input is escaped again, so there is no double-decode hole. | `packages/dom/src/tests/escape.test.ts`, `packages/dom/src/tests/dynamic-escape.test.ts` |
| ASVS V5.3 · CWE-83 | Untrusted data in an attribute **value** | Values are always emitted in double quotes and escaped with the same table, so a payload cannot close the quote or start a new attribute. Single quotes need no escaping precisely because the quoting style is fixed. | `packages/dom/src/tests/dynamic-escape.test.ts` |
| ASVS V5.3 · CWE-83 | Untrusted data in an attribute **name** | A name is checked when it is **declared** — `b.el('a', {href})`, `b.port('data-id')` — against an allowlist: a letter or `_`, then letters, digits, `_`, `.`, `:`, `$`, `-`. Anything else **throws**, naming the call the author made. | `packages/core/src/attr/tests/assertExoLegalAttrName.test.ts` |
| ASVS V5.3 · CWE-116 | Server state inside a `<script>` element | HTML escaping does not apply inside `<script>`: the parser looks only for `</script`, and a JS parser treats U+2028/U+2029 as line terminators. The payload escapes `<`, `>`, `&`, U+2028 and U+2029 as JSON `\uXXXX` escapes, so it still parses back to the original value. | `packages/ssr/src/tests/security.test.ts` |
| CWE-84 | The **scheme** of a URL in an `href`, `src` or `action` | **Nothing. This row is here because its absence read as "the question does not arise".** A `javascript:` URL is escaped as a string and rendered as written, on both backends. See [URL schemes are not filtered](#what-is-not-covered) below for what a guard would have cost and why it is not one. | — |

**Why a name is checked at all, when it is written in code.** A name cannot be
escaped — an escaped name is a different attribute — so it goes into the markup
verbatim, on **both** backends: the server prints it, and the DOM compiler writes
the identical bytes into the string it hands the HTML parser to build the
prototype every instance is cloned from. A port named `data-x" onclick="alert(1)`
does not become an oddly-named attribute; it closes the value, opens a second
attribute, and both backends serve a working `onclick`. That is not theoretical:
`data-` plus a key is a supported thing to be building, and the moment the key
comes from data the name is attacker-shaped.

Two details of that check are deliberate:

- **It is an allowlist, not the HTML spec's blocklist.** The spec forbids
  whitespace, quotes, `>`, `/`, `=` and the C0 controls in a name, which is the
  right rule for a string that is only sent to a browser. The same string is also
  *parsed as markup* here, and "the tokenizer tolerates this character" is much
  weaker than "this character cannot mean anything but itself". `<`, a backtick,
  `&` and every non-ASCII code point pass a blocklist, and none of them is a name
  a real component wants.
- **It throws instead of dropping the attribute.** The name is fixed before a
  single request arrives, so a throw costs no availability — and dropping would
  be worse than useless, because the port would still hold the **number** both
  backends index their plans by, which would move every later value onto the
  wrong element.

Beyond that name, a schema is code: it is built once when the module loads, there
is no prop spreading, and nothing merges an object of unknown keys into an
element. Values, and only values, arrive per render.

`packages/dom/src/tests/dynamic-escape.test.ts` pins **two separate properties**, and
the distinction is the point: *safety* (a value in a text position cannot open a
tag; a value in an attribute position cannot close the quote and start another
attribute), asserted on the resulting **tree** rather than on the bytes, because
a tree is what a browser acts on — and *agreement* (the bytes the server sent and
the tree the browser would have built are the same thing), because a value the
two backends escape differently is not an error on either side, it is a page that
adopts wrong. Two backends that are both wrong in the same way satisfy agreement
perfectly, which is why "they agree" is not a security claim and is not written
down as one.

## What is NOT covered

These are deliberate. They are pinned by tests too, so changing the policy is a
visible, intentional edit rather than a silent drift.

**URL schemes are not filtered** (CWE-84 stays the application to own). A `href`
port filled with `javascript:alert(1)` renders as written, on both backends.
Filtering schemes in the framework gives false comfort — it cannot know which of
`http`, `mailto`, `tel`, `blob` or a custom scheme your app legitimately uses.
**Validate URLs where they enter your system**, or use an allowlist at the point
of render.

Know what the neighbours do before you read that as a gap, because they do not
agree with each other. **React** rewrites a `javascript:` URL — on the client and
in the server renderer — into a URL that throws when clicked, silently, with no
warning; its pattern names that one scheme, so `data:text/html;base64,…` in an
`<object data>` passes it. **Angular** warns in dev and rewrites the value to
`unsafe:…`, and needs a second, stricter mechanism that *throws* for `<iframe
src>` and script sources, where rewriting is not enough. **Vue** filters nothing
and says so in its own security guide: "if you're ever doing URL sanitization on
the frontend, you already have a security issue. User-provided URLs should always
be sanitized by your backend before even being saved to a database."  **Svelte**
filters nothing; its escaper handles characters only. **DOMPurify**, which is a
sanitiser rather than a renderer, does not blocklist at all — it allowlists nine
schemes and expects to be reconfigured, because that is the only shape of the
check that actually works.

The reason we ship none of them is not only that the useful shape needs an
allowlist we cannot know. It is that a URL's value first exists **when a wire
fills it** — a schema knows the port's name when the module loads, and never the
value — so every possible guard runs per fill, on a path that also has to produce
the same bytes on both backends or hydration adopts wrong.

**The version that would have been affordable, and why it is still not shipped.**
`createExoAttrWrite` already branches on the port's name at schema-compile time and
hands back a different writer for a property, for `class`, for a namespaced
attribute and for the ordinary case
(`packages/dom/src/dom/factories/createExoAttrWrite.ts:27-67`); the choice is made ONCE per
port when the schema compiles, not per write, because the PORT KIND already carries it — the
builder mints a different kind for a plain attribute, a string attribute and a toggle
(`packages/string/src/schema/compileExoStrSchema.ts:294-308`), and the server reads the same
kinds.
A fifth branch for `href`, `src`, `action`, `formAction` and `xlink:href` would
therefore leave every other port's writer byte-identical, and the whole price
would be one scheme test on URL-bearing ports only. That is real but small: the
escaper's fast path is a single `/[&"<> ]/.test(value)` and an immediate return
(`packages/core/src/escape/escapeExoAttributeValue.ts:8`), so a clean URL makes one
pass today and would make two. **Cost is not what refuses it.** Two other things
do. First, the only guard shippable without configuration is a blocklist, and the
shipped blocklists name one scheme — a framework running React's pattern could
say it filters URLs while `data:text/html;base64,…` in an `<object data>` still
renders, which is exactly the false comfort this section is about. Second, a
guard that alters the value becomes a second pair of functions that the server
and the client must keep byte-identical or hydration adopts wrong (Angular's
rewrite would serve `unsafe:javascript:alert(1)`), and a guard that throws turns
an XSS *attempt* into a downed response, because it fires mid-stream on
request-shaped data.

**HTML is not sanitised, and the escape hatch says so in its own name.** A
children port that is its element's **only** child may be filled with raw markup
— `c.unsafeHtml(port, html)`, which the JSX dialect declares as `unsafeHtml={$.body}` — and that
string is printed verbatim on the server and assigned through `innerHTML` in the
browser. Nothing sanitises it in either place, deliberately: a renderer that
quietly ran a sanitiser would be making a security decision for an author who has
just typed the word `unsafe`. Never hand it a string built from user input
without running it through a real sanitiser such as DOMPurify first. Every other
children port refuses a raw string by name, so this is the one path in the
renderer that can produce markup from a value.

**A lowercase inline handler written as a static attribute passes through.**
`b.el('div', { onclick: '…' })` renders `onclick="…"`, like any other attribute,
because a schema's static attributes are markup and are not inspected. The
supported channel for events is an `eventPort`, which emits no markup at all.
This is only reachable by writing it into a schema — see the attribute-name note
above — so it is a thing you can do to yourself, not a thing request data can do
to you.

**Content Security Policy is your call.** `renderExoJsonScript` accepts a `nonce` and
escapes it, so a strict CSP works, but Exodra does not set headers.

## Running the checks

```bash
npm run test:run                 # the whole suite, security tests included
npx vitest run src/tests/dynamic-escape.test.ts --dir packages/dom
npx vitest run src/tests/security.test.ts --dir packages/ssr
```

The security tests are ordinary suite members — they run on every `npm run
release:check`, so a regression blocks a release rather than being noticed later.

## Release integrity

Packages are published from a GitHub Actions workflow with
[npm provenance](https://docs.npmjs.com/generating-provenance-statements): every
tarball carries a signed attestation binding it to this repository and the commit
it was built from. Verify what you installed with:

```bash
npm audit signatures
```

The same workflow re-runs the full gate — lint, typecheck, type tests, build, the
whole suite including these security tests, and a packed-artifact install — before
anything reaches npm.

## Reporting a vulnerability

See [SECURITY.md](https://github.com/abaikov/exodra/blob/master/SECURITY.md).
Please report privately rather than opening a public issue.


==============================================================================
# Limits and plans

What Exodra does not do yet, what it will never do, and why. Everything here was
measured against the current code rather than assumed — where a limit exists, the
test that pins it is named, so you can check the claim and watch it change.

## Custom elements

Rendering a custom element works today: the tag is created, the element upgrades,
and ordinary attributes reach it.

```tsx
import { exoJsx, type TExoSchemaElementProps } from '@exodra/jsx/schema';

declare module '@exodra/jsx/schema/jsx-runtime' {
    namespace JSX {
        interface IntrinsicElements {
            'my-widget': TExoSchemaElementProps;
        }
    }
}

export const WIDGET_SCHEMA = exoJsx(($) => <my-widget id="chart" title={$.heading} />);
```

**Event names work.** An event port carries its name verbatim
to `addEventListener`, so `on:sl-change={handleChange}` — the convention every
component library follows — is heard. Nothing is lowercased and nothing is
mapped, on either the direct or the delegated pack.

**Properties still are.** A custom element takes structured data through a JS
property, not through an attribute — `el.items = [...]`. An attribute port
writes an attribute, so an object or an array arrives as `"[object Object]"`.
Whether a name is a property is decided from a table (`EXO_DOM_PROPERTIES`) and, for
the names where the tag matters, from `exoDomPropertyKind(tag, name)` — which is how
`value`, `checked` and `selected` are resolved. A custom element cannot be in
that table and cannot be asked either: before it upgrades it has no properties at
all, so the intent has to come from whoever wrote the schema.

The JSX dialect has no way to say "write this one as a property" either: `attr={$.x}`
is an attribute port, `on:` is the only namespace, and any
other namespace (`prop:options={…}`) is refused by name. How the dialect should
spell a property write is still open.

One subtlety is worth knowing before it lands: if a component's definition is
loaded lazily, a property written before the element upgrades is shadowed by the
class field when it does. Writing after `customElements.whenDefined` avoids it and
costs a turn of the event loop, and which of the two Exodra should do is exactly
the question that is still open.

Until then, the way through is the child's own `mount` hook — it runs once the
element is in the tree, which is also when a widget wants to be measured or
focused:

```ts no-check
import { exoNodeDom } from '@exodra/dom';

const child = c.build(SELECT, 0, params);
exoNodeDom(child).mount = function () {
    (this.node as HTMLElement & { options: unknown }).options = items;
};
```

That hook is called by the children stack, so it fires for anything placed
through a children port — `c.one`, `c.list`, a child list (`c.childList`) or `c.keyedList` — and
not for the root instance `backend.render` puts in a parent itself.

## Pages that other software has edited

A browser translator, an extension, a password manager or a bookmarklet will
rewrite parts of your page without telling anyone. Chrome's translator, in
particular, does not edit a text node — it takes it out and puts a `<font>`
element in its place. Any renderer holding that node is then holding a node the
document has moved or discarded, and the classic result is a crash on the next
update.

Exodra does not crash, and it does not freeze either. A bound text port caches
the `Text` node it wrote so that an update is a `.data` store rather than a
`textContent` assignment — but the cache is trusted only while that node is still
its element's one and only child, and when it is not, the write falls back to
`textContent` and re-caches whatever the browser made
(`packages/dom/src/dom/tests/text-binding.test.ts`). That covers any software that
replaces the node, and both shapes a translator produces in particular:

- **Wrapped** — your `Text` node is moved inside a `<font>` that took its place.
  Without the guard, `cached.data = …` would keep succeeding on a node the
  element no longer renders, and the page would freeze at the translated text
  with no error anywhere. The fallback writes through and the wrapper goes with
  it.
- **Replaced** — your node is discarded and a copy of the text appears inside the
  translator's element. There is nothing to recover the mapping from, so the most
  any renderer can do is notice and rebuild, which is what happens: the next
  update prints the new value and clears the wrapper.

Lists are covered by the same rule at the element level: every insertion and
removal asks the document who a node's parent currently is rather than trusting
what it cached, so removing a row takes the `<font>` that swallowed it with it
(`packages/dom/src/dom/tests/reconcile-exo-order.test.ts`).

What no renderer can restore is the *translation*: after a rebuild the text is
your value, untranslated, until the translator gets to it again.

If a page mixes heavy reactivity with text that translators will attack, the
cheap insurance is to opt out of translation for that part:

```html
<meta name="google" content="notranslate" />
```

## Focus when a list is reordered

Moving a focused element loses focus — in Exodra, and in every other framework,
because the DOM specification removes a node before it re-inserts it, even when
the "move" is a single `insertBefore` call. Verified in Chromium, not deduced.
The caret position inside an input survives; the focus does not.

This is not on the list to fix: a renderer cannot tell a deliberate reorder from
a rebuild, and restoring focus behind your back would be wrong as often as it
would be right. If a list is reorderable while someone is typing in it, save
`document.activeElement` and restore it after the change.

## Server rendering

`@exodra/string` and `@exodra/ssr` render a schema to HTML, and hydration attaches
to it. Custom elements render as their tag with attributes — their shadow content
is theirs to produce, and Exodra does not attempt declarative shadow DOM.

## Known issues

These are known, measured where a measurement exists, and not yet solved. Each names where its number comes from, so it can be re-run and watched
as it moves.

### Components are longer than in React or Solid

The application every benchmark axis mounts is **477 lines** in Exodra, against
**208** in React and **220** in Solid, counted by the harness itself with
TypeScript's parser, comments and blank lines excluded (the `app LOC` column of
`initial-render`). A schema built with `createExoSchema` declares its ports by
hand, and a machine names every transition it runs. That is the cost of having
no compiler in the way, and nothing yet makes it shorter.

### Updates sit further from their floor than mounting does

Mounting is within 1.35–1.42× of a hand-written program producing the same DOM
([What the floor says](./why/what-the-floor-says.md)). Updates, each against a
hand-written program doing the same job (`update-floor.shuffled`): a list that
grows and shrinks is level with hand-written diff code (1.000×), and the rest
sit above their floor — `text-sweep` 1.522×, `text-one` 1.562×, `reorder`
1.566× and `wide` **2.242×**, the application-wide flip.

### A list cannot be told what changed

`c.bindList` once applied a list operation — insert here, remove there —
straight to the child list without diffing, and it was the fastest row on
`list-update`. That door is deleted (`list-reconcile.tsx` says so where the row
was struck): every list notification is now a bare "it moved", re-read and
diffed. Building children with `c.build` and placing them yourself is still
possible, but no axis measures it, and `benchmarks.md` still prints the old
op-source row.

### The runtime path of `@exodra/react-compat` is slower than React by default

Measured on the benchmark application with production builds, in narrowed runs
(ratios only, inside one run, `initial-render.compat4`): mounting through the
plain runtime path took 1.330 ms against React's 1.140. With
`enableExoReactHostTemplates()` it took 0.990, ahead of React, and the compiled
path, `@exodra/babel-plugin-schema/react`, took 0.890. On `app-update`
(`app-update.compat4`) the axis reports no resolution, so only the order is
known: compiled, then templates, then React, then the plain runtime.

Templates are off by default because a component that changes the shape of a
tree it already rendered has that subtree rebuilt once, where React would keep
the unchanged siblings ([Host templates](./guides/react-compat.md#host-templates-without-the-compiler)).

### React library compatibility is not checked by anything

`packages/react-compat-libraries/tests/` holds fifteen suites — Formik,
react-query, framer-motion, Radix, react-hook-form and others — that the default
test run does not collect, so none of what they assert is currently asserted.

### Toggling a large block rebuilds it by default

Tearing out 200 panels and building others takes 10.2 ms out of the box against
Solid's 9.2 (`toggle.base1`). Keeping the subtree alive takes 3.3, but that row
builds its panels in advance and so is not comparable with Solid or any other
framework; the default rebuilds.

### The cost of building a schema cannot be re-measured

`schema-build.published` puts a runtime schema at roughly 0.26–0.29 µs per
element, once per module load. The axis that produced it is no longer in the
tree, so the figure cannot be reproduced until it is written again.


==============================================================================
# Sugar, not restrictions

A framework earns its place by handing you shorter ways to say what you were
going to say anyway. It loses it the moment the short way is the **only** way —
when the one list on the page that needs a different reconciler, the one hot spot
that needs raw DOM, or the one subtree that belongs to somebody else's renderer
forces the whole application out.

So the rule this project holds itself to is: **every convenience is a layer over
something you can still reach.** `reconcileExoOrder` is a layer over the children
primitive — it maps items to rows and places them through the child list the backend already has, which is
what `reconcileExoOrder` takes as its first argument
(`packages/list-reconcile/src/reconcileExoOrder.ts`); keeping a port in step with outside data is a
transition that writes it plus an effect that calls the transition and subscribes, and
the composition is yours.

This page is about the last of those three — the named plugin interfaces, where a
part of the renderer is replaced rather than configured. What it costs is measured on
[What the abstraction costs](./abstractions-collapse.md); how much room is left
below the whole renderer, and every measured decision in one table, is on
[What the floor says](./what-the-floor-says.md); what other frameworks put behind
a fence, and how much of it is genuinely open here, is on
[Eight things frameworks forbid](./what-others-forbid.md).

## A plugin interface is a field on the backend, and a plugin is a bag of factories

One function in `@exodra/core` is the whole mechanism.

`composeExoPlugins(base, ...plugins)` composes a backend out of plugins, once, at
startup (`packages/core/src/plugins/composeExoPlugins.ts`). A plugin is an object whose
entries are **method factories** (`packages/core/src/plugins/types/TExoPlugin.ts`): each
receives whatever stands under that name right now — a method off the base's
prototype, a method an earlier plugin merged, or `undefined` for a name nobody has
used — and returns what stands there next.

```ts no-check
export type TExoPlugin = {
    readonly [name: string]: (next: never) => unknown;
};
```

There is no namespace, no registry, no `needs` / `provides`, and no resolution
pass. `new ExoDomBackend()` merges the connector surface onto itself in its
constructor — the class fields are already written when that runs — and every pack
an application composes is a unary decorator wrapped **around** the finished
object: `withExoHydration(withExoCompiler(new ExoDomBackend()))`. Each decorator is
`(base) => composeExoPlugins(base, ENTRIES)`, so the entries are still `(next) => …`
factories and a pack still never has to know whether it is replacing or wrapping.
`composeExoPlugins` mutates the object it is handed and returns it, so the whole
chain is **one identity** — which the plan cache requires, since it keys the
backend by pointer.

Three properties of that merge are what make "replace one thing" mean one thing:

- **Replacing and wrapping are the same act** — the property `super` gave a
  prototype chain. A plugin that never calls `next` has replaced; one that calls it
  has wrapped.
- **The last plugin to claim a name wins**, and the order is the nesting order —
  outermost last. That is the same last-provider-wins rule the deleted slot
  registry had, made visible at the composition site instead of resolved somewhere
  else, at the price that it now reads **inside-out** where a variadic constructor
  read left to right. It is also the one silent hazard: two plugins that both
  replace `writers` without calling `next` leave only the outer one, with nothing
  thrown.
- **The capability check is the type of the composed object.** Nobody declares a
  capability set. A decorator states its contribution in its return type —
  `composeExoPlugins(base, EXO_KEYED_LIST_VOCABULARY)` answers `typeof base &
  TExoKeyedListApi` — and they
  compose by intersection. A wire that touches `c.keyedList` infers a **connector**
  that has it, and a backend composed without the pack does not satisfy a parameter
  typed against that connector.

  **Where that refusal lands**, because the flattering version of this sentence was
  written here first: it is a **call-site** check. A wire written against a
  connector type without `keyedList` fails to compile on the line that calls it.
  The entry points perform it too, and against the composition they were built on:
  `ExoDomBackend.render` and `hydrate` declare their component against
  `this & TExoDomInstanceRecord`, so a component demanding a pack the backend never
  merged is refused in the file that built the backend. What no entry point can see
  is a pack composed and never named — `TExoDomNode` is the record plus the shipped
  surface and names none of them (`packages/dom/src/dom/types/TExoDomMachine.ts`).
  Following outside data needs no pack: a transition writes the port with
  `c.text` / `c.attr`, the fill doors every exonode has, and an effect calls it and
  subscribes.

A merged method **exists only where it was merged**. A slot is a name the engine
has to declare before anybody can fill it, so every capability that ever shipped
left a slot, a field on the plan or a field on every child behind it — a context
field on a page that never provides a context. The merge is here for what it makes
expressible.

## What `@exodra/dom` puts behind a plugin interface

Each is a **field on the backend**:

| Field | Interface | What ships in it |
|---|---|---|
| `events` | `TExoEventsApi` | `EXO_DIRECT_EVENTS` — one listener per element |
| `writers` | `TExoWritersApi` | `EXO_SHIPPED_WRITERS` — how a value reaches an attribute or a text node |
| `createInstance` / `createChild` | `TExoDomRecordFactories` | the two record factories the constructor builds over the backend |
| `hydrateSurface` | `TExoDomRecordFactories` | nothing, until `withExoHydration` writes the adopting surface |

They are **class field initialisers** on `ExoDomBackend`
(`packages/dom/src/dom/ExoDomBackend.ts`). The adopting half is not one of them and has no
default: a backend composed without `withExoHydration` carries no `hydrateSurface`, and the
hydrate compiler REFUSES rather than falling back
(`packages/dom/src/hydrate/requireExoHydrateSurface.ts:10-12`) — the refusal exists because
`__proto__: undefined` in an object literal is legal and silent, so without it the first write of
an adopted page is a `TypeError` on a method name that says nothing about hydration.
The ones that ship are defaults rather than providers for a stated reason: a library
whose every part is removable is a construction kit, not a framework.

Children and data-following are **not** fields. A changing list is `reconcileExoOrder`
called from a transition over `c.childList(port)`, and keeping a port in step with
outside data is a transition writing `c.text` / `c.attr` from an effect that
subscribes — functions over doors every exonode has, so a second strategy is a
second function rather than a field.

## Replacing one interface

Merge a plugin onto the backend. Everything you do not name keeps the shipped
value:

```ts no-check
import { composeExoPlugins } from '@exodra/core';
import { ExoDomBackend, createExoDelegatedEvents, withExoCompiler } from '@exodra/dom';

/** ONE pack per application, at module level. */
const DELEGATED = createExoDelegatedEvents(['click', 'input']);

// `writers` and the record factories are still the shipped ones.
// Nothing was restated, and nothing was rebuilt.
const backend = withExoCompiler(
    composeExoPlugins(new ExoDomBackend(), { events: () => DELEGATED })
);

// APP is your top-level component.
backend.render(APP, document.getElementById('root') as Element);
```

The composition **is** the backend, so it travels down into every nested component
and every list row through the schema's `backend` field: a row is built by `c.build`, which
compiles the child's declaration under the backend the parent is rendering through
(`packages/dom/src/dom/exoDomSchemaForChild.ts`) — a swapped
implementation is not something you get at the top level and lose at the first child
component. The backend is also the exonode's **prototype**, so `withSomething(backend)`
and `c.something` are the same act.

**Compose once, at module level.** The backend is the schema cache key, so one built
per render hands the cache a fresh index and recompiles every schema on every render.

## The evidence that the renderer reads the field

A replaceable field is easy to fake. Every assertion of the shape "the backend's
`writers` field holds my pack" would pass **at the same time as** the compiler
reaching the shipped writers through a static module import — the composition
would change what a field held and change nothing about what the renderer did.

The case that cannot pass by accident is in
`packages/dom/src/backend/tests/exo-composed-writers.test.ts`. It composes a backend
whose writers write **nothing**:

```ts no-check
composeExoPlugins(withExoCompiler(new ExoDomBackend()), withWriters(inert())).render(
    cardComponent(),
    parent
);

// The element is there — the compiler, the walk and the wiring all ran.
expect(parent.querySelectorAll('p')).toHaveLength(1);
expect(shown(parent)).toBe('-/-');
```

If any path in the renderer still reached the shipped writers directly, the
attribute and the text would appear anyway. They are absent exactly when the
`writers` field is the only route onto the page.

## What is not behind a plugin interface

Stated here rather than left to be discovered:

- **Still static imports:** the element builder, the schema compiler, the
  child-list anchoring, hydration's adoption **walk**, where an element comes from
  (`cloneExoNode` on the schema's prototype), and — deliberately — the *children* arm
  of the setter table the `writers` interface opened, because
  `compileExoHydrateSchema.ts` decides what an adopting fill on a raw-markup port means
  by pointer compare against `setExoHtml`. The four port kinds are a closed union in
  `@exodra/core`; and there is no plugin interface for a foreign *backend* — see
  [what others forbid](./what-others-forbid.md).
- **Where each field is read, and by whom.** Every one is a **field load** — there
  is no `get`, no map and no symbol. `backend.events` is read at the top of
  `compileExoDomSchema` (`packages/dom/src/dom/compileExoDomSchema.ts:686`), and
  `backend.writers` further down where the setters are built
  (`compileExoDomSchema.ts:777`) — once each per (schema, backend), inside the
  compile that already parses the schema's markup. The `writers` interface leaves
  **no field on the schema**: it is spent into `schema.setters`, the table every
  fill already loads from, so nothing per instance, per row, per update or per event
  changed shape at all.
- **There is no element→child direction.** An element carries no pointer back to
  its child, and `exoNodeDom` takes a child and refuses anything else
  (`packages/dom/src/dom/exoNodeDom.ts`), so there is nothing for a composition to
  take over there.
- **A hydrated page DOES inherit a reconciler, and this bullet used to say the
  opposite.** `openChildList` on a hydrating exonode answers `[]` and opens an
  adoption cursor over the rows the server printed, so a reconciler's opening
  pass adopts them instead of building beside them
  (`packages/dom/src/hydrate/EXO_HYDRATE_NODE_VOCABULARY.ts:214-232`). One shape
  is refused: a child list standing directly behind another with no static
  element between them, where the end of the first cannot be read off the markup
  (`packages/dom/src/hydrate/asserts/assertExoPluginChildList.ts:4-14`).

A framework that says "customisable" and means "configurable" is the failure this
page is written against. The items above are the parts where the claim is
narrower than it sounds, and they belong on the same page as the claim.


==============================================================================
# What the abstraction costs

"V8 collapses abstractions" is folklore. It is true often enough to be repeated
and false often enough to ruin a render loop, and quoting it is not evidence of
anything. This page is the version of that claim this project is willing to
defend: **one measurement, one mechanism read out of the code, and a plain
statement of what the measurement could not see.**

## The measurement

The change under test: the DOM renderer stopped reaching `attachExoChildren`
through a static module import and started taking its children reconciler from a
replaceable plugin interface — stored on the plan, read through the composed
surface, called through that field. On the day of the run that interface was still resolved
through a named lookup in a runtime map; that map has since been deleted and the reconciler is now
the plain `children` field on the backend, which is strictly less indirection than
what was measured here.

Measured on the mount axis of `packages/benchmarks` — the 80-card todo app,
batch 20, 100 rounds, medians — through `scripts/compare-axis.mjs`:

| | |
|---|---|
| Normalised move on the `exodra` row | **+0.1%** |
| That row's noise floor | **±3.3%** |
| Controls in the drift estimate | 10 |

**What that entitles anyone to say, and it is less than it looks.** The gate
prints it in its own words (`compare-axis.mjs:328`):

> `· exodra: +0.1% — inside this row's ±3.3% floor, so this run CANNOT say the change was free`

So the honest sentence is: *this pair of runs could not see a cost, and it could
have seen one of 3.3% or more.* Anything that indirection cost on this axis is under
3.3% of a mount. It is not zero, because a run cannot measure zero; it is under
the resolution of the best comparison this project knows how to make.

For scale, the same axis's medians on the same day, ms/mount, lower first
(`packages/benchmarks/.gate/initial-render.slots.json`, printed from that file):
stage0 0.345, mikado 0.355, **exodra 0.405**, solid 0.490, marko 0.505, sinuous
0.870, react 0.980, svelte 0.980, uhtml 1.075, lit 1.105, voby 1.155. Absolute
numbers do not compare across runs — the table on
[Benchmarks](../benchmarks.md) quotes `initial-render.post-repair`, a different
run, and reads differently.

## How the gate knows

A before/after read straight off two printed tables is mostly a reading of the
laptop. The file that does this comparison opens with the demonstration:
`packages/benchmarks/scripts/compare-axis.mjs:10-19` records three runs of one
axis with a single library line changed between runs 1 and 2 and **nothing**
changed between 1 and 3 — participants the change could not touch (mikado,
solid, stage0, react) moved 10-19%.

Four things make the number above mean something:

1. **Every axis runs a dozen participants interleaved in one browser session.**
   Whatever the ones that are not ours did between two runs is the machine.
   A control is a participant named in the explicit `FOREIGN` list of libraries
   this repository does not write (`compare-axis.mjs:128-142`, `:185`), and a name
   in neither list stops the comparison (`:217-224`) — mechanical, so a new row of
   ours cannot quietly be counted as a control and flatten the drift it should be measured against.
2. **Drift is the median of the controls' ratios** (`compare-axis.mjs:228`), and
   our row's move is divided by it.
3. **The resolution is what is left of the controls afterwards.** A perfect pair
   of runs leaves every control at 1.000; how far the worst *typical* one sits
   from 1 is the smallest move the comparison can call a move. It is the 80th
   percentile of the residuals and not the maximum (`compare-axis.mjs:257-260`) —
   re-derived from the two recordings on 2026-08-16, the ten controls' residuals
   after drift are 0.28, 0.28, 0.31, 0.44, 0.54, 0.56, 1.55, 3.31, 6.63 and
   16.93% — six under 1%, the 80th percentile at 3.31%, and `react` at 16.93%.
   A maximum would have put the floor at ±16.9% and blinded the gate over one
   row nothing in the change could touch. (This paragraph said "nine of ten
   under 1%" until the residuals were recomputed; the count was wrong and the
   conclusion was not, since the argument rests on the 5× gap between the 80th
   percentile and the maximum.)
4. **Plus a per-row quantum floor.** `performance.now()` is clamped at ~0.1 ms,
   so a median moves in tick steps; the gate takes the larger of the pooled
   scatter and one tick on that row (`compare-axis.mjs:287-288`). Batching
   divides the tick: unbatched, the `exodra` mount row carries ±23.8% and the
   gate is blind, which is why the run above is at batch 20.

That fourth rule was not reasoned into existence. The gate's first self-test —
two recordings of an **unchanged** build — reported `exodraKept` as a real +2.1%
regression, because the pooled scatter said 2.1% was outside the noise
(`compare-axis.mjs:271-273`).

## The mechanism, read from the code

A cost that does not show up should be explainable, or the measurement is just
luck. Here is where the indirection actually happens.

**Once per process.** `new ExoDomBackend()` calls `composeExoPlugins(this, …)` once,
in its constructor, to put the exonode surface on itself
(`packages/dom/src/dom/ExoDomBackend.ts`); every pack an application composes is
a unary decorator wrapped around the finished object —
`withExoHydration(withExoCompiler(new ExoDomBackend()))` — and each one is another
`composeExoPlugins` call, which mutates and returns the same object. That is the
whole of the resolution. There is no namespace, no slot registry and no provider
ordering: a plugin is a bag of factories, each receiving what already stands under
its name (`packages/core/src/plugins/types/TExoPlugin.ts`), and merging leaves the
overridden names as own properties on one flat object. An application that composes nothing holds
the shipped implementations in plain fields and pays for no lookup at all.

**Once per mounted root.** `render` reads `this.events` for the strategy's
`install` hook and passes `this` — the backend itself — into `exoDomSchemaOf`
(`packages/dom/src/dom/ExoDomBackend.ts`). Nothing is interned and no record is
minted: the key a caller hands down is the object it already holds.

**Once per (schema, backend).** Two interfaces are read as **fields** at this
frequency, and both reads are inside `compileExoDomSchema`, beside the build of the
`<template>` prototype that already happens there: `backend.events` at the top of it
(`packages/dom/src/dom/compileExoDomSchema.ts:699`), then `backend.writers` where the
setters are built (`compileExoDomSchema.ts:796`):

```ts no-check
// packages/dom/src/dom/compileExoDomSchema.ts
const writers = backend.writers;
```

The plan is cached on the machine, at the index the backend took when it was
constructed (`packages/dom/src/dom/exoDomSchemaOf.ts`):

```ts no-check
const held = machine.forms[backend.backendType];
if (held !== undefined) return held as TExoDomSchema;
```

One array read, one compare, return — whatever the number of backends in the
process. It was two compares (`plan.events === events && plan.runtime === runtime`)
until the interfaces became fields on one object.

**Once per instance.** There is no separate receiver to build. The object a wire
is handed **is** the instance record, minted by one constructor per composed
surface, whose prototype **is** that surface:

```ts no-check
// packages/dom/src/dom/factories/createExoDomInstanceFactory.ts
function ExoDomInstanceBody(this: TExoDomInstanceRecord, schema: TExoDomSchemaBase): void {
    this.nodes = EXO_EMPTY_NODES;
    // …twelve own fields, in one fixed order…
    this.live = null;
}
ExoDomInstanceBody.prototype = surface;
```

**One call per surface**, because every constructor function carries its own
initial map: two calls for one composition would split that composition's
instances across two hidden classes. `new` rather than an object literal with a
`__proto__` key is measured, and the note at that line says by how much.

**Per filled children port: nothing the composition decides.** `c.childList(port)`
is a shipped exonode method, and the reconciler is whatever function a transition
called over it — `reconcileExoOrder`, `createExoKeyedList`'s `reconcile`, or one of
the application's own.

**Per list row, per update, per dispatched event: nothing.** Nothing below this
line consults a composition. A plugin's factory receives `next` and runs **once**,
at merge, in the backend's constructor — it is handed no exonode, no plan and no
child, so there is nothing per-row it *could* consult
(`packages/core/src/plugins/types/TExoPlugin.ts`). "Resolve once, at composition, never per
row" is the shape of what a plugin is given rather than a rule it is asked to
follow.

## Why the call site stays monomorphic — and what would break it

This part is **read and reasoned, not profiled.** No inline-cache state was
inspected; what follows is the argument for why the shape is favourable, and it
should be read as a hypothesis consistent with the measurement rather than as its
explanation.

The field **load** is monomorphic because every instance record is built by one
constructor, writing one fixed field order, so every one of them in the process
shares a hidden class. (It has been a `class`, and an object literal with a
`__proto__` key; it is a constructor again, and the property that matters here is
the same one throughout — a fixed field order.) That holds regardless of
composition.

The **call** is monomorphic when the process has one composition: each entry of
`schema.setters` is then always the same function object for its port, so a call
site sees one callee.
An application that builds **one backend at module level** — the shape a nested
`with*` chain is meant for — has exactly that.

What would change it, stated plainly:

- **Two compositions live at once.** A page that renders one root under the
  shipped composition and another under a swapped one puts two different
  writer or event-attach functions through the same call site. Whether that costs anything
  measurable has not been measured here.
- **A backend per render.** This is the one that is not a micro-cost. The backend
  **is** the cache key and it is compared by pointer, so a
  `new ExoDomBackend()` written inside a component or a route handler takes a new
  `backendType` and **recompiles every schema, markup parse included, on every
  render**. It is not a slower render; it is a different program.
  `warnExoFormGrowth` (`packages/core/src/machine/warnExoFormGrowth.ts`) says so out
  loud in development once a machine holds eight schemas.

## What this measurement does not cover

- **One interface, one axis.** The A/B was the children reconciler on the mount
  axis. The event strategy was already threaded as a parameter before it became a
  named field, so it was not part of this comparison, and neither were the value
  writers.
- **Update, reconcile and toggle axes were not compared.** The reasoning above
  says the per-row path is untouched; the reasoning is not a measurement.
- **Hydration was not compared.**
- **A cost between 0% and 3.3% would be invisible here.** On a 0.405 ms mount
  that is up to ~0.013 ms per mounted app. If that matters to you, run the gate
  yourself: `node scripts/run-one-axis.js <axis> --record=<label>` twice, then
  `node scripts/compare-axis.mjs <axis> <before> <after>`.


==============================================================================
# The renderer interface that should not be built

A few parts of `@exodra/dom` are replaceable names — the `events` and `writers`
fields, the `createInstance` / `createChild` record factories, and `hydrateSurface`,
the one a backend may leave absent. The renderer is not, and "make `render` itself a composed
name, so a page picks its backend by composing a plugin instead of by importing
one" is the design somebody keeps almost writing. This page carries it far enough
to say what it would be, what it would cost, and what it would buy — and the
conclusion is that it buys nothing an entry point does not already buy, for a
reason about the shape of a replaceable name rather than about types.

The typing obstacle everyone stops at is **not the reason**. It is real, it is
worth killing candidate by candidate, and it dissolves under the one construction
that works. What survives the typing question is a worse problem: a composed name
holds **one** winner and is read by **one** call site, and the renderer question is
