"which of several, at once", asked by a page that has already answered it by
importing something.

The rationale for the ones that do exist is on
[Sugar, not restrictions](./sugar-not-restrictions.md); the reference for their
contracts is [Plugins](../guides/plugins.md); what one of them cost when it opened
is on [What the abstraction costs](./abstractions-collapse.md). None of that is
restated here.

## 1. What the interface would actually be

Take the three backends in this repository as the three implementors. Three are
packages and the fourth is a path, and all four are already registered together in
one array, which is where a lot of this page's evidence comes from.

| Implementor | Entry point | Host it needs | What it hands back |
|---|---|---|---|
| `@exodra/dom` | `ExoDomBackend.render(component, parent)` | an `Element` | a disposer |
| `@exodra/dom` (hydrate) | `backend.hydrate(component, parent)`, from `withExoHydration` | an `Element` already holding the markup | a disposer |
| `@exodra/string` | `ExoStrBackend.render(component)` | none | markup |
| `@exodra/term` | `ExoTermBackend.renderScreen(component, n)` | none | a screen: roots, a serialiser, a disposer |

Read from the four signatures: `packages/dom/src/dom/ExoDomBackend.ts`,
`packages/dom/src/hydrate/withExoHydration.ts`,
`packages/string/src/node/ExoStrBackend.ts` and
`packages/term/src/backend/ExoTermBackend.ts`.

**Three of the four already agree on more than they used to**, and that belongs
here before the disagreements are counted. `render` is the same method name on both
shipped backends, both take the component as one value, and **neither takes an
instance count**: each mounts ONE instance and hands its initial state `0` as its
index, because rows that vary are a LIST — a children port filled by `c.list`
or by `reconcileExoOrder` over `c.childList` — rather than a parameter. `@exodra/term` is the one that still
takes a count, and its own header states why rather than leaving it to be read as
an oversight: its output is a text SCREEN rather than a document, so there is no
parent to append roots into and no children port above them, and `roots` being an
array IS the shape a caller reads.

### The members, and what a second implementation has to do about each

**`name`.** Free. Several of the shipped plugin interfaces carry one for the same
purpose — it is what a refusal prints — and all three backends already carry one in
the conformance registry. No implementor fails it and nothing depends on it.

**The component parameter.** It must name ONE connector type, and the only
choice that all four can accept is the minimal shared surface rather than any
backend's connector class. That is not a guess: the conformance suite already
made it and states why — one value reaches all four entry points with no cast
because a wire's connector parameter is contravariant, and a component typed
against a backend's class is a backend-only component whatever the design
promised (`packages/conformance/src/types/TExoConformanceAdapter.ts:20-30`).

**The finding is that this parameter is strictly narrower than what
`ExoDomBackend.render` accepts today.** A wire that reaches for an element is a
client wire; the moment it calls `exoNodeDom` it cannot be served, and nothing on
the connector lets it ask which backend it is on. That is already written down as
an open hole
([what others forbid](./what-others-forbid.md#the-open-holes-in-one-place)). So
the composed name would refuse a class of component the DOM entry point renders
happily, and the refusal would be at the type, at the call, with no fix but "do
not use the composed name for this component".

**The host parameter.** Two of the four need an `Element`; two have nowhere to
put one. `@exodra/term`'s header states the reason as a fact about the backend
rather than an omission — a text tree has nothing to be inserted into
(`packages/term/src/backend/ExoTermBackend.ts`). Three ways out, and only one of
them is not a lie:

- typing it `unknown` and casting inside each implementation — which is the
  boundary cast, priced in section 2;
- a second type parameter for the host — which has exactly the problem the output
  type has, in section 2, and doubles it;
- **the implementation owns its host and the member does not take one.** This is
  what the conformance adapter does: the DOM adapter creates its own container
  and appends it to the document before rendering
  (`packages/conformance/src/adapters/exoDomAdapter.ts:34-40`), and the
  hydrating one renders markup with `@exodra/string` first, fills a container
  with it, and adopts (`packages/conformance/src/adapters/exoHydrateAdapter.ts:52-64`).

The third works. Its price is that **the caller can no longer say where**, which
for a browser application is the parameter it most wanted to pass.

**The render member's return type.** This is the one the project's own record
names as the obstacle, and it is real: a disposer, a string of markup and a live
text screen have nothing in common. The conformance adapter met it and did not
solve it — it **gave up the output**, deliberately. `render` is typed to return
`TExoConformanceRun` and not the backend's own artefact
(`packages/conformance/src/types/TExoConformanceAdapter.ts:56`): a neutral
handle with a `sketch`, a `fire`, a `translate` and a `dispose`
(`TExoConformanceAdapter.ts:34-43`). The sentence this page used to quote here —
that a suite handing out the real outputs "would have four comparison functions
instead of one artefact" — was in that file's header and the comment pass removed
it; it is nowhere in `packages/conformance` today, so the reasoning is stated
above rather than cited.

**A member half the backends cannot implement, and this is the finding section 1
was asked for.** Once the output is neutral, the handle has to carry the operations a
caller would have got from the output — and they are not universal. `@exodra/string`'s
handle answers two of them by throwing, with a message saying the call should
never be reached (`packages/conformance/src/adapters/exoStrAdapter.ts:31-36`).
That is not sloppiness: the suite routes around it by having every adapter
declare a capability set, cross-checked against every rule, so a rule needing a
capability a backend lacks is a first-class outcome rather than a skip
(`packages/conformance/src/types/TExoConformanceAdapter.ts:32-33, 52-53`). And the
adapter deliberately carries no `update` member at all, because a source has to
be fresh per backend and the adapter must never see the levers
(`TExoConformanceAdapter.ts:45-47`).

So the honest interface is five members — a name and its full package spelling for
messages, a declared capability set, a compile, and a render returning a neutral handle — and **it already exists**, as
`TExoConformanceAdapter`, written against three backends, with nothing composed
anywhere near it. That is the strongest single fact on this page and section 4 is
mostly its consequence.

## 2. Whether the typing obstacle is real

It is real, and **it is smaller than it used to be** — which is worth saying
carefully, because a design that was refused partly on types is now refused almost
entirely on meaning.

**What the merge gives for free.** A plugin is a bag of method factories, and what
a pack contributes is read off its factories' return types; the composed object's
type is those intersected in nesting order — a decorator declares its own
contribution in its return type, and `TExoMergedPluginMethods` computes it for one that would
rather infer (`packages/core/src/plugins/types/TExoPlugin.ts`). So the composed type is
**per composition**, not per name. `withTermRender(new ExoDomBackend())` would have
a `render` typed exactly as that pack's factory returned it, and the checker would
know it at the line that composed it. The predecessor of this system could not do
that: it keyed implementations by a registered symbol minted once for the life of
the process, so one name meant one fixed interface for every consumer of it, and
"generic over its output" was unspellable.

**What is still unspellable, stated exactly.** A merged name resolves per
composition, but the three backends do not differ by *composition* — they differ by
which package produced the object. `ExoStrBackend` and `ExoDomBackend` are two
classes with two `render` methods returning two unrelated types. To get `string`
out of one and `() => void` out of the other, a caller has to hold the right
object, and holding the right object is what importing the right package already
is. The type system will happily describe it; it just describes what the import
already decided.

### Every way out, and why each one dies

**One `render` name, one shared signature.** It has to name ONE return type, and a
disposer, a string of markup and a live text screen have nothing in common. Dead
at the first backend.

**One `render` name, generic in its output.** This types under the merge, per
composition, and it is the shape the old system could not express. It dies one
step later: to write down the type of what you got back you must name the
composition, and to name the composition you must name the pack, which is the
import. The genericity is real and buys nothing, because there was never a second
place the type could have come from.

**A separate name per output kind** — `renderToTree`, `renderToMarkup`,
`renderToScreen`. This one types cleanly too, and dies on meaning. To choose a
name you must know the output kind; to know the output kind you must know the
backend; and knowing the backend is what importing an entry point already is: an
entry point is what a page imports, so choosing one is how a backend is chosen,
and a composed name only moves that choice without removing it. Worse, it
multiplies where it was meant to divide: two of the four hand back a disposer, so
`renderToTree` has two candidates, and **last claim wins** — which under the merge
is the normal, unremarkable rule, and is exactly wrong here.

**Erasing to `unknown` and casting at the boundary.** A cast at every call is the
point at which the type system stops helping and the next wrong implementation
lands in it silently. The worked failure is a hand-written pack that compiles and
fails as a renderer with no methods, at the first mount, far from the line that
caused it. Dead.

**Not typing it at all.** The same as erasing to `unknown`, with the cast moved
into the reader's head. Dead.

**Erasing the OUTPUT rather than the interface — and this is the one that lives.**
It is section 1's construction and the conformance suite's. It types cleanly, it
needs no change to `TExoPlugin` or `composeExoPlugins`, and every one of the four can
implement it. Its price is stated in its own header: the caller does not get what
the backend produced. For a test harness that is correct, since what the harness
wants is one comparable artefact. For an application it is fatal in one direction —
a server that cannot have its markup has not rendered anything.

**So the obstacle is real, and the accurate sentence for the record is narrower
than the one on file.** It is not that a composed name cannot carry a generic API —
under the merge it can. It is that the only shape making three backends agree on one
name is one that discards their outputs, and that every way of recovering the
output routes back through naming the package.

## 3. What it costs at runtime

Stated per level, as this project requires, and the last two lines are the ones
that decide whether a design is allowed to exist.

**Per process.** Nothing. There is no name to register and no symbol to mint — a
plugin is a plain object and its entries are read at composition.

**Per composition.** One property read and one property write per merged name,
once, inside the backend's constructor
(`packages/core/src/plugins/composeExoPlugins.ts`). Nothing in the merge is reachable from
a render path; it runs before the first render and cannot run again.

**Per call.** Nothing beyond the call itself. A merged name is an **own property**
on one flat object, which is what the base's own methods already were — no chain
is walked and no map is consulted. This is the line where the design got cheaper
than its predecessor, and it is why the cost sheet is no longer the reason to
refuse it.

**Per schema.** Nothing, and there is nowhere for it to be anything. The existing
interfaces all amortise onto something: `events` and `writers` are read once per
(schema, backend) inside the schema compiler, on the same line that parses the
schema's markup, and spent into the schema; the record factories are built once per
backend.
A composed `render` cannot do any of that, because a plan is built
**by** a backend, and the value that decides which backend cannot be cached on the
artefact that backend produces. This is an absence of a place to amortise rather
than a cost.

**Per mount.** One field load and a call — and **the caller is not this library.**
Every one of the existing interface reads happens at a site `@exodra/dom` owns. A
composed `render` is called by application code, at a site nothing here can hoist
for it. The shape that would carry it is not hypothetical: `@exodra/react-mount`
picks between rendering and hydrating inside a React effect body, once per mount
and once per deps change, and it does so by testing `backend.hydrate` for
`undefined` — a backend composed without `withExoHydration` has no such method
— then calling `backend.render` (`packages/react-mount/src/useExoMount.ts`). A
composed `render` would sit on that same line.

**Per row and per event.** Zero — as long as the name is read only at the entry
point. Nothing below an entry point ever calls an entry point again: children go
through the connector, whose prototype is the backend and is composed once.

**And the version that would not be zero, which is the version worth wanting.**
A composed renderer meant to answer "another renderer inside part of the tree"
([item 6](./what-others-forbid.md#6-you-cannot-run-another-renderer-inside-part-of-the-tree))
has to be consulted where a children port is filled and where a row is built —
per filled port, per instance, per row. **That design is dead and this is the
sentence that kills it.** It is also not what the narrow version above would
deliver, so the narrow version cannot be defended by pointing at it.

**One cost this paragraph used to charge to the design, and no longer can.** It
said: `TExoCursorDeclaration` declares one plan slot per BACKEND, so admitting a backend the
reading side does not name would produce, for the first time, a backend that cannot
add a line to that type — and the mechanisms that would rescue it (a `Symbol` slot,
an integer id, a chain) were each enumerated and refused,
every refusal turning on the population being empty. **A composed renderer was the
thing that would have made it non-empty, and that was the cost.**

**The charge is withdrawn, because the population turned out never to have been
empty and the type was changed without any composed renderer.** A declaration
holds no compiled schema at all now: every backend stores its schema at
`machine.forms[backend.backendType]`, and every backend object takes its own
`backendType` from `nextExoBackendType()` when it is constructed
(`packages/core/src/machine/types/TExoMachine.ts`). What forced that was not a foreign
backend but the fact that the old shape's remedy had already been applied twice
inside this repository, as `termPlan` and as `stage0Plan` for a backend that has
since been deleted (`packages/term/src/schema/types/TExoTermSchema.ts`). So a backend
written outside this repository can cache a plan today with no core edit at all,
and the plan cache is no longer an argument for or against a composed renderer.
**What either storage costs is still unmeasured** — no recording in
`packages/benchmarks/measurements/` prices a plan lookup in any storage — so
nothing measured was gained or lost by the change.

**The one thing that did not move is the frequency, and it still belongs here.** A
plan lookup is not once per mounted root. `@exodra/term`'s connector pays it at
`build` and at `one`, and a reconciled list reaches it through `build` once per row —
its rows may be different components, so there is nothing to hoist — which means a

heterogeneous list pays it per row per update
(`packages/term/src/schema/exoTermSchemaOf.ts`). Whatever a foreign backend does to find
its plan, it does it at that frequency, and that belongs in the same paragraph as
any sentence promising an adapter over any backend.

## 4. What it would buy, honestly

The settled answer for the ones that do exist is **coherence**: an application composes
once and every entry point reads the same answer, instead of each render call
carrying it and one of them forgetting. That argument is not about polymorphism and
not about typing, and it is a real argument — it is why the `events` field exists
beside a parameter that already worked, and hydration is the sharpest case of it.
`hydrate` arrives as a pack **onto the backend that renders**
(`packages/dom/src/hydrate/withExoHydration.ts`), so a page cannot compose one
thing for the client and silently get a different composition on a server-rendered
page — which is exactly what happened when render and hydrate were two free entry
points each taking their own composition argument: nothing threw, and the wrong
reconciler owned every hydrated region from then on.

**It does not apply here, and the reason is a count.** Coherence is worth
something in proportion to the number of consumers that must agree. So count them.

1. **The application's own boot line.** One call. It already reads one answer,
   because it is one line, and the answer is which module it imported.
2. **A library that mounts on the application's behalf.** One exists —
   `@exodra/react-mount` — and it already takes a whole backend as an option and
   forwards it without inspecting anything but whether `hydrate` is there. A
   composed `render` would let it be backend-blind. It runs in a browser inside a
   React effect, where the markup and text-tree backends have no meaning, so
   backend-blindness here is a generality with no second case.
3. **Nested components and list rows.** Not consumers at all, per section 3.
4. **Something that needs several backends at once.** This exists, and it is the
   case that settles the question the other way. The conformance suite holds all
   four in a plain array, and its whole value is that adding a fifth breaks every
   rule at once by name until somebody states what the fifth does
   (`packages/conformance/src/exoConformanceTrees.ts`).

A composed name's semantics is **one winner**: plugins merge left to right and the
last one to claim a name is what stands there. The suite needs **all four,
simultaneously, distinguishable by name**. Those are different shapes, and
last-claim-wins is not a weaker version of an array — it is the wrong answer to the
question being asked.

So the honest ledger of what a composed `render` adds over a separate entry point:

- **A name a third-party backend could be discovered under** rather than imported.
  Real, and small: the discovery is still an import — of the plugin instead of the
  class.
- **A diagnostic for which backend is standing there.** There is always exactly one
  and it is the import at the top of the file.
- **The README sentence.** Which is section 5, and is the only item on this list
  anybody actually wants.

**The conclusion, plainly: it buys nothing, and the separate entry point is the
right shape.** The reason fits in one sentence — an entry point is what a page
imports, so choosing one is how a backend is
chosen. This page is that conclusion re-derived from the composition's side, and it
arrives at the same place by a different road: what composing a name provides is
one-answer-for-many-consumers, and the renderer has one consumer.

## 5. The condition the owner set

The condition is recorded in the foreign backend's own barrel: the project "has
deliberately withheld the phrase *adapter over any backend* from its README until
something proved it", and names `src/doc/` as that proof — two components copied
character for character out of `README.md`, checked against it by a test,
rendered with no cast and no adaptation
(`packages/term/src/index.ts`).

**Would this design satisfy it? It would satisfy the letter and not the point.**

**The letter.** This is no longer hypothetical on the composition side.
`@exodra/term` has a backend object — `new ExoTermBackend(...plugins)`, with every
connector method merged onto it first, so a pack naming one receives the shipped
body as its `next`. A pack claiming `render` composes into it today, an application
could call `backend.render`, and a foreign backend would have run through a
composed name. The sentence would be technically earned.

The package **deliberately does not** name its own entry point `render`, and its
header gives the reason rather than leaving it to be read as an oversight: `render`
on all three backends would be one name, one arity and three incompatible second
parameters, so `backend.render(APP, document.body)` written against the wrong
import would take an element as `n` and fail somewhere inside `new Array()` instead
of at the call (`packages/term/src/backend/ExoTermBackend.ts`).

**Why that is not the point, in three parts.**

1. **What ran through the composed name is one call at the top.** Nothing below it
   reaches that name, so nothing about the renderer became replaceable. The element
   builder, the plan compiler, the region anchoring and hydration's adoption are
   exactly as welded afterwards as before — and the *create* direction of a child
   is deliberately not replaceable either, because a second way in is the drift
   that arrangement exists to prevent. A reader who hears "adapter over any
   backend" will believe something about the inside of a render, and a composed
   `render` would say nothing about the inside of a render.
2. **The proof is already stronger without it.** The claim that matters is that
   `@exodra/core`'s exported surface is portable, and it has two witnesses that a
   composed name would not improve: everything in `packages/term/src` outside
   `src/doc/` imports `@exodra/core` and `@exodra/context` and nothing
   else (`packages/term/src/index.ts`), asserted by
   `packages/term/src/backend/tests/imports-only-core.test.ts`, and the README components are
   asserted verbatim by `packages/term/src/doc/tests/readme-verbatim.test.ts`. Adding an
   indirection to a proved claim does not prove it harder.
3. **The bar the existing ones clear cannot be cleared here in a way that means
   anything.** The precise statement of a plugin interface's contract in this project
   is the inert-implementation case — compose something that satisfies the type and
   does nothing, and show the page is measurably different, which is what separates a
   field the renderer reads from one that merely decorates a data structure
   (`packages/dom/src/backend/tests/exo-composed-writers.test.ts`). It is not universal
   even among them: the events interface has no inert case at all
   ([what a replacement has to do](../guides/plugins.md#what-a-replacement-has-to-do)).
   For a composed `render` the test can be written and it passes trivially, because
   there is one read site and it is the whole render: "does the renderer read the
   composed name" is answerable by looking at one line, and a test that confirms
   one line is not evidence about a mechanism.

**The sentence that IS earned, and should be written instead:** a backend written
against nothing but `@exodra/core` and `@exodra/context` runs this
project's own documented components unchanged — with the qualification from
section 3 stated beside it, which is that "written against only core" is not the
same as "written outside this repository". `@exodra/term` **used to** have a line
in `TExoCursorDeclaration` like every other backend, and that was the sharpest form of the
qualification. It does not any more — its plans are chain links on the shared
live-tree slot (`packages/term/src/schema/types/TExoTermSchema.ts`) — so the qualification
now rests on something weaker and should be stated as such: a backend that could
not edit `@exodra/core` has still never been built here, so nothing has walked the
path end to end, and the gaps such a backend would hit are the list above rather
than a plan lookup. That is a claim about the shared surface, it has two witnesses,
and it needs nothing composed at all.

## What would change this conclusion

Written down so this page can be refuted rather than merely disagreed with.

- **A second consumer that must not know the backend.** A router that mounts
  routes, a devtools that re-mounts a subtree, a test harness shipped inside a
  product. Today the only multi-backend consumer is the conformance suite, and it
  needs all four at once, which is an array and not a composed name. Two consumers
  that each need exactly one, and must agree, is the shape that makes coherence
  worth paying for — and it is the shape the `events` field had, and the shape
  `hydrate` has now.
- **A renderer reachable below the entry point.** If a children port could be
  handed to another backend, a composed `render` would be answering a question
  nothing else can. That question is asked per filled port and per row, so it is a
  different design with a different cost sheet, and section 3 says what it would
  have to beat.
- ~~**A backend that genuinely cannot edit `@exodra/core`.**~~ **DISCHARGED, and by
  something other than a composed renderer.** This item said that every backend can
  and does add one line to `TExoCursorDeclaration` for its plan slot, that a composed renderer
  would create the first backend in the other position, and that the plan-slot
  enumeration would then have to be re-argued with a non-empty population. The
  enumeration was re-argued in 2026-08 anyway, on the evidence that the line had
  been added twice inside this repository, and `TExoCursorDeclaration` now carries two fields
  named for the two kinds of OUTPUT with a chain under each
  (`packages/core/src/schema/types/TExoCursorDeclaration.ts`). A backend that cannot edit core
  therefore needs nothing composed to cache a plan, and this item is kept — struck
  rather than deleted — because it is a worked case of a trigger discharging
  without the change it was attached to.

Until one of those changes, the renderer stays where it is: chosen by an import,
typed by its own signature, and free.


==============================================================================
# What the floor says

Every performance page in this repository compares Exodra to other libraries.
This one does not. It compares `@exodra/dom` to **programs with no library in
them at all** — straight-line calls into Blink that produce the same DOM, byte
for byte, with no components, no schema, no reactivity, no plan and no
connector — and reports the distance.

That distance is **the entire remaining headroom for any framework whatsoever.**
Below the floor there is nothing left to beat anybody with, so the sentence it
produces bounds rivals as well as us:

> No framework can be more than X% faster than `@exodra/dom` at this job, because
> X% is all there is above the floor.

That is a stronger claim than "we beat Solid", and — this is the part that
matters — a **falsifiable** one. Anybody can write a cheaper floor program and
the number moves. Nobody has to take our word for a ranking.

**Two of the three sections below do that. The third does not**, and it says so in
its own place: [hydration](#hydration) has no framework-free program to stand on
and bounds nobody. It is here because it was measured beside the other two and
because its two answers disagree in a way that is worth publishing.

:::warning Two different things are called "the floor" in these docs
On [Benchmarks](../benchmarks.md#the-floor), `floor` is a **participant row**: the
harness's own cost, the 160 `querySelectorAll` matches and 160 dispatched
`MouseEvent`s every framework in that table pays for. It is not a renderer and it
is not this.

On this page a floor is a **program**: the cheapest way anyone knows to produce
the same DOM without a framework. The two words are unrelated and no number from
one page may be carried onto the other.
:::

## Where these numbers come from, before any of them

Three diagnostic axes in `packages/benchmarks`, all three written to the same
pattern — a phase per program, a resolution floor measured from a control whose
true value is zero, every way the axis can mislead written into its own header,
and **a run that refuses its own numbers when they are unreadable**:

-   `packages/benchmarks/src/benchmarks/axes/floors/mount-floor.ts` — 21 programs, mounting
-   `packages/benchmarks/src/benchmarks/axes/floors/update-floor.ts` — 5 transitions, updating
-   `packages/benchmarks/src/benchmarks/axes/floors/hydrate-floor.ts` — 3 censuses, hydration

**None of the three has a recording in `packages/benchmarks/.gate/`.** The
published-number gate (`scripts/check-doc-numbers.mjs`) can therefore check that
the reproducer exists and nothing else, so every table below carries an
`unrecorded` marker naming the command and the date, and every figure on this
page must be read as **the owner's measurement on one machine, quoted here, not
traced to a file.** That is a weaker provenance than the tables on
[Benchmarks](../benchmarks.md), and it is stated here rather than left for a
reader to discover.

One figure on this page is different and is marked as such: the `importNode`
decision in [the table below](#the-decision-table) is traceable to two recordings
on disk.

## Part 1 — the three floors

### Mounting

The app is the 80-card todo app every mount axis in this suite uses: **641
elements, 321 instances, 400 port fills**. Twenty-one programs build it. Every
one of them is checked **byte-identical against a real `mountExodraApp`** before
anything is timed, through the same `markupOf` the rest of the suite gates with,
and the run throws otherwise (`mount-floor.ts`, "WHAT IS GATED").

<!-- gate: axis=mount-floor label=published -->

| Program                 | what it is                                                                        | ms         |
| ----------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------- |
| `CENSUS/app-clone`      | ONE `cloneNode` of all 641 nodes, then a walk to the 480 ports; nothing is filled | 0.1800     |
| **`CENSUS/clone+refs`** | 321 clones, walk to the ports, fill, insert, keep 480 references                  | **0.2175** |
| `CENSUS/html·tpl`       | `template.innerHTML`                                                              | 0.2600     |
| `CENSUS/html`           | `innerHTML` of one precomputed string                                             | 0.2650     |
| `CENSUS/create`         | `document.createElement` per node, fill and forget                                | 0.2588     |
| `CENSUS/html·doc`       | `DOMParser.parseFromString`                                                       | 0.2625     |
| `CENSUS/html·adj`       | `insertAdjacentHTML`                                                              | 0.2663     |
| `CENSUS/html·range`     | `Range.createContextualFragment`                                                  | 0.2662     |
| `CENSUS/clone·frag`     | the same clones staged in a `DocumentFragment`                                    | 0.3613     |

Six of those nine rows are quoted verbatim inside this repository already, in
`hydrate-floor.ts`'s header, which cites them as the prior that decided its own
shape.

**The floor to quote is `clone+refs` at 0.2288 ms.** `app-clone` is cheaper and
is **not a technique anybody could adopt**: its prototype is built at module load
out of the app's own data — every `data-i`, every title, every tag label is
already inside the tree it clones, which is why it fills nothing. **A renderer is
handed its data after its templates compile**, so it can never contain any of it.
That distinction is machinery rather than etiquette: every row carries a
`dataBlind` flag, the axis prints **two** floors — the cheapest fair row, and "the
adoptable floor", the cheapest one a renderer could have been — and when they are
different rows it says so as a finding, in its own words, and labels the cheaper
one _"a BOUND only: addressable and retained, but its prototype contains the
data"_. Quote the adoptable one.

**What the table settles, and the size of each answer is the owner's:**

-   **Cloning beats creating.** `create` is +21% over `clone+refs`. This suite had
    been repeating "cloning is cheaper than creating" with no number beside it; now
    there is one. **One honest wrinkle in that row:** `create` is the _non-retaining_
    spelling (`retains: false` in `mount-floor.ts`), so the strict like-for-like
    against `clone+refs` is its twin `create+refs`, whose figure this page does not
    hold. The axis's own answer is that the distinction does not survive the
    instrument — it measured **retention at +0.0000 ms over 480 references**, quoted
    in `update-floor.ts`'s header — but that is the axis's finding, not a
    substitution performed here.
-   **The door into the parser does not matter.** Five separate entry points —
    `innerHTML`, `insertAdjacentHTML`, `Range.createContextualFragment`,
    `template.innerHTML`, `DOMParser` — land between 0.2763 and 0.2825, a spread of
    0.0075. One verdict covers the family, and the question never has to be
    reopened door by door.
-   **The parse is not the cheap half.** Every parser door is dearer than cloning
    the same 641 elements. Any argument that begins "but the browser's parser is
    fast" has already been measured and has already lost.
-   **`DocumentFragment` staging is the worst row in the table**, and the reason is
    the useful part: a fragment keeps insertions out of a live tree, and **this app
    assembles everything detached and inserts live exactly once**, so there are no
    live insertions for it to keep out. It is pure overhead here. On an app that
    inserts into the document repeatedly it would not be.
-   **Repetition moves the answer.** `clone·distinct` runs the identical program
    over **321 distinct prototypes**, each cloned once — same nodes, same walk,
    same fills, same insertions, same gated bytes, only the amount of repetition
    changed. It costs **+2.7%**, which is above the run's resolution floor. So
    "cloning is cheapest" is scoped to trees that repeat, and this app is close to
    the friendliest case there is: four shapes for 321 instances.

**And the granularity is forced, not chosen.** The obvious objection to
`clone+refs` is "why not clone bigger pieces". **Four shapes is the coarsest
data-blind granularity this app admits.** A whole-card prototype would have to
contain the tag rows and the details block — and both of those are things the
card's **wire** computes, not things its template knows. Coarser than four means
baking data in, which is `app-clone`, which is not a renderer. Everything below
`clone+refs` on the ladder measures per-call overhead, not something a renderer
could take.

#### The bound, and its imprecision is ours

Three runs of the axis, `exodra ÷ clone+refs`:

**1.351× · 1.418× · 1.339×** — so the headroom is **25–30%**, a range and not a
point.

Say plainly where the spread comes from: **the floor rows repeat to the third
decimal across runs. The row that moves is `exodra`** — 0.3262 in one run, 0.3063
in another, of an identical program. The instrument resolves the hand-written
programs better than it resolves the renderer, and until that is fixed the bound
is a range. **That imprecision is ours**, not the browser's and not the floor's.

Which gives the sentence this axis exists to produce, at its weaker and therefore
safer end:

> **No framework can be more than about 30% faster than `@exodra/dom` at mounting
> this app** — because roughly 30% is all that is left above a program with no
> components, no schema, no reactivity, no plan, no connector and no library,
> producing byte-identical DOM with every port addressable and retained. A rival
> that deleted **all** of its own abstraction and none of the browser's work would
> land there and no lower.

It is a bound. **It is not a target**, and the axis says so in the same breath:
everything inside the gap buys something — addressability that survives a
rebuild, lifetimes, teardown, reactivity, a component contract. The bound says
how much there is, not that any of it is free to take.

### Updating

There is no such thing as "the same program without the framework" for an update.
**A program with no reactivity does not update, it rebuilds** — and a rebuild is a
mount, already bounded above. So `update-floor.ts` bounds something narrower and
real: fix a before-state and an after-state, and the minimum set of DOM
operations that takes one to the other is a fact about the two states and the
browser. A program that performs exactly those operations, **having been told what
changed**, is a floor for that transition.

Two things make the comparison legitimate, and both are in the file rather than
in this page's good intentions:

-   **Every row declares a contract.** `told` means handed exactly what changed;
    `derive` means handed the new state and left to work it out. A `derive`
    renderer measured against a `told` floor is charged for the discovery twice.
    Every headline pairs rows on the same contract.
-   **The floor may not pre-bake its DOM calls.** It is handed indices and flags;
    it resolves nodes, finds anchors and fixes its own bookkeeping inside the timed
    region. A floor handed a list of calls to replay is not a bound, it is a replay,
    and it measures `insertBefore`.

100 rounds, **batch 16**, phases ordered by a per-round seeded shuffle. The
recording declares its own resolution bars: **0.260417 µs at floor scale** and
**5.729167–6.250000 µs at renderer scale**, and it refuses six of its own
attributions against them. **Batch 4 must not be quoted for this axis at all**: it
quantised every median onto the clock's 3.125 µs clamp, so its digits were the
timer, not the program. And raising the batch is not a remedy for a _bias_ here —
every figure is µs per transition, so more reps divide the measured region by the
same factor they multiply it. The previous recording of this axis was withdrawn
for exactly that reason — its phases ran in a rigid rotation, so its resolution
bar measured where a row had been declared rather than what the program did — and
nothing in the renderer changed between the two runs.

The new ordering is checked in the recording itself. `WIDE` now carries a null
declared far from its partner (`floor·twin·far`, 51.5625 against `floor`'s
51.5625) and one declared next to it (`exodra·twin·near`, 114.8437 against
`exodra`'s 115.625) — 0.0000 and −0.7813 µs, where under the old rotation the
distance between two declarations was worth several microseconds on its own.

<!-- EVERY ROW IS THE RECORDING'S OWN ROW NAME, and the ratio is not published as a column at all.
     That is `benchmarks.md`'s rule applied here — a column we computed on our own behalf is not
     evidence — and it is also what the gate can actually check: it matches a row by the table's
     FIRST cell, so a table of pairs traces one of the two and quietly leaves the other unchecked.
     Twelve rows instead of six pairs, every one of them checked cell by cell against
     `packages/benchmarks/measurements/update-floor.shuffled.json`, a file in this repository. The
     ratios follow in a sentence, as one division a reader can redo. -->

<!-- gate: axis=update-floor label=shuffled col=2 -->

| Row                      | µs      | what it is                          |
| ------------------------ | ------- | ----------------------------------- |
| `GROW-SHRINK/exodra`     | 6.0938  | grow-shrink · derive · the renderer |
| `GROW-SHRINK/floor·diff` | 6.0938  | grow-shrink · derive · its floor    |
| `REORDER/exodra`         | 33.8542 | reorder · derive · the renderer     |
| `REORDER/floor·diff`     | 21.6146 | reorder · derive · its floor        |
| `TEXT-SWEEP/exodra`      | 76.5625 | text-sweep · told · the renderer    |
| `TEXT-SWEEP/floor`       | 50.3125 | text-sweep · told · its floor       |
| `TEXT-ONE/exodra`        | 0.0806  | text-one · told · the renderer      |
| `TEXT-ONE/floor`         | 0.0516  | text-one · told · its floor         |
| `WIDE/exodra`            | 115.625 | wide · told · the renderer          |
| `WIDE/floor`             | 51.5625 | wide · told · its floor             |
| `GROW-SHRINK/exodraOps`  | 1.2656  | grow-shrink · told · the renderer   |
| `GROW-SHRINK/floor·told` | 0.3906  | grow-shrink · told · its floor      |

Renderer over its floor, one division of two rows above:
`grow-shrink`/derive **1.000×** · `reorder`/derive **1.566×** · `text-sweep`/told **1.522×** · `text-one`/told **1.562×** · `wide`/told **2.242×** · `grow-shrink`/told **3.240×**.

**Microseconds — this heading read `ms` until today, and it was wrong by 1000×.**
`update-floor` is the one floor axis of the four that emits microseconds; it
declares them row by row and returns `(dt / phase.reps) * 1000` where
`mount-floor.ts`, `ssr-floor.ts` and `hydrate-floor.ts` all return `dt / reps`.
The same error stood in nine other places and both numeric gates passed over it,
because a gate that compares a figure to a recorded row compares the digits and
never the unit. So: **the two tables on this page are in different units**,
because the mount table above and the hydration table below really are
milliseconds. Every ratio was unaffected — a ratio does not care what the unit
is — and every absolute in this table was out by three orders of magnitude.

**The first row is published because leaving it out would be the dishonest
choice.** It is the one row of the six that bounds nothing, and the reason it
bounds nothing is the most interesting result on this axis.

#### The row where the renderer drew level with the hand-written program

On `grow-shrink`, `@exodra/dom` measured **6.0938 µs against the floor's 6.0938
µs** — equal to the last digit the run records — and the run printed a refusal
rather than a headline:

> `NO BOUND FROM THIS ROW — @exodra/dom (6.0938 µs) measured AT OR BELOW the
"derive" floor "floor·diff" (6.0938 µs) at "grow-shrink". A floor a framework
can beat is not a floor.`

_(This page previously read "5.14 µs against the floor's 6.03 µs". That pair
resolves to no row in either recording of this axis; the figures above are the
recorded ones.)_

**The mechanism is named and it is the most important sentence on this page.**
The shipped reconciler trims the common head and tail by identity first, and a
middle that is only insertions or only removals is done in place with no map and
no allocation (`packages/list-reconcile/src/reconcileExoOrder.ts:107-128`). Only
a middle whose survivors changed order reaches the general pass, which keeps the
longest increasing run of old positions and moves the rest (`:66`). **The fast
paths are exactly the shapes that transition feeds it.** The floor is the general
case alone: stamp the survivors, drop the gone, read old positions, longest
increasing subsequence — with no special case at all.

That is how a framework catches hand-written code at all: **it knows the shape of
the data and a general program does not.** It is a finding about the floor, not a
victory over hand-written code in general — the floor stops bounding that
transition until it grows the same special cases, and the honest thing to publish
is the refusal.

#### Where the `wide` gap actually is

`wide` is the 80-card app flipping every details block and advancing every tag
list — 160 state changes in one transition, the transition where per-update
overhead should amortise if it amortises anywhere. The axis splits its gap in
two, by measuring the identical floor program **subscribed to identical
observable values and fired by identical `setValue` calls**:

-   **dispatch and the closures it calls: +10.1562 µs** — 160 `setValue` calls and
    the 160 closures a subscription needs, against a straight loop over flat arrays.
    That is `WIDE/floor·bound` (61.7187) minus `WIDE/floor` (51.5625). The renderer
    pays this and so would anybody, because a renderer nobody can notify is not a
    renderer.
-   **everything else: +53.9063 µs** — `WIDE/exodra` (115.625) minus
    `WIDE/floor·bound` — the children reconcile, the row records, the per-child
    node, the region anchors and the component boundary for every block built.

**Roughly five times more in the bookkeeping than in the dispatch** — 53.9063 ÷
10.1562 = 5.3, a division of the two figures above and not a column anybody
recorded. The two parts sum to 64.0625 µs, which is exactly `exodra − floor`, so
the split accounts for the whole gap and nothing is left over. If the update path
is to be attacked, that ratio says where. Two _other_ `WIDE` attributions in this
recording — the `bindList` façade and what survives when nothing is built or
dropped — the run refuses as ranges rather than numbers, so they are not quoted
here.

### Hydration

`hydrate-floor.ts` asks whether serving the markup and hydrating it beats cloning
and building on the client, for **one renderer doing one job two ways**, with the
network, the bundle, the compiler and the field all removed. The big census is
**5120 elements** (640 card instances), eight times the small one.

The wire runs **in full on both sides** — every closure, every effect,
every listener, from the same component values, with no second wire. Hydration
does not skip the application's work; it skips the browser's.

:::danger This one is not a floor, and its own file says so
`mount-floor` and `update-floor` bound their subjects with programs that have **no
framework in them at all**. There is no such program here. A hand-written adoption
of a hand-written string would bound "walking a tree" and would not bound
_hydration_, which is a contract about what the server already computed. **This
axis compares two real paths through one real renderer and that is all it does.**
It is on this page because it is the third of the three measurements produced
alongside the other two, not because it bounds anybody.
:::

**There are two answers and they disagree. Neither may ever be quoted as the
other.**

<!-- gate: unrecorded axis=hydrate-floor cmd="scripts/run-one-axis.js hydrate-floor 100 2" date=2026-08-20 -->
<!-- WHY THIS TABLE IS NOT TRACED CELL BY CELL, while the mount table above is: it
     publishes RATIOS, and a recording holds medians. Worse, `hydrate-floor` prints one table
     PER TRANSITION and every one of them names its rows `exodra`, `floor`,
     `floor·twin` — so the flat recording cannot tell the `exodra` of `wide` from the
     `exodra` of `text-one`. The recording IS committed
     (`packages/benchmarks/measurements/hydrate-floor.published.json`) and every number below
     comes out of it; what is missing is a way for the gate to check that mechanically.
     The fix is one change to the recorder — qualify a row name with its transition —
     and until it lands this marker is the honest state and not a waiver. -->

<!-- gate: axis=hydrate-floor label=published col=2 -->

| Row                      | ms     | what it is                                                 |
| ------------------------ | ------ | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ROWS·640/mount`         | 2.3667 | the client builds every node                               |
| `ROWS·640/parse`         | 2.1833 | one crossing into the parser, nothing addressable survives |
| `ROWS·640/hydrate`       | 0.9333 | the adopt walk, the checks, and the same whole wire        |
| `ROWS·640/parse+hydrate` | 3.1333 | both, in one region                                        |

-   **Serve-and-hydrate is 30% MORE total CPU work.** That is the right question
    for a worker, a second render into an existing page, a `renderToString`-and-swap,
    or any argument about battery and heat. It is the wrong question for a cold page
    load.
-   **Hydration alone is 62% LESS.** That is the right question for a page load, and
    it is realistic rather than generous **only** because the parse it does not pay
    for (the axis's own `parse` row, 2.13 ms) is real CPU that a real browser
    genuinely does off the framework's clock — streamed, fed
    by the network, finished before the script ran. It is still real, it is still on
    the **user's** clock, and it is still dearer than cloning would have been.

**The ranking held across 8× the rows** — 640 elements to 5120 — with both ratios
inside 2.5%. That is the part worth trusting; the sizes are one machine.

And the thing this axis proves that no string compare could: before it times
anything it captures every element in the container **in document order** and
checks the same **objects** are there afterwards, then clicks a real bubbling
`MouseEvent` into the first card and requires the details block it controls to
appear and disappear in that same served element. Without those two checks an
adoption that walked the tree, attached nothing and returned would have been the
fastest row in the table.

## Part 2 — the decision table {#the-decision-table}

Every decision this project has measured, one row each. **The `not covered`
column is the point of the table.** Where a decision is not proved, the row says
so; nothing in it is filled with reasoning dressed as evidence.

**This table is invisible to `npm run check:numbers`**, and that is worth saying
out loud rather than leaving as a quiet convenience. The gate's tripwire only
fires on a column of bare `number + unit` cells (`check-doc-numbers.mjs`, rules 1
and 2); every margin below is a sentence, so no column qualifies and no marker is
demanded. Each row therefore names its own source in its own `Where` cell, and a
row whose source is a `.gate` recording says which file.

| Decision                                                                        | Alternatives measured                                                                      | Margin                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              | Where                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  | What it does NOT cover                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Build instances by **cloning a prototype**                                      | `createElement` per node; five parser doors; whole-card and whole-app clone; shallow clone | create is +21% over the clone floor; every parser door is dearer, the five of them within a 0.0075 ms spread                                                                                                                                                                                        | `mount-floor`, one run, no `.gate` recording                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           | Trees that do not repeat. `clone·distinct` (321 distinct prototypes) costs +2.7%, so the ranking is scoped to repetitive markup and a genuine low-repetition census needs its own app and its own reference row, which **does not exist**                                                                                                                                                                    |
| **No `DocumentFragment` staging**                                               | the identical clone program with the clones staged in a fragment first                     | staging is the worst of the twenty-one programs                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     | `mount-floor`, same run                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                | Apps that insert into a **live** tree repeatedly. This app assembles detached and inserts once, which is the case where staging can only lose                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| **`document.importNode` removed** from the plan compiler                        | keeping the import; a size threshold in the predicate, swept 1…64 nodes                    | mount axis moved 0.413 → 0.375 ms, −9.2%, against a ±3.3% noise floor and machine drift ×1.000 over ten controls                                                                                                                                                                                    | **Traceable**: `.gate/initial-render.importnode-before.json` and `.gate/initial-render.importnode-after.json`. ONE further run agrees (it used to say two, and the second is struck below) — `import-node-trade` sweeps subtree size and finds the loss **growing** at ~14.9 ns per node over seven rungs. **The second half of that sentence is withdrawn**: it rested on a phase-by-phase axis that ran the schema core on a second backend, and both the axis and the backend have been deleted. Its one recording refused its own attributions before it went — the control rung moved 0.0297 ms where the whole gap is −0.0222, so by its own rule no contribution in it was attributable — and the ~95 ns / ~26 ns pair came from an unrecorded run that can no longer be checked against anything on disk. The withdrawal is stated rather than deleted so it stays visible; nothing left in the suite can re-derive that pair | Nothing about hydration, which adopts and never clones. The 0.413/0.375 pair is one app's shape                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| **Four template shapes** — the granularity of a prototype                       | coarser prototypes: whole card, whole app                                                  | not a margin. Coarser is **impossible**, not slower: a card prototype would have to contain the tag rows and the details block, which the card's wire computes                                                                                                                                      | Read from `exodra-app.tsx` and `mount-floor.ts`'s dataBlind flag                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       | **Not measured, and it cannot be.** The rows that would show a win (`card-clone`, `app-clone`) are data-baked and are published as bounds only. There is no measurement of what a _legitimately_ coarser template would cost, because none can be built for this app                                                                                                                                         |
| **Reconcile by object identity**, keys as an opt-in plugin                      | none                                                                                       | —                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   | Read from `packages/list-reconcile/src/index.ts`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     | **UNMEASURED.** No axis in this suite runs `createExoKeyedList` against `reconcileExoOrder`. The argument for identity is about the data layer (one permanent object per entity), not about a number, and the keyed plugin is a real deliverable rather than a fallback. The published `list-update` table measures the **op vs value** contract, which is a different question and must not be read as this one |
| **No node bank** — removed, and not offered as a plugin                         | `cloneNode(true)` against a bank of parked elements                                        | the `bank-vs-clone` ladder priced this app's CARD prototype at 875 ns to clone against 3.1 ns for a bare pop, 125 ns for a pop plus a port reset, 625 ns for a pop plus a full reset; the mount axis splits into clone 34.8% / walk 6.1% / insert 15.2% / wire 43.9% | the ladder's recording, `packages/benchmarks/measurements/bank-vs-clone.published.json`; its source is gone with the bank | Removed by the owner on 2026-09-20: caching a whole exonode by hand and reusing it does the bank's job without an engine-side reset, and a bank had to refuse every template with an event port. |
| **Keep-alive via `unmount = NOTHING`** rather than a caching policy in the list | out-of-the-box teardown-and-rebuild; Mikado's pooled mode                                  | 10.2 → 3.3 ms on the toggle axis, and ahead of the pooled hand-written participant                                                                                                                                                                                                                  | `.gate/toggle.base1.json`, published in [Eight things frameworks forbid](./what-others-forbid.md#4-you-cannot-keep-a-subtree-alive-or-pool-it)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         | The toggle axis is Exodra's **weakest** out of the box (10.2 against mikado's 7.4). The extension point is what closes it; nothing here says the default is good                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |

## Part 3 — what none of it bounds

Read this before quoting a single number above.

-   **This machine, this browser, one operator.** Every figure is one person's
    measurement on one laptop, and all three floor axes have no recording on disk at
    all — nothing here can be re-read against the run that produced it.
-   **These apps and these shapes.** The mount bound is 321 instances averaging
    ~3.5 nodes each. A floor is not scale-invariant: a component with **more static
    markup per instance** moves the gap towards zero because the clone dominates;
    one with **more ports per element** moves it the other way. One shape.
-   **These five transitions.** The update floor is five transitions on two apps. A
    transition with more DOM work per dispatch pulls every ratio towards 1; one with
    less pushes it away.
-   **Not teardown.** Every floor's cleanup is `container.remove()` and ends no
    subscriptions, because it has none. `teardown-phases` is that direction and it
    is not a floor.
-   **Not memory.** No heap column is printed and none would mean anything: a floor
    retains 480 flat references where a framework retains records, listeners,
    registries and subscriber lists. That is a different axis and nobody has built
    it.
-   **Not page load, TTI, or any wall-clock quantity.** The hydration axis's parse
    is an `innerHTML` call on a string already in memory. A real parse is streamed,
    interleaved with the network and with the script's own download and compile.
    `packages/benchmarks/ssr/` is the wall-clock instrument and it is a different
    claim.
-   **The hydration section bounds nothing.** It has no framework-free program in
    it and cannot have one. It is a comparison of two paths through one renderer,
    and the word "floor" in `hydrate-floor.ts` names the _set of axes it was written
    to_, not what it produces.
-   **Not other renderers, directly.** No third-party participant appears in any of
    these three axes. The bound applies to everybody for the same reason it applies
    to us — nothing can be further below the floor than the floor — but no row here
    measures a rival.
-   **These are throughput measurements.** A timed region performs thousands of
    transitions back to back; a real page performs one and yields. Nothing reads
    layout back, so no row pays a forced style recalculation and every row defers
    the same invalidation to whatever runs next.
-   **And the mount bound's imprecision is ours.** 1.351× / 1.418× / 1.339× is a
    range because the `exodra` row moved between runs of an identical program while
    the floor rows repeated to the third decimal. Tightening it is our work, not the
    reader's problem to discount.

## Reproducing any of it

From `packages/benchmarks`:

```bash
node scripts/run-one-axis.js mount-floor 100 4
node scripts/run-one-axis.js update-floor 100 16   # batch 4 quantises every median — do not quote it
node scripts/run-one-axis.js hydrate-floor 100 2
```

Each run prints its own resolution floor, its own refusals, and the whole "what
this does not bound" list again in its own words. If a run refuses a row, that row
is not a number.


==============================================================================
# Order without recomputing

This renderer reconciles children by the pointer identity of the child object. It never keys, and it
never treats a position as an identity. Each child also remembers where it last sat, on itself. So
the question arrives on its own:

> If identity already gives us the mapping, and the old position is already on the child, why is a
> longest-increasing-subsequence pass still needed? Store the **order** in the identity, and a move
> becomes a link update rather than a rebuilt subsequence.

The narrow answer is that the subsequence is not there to *find* the children — it is there to decide
which of them may stay still. But "why this algorithm and not another" deserves the whole space
rather than one rebuttal, so this page enumerates every way this problem is known to be solved and
says, for each, what it would cost **here**. Where a candidate cannot be priced from anything in this
repository, it says so and names the row that would settle it.

## The problem, and the objective

Given a sequence of items in an old order, and the same items — plus insertions, minus deletions — in
a new order, with a stable identity per item, produce a sequence of DOM operations that realises the
new order.

**The cost is not comparisons.** It is `insertBefore` calls plus whatever bookkeeping the algorithm
needs to decide on them. On the transition where this matters most, the axis prices *discovery* —
stamping survivors, reading old positions, computing the move set — at **3.1250 µs against a
hand-written reconciler's 21.6146, or 14.5%** *(my subtraction on two recorded medians, below; not a
run)*. Every algorithm in this page's Family A and Family C competes inside that 14.5%. The other
85.5% is the moves.

### One fact closes most of the space before it opens

A node may stay where it is only if every node it must remain behind also stays. So the set of nodes
that do not move is an increasing subsequence of the old positions, and **the minimum number of
single-node moves is exactly `n` minus the length of a maximum increasing subsequence.** That is a
property of the problem, not a claim about this code; the shipped pass's own header claims only that
every backend moving DOM nodes uses it, because two placement passes are interchangeable only if they
keep the same rows in place (`packages/list-reconcile/src/getExoSequence.ts:1-6`).

**The incumbent is therefore already optimal on the expensive term.** No algorithm can move fewer
nodes. Everything below either

- trades *more moves* for *less bookkeeping* (Family A),
- makes a move cost less than one `insertBefore` (Family B),
- makes the bookkeeping cheaper without changing the moves (Family C — where order maintenance
  lives), or
- changes the problem so that no move set is derived at all (Family D — where this renderer already
  has an answer, and it is the one that wins).

## The enumeration

### Family A — choose which nodes move

Same objective, different algorithm. All of these are `O(n)` or `O(n log n)` and none allocates a
per-row structure that survives the update.

*The library names in the left column are attributions from the literature, not readings of those
libraries' source. Nothing in this repository checks them, and only the rows marked **shipped** are
claims about code here.*

| candidate | moves | bookkeeping | why it wins or loses here |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Longest increasing subsequence** (Vue 3, ivi, and this renderer) | minimal, by the fact above | one `number[]` in, two arrays out per reordering update | shipped. Its cost is the one term this family can still argue about, and it is unmeasured here — see below |
| **Naive: move everything not in place** | up to `n` | none | the honest rival: with the subsequence forced empty, the placement pass moves every surviving row it does not keep (`packages/list-reconcile/src/reconcileExoOrder.ts:72-90`). Nobody has counted the difference. **This is the one candidate in the whole page that could beat the incumbent on a real transition, and it is untested** |
| **Greedy ascending run** (React's `lastPlacedIndex`) | between the two — a *greedy* increasing run, not a maximum one | none beyond a running maximum | this renderer already computes exactly that running maximum, for a different purpose: `inOrder` skips the subsequence whole when no survivor is out of order (`packages/list-reconcile/src/reconcileExoOrder.ts:46-60`). Adopting React's rule would mean *stopping* there and moving more nodes — the same trade as the naive row, with a smaller saving |
| **Two-ended prefix/suffix scan** (Vue 2, Snabbdom, Inferno) | depends on the shape | four cursors | **shipped, and it runs first.** The position-only path and the two contiguous-splice paths are this technique; the subsequence is only what is left when they cannot answer (`:108-129`). It is why `GROW-SHRINK/exodra` measures *level with* the hand-written general floor in the table below, which the run refuses as a bound in either direction |
| **Edit-script diffing** (Myers, Hunt–Szymanski, Wu) | minimal *edits*, which is a different objective | `O(nd)` time and an `O(n)`–`O(n²)` table | it optimises insert/delete counts and treats a move as a delete plus an insert. Here a move is one call and a delete is a teardown plus a rebuild, so minimising edits maximises the expensive thing. **Never considered here — my judgement** |
| **Cycle decomposition of the permutation** | minimal *transpositions*, `n −` (number of cycles) | one visited-flag per row | swaps are not the primitive. `insertBefore` moves one node into a position; realising a transposition takes two of them. Minimal transpositions and minimal insertions are different numbers, and the second is what the LIS gives. **Never considered here — my judgement** |
| **Patience / LCS-based diffing** | — | — | not a separate candidate: patience diff *is* a longest-increasing-subsequence pass over matched positions. It is the incumbent under another name |

### Family B — make one move cost less

These leave the move set alone and attack the price of a move. None is shipped.

| candidate | what it would buy | why it is not here |
|---|---|---|
| **Run moves** (`Range`, or a `DocumentFragment` round trip) | *k* contiguous movers in fewer calls | the movers are scattered *because* the subsequence already kept the long runs still, so there is usually little contiguity left to batch. The one place a contiguous run is known in advance is a caller telling the list the move, and `move` relocates one row per call, one `insertBefore` each (`packages/dom/src/dom/factories/createExoChildList.ts:82-99`). **Unpriced. What would settle it is a `GROW-SHRINK` or `REORDER` row that is the shipped op path with the run relocated through a fragment** |
| **CSS `order` / grid placement** | zero DOM mutations — a permutation becomes `n` style writes | it changes *visual* order only: hit-testing, tab order, selection and assistive technology continue to see the document order. It also costs a write per row where a move set costs a call per mover, so it loses on the shapes this renderer is fast on. It works only inside a flex or grid container, which a children port cannot assume. **Never considered here — my judgement** |
| **Detach the region, rebuild it, reattach** | one insertion instead of many | this is Family D's rebuild row, and the numbers there are against it |

### Family C — answer "where was this child" faster

This is where **order-maintenance structures** sit, and the whole family competes for one term only:
what it costs to find out where each child was. In a program with no framework in it that term is
**3.1250 µs of 21.6146, 14.5%** — the whole of it, stamping and subsequence included. That figure
bounds the *floor's* discovery and not this renderer's, whose own version of the same machinery
carries a per-row record and a `Map`. The four rungs below were finally run in the shuffled recording;
two of them resolve, two are refused as under the axis's own resolution bar, and two of the four
price things no structure here would touch.

| candidate | per-row cost | what it answers | status |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A field on the child** (`index`) | one slot in an object that already exists | old position, membership and the subsequence's input, in one load | **removed**: the shipped reconciler stopped reading it, so the child list stopped writing it — `reconcileExoOrder` works from the caller's own mirror of keys (`packages/list-reconcile/src/reconcileExoOrder.ts:94-130`) |
| **Read it off the document** | nothing stored | old position, by walking back from the region's end anchor | was shipped as a plugin and is **not in the tree today** — the seam it stood in is now a whole package over two backend doors (`packages/list-reconcile/src/reconcileExoOrder.ts`) |
| **A `Map` from key to old position, rebuilt per update** | a hash entry per row of the changed middle, per update | old position and membership | **what ships today**: a `Map` from key to its first old position plus an `Int32Array` chain for repeated keys, built only over the middle that differs and dropped when the pass ends (`packages/list-reconcile/src/reconcileExoOrder.ts:17-34`). An earlier node-keyed table that outlived the pass, and so pinned every element the list ever held, is gone |
| **Order maintenance** (Dietz–Sleator; Bender et al.) | a label, and prev/next if insertion is to be `O(1)` | *does A come after B* in `O(1)`, insert-after in amortised `O(1)` | **the subject of this page.** It answers a question this pass asks once and answers already — see the next section |
| **Order-statistic / balanced tree keyed by position** (splay, AVL with subtree counts) | a tree node per row | rank in `O(log n)`, and a move is a splice | it answers *rank*, which the renderer has as an integer for free, and it pays a pointer chase where the incumbent pays an array index. **Never considered here — my judgement** |
| **Successor structures over a bounded universe** (van Emde Boas, y-fast tries) | a universe-sized or hash-backed index | successor in `O(log log u)` | the renderer never asks for a successor: the new order *is* the successor list, handed over. **Never considered here — my judgement** |

### Family D — do not derive a move set at all

| candidate | status | evidence |
|---|---|---|
| **Be told what changed** (a transition calling the child list's own `insert` / `move` / `remove`) | **shipped, and it is the answer** | 10.9× and 4.81×, in the tables below |
| **Rebuild instead of reordering** | measured, and the numbers are against it | `exodraKept` 3.3 against `exodra` 10.2 on `toggle`, and `WIDE/exodra·kept` 56.25 against `WIDE/exodra` 115.625 — below |
| **Do not have the rows** (windowing) | shipped as an application technique, not a reconciler one | a sliding window preserves ascending order, so `anyMoved` stays false and the subsequence is skipped whole. It removes this problem rather than solving it |

## The two tables everything above quotes

<!-- gate: axis=list-update label=rec1 -->

| row | median (ms) | what it is |
|---|---|---|
| `exodraOps` | 0.075 | four mutations, told to the list as operations |
| `exodra` | 0.815 | the same four, handed over as a new array and diffed |

<!-- gate: axis=update-floor label=shuffled -->

| row | median (µs) | what it is |
|---|---|---|
| `GROW-SHRINK/exodraOps` | 1.2656 | told |
