| `GROW-SHRINK/exodra` | 6.0938 | deriving — *level with* the hand-written floor beneath it, because the two-ended paths recognise this shape |
| `GROW-SHRINK/floor·diff` | 6.0938 | a hand-written general reconciler, deriving |
| `REORDER/floor·told` | 18.4896 | handed the minimum move set in advance |
| `REORDER/floor·diff` | 21.6146 | the hand-written general reconciler |
| `REORDER/exodra` | 33.8542 | this renderer, on a shuffle |
| `WIDE/exodra·kept` | 56.25 | the same app keeping what the reference rebuilds |
| `WIDE/floor` | 51.5625 | a hand-written program that rebuilds |
| `WIDE/exodra` | 115.625 | the shipped app, rebuilding |

<!-- gate: axis=toggle label=base1 -->

| row | median (ms) | what it is |
|---|---|---|
| `exodraKept` | 3.3 | a block that survives being taken out and comes back with one insertion |
| `exodra` | 10.2 | the same block rebuilt |

*My arithmetic on those medians, not a run:* being told is **10.9×** the deriving path on
`list-update` and **4.81×** on `GROW-SHRINK`; keeping is **3.1×** rebuilding on `toggle` and
**2.06×** on `WIDE`. Read the `WIDE` pair with the axis's own caveat: `exodra·kept` is a diagnostic
row that "keeps what the reference rebuilds", and the file says outright that it bounds nothing
(`packages/benchmarks/src/benchmarks/axes/floors/update-floor.ts:208-212`).

The `update-floor` figures here are re-read from `update-floor.shuffled.json`. The earlier recording
of that axis is withdrawn — its phases ran in a rigid rotation, so its resolution bar was measuring
where a row had been declared rather than what the program did; nothing in the renderer changed
between the two runs.

## Why Family D comes first

Telling the child list directly already skips the diff, the old-position table and the subsequence
entirely: a transition that knows what changed calls the command, nothing is derived — `insert`,
`move` and `remove` are three short bodies on the child list
(`packages/dom/src/dom/factories/createExoChildList.ts:64-108`). "A move updates a link
rather than rebuilding a subsequence" is not a design this renderer lacks — it is the design it
ships, and the link it updates is the document.

So the case any Family A or C candidate has to serve is what is left after that: **a list that
reorders by handing over a new order rather than the move.** Counted in this repository's own
examples and benchmarks:

| where | reorders | tells the child list the move |
|---|---|---|
| `packages/benchmarks/src/benchmarks/axes/list/reconcile.tsx:329` | yes — 30 shuffles of 200 rows per batch | no (a new array) |
| `packages/benchmarks/src/benchmarks/axes/list/list-reconcile.tsx:665` | yes — one run move per cycle | no (the plain array the diffing rows share) |
| `packages/benchmarks/src/benchmarks/axes/floors/update-floor.ts:1568-1570` | yes — the `REORDER` transition | no |
| `packages/examples/no-build/global.html` | yes — rotate | no — the rotated array goes to `reconcileExoOrder` |
| `packages/examples/no-build/esm.html` | yes — rotate | no — the rotated array goes to `reconcileExoOrder` |
| every other list in the examples | no | — |

**Five: three in the benchmark suite, written to measure the general path, and the rotate in the
no-build pair, which hands over a new array where one `move` would say it.** That is not an argument
that the general path is unimportant — it is what a caller that does not track its own moves falls
back to, and it must be correct and fast for exactly that reader. It is an argument that the
population any new structure would serve is, here and today, the population that already has a
cheaper answer one call away and does not take it.

## What the reconciler actually asks, pass by pass

Every question the diffing path puts, in order. The last column is why Family C's most interesting
member does not apply.

| pass | the question | kind | answered by an order structure? |
|---|---|---|---|
| prefix scan | is the key now at position *i* the key that was at *i*? (`packages/list-reconcile/src/reconcileExoOrder.ts:110`) | identity equality | no — not an order question |
| tail scan | the same, walking back from the end (`:113-116`) | identity equality | no |
| fast paths | did the middle only grow, or only shrink? (`:117-128`) | two integer compares | no |
| resolve | where was this key, and was it here at all? (`:17-34`) | a hash lookup in a `Map` built for this pass | no — such a structure has no absolute position; that is its defining property |
| removals | which old rows did nobody claim? (`:39-41`) | a rank of zero | no |
| ascending? | `at < last` over the survivors' ranks (`:47-53`) | **an order comparison** | yes, and it is already one integer compare on a value in a register |
| subsequence | which maximal subset of the old positions is increasing? (`:66`) | **an optimisation over the whole permutation** | **no** |
| place | is this row in the increasing run the subsequence kept? (`:72-89`) | a bit set from the subsequence | no |

Eight questions. **One is a comparison, and it is the cheapest line in the pass** — each survivor's rank
compared with the one before it, integers the loop has already loaded, whose whole output is a boolean deciding whether the
subsequence runs at all. The question that costs is the seventh, and it is not a comparison query. An
oracle answering *is A before B* perfectly and for free would leave it exactly where it is.

**The subsequence is comparison-shaped, and that changes nothing.** `getExoSequence` touches its
input only through `<` and a `!== 0` sentinel (`packages/list-reconcile/src/getExoSequence.ts:12-33`), so it
*could* run over opaque labels from an order structure with no change to the algorithm. That is the
strongest form of the idea and it still loses: the same `O(n log n)` binary search would run with an
indirect comparison in place of an integer compare, inside the binary search itself
(`packages/list-reconcile/src/getExoSequence.ts:21-27`).

**Membership comes from the hash, and an order label would not replace it.** A key that is not in
the caller's mirror of what was shown has no entry in the pass's `Map` and is built as new
(`packages/list-reconcile/src/reconcileExoOrder.ts:26-34`). An order structure carries relative
order and no membership, so it would sit beside that lookup rather than replacing it.

**And it cannot replace the arrays it would sit beside.** The reconciler's own state is the caller's
array of keys, `shown`, rewritten in place or replaced by the return value
(`packages/list-reconcile/src/reconcileExoOrder.ts:117-130`). The child list keeps its own `order`
array of children, and that one is not scratch either: it is published to the child list in front so
that list can end at this one's first node, so it is emptied in place and never handed out
(`packages/dom/src/dom/factories/createExoChildList.ts:14-16`).

## Does identity make the per-element price already paid?

This is the strongest form of the intuition, and it is a fair question with a three-part answer. An
order-maintenance structure needs a stable per-element node. A key-based renderer must derive a key
and map it to something; **this one already holds the item object, and a record already hangs off
every child.**

**The allocation: yes, already paid.** `TExoDomChild` exists per child regardless, it is built whole in
one literal, and until recently it carried a position field, `index`, which was removed once nothing read it
(`packages/dom/src/dom/types/TExoDomChild.ts`). A label, or a prev/next pair, could be two or
three more slots in that same literal rather than a new object per row. Adding a field there is a
thing this package has already done: `node` itself went in that way. **The owner's intuition holds on
this point and it should be recorded as holding.**

**The width: not paid, and the number usually quoted does not bound it.** The measured hazard beside
that literal is about growing an object *after* construction: "an earlier attempt to cut per-node
allocations made a build 11% *slower*, and the lesson recorded from it was about V8's in-object
sizing, not allocation counts" (a measurement note whose source file is no longer in the tree), which is why
`ExoDomChildBody` assigns every field in its constructor — "a field added later spills the object
out of its in-object store" (`packages/dom/src/dom/factories/createExoDomChildFactory.ts:64`). The sentence this
page used to quote here, naming the regression as a fact about `TExoDomChild`'s own literal, is no
longer in that file and was not re-cited to another: what survives is the rule and the 11% figure
above, neither of which prices a widened literal. A **wider literal** is a different
thing from a **grown object**, and that figure does not price it. What would price it is a
`mount-floor` or `initial-render` A/B with the literal widened by three slots and nothing else
changed. **No such row exists, and this page cannot tell you what three more slots per child cost.**

**The maintenance: not paid, and this is the part identity does not help with.** Today nothing per
child records a position at all: the child list's `order` array is the only record, and a splice keeps
it right (`packages/dom/src/dom/factories/createExoChildList.ts:52-85`). A structure whose value *is*
its links has no equivalent: a link is either right or it is not, and label space runs out and has to
be rebuilt. So a splice that stores nothing per element today would start costing per-element work on
paths that reorder nothing.

**And none of it changes the outcome**, because the price being paid or unpaid is not what decides
this. Even at zero cost per element, the structure answers the fifth question in the table above —
the one already answered in a register — and does not answer the subsequence, which is the one with
the work in it.

## What the subsequence buys is unmeasured, and the file says so

The claim under audit is the incumbent's, not the challenger's. `getExoSequence` used to quote "3
moves vs 7 on a 10-row rotation, 38 vs 48 on a 50-row shuffle" against a naive "reposition everything
out of place" pass. Those figures were attributed to a test file that does not exist here, and they
resolve to no row in `packages/benchmarks/measurements/`
(`packages/list-reconcile/README.md:46-52`). **So minimising moves is, in this repository, an
unmeasured premise** — and Family A's naive row is the candidate that premise is holding off.

One thing makes the doubt larger than the deleted figures suggested:

- The cost side is bounded and small. `REORDER/floor·diff` minus `REORDER/floor·told` is what
  *discovery* costs a program with no framework in it: **3.1250 µs, 14.5% of the deriving floor and
  9.2% of this renderer's 33.8542** *(my subtraction on two recorded medians, not a run)* — stamping,
  position reads and the subsequence together.

**The row that would settle it** is a `REORDER` row that is the shipped renderer with the placement
pass handed an empty subsequence, gated by the same step-by-step markup diff every other row on that
axis passes, and differenced against `REORDER/exodra`. A negative difference kills the subsequence; a
positive one prices what it saves. **That row still does not exist.** The axis's `floor·seq` rung,
which priced the other half — what the computation costs, separately from what it saves — was run
once and is now struck with the reconciler it decomposed
(`packages/benchmarks/src/benchmarks/axes/floors/update-floor.ts:1736-1740`); it came back
at **+0.0000 µs over `floor·record`**, a difference the run refuses as a number because it sits under
4× its floor-scale null of 0.260417 µs. So the computation is somewhere between nothing and a quarter
of a microsecond, and what it saves is still unmeasured.

## Which of the four rungs any of this would move

`update-floor` carried four nested attribution rungs for the `REORDER` gap, and **the shuffled
recording is the only one to have executed them** — all four are struck now, because the reconciler
they decomposed is deleted (`packages/benchmarks/src/benchmarks/axes/floors/update-floor.ts:239-243`). Each rung is the row
above it with exactly one substitution:

| rung | what it prices | measured | moved by a Family C structure? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `floor·record` | the position and survival tables moving onto per-row records | **+0.2604 µs** over `floor·diff` — *refused as a number*, under 4× the floor-scale null of 0.260417 µs | it would **add** to this term: more slots per record |
| `floor·seq` | the shipped subsequence instead of the floor's | **+0.0000 µs** over `floor·record` — *refused as a number*, same bar | at most this one, and it was predicted the smallest |
| `floor·place` | the shipped placement walk, including its DOM read per moved child | **+6.5104 µs** over `floor·seq` — the largest single rung on the ladder | no |
| `floor·registry` | the item-to-child `Map`, 200 lookups per transition | **+3.3854 µs** over `floor·place` | no — it had been predicted the **largest** named part, at least 5.0 µs, derived from a measured 35.5 ns per `Map` operation |

Two things the run changed. **The registry prediction missed**: it named the registry as the largest
named part at 5.0 µs or more, and the registry came in at 3.3854 µs behind the placement walk's
6.5104. **And the two rungs a Family C structure could touch are precisely the two the run cannot
resolve** — both sit under the axis's own resolution bar, so what an order structure would displace is
somewhere between nothing and about half a microsecond, on a gap of 12.2396.

So the idea reaches one term, the term measured smallest and refused as a number, and enlarges
another. **If the gap is the placement walk and the registry, this addresses the wrong one** — and the
two rungs that carry almost all of it, at 9.8958 µs of the 12.2396 between them, are the two no
storage change would move.

## Where the old order lives is a separable question

The strongest evidence that *where the old order lives* is not the term is that the placement pass
does not care where its input came from.

The shipped reconciler reads the old position off its own mirror of what it showed. Reading it off
the **document** instead — walking back from the region's end anchor to build the same `shown`
array — would feed the same placement pass, because that pass takes the old order as the `shown` array it
is handed (`packages/list-reconcile/src/reconcileExoOrder.ts:5-14`). No such reconciler is in the
tree; the argument depends only on the two questions being separable.

A third backend refuses the pass outright, and its reason is about the destination rather than the
storage: `@exodra/term`'s region is an array and the new order is one store, so a subsequence would
compute an answer nothing then reads. That is the shape of an argument
that removes the pass: it names a destination where a move costs nothing. Family C names a different
place to keep the input.

## Two things that are not this, and survive

**A command that carries a permutation.** The child list answers four commands — `insert`,
`move`, `remove`, `removeAll` (`packages/list-reconcile/src/types/TExoPlacedChildren.ts`). A `move`
relocates one row, so a re-sort cannot be told as one; a whole new order goes through
`reconcileExoOrder` and the same diff, and the only wholesale path is an empty order, which clears
the list outright (`packages/list-reconcile/src/reconcileExoOrder.ts:102-106`). That is a real gap,
it is in the command set rather than in the storage, and it is where a caller that re-sorts would be
served. **It would not
remove the subsequence either.** Being handed the new order is not being handed the move set;
minimising moves is a function of the permutation, however you learned it. The axis has a row for
being handed the answer — `floor·told` — and says of it that it is "THE MAXIMAL FREE LUNCH and it is
not a technique anybody could ship" (`packages/benchmarks/src/benchmarks/axes/floors/update-floor.ts:134-138`).

**The interface.** If somebody wants to build any of this, there is a door, and it does not require the
argument above to be wrong. Reconciling is a whole package that stands on two doors the backend
already has — `build` to make a row and the child list to place one — so a second strategy is a
second function, not a fork of the renderer
(`packages/list-reconcile/src/reconcileExoOrder.ts`). A third strategy costs the people
who do not install it nothing, and it would be measured against `REORDER/exodra` on an axis that
already exists.

## What this page does not settle

- **It is an argument from the code and from recorded rows, not a run.** No axis was executed to write
  it. Every figure in the three gated tables is a median already recorded in
  `packages/benchmarks/measurements/`; every ratio in the prose is arithmetic on those medians and is
  labelled where it appears.
- **It does not prove the subsequence is worth its computation.** It says the opposite: that claim is
  unmeasured here, Family A's naive row is the live challenger, and the row that would settle it is
  named.
- **It cannot price a wider `TExoDomChild`.** Three more slots per child is the one cost in the
  order-maintenance case that identity might genuinely have already paid, and nothing here measures
  object width.
- **It prices nothing in Family B.** Run moves and CSS ordering are named, argued from their
  semantics, and left unmeasured.
- **It does not rule out these structures for a different problem.** The argument is about the
  question *this* reconciler puts. A renderer whose region is not a document, or whose caller asks
  *where does this go relative to that*, is asking something else, and nothing here transfers.


==============================================================================
# Eight things frameworks forbid

Eight sentences that begin "you can't" in most UI frameworks. For each one: what
the common arrangement is, what Exodra does instead, and — the part that matters
— **the current state, with the file that proves it or the gap that undoes it.**

:::note How the eight map onto plugin interfaces
They do not line up one-to-one. **Two of the eight are backed by a field on
`ExoDomBackend`**: the event pack (7) and the value writers (8). The reconciler (2)
and keys (3) are free functions in `@exodra/list-reconcile` over the child-list door
every exonode has; keeping a subtree (4) is that same child list's `detach` /
`attach`; no build step (1) is a property of the component form; a foreign node (5)
is an escape from the schema rather than a part of it; and another renderer (6) has
no interface at all. See [Sugar, not restrictions](./sugar-not-restrictions.md).
:::

:::note About the "what others do" half
Those paragraphs describe the common arrangement as a shape, not as a claim about
any particular framework's source. Nothing in this repository measures or reads
React, Svelte, Solid, Lit or Vue internals, so no sentence here should be quoted
as a finding about them. The Exodra half of each item is read from this
repository and cited.
:::

## 1. "You need a build step"

**The common arrangement.** A template dialect or a JSX transform is the primary
way to write a component, so the framework's own documentation begins with a
bundler.

**Here.** A component is plain function calls —
`createExoSchema(build)` and `createExoMachineBuilder(schema)` — so there is nothing to compile. Two pages in
`packages/examples/no-build/` run a real application with nothing installed and
nothing bundled: `esm.html` reaches the three packages by **bare name** through
an `importmap`, a browser feature; `global.html` loads three `<script src>` IIFE
builds onto one `window.Exodra` namespace. Both were opened in a browser and run
on 2026-08-15.

**Current state.** The pages load this repository's own `dist/`, so those have to
be built first — the last *published* `@exodra/core` is `0.2.0`, a renderer that
has since been deleted, so a CDN URL would load a different program that happens
to share a name (`packages/examples/no-build/README.md`).

**And the honest exception: JSX does need a compiler, by design.** The JSX
runtime exists only so a `tsc` emit resolves, and every entry point throws:

```ts no-check
// packages/jsx/src/schema/jsx-runtime.ts:539
throw new Error(
    'Exodra schema JSX reached the runtime, which means this module was never compiled. ' +
        'Add @exodra/babel-plugin-schema to the build …'
);
```

There is no interpreter for a JSX element, and there is deliberately no
`Fragment`. Writing JSX means adopting a build step; writing Exodra does not.

## 2. "The reconciler is the framework"

**The common arrangement.** How children are diffed and moved is the framework's
central algorithm, and there is no interface anybody outside it can implement.

**Here.** The reconciler is not part of the backend at all. It is a free function,
`reconcileExoOrder(kids, shown, keys, want, build)`, which a transition calls over two
doors every exonode has — `c.childList(port)` to place a row and
`c.build(component, index)` to make one
(`packages/list-reconcile/src/reconcileExoOrder.ts`). It is handed the order shown
and the order wanted and returns the new order shown, so the machine keeps that in
its own state. A second strategy is a second function over the same doors, with no
reconciler to subclass and nothing to opt out of. One ships beside it:
`createExoKeyedList`, the same pass over an extracted key instead of the item
object — see item 3.

**Current state.** A reconciler that reads a child's old position off the
**document** instead of off its own mirror — so a region repairs itself when a
browser extension or a page translator moves a child — is not in the tree. It would
be one more function over the same two doors.

## 3. "Rows are matched by key, and the key rules are ours"

**The common arrangement.** A list requires a key, and identity is not offered as
a choice.

**Here.** The core reconciles by **object identity** — a child that is still in
the array is moved, a child that is not is dropped, and neither is rebuilt
(`reconcileExoOrder`, `packages/list-reconcile/src/reconcileExoOrder.ts`).
Keys are an opt-in pack, `EXO_KEYED_LIST_VOCABULARY` from `@exodra/list-reconcile`,
which puts `c.keyedList(port, keyOf, build, update)` on the exonode of a backend
that composed it and on no other; it returns `{ reconcile(items) }`, kept in the
machine's state and called from a transition (`createExoKeyedList` is the same list
as a free function over a child list). It is a case about a data layer: a caller whose rows arrive as freshly
parsed JSON on every poll has a new object per row per refetch, and telling them
to build a stable object per entity first is telling them to write that file.

**A page you can open.** `packages/examples/plugin-slots/keyed-list.html` renders
one row component twice over the same data — left through `reconcileExoOrder`,
right through `c.keyedList` with `item => item.id`. Button 1 hands both panels a
**refetch**: the same ids and labels as `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(…))`. The left
panel has three rows it has never seen and rebuilds all of them; the right keeps
all three and the build stamps stand still. Button 2 changes the labels: the right
panel's rows stay and their labels move, through the `update` argument the call
site passes (`(row, item) => …`, the row's own transition — there are no props).
Button 3 repeats an id: a repeated key is one row per occurrence, as a repeated
item is in an identity list.

**On the server and under hydration.** The string backend prints a row at `build`,
so a row there takes its data inside its own initial state, and a list is printed once and
never updated. Under hydration the child list opens an adoption cursor and each
`build` adopts the next served row, as for an identity list; the keyed list has no
hydration test of its own.

## 4. "You cannot keep a subtree alive, or pool it"

**The common arrangement.** A view that leaves the tree is destroyed, and reuse
is the framework's business.

**Here.** The lifecycle object *is* the child, and it is the public extension
point:

```ts no-check
// packages/dom/src/dom/types/TExoDomChild.ts — `mount`/`unmount` are called blindly
const block = c.build(DETAILS, i);
exoNodeDom(block).unmount = NOTHING;   // keep my subscriptions, I am coming back
```

From then on, taking it out of the source array detaches the node and changes
nothing else; putting it back is one `insertBefore`. The list is not involved in
that decision and contains no word about caching.

**What that is worth, measured.** The toggle axis — 20 × tear down a 200-panel
block and build a different one, ms per timed region, lower is better:

<!-- gate: axis=toggle label=base1 -->

| Participant | ms |
|---|---|
| exodraKept (panels kept alive) | **3.3** |
| mikadoPooled | 3.5 |
| mikado | 7.4 |
| exodra (out of the box) | 10.2 |

Out of the box this axis is Exodra's weakest: 10.2 against mikado's 7.4, because
the axis is dominated by rebuilding. The extension point is what closes it — 10.2 → 3.3,
which is **3.1×**, and ahead of the pooled hand-written participant.

**Which run this is, and what the figures used to say.** The four numbers above
are the medians in `packages/benchmarks/.gate/toggle.base1.json`. The figures
printed here before — 3.8 / 4.1 / 8.3 / 11.1 — were in neither toggle recording
and were retyped from somewhere the repository does not hold; they have been
replaced rather than defended. The second recording, `toggle.base2.json`, has the
same four rows at 3.0 / 3.1 / 6.6 / 9.1 — the whole table sits 10–14% lower
and the argument is unchanged, because it is 3.1× in one run and 3.0× in the
other. Both recordings are of the **rescaled** toggle axis (200 panels ×20; the
old axis measured 25 panel builds per sample and landed five participants on one
timer tick), and [Benchmarks](../benchmarks.md) now publishes both columns in
full.

**The hook-free form.** The child list itself has a placement pair that runs no hook
at all: `detach(i)` takes a child's node out without unmounting or disposing it, and
`attach(child, i)` puts it back without mounting it
(`packages/dom/src/dom/types/TExoChildList.ts`). A kept child is ended by putting it
back and calling `remove`, which disposes it
(`packages/dom/src/dom/tests/make-exo-child-list.test.ts`).

**There is no element pool.** The pooling half of the heading — handing an element
that served one wiring to the next — has no seam: every instance's element is
`cloneExoNode` on the schema's prototype. What an application keeps instead is the
**whole exonode**, wired and subscribed, through either form above.

## 5. "You cannot drop to vanilla JS in one hot spot"

**The common arrangement.** An element the framework did not create is not
something a list can hold, so a hand-written hot spot means an escape container
plus a lifecycle hook plus a rule about not letting the framework near it.

**Here.** `exoForeignNode(c, element, hooks?)` gives an element the half a child
needs — `mount`, `unmount`, disposers, the list's scratch — so that from the
list's point of view nothing foreign is happening
(`packages/dom/src/foreign/exoForeignNode.ts:22-63`). It travels the same lines as
every other child: placed, moved, dropped, disposed.

**Current state.** `packages/examples/escape-hatches/` runs it: one row of an
ordinary list built with `document.createElement` and `addEventListener`, standing
among schema-built siblings, reordered with them and put back with its own state.
The hand-built row is `escape-hatches/index.html:211-273` — no schema, no ports, no
wiring function, no `c.attr` — and it goes into the same children array as three
schema rows at `:451-456`. Opened in a browser and run on 2026-08-15. How to use it —
and the trap in the `onMount` hook — is [the next page](./imperative-escape.md).

## 6. "You cannot run another renderer inside part of the tree"

**The common arrangement.** Two renderers in one document means two roots and a
manual boundary between them.

**Here, in the narrow sense: the same door.** A subtree owned by something that
has never heard of Exodra arrives through `exoForeignNode` and is placed, moved
and disposed like any other child. The escape-hatches page runs a canvas widget
with its own `requestAnimationFrame` loop between two schema-built cards. The
widget is `packages/examples/escape-hatches/index.html:287-325` — lines that
know nothing about schemas, ports or children. Its whole contract with Exodra is
two hooks at `packages/examples/escape-hatches/index.html:338-354`, and the
`onUnmount` one is what stops the loop; the page shows the frame counter
freezing when it does. It sits between two schema cards
in one children array at `:382-386`. What must be true of such a widget is stated
where it is built (`:203-208`): it renders **inside** the box it hands out and never
moves or replaces that box, because removal and placement climb `parentNode` only
as far as the list's parent, so a box moved out of that parent is beyond reach. Opened
in a browser and run on 2026-08-15.

**Not yet true as a general claim, and this is the item to be blunt about.**
There is **no foreign backend behind a plugin interface.** An element carries no
pointer back to its child and `exoNodeDom` takes a child and refuses anything else
(`packages/dom/src/dom/exoNodeDom.ts`): the renderer holds children as `TExoDomChild`s
directly and never needs an element→child read at all. What is deliberately outside every plugin interface is the
*create* direction — `makeNodeDom` is the one place a child is constructed and is not exported. So:

- What works is **one element handed in**, filled by whatever you like, treated as
  an opaque child. Client render only.
- What does not exist is a second *renderer* plugged into the schema — there is no plugin
  interface for the element builder, the schema compiler, or hydration's adoption **walk**. The
  attribute and text **setters** are behind the `writers` interface, which is
  [item 8](#8-you-cannot-change-what-a-value-means-on-the-way-to-the-element).
  The *children* arm of that same branch stays welded on
  purpose — `compileExoHydrateSchema.ts:44-49` identifies a raw-markup port by
  pointer-comparing its setter against `setExoHtml`.
- On the server a foreign node is markup the caller supplies: `c.foreign(t)` calls
  `t.createStr()` there (`packages/string/src/foreign/constants/EXO_STR_FOREIGN_VOCABULARY.ts:7-9`),
  and `exoForeignMarkup(markup)` is the unescaped string it hands back. The parameter
  type is the only guard — nothing at runtime tells markup from `[object Object]`.

## 7. "How a listener gets attached is the framework's business"

**The common arrangement.** Either every handler is a real `addEventListener` on
its element, or every handler goes through one delegated document listener. Which
one it is was decided by the framework's authors, and an application that wanted
the other has no way to say so.

**Here.** `ExoDomBackend.events`
(`packages/dom/src/events/types/TExoEventsApi.ts`) holds a `TExoEventsApi`,
and this library already had two: `EXO_DIRECT_EVENTS` — one listener per element,
which is what composing nothing gives you — and `createExoDelegatedEvents(['click',
'input'])`, which puts one listener per named event on the render root.
Both are exported. Swapping is the five-line composition on
[Every convenience is sugar](./sugar-not-restrictions.md#replacing-one-interface).

**A page you can open.** `packages/examples/plugin-slots/events.html` renders 200 rows
of one component twice and counts `addEventListener` for the duration of each render —
the only honest observable for this interface, since no DOM API reports how many listeners
exist. Both panels answer clicks; only the counts differ. The whole of what an
application writes is `events.html:150, 183-184`. The page also carries the constraint the
interface imposes and does not hide it (`:79-84`; the refusal is
`packages/dom/src/events/attachExoDelegatedEvent.ts:7`): **a delegated pack refuses a fill with no
subject**, because a listener on the render root finds the handler by reading the element
and the subject beside it is the only thing that tells one shared function which row fired.
That form — a module-level function plus a subject — works under both packs, which is what
lets one component be rendered twice with only the composition changed. **Not opened in a
browser**, and the `addEventListener` count is an instrument, not something an
application should do.

**The interface is the model the rest follow**, and it is worth reading for
that alone: an inert **value** — `{ name, attacher(event), install?(root) }` — with
no registration call, no lifecycle and no global. `attacher` is called **once per
event port per schema**, while the plan is compiled, and what it returns is stored
in `plan.setters` beside the attribute writers. So filling an event port stays two
array loads and one indirect call, **with the strategy already baked into which
function got loaded** — the choice is spent at compile time and never consulted per
row, per update or per dispatch. `install` is the once-per-render-root half that
the delegated strategy needs, and a pack that needs nothing leaves it undefined, so
the common path does not test for it.

**Current state, and two behaviours legitimately change with the pack** — which is
why they are documented rather than tested for. A node moved out of its root
**stops responding** under a delegated pack. And disposal is not symmetric: direct
listeners die with their node, delegated ones die with the render's scope. A second
pack also has two rules on it, both because getting either wrong double-dispatches
silently, which looks like nothing happening: namespace the per-element event slots
through `exoEventSlotsFor(packId, event)` with a pack id unique to the pack, and
reference-count anything put on a root, because `install` runs once per **render**
and two renders can share one parent (`installExoDelegatedRoot` is the counted
implementation and is exported).

## 8. "You cannot change what a value means on the way to the element"

**The common arrangement.** The framework decides whether `foo={x}` is an
attribute or a property, usually by a name table it owns, and a value that is not
a string has no route to the element at all.

**Here.** `ExoDomBackend.writers`
(`packages/dom/src/backend/types/TExoWritersApi.ts`) decides how an
attribute or text port's value reaches an element. `EXO_SHIPPED_WRITERS` is the
default; `withExoPropertyWriters` (`packages/dom/src/plugins/exo-property-writers/`) is
the second implementation, and it writes a custom element's ports as JavaScript
**properties** (`chart.series = rows`), delegating every other element, every
global attribute and every text port to the shipped pack unchanged.

**A page you can open.** `packages/examples/plugin-slots/value-writers.html` defines a
`<price-chart>` custom element that draws whatever array it is handed
(`value-writers.html:83-118`) and renders **one** schema twice
(`:130-152`): on the left the port becomes `setAttribute('series', String(rows))` and
the element receives nothing it can use; on the right it receives the array itself. The
readout prints `el.series` and `el.getAttribute('series')` side by side, so the
difference is not a claim. The page also carries the upgrade dance any element needs
that expects a property before it is upgraded (`:91-105`) — an instance is wired and
inserted afterwards, so the write lands while the element is still a plain
`HTMLElement` — and names the leftover ` series=""` placeholder out loud. **Not opened
in a browser**, and it is a client render for the first reason listed below.

**This is the one plugin interface that exists because the shipped answer CANNOT
do something, rather than because it might be beaten.** `setAttribute` takes a
string. A custom element that accepts an array of rows, a `Date`, a `Map` or a
callback is not badly served by this renderer — it is **unreachable from a
schema**, and the only escape was `exoForeignNode`, i.e. building that subtree by
hand outside the schema entirely. The second case is the one enterprise pages hit:
a policy in front of the write — Trusted Types wanting every `src`, `href` and
`srcdoc` through a policy object; an audit build recording every attribute write
with its port. Both are "wrap what the shipped pack returned", both are five lines
against this interface, and both were unspellable.

**What it costs on the hot path is structurally zero**, which is a stronger
statement than "measured at zero". The pack is resolved once per (schema,
composition) and spent immediately into `plan.setters` — the table every fill
already loads from — so `TExoDomNode.set`, `.bind` and the three hydrate fill
sites are byte-for-byte the code they were. There is no added load, branch or call
on any per-instance, per-row, per-update or per-event line. The added work is one
map lookup and one call per port, per schema, per process, next to a `<template>`
parse.

**Current state, and what it gives up.**

- **The server is not composed.** `@exodra/string` compiles through its own
  `EXO_STR_WRITERS` by module import, so it prints the stringified attribute for the
  same port. **Byte parity between the backends is a
  property of the shipped pack alone.**
- **Hydration keeps the live writer for a taken-over port.** A pack declares
  `markupCarries: false` for a port whose value no bytes could have carried, and
  `compileExoHydrateSchema` does not give those ports a repairing fill
  (`packages/dom/src/hydrate/compileExoHydrateSchema.ts`), so an adopted element
  receives its first property write.
- **One route bypasses it.** `portNodeWriter()` loads the setter table once and
  addresses ports by number from then on, so a pack sees the write it handed over and
  nothing after it. Every other route — `c.attr`, `c.text`, and the repeat writes
  a transition makes through them — goes through the table on every
  fill.

## The open holes, in one place

**Hydration DOES hand a reconciler the server's rows, and this paragraph said
the opposite.** `openChildList` on a hydrating exonode answers `[]` and opens an
adoption cursor over what the server printed, so the reconciler's opening pass —
one `build` per item — adopts those rows instead of building beside them
(`packages/dom/src/hydrate/EXO_HYDRATE_NODE_VOCABULARY.ts:214-232`). One shape is
refused, and only one: a child list standing directly behind another with no
static element between them, where no walk can find the first list's end
(`packages/dom/src/hydrate/asserts/assertExoPluginChildList.ts:4-14`).

**A machine that reaches for an element cannot be server-rendered.** The declarative
surface runs on all three backends; the moment a machine calls `exoNodeDom` it is a
client machine, and nothing on the exonode lets it ask which backend it is on.

This is [page four's subject](./imperative-escape.md#the-backend-split).

**Three defects the suite was red on. Two are closed; the third is closed too, and
this section is kept because how they closed is the argument.** None was ever pinned
as a green `it.fails`.

1. ~~**A `checked={false}` box comes back ticked after `form.reset()`.**~~ **Closed
   2026-08-16.** A port has to occupy a position, so the prototype markup carried
   `checked=""` for every `checked` port and every clone parsed as
   `defaultChecked === true`, while the server printed no attribute at all — one
   component, one wire, two different answers to `form.reset()`. The fix is in the
   DOM setter: write the PROPERTY, then the attribute. Assigning the property sets
   the control's dirty flag, and HTML only re-derives live state from an attribute
   while that flag is clear, so the second write moves the reset value and cannot
   move the control. The same line covers `value`→`defaultValue` and
   `selected`→`defaultSelected`. Its price is one extra
   `setAttribute`/`removeAttribute` per fill of such a port.
2. ~~**A `<select>` serves the first option where the data says the second.**~~
   **Closed 2026-08-16, by refusal rather than by machinery.** "This option is
   chosen" is a `selected` attribute on the **option** — a different element, later
   in the document than the port's own slot, and a writer standing in a `<select>`'s
   open tag can never reach it. The alternative was a port that writes into more than
   one slot of the plan: a change to the wire format, whose static-options-only
   version would have left the common case (options from a list) silently wrong. So
   `port('value')` on a `<select>` now throws from `ExoSchemaBuilder.port()`, before
   either backend exists, naming `port('selected')` on the option as the replacement.
   `@exodra/forms` marks a select accordingly: one `selected` port per option, the
   same shape as a radio group's `checked` ports, and `writeExoChoice` writes `true`
   to the one option whose value is chosen. The browser clears the rest of a single
   `<select>` itself, so it is one write whatever the number of options. A selection
   a person makes moves the mark natively and writes nothing.
3. ~~**A raw-markup port does not repair a stale server value on hydration.**~~
   **Closed 2026-08-16.** The objection that blocked it for so long was sound: the
   parser normalises what it parsed (`<br/>`→`<br>`, quoting, attribute order), so a
   byte compare against `el.innerHTML` reports mismatches on markup that is nothing
   of the kind. The answer is two comparisons — the cheap one first, and on a miss,
   parse the candidate into a **shallow clone of the element** so it gets the same
   fragment-parsing context, and compare the two serialisations. Equal writes
   nothing. It costs one `innerHTML` read per bound raw-markup port per hydrated
   instance, and nothing on any render, update or reconcile path.

**What is still red: nothing.** The suite is green. That sentence is only worth
anything for as long as it is true, so it is the first thing to check against a run
rather than to trust from this page.


==============================================================================
# The imperative escape

Some views are not worth describing declaratively. A body of text that has to be
re-marked on every keystroke, a canvas, a widget somebody else wrote, a
measurement that only the live element can answer — for these, the shortest
correct program is imperative, and a framework that will not let you write it
makes you write a worse one instead.

So this page is two halves: **we give you the element**, and **here is a real
imperative hot spot, done almost vanilla**.

## We give you the element

`exoNodeDom(child)` opens the lifecycle object behind a built child, and
`.node` is the element (`packages/dom/src/dom/exoNodeDom.ts:10-15`):

```ts no-check
import { exoNodeDom, exoOnTeardown } from '@exodra/dom';

const panel = c.build(DETAILS, i);

const element = exoNodeDom(panel).node;   // the real Element, right now
exoOnTeardown(exoNodeDom(panel), () => socket.close());   // run this when it leaves
```

`exoOnTeardown(child, off)` pushes a teardown onto the child's own `disposers`
(`packages/dom/src/dom/exoTeardownScope.ts:30-38`); the child's default `unmount`
runs them. Assigning `exoNodeDom(child).unmount = NOTHING` is the other direction
— it is how a child says "keep my subscriptions, I am coming back", and it is
what the toggle-axis numbers on
[the previous page](./what-others-forbid.md#4-you-cannot-keep-a-subtree-alive-or-pool-it)
measure.

### What the two hooks guarantee

- **`onUnmount` runs while the element is still attached.** `dropExoChild` calls
  `child.unmount()` first and removes the node afterwards
  (`packages/dom/src/dom/dropExoChild.ts:12-17`), and `clearOwnedExoChildList` calls
  every one of them with the whole child list still in the document. A widget that has to
  tear itself down against a live tree can.
- **`onMount` runs after the element has been put in its parent.** The child list's
  `insert` calls it after its `appendChild`/`insertBefore`
  (`packages/dom/src/dom/factories/createExoChildList.ts:53-67`); `attach` is the one
  placement that skips it (`createExoChildList.ts:160-171`).
- **Both fire again on every re-entry and re-exit.** A child that leaves a list
  and comes back is moved, not rebuilt, so its hooks run again.

### The trap: the first `onMount` is not in the document

`onMount` promises a **parent**, not a connection. `mountExoInstance` clones the
prototype, **arms the machine** on it — which is when its children ports are filled and its
children are inserted and mounted — and inserts the whole clone into the page
**afterwards**:

```ts no-check
// packages/dom/src/dom/mountExoInstance.ts:23-47, cut to the four lines that matter
const root = schema.acquireNode(schema);
createExoNode(schema, root, machine, index, ownerChild, record, context);
if (before === null) parent.appendChild(root);
else parent.insertBefore(root, before);
```

So on a first render a child's `onMount` fires inside a clone that nobody has
appended yet: `element.parentNode` is set and `element.isConnected` is **false**.
Put the same child back later, into a page that is already on screen, and the
same hook reports `true`. This is visible on the escape-hatches example page,
whose first log line reads `in the document: false`
(`packages/examples/escape-hatches/README.md`).

A hook that measures a box, focuses something, or hands the element to a library
that reads layout has to check `isConnected` rather than assume it. There is no
"connected" hook today.

### The backend split

**A wiring function that reaches for an element is a client-side wiring
function.** This is not a style rule; it is a throw.

The same machine runs on `@exodra/string`, where a `TExoNode` **is** a string of
markup. `c.build` there hands back markup, so `exoNodeDom` refuses with *"this
node was not built by c.build(...)"* — during the **server render**, before the
browser is anywhere near it. The type system says so first: a machine built with
`createExoMachineBuilder<TExoDomNode>` is not one `ExoStrBackend.render` accepts, and the
case that pins the runtime half casts past that on purpose
(`packages/conformance/src/tests/an-element-wire-is-client-only.test.ts`).

Two consequences:

1. **The declarative surface is the portable one** — `attr`, `text`, `on`, `one`,
   `list`, `build`, `childList`, and `reconcileExoOrder` over them.
   `exoNodeDom` and `exoForeignNode` are `@exodra/dom`'s doors to a DOM node, and
   importing one pins the module that calls it to the browser — `exoForeignNode`
   takes an `Element` in its signature (`packages/dom/src/foreign/exoForeignNode.ts:21-25`).
2. **The portable way in is `c.foreign(t)`**, a pack every backend composes
   (`EXO_DOM_FOREIGN_VOCABULARY`, `EXO_STR_FOREIGN_VOCABULARY`,
   `EXO_TERM_FOREIGN_VOCABULARY`). `t` carries one half per backend — `createDom`,
   `createStr`, `createTerm` — and each backend calls its own, so the element is
   only ever touched by the browser half. `exoBackendCompatible(BACKENDS,
   'foreign', t)` checks at compile time that `t` has a half for every backend the
   application lists, and that every listed backend composed the door. There is
   still no capability query: nothing in a machine asks which backend it is on.

Everything below is therefore **client-rendered**. It is not written as something
that server-renders, because it does not.

## Search highlighting in rich text

The view: a long body of text, and a search box. Every hit of the query has to be
wrapped in a `<mark>`, live, as the user types.

**Why a schema tree is the wrong shape here.** The number of nodes is a function
of the *query*, not of the data — one keystroke can take the text from one node
to two hundred and back to one. Expressing that declaratively means turning a
string into an array of segments on every keystroke, diffing that array,
building a child per segment and reconciling them, to produce a result the
browser can also get from clearing one element and appending text nodes into it.
The reconciler would be doing careful work to avoid work that is cheaper than the
care.

The right shape is the imperative one: **one element you own, repainted.**

### The code

```ts no-check
import { createExoMachineBuilder, createExoSchema } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoChildrenPort, TExoEventPort } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoDomNode } from '@exodra/dom';
import { ExoDomBackend, exoForeignNode, withExoChildList, withExoCompiler } from '@exodra/dom';

/** What the user typed: a tiny store of the application's own, nothing Exodra about it. */
function createTextStore(initial: string) {
    let value = initial;
    const listeners = new Set<() => void>();
    return {
        getValue: () => value,
        setValue(next: string): void {
            value = next;
            listeners.forEach((listener) => listener());
        },
        onChange(listener: () => void): () => void {
            listeners.add(listener);
            return () => listeners.delete(listener);
        },
    };
}
const query = createTextStore('');

const ARTICLE =
    'Exodra compiles a component once, at module load, into a prototype element ' +
    'and a setter per port. A render is a clone plus one indirect call per port. …';

/**
 * PAINT THE TEXT INTO A BOX, WITH EVERY HIT IN A <mark>.
 *
 * Not one line of this is Exodra — createElement, textContent, append. It is the
 * program you would write if there were no framework on the page, and that is
 * the point: the framework's job here is to place this box and tell it when it
 * comes and goes, not to have an opinion about how the text is marked.
 */
function paintHighlights(box: Element, text: string, needle: string): void {
    box.textContent = '';
    if (needle === '') {
        box.append(text);
        return;
    }
    const hay = text.toLowerCase();
    const q = needle.toLowerCase();
    let at = 0;
    for (;;) {
        const hit = hay.indexOf(q, at);
        if (hit === -1) break;
        if (hit > at) box.append(text.slice(at, hit));
        const mark = document.createElement('mark');
        mark.textContent = text.slice(hit, hit + q.length);
        box.append(mark);
        at = hit + q.length;
    }
    if (at < text.length) box.append(text.slice(at));
}

/** The hot spot, as a child Exodra can place, move and dispose. */
function highlightedText(c: TExoDomNode, text: string) {
    const box = document.createElement('div');
    box.className = 'rich-text';
    let off: (() => void) | null = null;

    return exoForeignNode(c, box, {
        // SUBSCRIBE HERE, NOT AT CREATION, and see the open questions below for
        // why this is not the same as `exoOnTeardown`: `onMount` fires again every time
        // this child re-enters, and `onUnmount` every time it leaves.
        onMount() {
            paintHighlights(box, text, query.getValue());
            off = query.onChange(() => paintHighlights(box, text, query.getValue()));
        },
        // Runs while the element is STILL ATTACHED (drop-child.ts:34-39).
        onUnmount() {
            if (off !== null) {
                off();
                off = null;
            }
        },
    });
}

const READER_SCHEMA = createExoSchema((b) => {
    let field!: TExoEventPort;
    let body!: TExoChildrenPort;
    b.el('div', { class: 'reader' }, (div) => {
        div.el('input', { class: 'reader-search', type: 'search' }, (input) => {
            field = input.eventPort('input');
        });
        div.el('div', { class: 'reader-body' }, (host) => {
            body = host.childrenPort();
        });
    });
    return { field, body };
});
const mReader = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoDomNode>(READER_SCHEMA);
mReader.createInitialState((c) => {
    // ONE CHILD THAT NEVER CHANGES, built by the CALLER and placed through the
    // child list's own `insert` — there is no order to reconcile.
    c.childList(READER_SCHEMA.ports.body).insert(highlightedText(c, ARTICLE));
});
mReader.on(READER_SCHEMA.ports.field, (c, event) => {
    query.setValue((event.currentTarget as HTMLInputElement).value);
});
const READER = mReader.done();

const backend = withExoChildList(withExoCompiler(new ExoDomBackend()));
backend.render(READER, document.getElementById('root') as Element);
```

This matches the idiom in `packages/examples/escape-hatches/index.html`, which
does the same thing for a canvas widget: a container the widget owns, an `onMount`
that starts it, an `onUnmount` that stops it, and `c.childList(port).insert(node)`
as the door.

### Where the boundary sits

- **The box is the boundary, and it never moves.** Hand in an element and render
  *inside* it. Removal and placement both climb `parentNode`, so a wrapper put
  around the box travels with it, but **an element moved out of the parent is
  beyond the climb** — it is `exoForeignNode`'s one rule for the caller, stated
  in its own header (`packages/dom/src/foreign/exoForeignNode.ts:14-19`). Never
  let the imperative code move or replace the element you handed over.
- **The search input is ordinary Exodra.** It has a port, its handler is a normal
  machine handler, and it writes into a plain store. Only the repaint is imperative.
- **The query store is the seam.** The foreign node subscribes to it and the
  input's handler writes it; neither knows anything about the other.

### What you give up in that port

- **Server rendering, unless you hand the server its own half.** `c.foreign(t)` —
  a pack, composed on each backend — calls `t.createDom(c)` on the DOM backend and
  `t.createStr()` on the server
  (`packages/string/src/foreign/constants/EXO_STR_FOREIGN_VOCABULARY.ts:7-9`), so one `t`
  carrying both serves both, and `exoBackendCompatible(BACKENDS, 'foreign', t)`
  refuses at compile time a `t` that misses a backend the application lists; `exoForeignMarkup(markup)` builds the server half,
  and it does not escape — the caller owns that string.
- **Nothing is adopted for the foreign node itself.** While hydrating,
  `exoForeignNode` takes the server's row for that position off the adoption
  cursor and removes it, and builds a fresh element in its place;
  the rows around it are adopted as usual
  (`packages/conformance/src/tests/a-foreign-node-in-a-hydrated-list.test.ts`).
  `exoForeignNode` called directly, not through `c.foreign`, takes its row the same way.
- **Ports and bindings inside it.** A foreign node has no schema, so `c.attr`,
  `c.text` and `c.on` have nothing to address
  (`packages/dom/src/foreign/exoForeignNode.ts`). The two hooks are the
  whole interface.
- **Contexts.** A foreign node is not a wiring, so it neither provides nor
  injects. A machine that wants the foreign renderer to see a context value injects
  it in its initial state and hands it over as data.

## Open questions

This scheme is not finished, and these are the places where writing the page ran
into the API rather than around it. They are stated as questions because none of
them has been decided.

**1. How should a machine ask which backend it is on?** Today it cannot, and the
consequence is that a component with one imperative hot spot cannot be
server-rendered at all — it throws during SSR. Three shapes have been named and
none chosen:

- *A capability test* (`c.isDom`, or a kind tag on the connector). Cheapest to
  add; it also puts a branch into wiring functions and invites `if` ladders that
  each backend has to keep true.
- *A second, client-only initial state on the component.* Keeps every machine honest about
  its backend and makes the split visible at the component boundary; it is a new
  member on the component value and a second thing hydration has to reason about.
- *A backend-tagged escape that no-ops on the server* — `exoForeignNode` returning
  an empty string on `@exodra/string`. Least disruptive to write against; it also
  makes a page that silently renders a hole on the server look like a page that
  worked.

**2. Which channel ends an imperative subscription — the hook or `exoOnTeardown`?** Both
exist and they have different lifetimes. `exoOnTeardown` pushes onto `disposers`, and
the shared default `unmount` — `disposeExoChildSelf` — runs them and then
**clears the array**
(`packages/dom/src/dom/factories/createExoDomChildFactory.ts:22-36`), so an `exoOnTeardown` teardown is
one-shot: a child that leaves and re-enters has none. The `onMount`/`onUnmount` pair
fires on every entry and exit, which is why the example above subscribes in
`onMount`. Nothing in the API says which to reach for, and the wrong choice is
silent — a hot spot that stops updating after its first round trip through a
list.

**3. Is the child list the right and only door?** `reconcileExoOrder` is handed a *build
callback* and places whatever it returns
(`packages/list-reconcile/src/reconcileExoOrder.ts`), so a foreign node travels
through it only as an item of an order of nodes, with `(node) => node` as the callback.
Underneath is the imperative door the example above uses directly —
`c.childList(port)` and its `insert`
(`packages/dom/src/dom/factories/createExoChildList.ts`). An imperative hot spot
**inside a reconciled row of data** therefore means that row's own children are a second,
node-valued order. Whether the reconciler should accept a "this one is already built"
entry beside data items is open.


**4. Should a foreign node be able to declare what it depends on?** In the example
the box reaches `query` itself, from module scope. The machine cannot see that

dependency, so nothing in the component describes what makes this subtree change
— which is exactly the information the rest of the framework is built to make
explicit. A port that carried a source into a hook, without giving the foreign
node a schema, would close that; it does not exist and it is not obviously worth
its weight.

**5. Is there a "connected" hook?** No. `onMount` guarantees a parent, and the first
one is not in the document. Anything that measures has to test `isConnected` and
decide for itself what to do when it is false.


==============================================================================
# Core Concepts

Four ideas carry the whole runtime: a component is a **schema plus a wiring
function**, the schema declares **ports** that a backend fills through an
**exonode**, change is **explicit** — transitions write ports and effects
subscribe — rather than automatic tracking,
and children are reconciled by **identity** rather than by keys. The rest
follows from these four.

## Schema and wiring

A component is one value carrying two halves:

| Half | When it runs | What it is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| the **schema** | once, at module load | the constant shape — static markup, plus the ports where values may later be put |
| the **wiring function** | once per instance | the code that fills those ports |

That split is where the performance comes from. Deciding what the markup is,
which attribute lives where, how deep a node sits — all of it happens once per
component for the life of the process. A render is a clone of the prepared
element plus one indirect call per port. Nothing is diffed and nothing is walked
at render time.

```ts
import { createExoMachineBuilder, createExoSchema } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoAttrPort, TExoMachineNode, TExoTextPort } from '@exodra/core';

/** The row's own datum, by index. A view is handed its index and nothing else. */
const BUILDING: string[] = [];

const ROW_SCHEMA = createExoSchema((b) => {
    let id!: TExoAttrPort;
    let label!: TExoTextPort;
    b.el('li', { class: 'row' }, (li) => {
        id = li.port('data-id');
        li.el('span', null, (span) => {
            label = span.textPort();
        });
    });
    return { id, label };
});
const mRow = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoMachineNode, unknown, string>(ROW_SCHEMA);
mRow.createInitialState((_c, index) => BUILDING[index]);
mRow.wire((c) => {
    const name = c.state;
    c.attr(ROW_SCHEMA.ports.id, name);
    c.text(ROW_SCHEMA.ports.label, name.toUpperCase());
});
const ROW = mRow.done();
```

## Ports

A port is a **place**, declared once and named by **identity**. `port(name)` is
an attribute, `eventPort(name)` a listener, `textPort()` an element's whole text
content, and `childrenPort()` a variable-length sequence of children.

Everything else — the tags, the static attributes, the static text — is folded
into prepared markup and costs nothing per instance. An attribute whose value
varies is not an attribute; it is a port.

Ports are numbered after the whole shape is known, in **document order**. That
numbering is the contract between the backends: the server and the browser never
speak to each other, and they agree because both index their prepared plans by
the same numbers. Change the order and a page hydrates into nonsense rather than
crashing — which is why it is stated as a rule and not an implementation detail.

## Exonodes

An initial state is handed an **exonode** — the instance itself, with the
backend's methods on its prototype. The exonode is what differs between backends:
`TExoStrNode` writes into a value array, `TExoDomNode` into cloned nodes,
`TExoHydrateNode` into the server's own nodes. All three are **types**, not
classes — an exonode is a plain object whose prototype is the composed backend,
which is what lets a plugin add or wrap one of its methods. All three carry the
same `attr` / `text` / `unsafeHtml` / `on` / `one` / `list` / `build` /
`onTeardown` surface, so **one hand-written machine drives all three** —
the server render, the client render and hydration — with no cast.

An exonode is not a cursor: nothing walks, nothing descends, and no method
depends on the order the others were called in. It IS the instance the machine is
filling, so a subscription that closes over it closes over that one row and
nothing else.

## Identity & reconciliation

`reconcileExoOrder(kids, shown, keys, want, build)` from `@exodra/list-reconcile`,
called from a transition over `c.childList(port)`, makes a children port equal to
the array it is handed, reconciled by **object identity**, and returns the new
order shown for the machine to keep in its state:

- **Same item object** as before → the **same element is reused** (moved if its
  position changed, never rebuilt).
- **A new item object** → a child is built and inserted.
- **An item that disappeared** → its child is removed and its effects are
  stopped.

There is no `key` prop on this path and no heuristic: the reference *is* the key.
Whether a row survives an update depends entirely on whether you hand back the same
object — which is what preserves input focus, scroll position and per-row state.

A key is available as an **opt-in plugin**, never as a core default:
`EXO_KEYED_LIST_VOCABULARY` from `@exodra/list-reconcile` puts
`c.keyedList(port, keyOf, build, update)` on the exonode of a backend that
composed it — it returns a list whose `reconcile(items)` a transition calls — over
the free function `createExoKeyedList`, for the case where
identity genuinely is not available — rows arriving as freshly parsed JSON on every
refetch. See
[Keys, when identity is not available](../guides/lists.md#keys-when-identity-is-not-available).

This is the functional idiom of **structural sharing**: keep the reference for
what is unchanged, mint a new one for what changed. React hides identity and
hands you `key` / `memo` as escape hatches; Exodra makes identity first-class.

Underneath the reconciler, a child is a value you can hold: `c.build(component,
index)` returns one, and `c.childList(port)` is the placement door — `insert`,
`move`, `remove` — that holds whatever is put in it. Whoever drives that door
decides everything else — which item reuses which child, and what a key would mean
if you wanted one. See
[Lists & Reconciliation](../guides/lists.md).

## State, transitions and effects

A machine's state is what `createInitialState` returns, once per instance; it is
`c.state` from then on. A **transition** — `m.transition((c) => …)` — is the one
place that turns state into port writes, and the wire, the handlers and the
effects all call it. Data that lives **outside** the instance is followed by an
**effect** that draws first, then subscribes, and returns the unsubscribe:

```ts
import { createExoMachineBuilder, createExoSchema } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoMachineNode, TExoTextPort } from '@exodra/core';

const count = {
    value: 0,
    listeners: new Set<() => void>(),
    getValue(): number {
        return this.value;
    },
    increment(): void {
        this.value++;
        for (const listener of Array.from(this.listeners)) listener();
    },
    onChange(listener: () => void): () => void {
        this.listeners.add(listener);
        return () => {
            this.listeners.delete(listener);
        };
    },
};

const COUNTER_SCHEMA = createExoSchema((b) => {
    let text!: TExoTextPort;
    b.el('output', null, (output) => {
        text = output.textPort();
    });
    return { text };
});
const mCounter = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoMachineNode>(COUNTER_SCHEMA);
const showCount = mCounter.transition((c) => {
    c.text(COUNTER_SCHEMA.ports.text, count.getValue());
});
mCounter.effect((c) => {
    showCount(c);
    return count.onChange(() => showCount(c));
});
const COUNTER = mCounter.done();
```

The source is anything with a read and a subscription — a store, an
[OIMDB](https://oimdb.org/) collection, a socket. Exodra ships no
cell of its own, and a derived value is computed in the transition that writes it.

## Composition

A component nests another by filling a **children port** with it. There are three
calls, and the difference between them is how much may change later:

| Call | What it puts in the port |
| --- | --- |
| `c.one(port, COMPONENT)` | one instance, built now |
| `c.list(port, COMPONENT, count)` | a fixed list of `count` instances — rendered once, never reconciled |
| `reconcileExoOrder(c.state.rows, c.state.shown, want, want, build)` in a transition | a live list, reconciled by object identity |

A children port **is a child**: it renders exactly where `childrenPort()` was
called, so it may stand between static siblings.

```ts
import { createExoMachineBuilder, createExoSchema, createExoStatic } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoChildrenPort, TExoChildrenWiring, TExoMachineNode } from '@exodra/core';

// A component with nothing to fill — an icon, a separator, a masthead.
const MASTHEAD = createExoStatic((b) => {
    b.el('h1', { class: 'masthead' }, (h1) => h1.text('Exodra'));
});

const PAGE_SCHEMA = createExoSchema((b) => {
    let head!: TExoChildrenPort;
    b.el('div', { class: 'app' }, (div) => {
        div.el('header', null, (h) => { head = h.childrenPort(); });
        div.el('main', null, (m) => { m.text('…'); });
    });
    return { head };
});
const mPage = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoChildrenWiring & TExoMachineNode>(PAGE_SCHEMA);
mPage.createInitialState((c) => {
    c.one(PAGE_SCHEMA.ports.head, MASTHEAD);
});
const PAGE = mPage.done();
```

## Cleanup

An effect's stop — the function it returns — runs when the instance leaves.
Something started outside an effect is registered against the child being wired
with `c.onTeardown`:


```ts
import type { TExoDomNode } from '@exodra/dom';

export function startTicker(c: TExoDomNode, tick: () => void): void {
    const id = setInterval(tick, 1000);
    c.onTeardown(() => clearInterval(id));
}
```

`exoTeardownScope(fn)` opens a scope and hands back a disposer for everything
`exoOnTeardown` registered inside it — which is exactly what `ExoDomBackend.render` is
around its mount, and why the disposer it returns ends everything the render
started.
A subscription with nothing to end it is refused rather than left to outlive the
page that made it.

## Performance

Correctness never depends on an optimization: the fast path is the only path.
The shape is compiled once per process into a prototype element, a walk plan and
a setter per port, and a render is a clone plus one indirect call per port. There
is no hoisting switch to forget and no cache key to name — the schema *is* the
hoisted template.

Two things are worth knowing anyway:

- **A list pass costs what changed.** `reconcileExoOrder` trims the common head
  and tail first and runs the identity match only over the middle, so an append
  or a single edit is a short pass, not a walk of the whole array.

- **Event delegation is a choice.** `createExoDelegatedEvents(names)` puts one listener
  on the root for every row instead of one per element. It requires a **subject**
  in every fill — `c.on(port, handler, subject)` — because the subject is how one
  module-level function learns which row it fired on, rather than one closure
  per row carrying its own.

See **[Optimizations](../guides/optimizations.md)** for what you get for free and
what you reach for by hand.


==============================================================================
# JSX in Exodra

Exodra JSX is **not** React JSX, and it is not a template language either. It is
a way of writing a **schema declaration** — the markup of a component and its
named ports — and nothing else. What the ports show, when they change and what
happens on a click is the [machine](./components.md), written in TypeScript
around the declaration.

```tsx
import { exoJsx } from '@exodra/jsx';
import { createExoMachineBuilder } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoAttrPort, TExoEventPort, TExoMachineNode, TExoTextPort } from '@exodra/core';

interface TCounterPorts {
    step: TExoAttrPort;
    count: TExoTextPort;
    increment: TExoEventPort;
}

const COUNTER_SCHEMA = exoJsx<TCounterPorts>(($) => (
    <div class="counter" data-step={$.step}>
        <span class="counter__value">{$.count}</span>
        <button type="button" onClick={$.increment}>
            +
        </button>
    </div>
));
const P = COUNTER_SCHEMA.ports;

type TCounterState = { n: number };

const m = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoMachineNode, unknown, TCounterState>(COUNTER_SCHEMA);
m.createInitialState((c): TCounterState => {
    c.attr(P.step, 1);
    c.text(P.count, 0);
    return { n: 0 };
});
const show = m.transition((c) => {
    c.text(P.count, c.state.n);
});
m.on(P.increment, (c) => {
    c.state.n += 1;
    show(c);
});
export const COUNTER = m.done();
```

`@exodra/babel-plugin-schema` compiles the `exoJsx(…)` call away. What it
emits is the hand-written form of the same declaration, hoisted to module scope:

```js no-check
import { createExoNamedSchema } from '@exodra/core';

const _s0 = createExoNamedSchema((_b0) => {
    _b0.el('div', { class: 'counter' }, (_b1) => {
        _b1.port('data-step', 'step');
        _b1.el('span', { class: 'counter__value' }, (_b2) => {
            _b2.textPort('count');
        });
        _b1.el('button', { type: 'button' }, (_b2) => {
            _b2.eventPort('click', 'increment');
            _b2.text('+');
        });
    });
});

const COUNTER_SCHEMA = _s0;
```

Every port is created under the name written after `$.`, so
`COUNTER_SCHEMA.ports.count` is the text port and `COUNTER_SCHEMA.ports.increment`
the event port. The type argument `TCounterPorts` types those names: a port used
in the wrong place, or one the interface does not declare, is a type error.
Without a type argument every `$.name` is accepted and `.ports` is a record of
untyped ports.

The schema is built **once**, when the module loads, however many instances are
rendered from it. Hoisting is not a switch: every backend indexes its prepared
plans by the schema's ports, so a schema rebuilt per render would be a different
program, not a slower one. The output imports `@exodra/core` and nothing else.

The machine is an ordinary machine, so it goes straight into a backend:

```ts
import { ExoDomBackend, withExoCompiler } from '@exodra/dom';
import type { TExoDomMachine } from '@exodra/dom';

declare const COUNTER: TExoDomMachine;

const backend = withExoCompiler(new ExoDomBackend());

backend.render(COUNTER, document.body);
```

## The dialect

A declaration holds **markup and named ports, and nothing else**. Every JSX form
maps to exactly one schema call:

| written in JSX | what it is | schema call | filled by the machine with |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `class="row"`, `tabindex={0}`, `disabled` | markup | folded into `el(tag, attrs)` | — |
| plain text between tags | markup | `text('…')` | — |
| `data-id={$.id}` | attribute port `id` | `port('data-id', 'id')` | `c.attr(P.id, value)` |
| `<span>{$.label}</span>` | text port `label` | `textPort('label')` | `c.text(P.label, value)` |
| `onClick={$.toggle}` | event port `toggle`, event `click` | `eventPort('click', 'toggle')` | `m.on(P.toggle, handler)` |
| `on:dblclick={$.edit}` | event port `edit`, event `dblclick` | `eventPort('dblclick', 'edit')` | `m.on(P.edit, handler)` |
| `ref={$.box}` | ref port `box` | `refPort('box')` | read, never written |
| `<div unsafeHtml={$.body} />` | children port `body` | `childrenPort('body')` | `c.unsafeHtml(P.body, markup)` |
| `<$.rows />` | children port `rows` | `childrenPort('rows')` | `c.one`, `c.list`, or `c.childList` + `reconcileExoOrder` |

### Literal attributes are markup

```tsx
import { exoJsx } from '@exodra/jsx';

export const CHECKBOX_SCHEMA = exoJsx(() => (
    <input type="checkbox" tabindex={0} checked disabled={false} />
));
```

A string, a number, a boolean, or a bare attribute meaning `true`. It is folded
into the schema and never touched again. A declaration with no ports takes no
parameter.

### `attr={$.name}` is an attribute port

The attribute name is passed through verbatim. The machine writes it with
`c.attr(port, value)`; `null` and `undefined` leave the attribute out.

### `{$.name}` is a text port

A text port is the element's **whole content**, so `{$.name}` must be the only
child of its element. Text that varies beside static text or other elements
goes in an element of its own:

```tsx
import { exoJsx } from '@exodra/jsx';
import type { TExoTextPort } from '@exodra/core';

export const GREETING_SCHEMA = exoJsx<{ name: TExoTextPort }>(($) => (
    <p class="greeting">
        Hello, <b>{$.name}</b>!
    </p>
));
```

### Event ports: `onClick` and `on:`

`onClick={$.toggle}` declares an event port for `click`: the compiler drops `on`
and lowercases the rest, so `onDblClick` listens for `dblclick` and `onKeyDown`
for `keydown`. `on:` keeps the event name exactly as written — `on:dblclick`,
`on:focusin`, `on:my-thing` — for a name whose case or spelling must survive.
Both forms are typed per DOM event, so `on:clik` is a type error.

The handler is attached by the machine, `m.on(P.toggle, (c, event) => …)`: one
function for every instance, with the instance as `c`. This is also the form
[`createExoDelegatedEvents`](../api/dom.md#events-as-a-plugin) serves with one
root listener per event name.

### `ref={$.name}` is a ref port

A reference to the element and no way to write to it — see
[`refPort()`](../api/core.md).

### `unsafeHtml={$.name}`

Declares a children port standing for the element's whole content, which the
machine fills with unescaped markup through `c.unsafeHtml(P.name, markup)`.
Nothing on this path escapes and nothing sanitises — see
[Security](../security.md). An element with `unsafeHtml` takes no children.

### `<$.name />` is a children port

A schema has no notion of a component. Where other components' instances stand,
the declaration names a **children port**, and it may stand between static
siblings:

```tsx
import { exoJsx } from '@exodra/jsx';
import type { TExoChildrenPort } from '@exodra/core';

export const PANEL_SCHEMA = exoJsx<{ body: TExoChildrenPort }>(($) => (
    <section class="panel">
        <h3>Panel</h3>
        <$.body />
        <footer>end</footer>
    </section>
));
```

The tag takes no attributes and no children. The machine fills it with one of
three calls, and the choice is a choice of cost:

| call | what it is | pays for diffs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `c.one(P.body, MACHINE, params?)` | one instance, for the life of this one | no |
| `c.list(P.rows, MACHINE, count)` | a fixed number of instances, each built with its index | no |
| `c.childList(P.rows)` + `reconcileExoOrder` | a list that changes, reconciled by identity | yes |

## A list

The changing list is a children port whose child list the machine keeps in its
state and reconciles inside a transition with `reconcileExoOrder` from
`@exodra/list-reconcile`. Rows are matched by **identity of the item**: a row
that survives an update is the same element with the same instance.

```tsx
import { exoJsx } from '@exodra/jsx';
import { createExoMachineBuilder } from '@exodra/core';
import type {
    TExoAttrPort,
    TExoChildrenPort,
    TExoEventPort,
    TExoMachineNode,
    TExoTextPort,
} from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoChildList, TExoDomNode } from '@exodra/dom';
import { reconcileExoOrder } from '@exodra/list-reconcile';

type TTask = { id: string; title: string };

const TASK_SCHEMA = exoJsx<{ id: TExoAttrPort; title: TExoTextPort }>(($) => (
    <li class="task" data-id={$.id}>
        <span class="task__title">{$.title}</span>
    </li>
));
const mTask = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoMachineNode, TTask>(TASK_SCHEMA);
mTask.createInitialState(() => null);
mTask.wire((c, task) => {
    c.attr(TASK_SCHEMA.ports.id, task.id);
    c.text(TASK_SCHEMA.ports.title, task.title);
});
const TASK = mTask.done();

const TASK_LIST_SCHEMA = exoJsx<{
    rows: TExoChildrenPort;
    add: TExoEventPort;
    reverse: TExoEventPort;
}>(($) => (
    <section class="tasks">
        <h2>Tasks</h2>
        <ul class="tasks__list">
            <$.rows />
        </ul>
        <button type="button" onClick={$.add}>
            Add
        </button>
        <button type="button" onClick={$.reverse}>
            Reverse
        </button>
    </section>
));
const P = TASK_LIST_SCHEMA.ports;

type TTaskListState = { rows: TExoChildList; tasks: TTask[]; shown: TTask[] };

const mTaskList = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoDomNode, unknown, TTaskListState>(
    TASK_LIST_SCHEMA
);
mTaskList.createInitialState(
    (c): TTaskListState => ({
        rows: c.childList(P.rows),
        tasks: [
            { id: 't1', title: 'Write the schema' },
            { id: 't2', title: 'Write the machine' },
        ],
        shown: [],
    })
);

const showRows = mTaskList.transition((c) => {
    const state = c.state;
    state.shown = reconcileExoOrder(state.rows, state.shown, state.tasks, state.tasks, (task, at) =>
        c.build(TASK, at, task)
    );
});

mTaskList.effect((c) => {
    showRows(c);
    return null;
});

let nextTask = 3;
mTaskList.on(P.add, (c) => {
    c.state.tasks = [...c.state.tasks, { id: `t${nextTask}`, title: `Task ${nextTask}` }];
    nextTask += 1;
    showRows(c);
});
mTaskList.on(P.reverse, (c) => {
    c.state.tasks = [...c.state.tasks].reverse();
    showRows(c);
});

export const TASK_LIST = mTaskList.done();
```

`reconcileExoOrder(kids, shown, keys, items, build)` takes the child list, the
keys it showed last time, the keys and items to show now, and a `build` for an
item it has not seen; it returns the keys it now shows. Here the item is its own
key. Data from a store reaches the list the same way: an effect subscribes to the
store directly and calls the transition — see [Lists](./lists.md).

## What is refused

There is no runtime under this JSX to defer a decision to, so everything outside
the table above is a **compile error**, naming the element and the fix:

- Any expression other than `$.name`: a closure (`onClick={() => …}`), a value
  (`data-id={item.id}`), a conditional, a template literal, a call.
