- A component tag (`<Row />`, `<Ui.Row />`) — declare `<$.rows />` and build the
  instances from the machine. There is no `list=` or `props=` operand.
- Attributes or children on `<$.name />`.
- A fragment (`<></>`), anywhere.
- `{...spread}`.
- A lowercase inline handler, `onclick="…"` — write `onClick={$.name}`.
- A namespace other than `on:`.
- A text port beside other children: `<b>Hi {$.name}</b>` — write
  `<b>Hi <span>{$.name}</span></b>`.
- `unsafeHtml` on an element that also has children.
- The same port name twice. A port is one place in the markup; two places that
  show the same value are two ports the machine writes.
- JSX outside `exoJsx(…)`.
- A declaration that does anything but return one element: statements before
  the `return`, a second parameter, a destructured parameter, or a function
  declared elsewhere (`exoJsx(build)`).

## Setup

### Babel

```bash
npm install --save-dev @exodra/babel-plugin-schema
npm install @exodra/jsx
```

`@babel/core` is a peer dependency. The plugin needs JSX parsed with namespaced
attribute names (`on:click`) left alone:

```js
// babel.config.js
module.exports = {
  plugins: [
    ['@babel/plugin-syntax-jsx', { throwIfNamespace: false }],
    '@exodra/babel-plugin-schema',
  ],
};
```

Or through [`babel-preset-exodra`](../tooling/babel-preset.md), which wires the
same thing plus TypeScript in one line:

```js
// babel.config.js
module.exports = { presets: ['exodra'] };
```

The bundler plugins ([Vite](../tooling/vite-plugin.md),
[Rollup, esbuild and Bun](../tooling/bundlers.md)) call the same runner, so a
project using one of them configures nothing else. They forward `schemaSource`;
the preset forwards all three options.

Plugin options — all three are for a build that renames things, and most
projects set none of them:

| option | default | what it is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `schemaSource` | `'@exodra/core'` | where the schema factory is imported from |
| `schemaImport` | `'createExoNamedSchema'` | the exported name of the schema factory |
| `markerName` | `'exoJsx'` | the marker call the plugin compiles away |

### TypeScript

```json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "jsx": "react-jsx",
    "jsxImportSource": "@exodra/jsx/schema"
  }
}
```

`@exodra/jsx/schema` carries the types for this dialect: the intrinsic elements
and their attributes, the five port kinds `$` hands out, `onClick`-style and
`on:` event names typed per DOM event, `unsafeHtml` and `ref`.

## The marker at runtime

`exoJsx` is a real export of `@exodra/jsx`, so TSX authors have a symbol to
import and a type to hover. The compiler removes it; if JSX ever reaches the
runtime uncompiled it throws, naming the missing plugin — a build that forgot it
would otherwise render nothing and say nothing.

## Where to go next

- [Components](./components.md) — schemas and machines by hand. Everything on
  this page compiles to that.
- [Lists & Reconciliation](./lists.md) — what `reconcileExoOrder` reconciles by.
- [SWC plugin](../tooling/swc-plugin.md) — the same dialect in Rust, with the
  same three options.


==============================================================================
# Components in Exodra

A component is **one value carrying two halves**:

| Half | When it runs | What it is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| the **schema** | once, when the module loads | the constant shape — static markup, plus the **ports** where values may later be put |
| the **wiring function** | once per instance | the code that puts values in those ports, through a **connector** |

That split is the whole design. Everything expensive — deciding what the markup
is, which attribute lives where, how deep a node sits — happens once per
component for the life of the process. What a render repeats is: clone the
prepared element, then one indirect call per port.

There is no per-render tree, no props object to diff, and no walk at render
time. A port is named by **identity**, so a wiring function cannot count wrong
and does not look anything up.

## The smallest component

```ts
import { createExoMachineBuilder, createExoSchema } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoMachineNode, TExoTextPort } from '@exodra/core';
import { ExoDomBackend, withExoCompiler } from '@exodra/dom';

/** ONE backend for the application, at module level — it is the schema cache key.
 *  `render` arrives with the compiler: a bare backend has no way to turn a
 *  declaration into a schema, and says so at the type level. */
const backend = withExoCompiler(new ExoDomBackend());

// ── the schema: runs once, at module load ────────────────────────────
const GREETING_SCHEMA = createExoSchema((b) => {
    let name!: TExoTextPort;
    b.el('p', { class: 'greeting' }, (p) => {
        p.text('Hello, ');
        p.el('strong', null, (strong) => {
            name = strong.textPort();
        });
    });
    // Whatever this returns IS the component's API.
    return { name };
});

// ── the machine: its wire writes the ports of each instance ─────────
const mGreeting = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoMachineNode>(GREETING_SCHEMA);
mGreeting.wire((c) => {
    c.text(GREETING_SCHEMA.ports.name, 'world');
});
const GREETING = mGreeting.done();

backend.render(GREETING, document.body);
```

`backend.render` mounts **one** instance and hands it `0` as its **index**.
There is no instance count, because a lone root has nothing else to be about and
no library asks an application how many copies of its root to make. Rows that
vary are a **list** — a children port filled by `c.list` (fixed) or by a
transition calling `reconcileExoOrder` over `c.childList` (live). That is also what a rival framework's
participant is doing when a benchmark says "render 1000 rows": the count belongs
to the list, never to the mount.

**There are no props, anywhere.** The initial state's second argument is the
instance's **index**, and that is the whole of what a view is told about itself. A row
reads its own datum by that index, from wherever the caller put it — the build
callback that constructs the row is the place that knows both, so it writes the
datum down and then builds. Props would have to be *serviced*: stored per
instance, compared on every update, and turned into a decision about which
transitions to re-run. An index costs a number.

Read `createExoMachineBuilder<TWiring>` by its type argument. **`TWiring`** is what
every transition may assume about the exonode it is handed: `TExoMachineNode` from
`@exodra/core` is the surface all backends share — `attr`, `text`, `on`,
`provide`, `inject` — so a component naming it is served, client-rendered and
hydrated as one value. A machine that also nests components takes
`TExoChildrenWiring & TExoMachineNode`, which adds `one`, `list` and `build`. Naming
one backend's exonode instead — `createExoMachineBuilder<TExoDomNode>` — types the
component against the browser alone, because a machine's exonode parameter is
contravariant. What the initial state **returns** is what the instance keeps: the
value lands in `enode.state` and is read back with `readState()`. A machine that
only fills ports returns nothing.

Two details are worth reading twice:

- **The schema is a value before the machine is.** `createExoSchema` runs the
  builder once, at module load, and `createExoMachineBuilder` is handed the result,
  so the ports are named once as `GREETING_SCHEMA.ports` rather than passed to
  every instance. It also makes the order structural: a transition cannot be
  written before the ports it fills exist.
- **`p.text('Hello, ')` is folded into the prepared markup.** It costs nothing
  per instance. `strong.textPort()` is a *place*, and costs one call. A text
  port stands for an element's **whole** content, so it gets an element of its
  own rather than sitting beside static text.

## Static is not a bucket, it is an argument

Anything passed to `el()` is known now and is baked into the markup:

```ts
import { createExoStatic } from '@exodra/core';

export const EMPTY_STATE = createExoStatic((b) => {
    b.el('div', { class: 'empty', role: 'status' }, (div) => {
        div.el('span', { class: 'empty__icon', 'aria-hidden': 'true' }, (icon) => {
            icon.text('∅');
        });
        div.text('Nothing here yet');
    });
});
```

`createExoStatic` is for a component with **nothing to fill** — an icon, a separator,
a conditional block's body, an empty state. It refuses a builder that declares
ports, because a component with ports and no wiring is an attribute stuck empty:
a silent wrong page rather than an error.

An attribute whose value **varies** is not an attribute here. It is a port.

## The builder

| Call | Declares |
| --- | --- |
| `el(tag, attrs?, fn?)` | a child element with its static attributes, and optionally a body |
| `text(value)` | static text |
| `port(name)` | a port for one **attribute** |
| `eventPort(name)` | a port for one **listener** |
| `textPort()` | a port for the **whole text content** of the current element |
| `childrenPort()` | a port for a **variable-length sequence of children** |

A children port **is a child**: it is appended where the call appears, so a
conditional block between a heading and a footer is the ordinary case, not an
awkward one.

## The wiring function

```ts no-check
(connector, index) => state
```

- `index` is the **only** thing this instance is told. A row of `c.list` gets its
  position in the run, `c.build(component, index)` passes whatever the caller
  hands it, and an instance placed by `one()` or mounted by `backend.render`
  gets `0`.
- It is the position **at build time and nothing more**. When rows move,
  the reconciler moves nodes — it does not re-run wiring — so a component that
  needs a live position must be handed it by a transition, not capture this.

What the connector offers:

| Call | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `c.attr(port, value)` | write an attribute, once |
| `c.text(port, value)` | write an element's whole text, once |
| `c.unsafeHtml(port, markup)` | write raw markup into a children port |
| `c.on(port, handler, subject?)` | a listener |
| `c.one(port, component)` | one nested instance |
| `c.list(port, component, count)` | a fixed run of `count` instances |
| `c.build(component, index?)` | a child as a value, placed nowhere |
| `c.childList(port)` | the port's live children, for a reconciler to drive |
| `c.onTeardown(off)` | hand the instance a disposer to run when it goes |
| `c.provide(token, value)` / `c.inject(token)` | contexts |

**Nothing in that table watches a source, and that is the design.** A machine
writes "state → ports" in **transitions** — `m.transition((c) => …)`, one place the
wire, the handlers and the effects all call. Following data that lives outside
the instance is an **effect** that runs the transition once, then subscribes, and
returns the unsubscribe. Keeping a child list in step is a transition that calls
`reconcileExoOrder` from `@exodra/list-reconcile` over `c.childList(port)`. A door
would have made every page link subscription machinery it may never use, and
would have let the backend decide what counts as a source. As plain calls inside
transitions and effects, the application composes them — or does not, and pays
nothing.

The **same wiring function** runs on the server, on a client render and through
hydration. Write it against the methods it actually uses and all three backends
accept it with no cast.

## State and transitions

State that belongs to one instance is **machine state**: `createInitialState`
returns it once per instance, a handler changes it, and a transition writes it to
the ports.

```ts
import { createExoMachineBuilder, createExoSchema } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoAttrPort, TExoTextPort, TExoEventPort } from '@exodra/core';
import { ExoDomBackend, withExoCompiler } from '@exodra/dom';
import type { TExoDomNode } from '@exodra/dom';

const backend = withExoCompiler(new ExoDomBackend());

const TOGGLE_SCHEMA = createExoSchema((b) => {
    let rootClass!: TExoAttrPort;
    let click!: TExoEventPort;
    let text!: TExoTextPort;
    b.el('div', null, (div) => {
        rootClass = div.port('class');
        div.el('button', { type: 'button' }, (btn) => {
            click = btn.eventPort('click');
            text = btn.textPort();
        });
    });
    return { rootClass, click, text };
});
const P = TOGGLE_SCHEMA.ports;

const mToggle = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoDomNode, unknown, { on: boolean }>(TOGGLE_SCHEMA);
mToggle.createInitialState(() => ({ on: false }));
const show = mToggle.transition((c) => {
    c.attr(P.rootClass, c.state.on ? 'toggle toggle--active' : 'toggle');
    c.text(P.text, c.state.on ? 'ON' : 'OFF');
});
mToggle.wire((c) => {
    show(c);
});
mToggle.on(P.click, (c) => {
    c.state.on = !c.state.on;
    show(c);
});
const TOGGLE = mToggle.done();

backend.render(TOGGLE, document.body);
```

A derived value is computed **in the transition** — the label and the class above
are both read off one boolean at the moment they are written.

:::caution The one rule that has no exception
A connector is **reused**: one of them serves every row of a list. A callback
that read the connector's fields would follow it onto the next row and update
the wrong element — a bug with no assertion failure and no wrong-looking line,
just a table where every row shows the last row's data. A transition is handed
the exonode it runs on, and an effect's subscriber closes over the `c` that effect
was started for, which is that instance's own. If you write a subscription by
hand anywhere else, capture the node, never the connector.
:::

## Composition

Components nest through a **children port**. `one` puts a single instance in it.
It takes the port and the component, and nothing else — the child is not handed
data, it goes and reads it.

```ts
import { createExoMachineBuilder, createExoSchema } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoChildrenPort, TExoTextPort } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoDomNode } from '@exodra/dom';

function createStore<TValue>(value: TValue) {
    const listeners = new Set<() => void>();
    return {
        getValue: () => value,
        setValue(next: TValue) {
            value = next;
            for (const listener of Array.from(listeners)) listener();
        },
        onChange(listener: () => void): () => void {
            listeners.add(listener);
            return () => {
                listeners.delete(listener);
            };
        },
    };
}

type TUser = { readonly name: string; readonly role: string };

const user = createStore<TUser>({ name: 'Ada', role: 'author' });

const AVATAR_SCHEMA = createExoSchema((b) => {
    let initials!: TExoTextPort;
    b.el('span', { class: 'avatar' }, (span) => {
        initials = span.textPort();
    });
    return { initials };
});
const mAvatar = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoDomNode>(AVATAR_SCHEMA);
const showInitial = mAvatar.transition((c) => {
    c.text(AVATAR_SCHEMA.ports.initials, user.getValue().name.slice(0, 1).toUpperCase());
});
mAvatar.effect((c) => {
    showInitial(c);
    return user.onChange(() => showInitial(c));
});
const AVATAR = mAvatar.done();

const USER_CARD_SCHEMA = createExoSchema((b) => {
    let slot!: TExoChildrenPort;
    let name!: TExoTextPort;
    let role!: TExoTextPort;
    b.el('div', { class: 'user' }, (div) => {
        // The children port sits between two static siblings — and renders there.
        div.el('div', { class: 'user__avatar' }, (holder) => {
            slot = holder.childrenPort();
        });
        div.el('strong', null, (strong) => {
            name = strong.textPort();
        });
        div.el('em', null, (em) => {
            role = em.textPort();
        });
    });
    return { slot, name, role };
});
const P = USER_CARD_SCHEMA.ports;
const mUserCard = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoDomNode>(USER_CARD_SCHEMA);
mUserCard.createInitialState((c) => {
    c.one(P.slot, AVATAR);
});
const showUser = mUserCard.transition((c) => {
    const { name, role } = user.getValue();
    c.text(P.name, name);
    c.text(P.role, role);
});
mUserCard.effect((c) => {
    showUser(c);
    return user.onChange(() => showUser(c));
});
const USER_CARD = mUserCard.done();
```

The effect draws **first** and subscribes second, synchronously: hydration adopts
the server's markup only while the instance is being armed, which is when effects
start. What it returns is its stop, run when the instance leaves.

`AVATAR` names the source it reads. That is the trade the no-props design makes
and it is worth stating plainly: a component is **not** a function of arguments
you can call with anything — it is wired to where its data lives. Reuse comes
from the data layer, not from the parameter list: the same component over a
different user is a different source, and the same component over a thousand
rows reads a **slot by its index**, which is what the build callback of a
reconciled list writes before it builds. See
[Rendering](./rendering.md#where-children-come-from).

`backend.render` is for the top of a page, where the index is `0` — so the root
component is the one that goes and *gets* the data, which is what every
component here does.

Note what is **not** here: no props object, no bucket, no `children` key, and
no diffing of any of them.

### "Slots"

A slot is a children port. A component with two of them takes two nested
instances; which component goes in each is decided by the wiring function that
fills them, so a layout is written once and reused by naming different
components at the call site.

## Lists

`reconcileExoOrder` from `@exodra/list-reconcile` reconciles a children port
against an array, **by object identity**, from inside a transition: it is handed
the port's child list, the order shown, and the order wanted, and returns the new
order shown, which the machine keeps in its state. A row that survives is the same
element it was; a row that leaves is disposed. No keys are involved on this path —
and where identity is not available, `c.keyedList` (the `EXO_KEYED_LIST_VOCABULARY`
pack) supplies one. See
[Keys, when identity is not available](./lists.md#keys-when-identity-is-not-available).

```ts
import { createExoMachineBuilder, createExoSchema } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoAttrPort, TExoTextPort, TExoChildrenPort } from '@exodra/core';
import { ExoDomBackend, withExoChildList, withExoCompiler } from '@exodra/dom';
import type { TExoChildList, TExoDomNode } from '@exodra/dom';
import { reconcileExoOrder } from '@exodra/list-reconcile';

const backend = withExoChildList(withExoCompiler(new ExoDomBackend()));

function createStore<TValue>(value: TValue) {
    const listeners = new Set<() => void>();
    return {
        getValue: () => value,
        setValue(next: TValue) {
            value = next;
            for (const listener of Array.from(listeners)) listener();
        },
        onChange(listener: () => void): () => void {
            listeners.add(listener);
            return () => {
                listeners.delete(listener);
            };
        },
    };
}

type TItem = { readonly id: string; readonly label: string };

/** Where a row's item waits for it. The build callback writes it, then builds. */
const BUILDING: TItem[] = [];

const ROW_SCHEMA = createExoSchema((b) => {
    let id!: TExoAttrPort;
    let label!: TExoTextPort;
    b.el('li', null, (li) => {
        id = li.port('data-id');
        label = li.textPort();
    });
    return { id, label };
});
const mRow = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoDomNode, unknown, TItem>(ROW_SCHEMA);
mRow.createInitialState((_c, index) => BUILDING[index]);
mRow.wire((c) => {
    const item = c.state;
    c.attr(ROW_SCHEMA.ports.id, item.id);
    c.text(ROW_SCHEMA.ports.label, item.label);
});
const ROW = mRow.done();

const items = createStore<readonly TItem[]>([
    { id: 'a', label: 'First' },
    { id: 'b', label: 'Second' },
]);

const LIST_SCHEMA = createExoSchema((b) => {
    let rows!: TExoChildrenPort;
    b.el('ul', { class: 'list' }, (ul) => {
        rows = ul.childrenPort();
    });
    return { rows };
});
type TListState = { rows: TExoChildList; shown: TItem[] };
const mList = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoDomNode, unknown, TListState>(LIST_SCHEMA);
mList.createInitialState((c) => ({ rows: c.childList(LIST_SCHEMA.ports.rows), shown: [] }));
const showRows = mList.transition((c) => {
    const want = items.getValue();
    c.state.shown = reconcileExoOrder(c.state.rows, c.state.shown, want, want, (item, i) => {
        BUILDING[i] = item;
        return c.build(ROW, i);
    });
});
mList.effect((c) => {
    showRows(c);
    return items.onChange(() => showRows(c));
});
const LIST = mList.done();

backend.render(LIST, document.body);

items.setValue([...items.getValue(), { id: 'c', label: 'Third' }]);
```

The child list is opened in `createInitialState`, which runs once per instance; a
wire can run again, and opening a children port there is refused.

When the contents cannot change, use `c.list(port, component, count)` instead: a
fixed list pays for no row records, no diff and no teardown.

For a filtered view, compute the subset in the transition and hand that as
`want`: rows are matched by the item objects, so a row the filter keeps is the
same element it was. See the [Lists guide](./lists.md).

## Side effects and cleanup

An effect owns what it starts: the function it returns is its stop, run when the
instance leaves, and `backend.render` hands back a disposer that ends everything
at once. Anything started outside an effect is registered with `c.onTeardown`,
against the child the exonode is currently wiring:

```ts
import { createExoMachineBuilder, createExoSchema } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoTextPort } from '@exodra/core';
import { ExoDomBackend, withExoCompiler } from '@exodra/dom';
import type { TExoDomNode } from '@exodra/dom';

const backend = withExoCompiler(new ExoDomBackend());

const TIMER_SCHEMA = createExoSchema((b) => {
    let text!: TExoTextPort;
    b.el('div', { class: 'timer' }, (div) => {
        text = div.textPort();
    });
    return { text };
});
const mTimer = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoDomNode, unknown, { seconds: number }>(TIMER_SCHEMA);
mTimer.createInitialState(() => ({ seconds: 0 }));
const show = mTimer.transition((c) => {
    c.text(TIMER_SCHEMA.ports.text, `Time: ${c.state.seconds}s`);
});
mTimer.wire((c) => {
    show(c);
});
mTimer.effect((c) => {
    const id = setInterval(() => {
        c.state.seconds++;
        show(c);
    }, 1000);
    return () => clearInterval(id);
});
const TIMER = mTimer.done();

const dispose = backend.render(TIMER, document.body);

// Stops the interval along with every other effect this render started.
dispose();
```

A subscription with nothing to end it is **refused**, rather than quietly
outliving the page that made it.

**`onTeardown` is on every backend, including the server's** — what differs is
*when* it runs. In the browser it runs when the instance leaves. On the server
it runs at the end of the render, in registration order, after the markup has
already been taken: a disposer that writes to a port cannot change the bytes
that were printed
(`packages/string/src/node/tests/render-exo-instance.test.ts:105-129`). That is
what makes a disposer safe to register on three backends — whatever it stops is
started and ended in both places, and only the browser keeps it running between
the two.

## Contexts

A context token is an identity, not a string, so two packages cannot collide on
a name. `provide` and `inject` are methods on the connector — there is nothing
to import to use them, because a context exists only while a wiring is running.

```ts
import { createExoMachineBuilder, createExoSchema } from '@exodra/core';
import type {
    TExoAttrPort,
    TExoChildrenPort,
    TExoChildrenWiring,
    TExoMachineNode,
} from '@exodra/core';
import { exoContextToken } from '@exodra/context';
import { ExoDomBackend, withExoCompiler } from '@exodra/dom';

const backend = withExoCompiler(new ExoDomBackend());

const THEME = exoContextToken<string>('theme');

const LABEL_SCHEMA = createExoSchema((b) => {
    let cls!: TExoAttrPort;
    b.el('span', null, (span) => {
        cls = span.port('class');
    });
    return { cls };
});
const mLabel = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoMachineNode>(LABEL_SCHEMA);
mLabel.wire((c) => {
    // `undefined` when nobody provided it — not a throw.
    c.attr(LABEL_SCHEMA.ports.cls, 'label label--' + (c.inject(THEME) ?? 'light'));
});
const LABEL = mLabel.done();

const SHELL_SCHEMA = createExoSchema((b) => {
    let slot!: TExoChildrenPort;
    b.el('div', { class: 'shell' }, (div) => {
        slot = div.childrenPort();
    });
    return { slot };
});
const mShell = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoChildrenWiring & TExoMachineNode>(SHELL_SCHEMA);
mShell.createInitialState((c) => {
    c.provide(THEME, 'dark');
    c.one(SHELL_SCHEMA.ports.slot, LABEL);
});
const SHELL = mShell.done();

backend.render(SHELL, document.body);
```

The chain `provide` returns travels downwards as an ordinary **value**: it goes on
the exonode, and every `one`, `list` and `build` wired after it
inherits it. A reconciled list captures the chain when it is wired and holds it for its whole
life, so a row added an hour later — from inside a subscriber, with no render on
the stack — resolves what the page provided without touching the DOM at all.

**A context does not travel through the document.** A second, independent
`render()` into an element that some other render provided into starts from
nothing: it reads `undefined`, not the surrounding page's value. There used to be
a second channel — `provide` marked the instance's root element and each entry
point climbed `parentNode` from the parent it was handed — and it was removed. A
host that wants a separately-mounted widget to see a value **hands it over**: by
putting it where the widget's root component reads it, or by rendering the widget
inside the same render that provided.

The reasoning: it was a whole per-provider storage scheme on
the element, paid by every page, for a case where the host already owns the mount
call and can pass the value at it. What the DOM bought over passing it was the
absence of an **interface**; what it cost was a channel that depended on mount
order and document position.

`inject` walks a **frame chain, never the DOM**: 1.67 ns at one link, 7.67 ns at
eight (`context-cost` axis, `b4` label).

Providing a token something above already provided **shadows** it for that
subtree and nothing else.

:::caution Contexts are not reactive by themselves
What you provide is what a consumer holds forever. Put a *source* in the context
and follow it with an effect: read `c.inject(THEME)`, run the transition, and
return `theme.onChange(() => show(c))`. A context that tried to be
reactive itself would be a second, weaker subscription mechanism on top of the
one that already works.
:::

## Writing the schema in JSX

[Exodra JSX](./jsx.md) is another way to write the schema half:
`exoJsx<TPorts>(($) => <markup/>)` declares markup and named ports —
`data-id={$.id}`, `{$.title}`, `onClick={$.toggle}`, `<$.rows />` — and
`@exodra/babel-plugin-schema` compiles it into the module-level schema this page
builds by hand. The machine is the same machine, written as on this page and
filling the ports through `SCHEMA.ports`. Nothing on this page depends on JSX — a
hand-written schema needs no build step at all.

## Performance notes

- **Declare in `el()`, not in a port.** A port costs a slot and a call per
  instance; a static attribute costs nothing.
- **A bare `c.attr` in the wire when it cannot change, an effect when it can.**
  The bare write is two array loads and a call, with nothing retained.
- **`c.list` for a fixed list, `reconcileExoOrder` in a transition for a live one.** A list whose
  contents cannot change should not pay for the possibility that they might.
- **Use a shared handler for a repeated handler.** A module-level function taking
  `(event, subject)` is one function object for the whole template; a closure is
  one per row — and the subject is what the
  [delegated event pack](../api/dom.md#events-as-a-plugin) needs a fill to carry.
- **Let effects own their subscriptions.** An effect returns its stop; registering
  teardown by hand is only for what you start outside one.


==============================================================================
# Lists & Reconciliation

Exodra has no virtual DOM. When a list changes, the renderer reconciles the
**actual** DOM against the new contents **by object identity**. Understanding
that one rule is the key to fast, focus-safe lists.

## A list is a children port reconciled in a transition

The samples on this page read their items from a store object of a dozen lines —
anything that can answer "what is there now" and "tell me when it changes". In an
application it is the data layer.

```ts setup
function createStore<TValue>(value: TValue) {
    const listeners = new Set<() => void>();
    return {
        getValue: (): TValue => value,
        setValue(next: TValue): void {
            value = next;
            listeners.forEach((listener) => listener());
        },
        onChange(listener: () => void): () => void {
            listeners.add(listener);
            return () => listeners.delete(listener);
        },
    };
}
```

```ts
import { createExoMachineBuilder, createExoSchema } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoTextPort, TExoChildrenPort } from '@exodra/core';
import { ExoDomBackend, withExoChildList, withExoCompiler } from '@exodra/dom';
import type { TExoChildList, TExoDomNode } from '@exodra/dom';
import { reconcileExoOrder } from '@exodra/list-reconcile';

const backend = withExoChildList(withExoCompiler(new ExoDomBackend()));

type TItem = { readonly id: string; readonly label: string };

const ROW_SCHEMA = createExoSchema((b) => {
    let label!: TExoTextPort;
    b.el('li', null, (li) => {
        label = li.textPort();
    });
    return { label };
});
const mRow = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoDomNode>(ROW_SCHEMA);
const showItem = mRow.transition((row: TExoDomNode, item: TItem) => {
    row.text(ROW_SCHEMA.ports.label, item.label);
});
const ROW = mRow.done();

const items = createStore<readonly TItem[]>([{ id: 'a', label: 'First' }]);

const LIST_SCHEMA = createExoSchema((b) => {
    let rows!: TExoChildrenPort;
    b.el('ul', null, (ul) => {
        rows = ul.childrenPort();
    });
    return { rows };
});

type TListState = { rows: TExoChildList; shown: TItem[] };

const mList = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoDomNode, unknown, TListState>(LIST_SCHEMA);
mList.createInitialState((c) => ({ rows: c.childList(LIST_SCHEMA.ports.rows), shown: [] }));
const showItems = mList.transition((c) => {
    const want = items.getValue();
    c.state.shown = reconcileExoOrder(c.state.rows, c.state.shown, want, want, (item, i) => {
        const row = c.build(ROW, i);
        showItem(row, item);
        return row;
    });
});
mList.effect((c) => {
    showItems(c);
    return items.onChange(() => showItems(c));
});
const LIST = mList.done();

backend.render(LIST, document.body);
items.setValue([...items.getValue(), { id: 'b', label: 'Second' }]);
```

On the DOM backend `c.childList` is a pack:
[`withExoChildList`](../api/dom.md#withexochildlist), composed once where the backend is
built. A backend without it throws [EXO0109](../errors.md#exo0109) at the first
`c.childList`, and a page whose children are only `c.one` and fixed `c.list` never links it.

Three pieces, each in one place:

- **`createInitialState`** opens the child list once and keeps it, with the order
  currently shown, in the machine's state. It is the only place a child list may be
  opened.
- **The transition** is "state → rows": it reads what should be shown and hands
  `reconcileExoOrder(kids, shown, keys, want, build)` the order shown and the order
  wanted. For an identity list `keys` and `want` are the same array. It returns the
  new shown order.
- **The effect** draws first, synchronously, then subscribes and returns the
  unsubscribe. On a hydrated page the first draw is what adopts the server's rows,
  and it must happen while the instance is being armed — which is where effects
  start.

In [JSX](./jsx.md) the list is a children port, `<$.rows />`, and the machine
fills it with exactly this composition.

Three levels are available, and the cheapest one that fits is the one to use:

| Call | When |
| --- | --- |
| `c.list(port, component, count)` | the contents **cannot** change — rendered once, no row records, no diff, no teardown |
| `reconcileExoOrder(c.state.rows, c.state.shown, items, items, build)` in a transition | the ordinary reactive list, reconciled by item identity |
| `c.keyedList(port, keyOf, build, update)` → `{ reconcile(items) }` | rows with no stable identity, reconciled by key |

The second one **is** the open one. The two halves it is written over —
`c.childList(port)`, which hands back the port's live children, and
`c.build(component, index)`, which makes a child and places it nowhere — are both
doors on the exonode. A caller who wants a different reuse policy writes a
different function over the same two doors, with no reconciler to subclass and
nothing to opt out of; the keyed policy is exactly that, already written:
[`createExoKeyedList`](#keys-when-identity-is-not-available) runs the same pass
over an extracted key instead of the item object.

:::caution A reconciled list adopts on a hydrated page — at a price worth reading
The mechanism is a CURSOR over the rows the server printed: opening a child list on a
hydrating page collects them, `c.build` takes the next one per item, and whatever is
left when the instance has been armed is surplus the data did not want (`packages/dom/src/dom/EXO_ADOPT_CURSOR.ts:16-21`). What that costs, read at
the bodies:

- **No placeholder element, and no build record.** `c.build` on a hydrating page asks
  the cursor for the next served row and wires the instance onto THAT element
  (`packages/dom/src/hydrate/EXO_HYDRATE_NODE_VOCABULARY.ts:165-171`), so nothing is
  created to be repointed later and nothing has to be remembered between the build and
  the adoption. `buildAdoptedExoChild`
  (`packages/dom/src/hydrate/buildAdoptedExoChild.ts:27-29`) runs the initial state once, on the
  server's element.
- **A row is taken once because the cursor advances.** `takeExoAdoptedRow` returns the
  element at `at` and moves on (`EXO_ADOPT_CURSOR.ts:28-36`), so the same row cannot be
  claimed twice — it is the shape of the reader, not a check.
- **The rows are collected eagerly, in ONE walk, and the reason is a measurement.**
  `ExoChildList.insert` places an adopted row with `appendChild`, which MOVES it behind
  its own siblings, so reading `nextElementSibling` after the first insert answers with a
  row already taken — three served rows came out as the whole list swept away
  (`EXO_ADOPT_CURSOR.ts:6-9`). The same `openChildList` walk also finds the list's end,
  which a child list standing behind this one resolves its own start from
  (`EXO_HYDRATE_NODE_VOCABULARY.ts:218-231`).
- **When the data wants more rows than the server printed, the client builds the rest.**
  `takeExoAdoptedRow` answers `null` past the last served row and `build` takes the
  ordinary path — that is how a list whose data grew past its markup gets its extra rows
  (`EXO_HYDRATE_NODE_VOCABULARY.ts:162-166`).
- **Surplus is removed with no shape check at all**, because the span was bounded by the
  list's own end when it was collected, so everything in it is a row of this list
  (`EXO_ADOPT_CURSOR.ts:38-45`). An instance that opens a SECOND child list drops the
  first one's surplus before the cursor is overwritten, or rows the data refused would
  stay on the page for good.
- **`EXO_ADOPT_CURSOR` (`EXO_ADOPT_CURSOR.ts:21`) is a module cell, not a field on the
  record**, because that record is the render record too and a field there is a field on
  every instance a page builds; adoption is depth-first and synchronous, so the cell is
  saved and restored around each instance's wiring.

A build callback that names a *component* (`(item, i) => c.build(ROW, i)`) takes the
same cursor by the same `build`, and nothing above is special to it. **How much a list of
caller-built nodes costs on a hydrated page has never been measured** — a build callback
that hands back a node it did not get from `c.build`. It is a real option on a hydrated
page rather than a refusal.
:::

## The golden rule: identity = the same node

The identity that matters is the **item object**. On every update the renderer
diffs the new items against the previous ones:

- **the same item object** as before → the **same DOM node is reused**, moved if
  its position changed, never rebuilt;
- a **new item object** → a child is built and wired;
- an item that **disappeared** → its child is removed and its subscriptions end.

There is no `key` prop on the core path: whether a row keeps its DOM node depends
entirely on whether you hand back the same object — which is what preserves input
focus, scroll position and per-row DOM state across an update.

There **is** something to opt into, and it is a plugin rather than a core default.
See [Keys, when identity is not available](#keys-when-identity-is-not-available)
below.

The rule says nothing about **the same object at two positions**, because that is
one identity for two entries. The reconciler answers it by position — one row per
occurrence, on every backend — and identity only decides which of them survives an
update. Why, and how to avoid the ambiguity:
[The same object twice in one list](../troubleshooting.md#the-same-object-twice-in-one-list).

## Identity comes from your data layer

The trap is upstream of the renderer. If a recompute rebuilds every item object,
every row is a new identity → every node is rebuilt → **the input you were
typing in loses focus**, even though only one field changed.

The fix is not a renderer feature, it is keeping the item objects stable:

- A store that hands back the **same entity object** until that entity actually
  changes gives you focus-safe lists for free. Reactive stores like
  [`@oimdb/*`](https://oimdb.org/llms.txt) are built this way — a
  row's identity is the entity's permanent slot, not a projection made per read.
- A field edit should reach the row through the row's **own** effect, not
  through a new list. Subscribe to the field inside `ROW` and a change to it writes
  one attribute; it never reaches the reconciler at all.
- If a projection is unavoidable (a filter, a sort), either cache the projected
  objects by their stable id so that re-running the projection yields the same
  objects for the rows that survived — or stop hand-rolling that cache and use the
  keyed plugin below, which is the same idea written once inside the renderer.

## Keys, when identity is not available

**Why it exists.** The identity rule is an argument about a *data layer*. A caller
whose rows arrive as freshly parsed JSON on every poll has no stable object to
reconcile by — every item is new on every refetch, so an identity list rebuilds
every row and throws away its DOM, its listeners, its scroll position and anything
focused inside it. That caller is not being told to go and write a cache first.

**It is a pack, from `@exodra/list-reconcile`, and it works on any backend that has
a child list.** `EXO_KEYED_LIST_VOCABULARY` puts `c.keyedList` on the exonode; a
backend that did not compose it has no such method. `keyedList` opens a child list, so on the
DOM backend it stands on `withExoChildList` too:

```ts
import { composeExoPlugins, createExoMachineBuilder, createExoSchema } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoChildrenPort, TExoTextPort } from '@exodra/core';
import { ExoDomBackend, withExoChildList, withExoCompiler } from '@exodra/dom';
import type { TExoDomNode } from '@exodra/dom';
import { EXO_KEYED_LIST_VOCABULARY } from '@exodra/list-reconcile';
import type { TExoKeyedList, TExoKeyedListApi } from '@exodra/list-reconcile';

const backend = composeExoPlugins(
    withExoChildList(withExoCompiler(new ExoDomBackend())),
    EXO_KEYED_LIST_VOCABULARY
);

type TUser = { readonly id: number; readonly name: string };

const ROW_SCHEMA = createExoSchema((b) => {
    let name!: TExoTextPort;
    b.el('li', null, (li) => {
        name = li.textPort();
    });
    return { name };
});
const mRow = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoDomNode>(ROW_SCHEMA);
const setUser = mRow.transition((row: TExoDomNode, user: TUser) => {
    row.text(ROW_SCHEMA.ports.name, user.name);
});
const ROW = mRow.done();

const users = createStore<readonly TUser[]>([
    { id: 1, name: 'ada' },
    { id: 2, name: 'bob' },
]);

const LIST_SCHEMA = createExoSchema((b) => {
    let rows!: TExoChildrenPort;
    b.el('ul', null, (ul) => {
        rows = ul.childrenPort();
    });
    return { rows };
});
const mList = createExoMachineBuilder<
    TExoDomNode & TExoKeyedListApi,
    unknown,
    { users: TExoKeyedList<TUser> }
>(LIST_SCHEMA);
mList.createInitialState((c) => ({
    users: c.keyedList(
        LIST_SCHEMA.ports.rows,
        (user: TUser) => user.id,
        (user, i) => {
            const row = c.build(ROW, i);
            setUser(row, user);
            return row;
        },
        setUser
    ),
}));
const showUsers = mList.transition((c) => {
    c.state.users.reconcile(users.getValue());
});
mList.effect((c) => {
    showUsers(c);
    return users.onChange(() => showUsers(c));
});
const LIST = mList.done();

backend.render(LIST, document.body);
users.setValue([
    { id: 2, name: 'bob' },
    { id: 1, name: 'ada lovelace' },
]);
```

`c.keyedList(port, keyOf, build, update)` opens the child list and hands back a
handle with one method, `reconcile(items)`. It holds no data of its own: the machine
keeps the handle in its state, opened in `createInitialState`, and calls
`reconcile` from a transition with whatever items it has now. `setUser` is the
row's own transition. There are no props, so the data reaches a row twice and both
times through it: inside `build`, before the row is placed, and on every later
`reconcile` whose object under that key is a **different** one — the same object
again calls nothing.

Underneath is `createExoKeyedList(kids, keyOf, build, update)`, exported for a
caller that drives a child list itself, and underneath that the same
`reconcileExoOrder` pass an identity list runs, over `keyOf(item)` instead of the
item (`packages/list-reconcile/src/createExoKeyedList.ts`).

**What a keyed pass costs that an identity pass does not:** one `keyOf` call and one
key per item per update, and a `Map` from key to item, rebuilt per update, which is
how it tells a fresh object from the same one. A repeated key is not refused: like a
repeated item in an identity list, it is one row per occurrence.

**On the server** a list is printed once and never updated. `build` there returns the
printed markup, so a transition called after `c.build` cannot reach it: a row printed
by the string backend takes its data inside its own initial state. **Under hydration** the
child list opens an adoption cursor and each `build` adopts the next served row, as
for an identity list; a keyed list under hydration has no test of its own.

Encode into your own identity whatever must force a rebuild, and leave out whatever
should flow through a transition instead. Where the data layer can answer that, it is
the cheaper answer; where it cannot, the pack above is the one that exists.

## Rows that own a subscription

If a row subscribes to something of its own — a per-entity store key — register
the teardown against the child being wired. It ends when that row leaves,
**including a row added by a later update**, so in a windowed list the
subscription cost is `O(visible)` rather than `O(total)`:

```ts
import { createExoMachineBuilder, createExoSchema } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoAttrPort } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoDomNode } from '@exodra/dom';

type TItem = { readonly id: string };

declare const store: {
    subscribeOnKey(id: string, cb: () => void): () => void;
};

const ROW_SCHEMA = createExoSchema((b) => {
    let id!: TExoAttrPort;
    b.el('li', null, (li) => {
        id = li.port('data-id');
    });
    return { id };
});
const mRow = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoDomNode>(ROW_SCHEMA);
export const showItem = mRow.transition((row: TExoDomNode, item: TItem) => {
    row.attr(ROW_SCHEMA.ports.id, item.id);
    row.onTeardown(store.subscribeOnKey(item.id, () => {}));
});
export const ROW = mRow.done();
```

An effect's returned unsubscribe is already owned by the instance —
`c.onTeardown` is for what you start yourself outside an effect. The disposer
joins the instance record's child when there is one, and the ambient render scope
otherwise, so a top-level instance and a list row behave the same. A subscription
with nothing to end it is refused rather than left to outlive the page that made
it.

**Both examples above build on a DOM-only exonode type
(`createExoMachineBuilder<TExoDomNode>`), and that is the honest type for them.** `c.nodes`, `c.schema`, `c.openChildList` and
`c.childListEndNode` are fields and methods of the DOM and hydration exonodes;
`TExoStrNode` has none of them, and has nothing for them to be about — it
writes strings into an array. A machine built over `TExoWiring` from
`@exodra/core` is what makes one component serve, render and hydrate. A machine
that reaches past the shared surface is browser-only, and
`createExoMachineBuilder<TExoDomNode>` is how it says so.

## Choosing

| You have… | Use |
|---|---|
| contents that cannot change | `c.list(port, ROW, count)` |
| "the current set of items" from a store | `reconcileExoOrder(c.state.rows, c.state.shown, items, items, build)` in a transition — identity-stable items |
| rows with no stable identity (freshly parsed JSON per refetch) | `c.keyedList(port, keyOf, build, update)` from `EXO_KEYED_LIST_VOCABULARY`, kept in state, `reconcile(items)` from a transition |
| a producer that knows the exact mutation, or a reuse policy of your own | `c.childList(port)` and its `insert`/`move`/`remove`, driven by hand |


==============================================================================
# Rendering patterns

A component is one value carrying two halves: a **schema** built once when the
module loads, and a **wiring function** run once per instance against a
**connector**. If that sentence is new, read the
[Components guide](./components.md) first — this page assumes it and is the
toolkit for everyday layout on top of it: static structure, reactive text and
attributes, conditional rendering, and mixing static with dynamic.

Lists have their [own guide](./lists.md).

## Static structure is an argument, not a bucket

Anything passed to `el()` is known when the module loads, and is folded into the
markup the prototype is parsed from. It costs nothing per instance — there is no
subscription, no setter and no slot in the instance's node array. Whole subtrees
with no ports in them are never even walked into at render time.

```ts
import { createExoStatic } from '@exodra/core';

export const CARD_HEADER = createExoStatic((b) => {
    b.el('header', { class: 'card__header' }, (header) => {
        header.el('h2', { class: 'card__title' }, (h2) => {
            h2.text('Recent activity');
        });
        header.el('p', { class: 'card__hint' }, (p) => {
            p.text('Updated hourly');
        });
    });
});
```

`createExoStatic` is for a component with nothing to fill. It **refuses** a builder
that declares ports, because a component with ports and no wiring is an
attribute stuck empty — a silently wrong page rather than an error.

It has no initial state at all, deliberately: a component with nothing to fill has
nothing to be about, so it does not even read the index it is handed. It is nested
by a machine above it like any other component (`c.one(P.slot, CARD_HEADER)`).

## Text and attributes that change

A value that varies is not an attribute. It is a **port**, and a **transition**
writes it. Data that lives outside the instance is followed by an **effect**
that runs the transition first, then subscribes, and returns the unsubscribe.

```ts
import { createExoMachineBuilder, createExoSchema } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoTextPort, TExoAttrPort } from '@exodra/core';
import { ExoDomBackend, withExoCompiler } from '@exodra/dom';
import type { TExoDomNode } from '@exodra/dom';

/** ONE backend for the application, at module level — it is the plan cache key. */
const backend = withExoCompiler(new ExoDomBackend());

function createStore<TValue>(value: TValue) {
    const listeners = new Set<() => void>();
    return {
        getValue: () => value,
        setValue(next: TValue) {
            value = next;
            for (const listener of Array.from(listeners)) listener();
        },
        onChange(listener: () => void): () => void {
            listeners.add(listener);
            return () => {
                listeners.delete(listener);
            };
        },
    };
}

const status = createStore<'on' | 'off'>('off');

const BADGE_SCHEMA = createExoSchema((b) => {
    let cls!: TExoAttrPort;
    let label!: TExoTextPort;
    b.el('span', { role: 'status' }, (span) => {
        cls = span.port('class');
        label = span.textPort();
    });
    return { cls, label };
});
const mBadge = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoDomNode>(BADGE_SCHEMA);
const showStatus = mBadge.transition((c) => {
    const s = status.getValue();
    c.attr(BADGE_SCHEMA.ports.cls, s === 'on' ? 'badge badge--on' : 'badge');
    c.text(BADGE_SCHEMA.ports.label, s.toUpperCase());
});
mBadge.effect((c) => {
    showStatus(c);
    return status.onChange(() => showStatus(c));
});
const BADGE = mBadge.done();

backend.render(BADGE, document.body);

status.setValue('on'); // one attribute write and one text write, nothing else
```

There is no diff and no virtual DOM: a change runs the setter the schema compiled
for that port, against the node that port resolved to. Call `c.attr` or `c.text`
**directly** when the value is decided once per instance and will never change —
a bare write retains nothing and subscribes to nothing, and an effect is nothing
but that write plus `onChange`.

:::note A bare write is repaired during hydration too
On a page that is **hydrated**, every fill reads what the server printed and writes
only on disagreement — a direct `c.attr` in the wire as much as one an effect makes
(`packages/dom/src/hydrate/factories/createExoRepairingFill.ts:13-15`). A value that is
constant but **environment-dependent** — a media query, the client's locale, a flag that
flipped while the bundle downloaded — therefore comes out right either way; what an
effect adds is the subscription for later changes. See
[SSR & hydration](./ssr.md#what-hydration-actually-does).
:::

:::note A text port owns its element's whole content
`textPort()` stands for **everything** inside its element, so an element cannot
have both a text port and static children — the schema compiler refuses that
combination by name at module load. Static text beside a reactive value means
two elements: `<span>Hello, </span><strong>«port»</strong>`, which is exactly
what the [Components guide's first example](./components.md#the-smallest-component)
builds.
:::

## Where children come from

A **children port** is declared with `childrenPort()`, and it *is* a child: it
renders exactly where the call appears in the builder. There are four ways to
fill one, and choosing between them is most of what this page is about.

| Call | What stands there | Reactive? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `c.one(port, component)` | one instance, fixed | no |
| `c.list(port, component, count)` | a fixed run of `count` instances | no |
| `c.build(component, index)` | an instance placed **nowhere** — the caller decides where it goes | no |
| `reconcileExoOrder(c.state.rows, c.state.shown, want, want, build)` in a transition, over `c.childList(port)` | rows that follow the array the transition hands it | yes |

The three fixed forms subscribe to nothing and keep no row records — a list whose
contents cannot change should not pay for the possibility that they might.

The live form is **one function and not four doors**, because its `build(item,
index)` callback is handed the item and returns the node: a callback that always
names the same component is a list of one kind, and one that picks a component per
item is a list of many kinds. The difference is in the callback the application
writes, so the engine carries no case for it. `reconcileExoOrder` comes from
`@exodra/list-reconcile`, which no backend depends on — a page that never
reconciles anything never links it.

:::note A reconciled list ADOPTS what the server printed
It used to refuse by name. It does not any more — opening a child list on a hydrating page
collects the rows the server printed, and `c.build` wires the instance straight onto the
next one, through `hydrateExoInstance`
(`packages/dom/src/hydrate/buildAdoptedExoChild.ts:27-29`).

The child list is opened in `createInitialState`, which runs **once**, and there is nothing to pay for it: no placeholder element and no
record. A row is taken once because the cursor advances — `takeExoAdoptedRow` returns the
element at its position and moves on (`packages/dom/src/dom/EXO_ADOPT_CURSOR.ts:28-36`)
— so the same row cannot be claimed twice, by the shape of the reader rather than by a
check. Once the printed rows run out, `build` goes on constructing client-side, which is
why a list that **grew** between the server's render and the client's is not a special
case.

How much the adoption saves over simply rebuilding has never been measured. See
[Lists & Reconciliation](./lists.md)
for the full cost list.
:::

## Conditional rendering

Pick the idiom by whether the hidden branch should be **removed** or merely
**hidden**, and by whether the *component* changes or only the data.

### One component, present or absent — a reconciled list of one item or none

The narrow conditional is a list of length one or zero. Nothing else is needed:
the same reconcile that runs a thousand rows runs this.

```ts
import { createExoMachineBuilder, createExoSchema } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoTextPort, TExoEventPort, TExoChildrenPort } from '@exodra/core';
import { ExoDomBackend, withExoChildList, withExoCompiler } from '@exodra/dom';
import type { TExoChildList, TExoDomNode } from '@exodra/dom';
import { reconcileExoOrder } from '@exodra/list-reconcile';

const backend = withExoChildList(withExoCompiler(new ExoDomBackend()));

/** Where a row's own datum waits for it: a view is handed its INDEX and nothing else. */
const BUILDING: string[] = [];

const DETAILS_SCHEMA = createExoSchema((b) => {
    let text!: TExoTextPort;
    b.el('div', { class: 'details' }, (div) => {
        text = div.textPort();
    });
    return { text };
});
const mDetails = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoDomNode, unknown, string>(DETAILS_SCHEMA);
mDetails.createInitialState((_c, index) => BUILDING[index]);
mDetails.wire((c) => {
    c.text(DETAILS_SCHEMA.ports.text, c.state);
});
const DETAILS = mDetails.done();

const ROW_SCHEMA = createExoSchema((b) => {
    let toggle!: TExoEventPort;
    let body!: TExoChildrenPort;
    b.el('div', { class: 'row' }, (div) => {
        div.el('button', { type: 'button' }, (btn) => {
            toggle = btn.eventPort('click');
            btn.text('Toggle');
        });
        body = div.childrenPort();
    });
    return { toggle, body };
});
type TRowState = { open: boolean; body: TExoChildList; shown: string[] };
const mRow = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoDomNode, unknown, TRowState>(ROW_SCHEMA);
mRow.createInitialState((c) => ({
    open: false,
    body: c.childList(ROW_SCHEMA.ports.body),
    shown: [],
}));
// One item when open, none when closed.
const showBody = mRow.transition((c) => {
    const want = c.state.open ? ['Everything about this row'] : [];
    c.state.shown = reconcileExoOrder(c.state.body, c.state.shown, want, want, (item, i) => {
        BUILDING[i] = item;
        return c.build(DETAILS, i);
    });
});
mRow.wire((c) => {
    showBody(c);
});
mRow.on(ROW_SCHEMA.ports.toggle, (c) => {
    c.state.open = !c.state.open;
    showBody(c);
});
const ROW = mRow.done();

backend.render(ROW, document.body);
```

Appearing mounts the instance; disappearing removes its element and ends its
subscriptions.

### A different component in the same place

A tab, a modal, a route: the *component* standing in the position changes, not
just its data. That is a list of **one item, and the item is the component** —
the reconciler compares items by identity, so a new component value drops the
old instance and builds the new one in its place. An empty array empties the
position.

```ts
import { createExoMachineBuilder, createExoSchema } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoTextPort, TExoChildrenPort } from '@exodra/core';
import { ExoDomBackend, withExoChildList, withExoCompiler } from '@exodra/dom';
import type { TExoChildList, TExoDomMachine, TExoDomNode } from '@exodra/dom';
import { reconcileExoOrder } from '@exodra/list-reconcile';

const backend = withExoChildList(withExoCompiler(new ExoDomBackend()));

function createStore<TValue>(value: TValue) {
    const listeners = new Set<() => void>();
    return {
        getValue: () => value,
        setValue(next: TValue) {
            value = next;
            for (const listener of Array.from(listeners)) listener();
        },
        onChange(listener: () => void): () => void {
            listeners.add(listener);
            return () => {
                listeners.delete(listener);
            };
        },
    };
}

const OVERVIEW_SCHEMA = createExoSchema((b) => {
    let title!: TExoTextPort;
    b.el('section', { class: 'overview' }, (s) => {
        s.el('h1', null, (h1) => {
            title = h1.textPort();
        });
    });
    return { title };
});
const mOverview = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoDomNode>(OVERVIEW_SCHEMA);
mOverview.wire((c) => {
    c.text(OVERVIEW_SCHEMA.ports.title, 'Overview');
});
const OVERVIEW = mOverview.done();

const SETTINGS_SCHEMA = createExoSchema((b) => {
    let body!: TExoTextPort;
    b.el('article', { class: 'settings' }, (a) => {
        a.el('p', null, (p) => {
            body = p.textPort();
        });
    });
    return { body };
});
const mSettings = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoDomNode>(SETTINGS_SCHEMA);
mSettings.wire((c) => {
    c.text(SETTINGS_SCHEMA.ports.body, 'Nothing configured yet');
});
const SETTINGS = mSettings.done();

// The ITEM is the component. One of them, or none.
const page = createStore<readonly TExoDomMachine[]>([OVERVIEW]);

const SHELL_SCHEMA = createExoSchema((b) => {
    let outlet!: TExoChildrenPort;
    b.el('main', { class: 'shell' }, (main) => {
        outlet = main.childrenPort();
    });
    return { outlet };
});
type TShellState = { outlet: TExoChildList; shown: TExoDomMachine[] };
const mShell = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoDomNode, unknown, TShellState>(SHELL_SCHEMA);
mShell.createInitialState((c) => ({ outlet: c.childList(SHELL_SCHEMA.ports.outlet), shown: [] }));
const showPage = mShell.transition((c) => {
    const want = page.getValue();
    c.state.shown = reconcileExoOrder(c.state.outlet, c.state.shown, want, want, (component, i) =>
        c.build(component, i)
    );
});
mShell.effect((c) => {
    showPage(c);
    return page.onChange(() => showPage(c));
});
const SHELL = mShell.done();

backend.render(SHELL, document.body);

// Later — a different component, in the same position:
page.setValue([SETTINGS]);
```

The outgoing instance is dropped the way a list row that leaves is: its element
comes out and its subscriptions end.

**Many** mixed positions at once — a page of blocks, a feed of mixed card types,
a form generated from a schema — is the same call with a longer array. Nothing
in the engine distinguishes the two cases, because nothing in it knows how the
callback picks: `build` is handed the item and returns a node, so a source of
components gives mixed kinds and a source of data gives one kind, from one
reconciler with no case for either.

### Keep it mounted — toggle a class

When the branch is cheap and its state must survive (an input mid-typing, a
scroll position), do not remove it. Write a class from a transition and hide
with CSS:

```ts
import { createExoMachineBuilder, createExoSchema } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoAttrPort } from '@exodra/core';
import { ExoDomBackend, withExoCompiler } from '@exodra/dom';
import type { TExoDomNode } from '@exodra/dom';

const backend = withExoCompiler(new ExoDomBackend());

const PANEL_SCHEMA = createExoSchema((b) => {
    let cls!: TExoAttrPort;
    b.el('section', null, (section) => {
        cls = section.port('class');
        section.el('input', { type: 'text', placeholder: 'Keeps its focus' });
    });
    return { cls };
});
const mPanel = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoDomNode, unknown, { expanded: boolean }>(PANEL_SCHEMA);
mPanel.createInitialState(() => ({ expanded: false }));
const showPanel = mPanel.transition((c) => {
    c.attr(PANEL_SCHEMA.ports.cls, c.state.expanded ? 'panel' : 'panel panel--hidden');
});
mPanel.wire((c) => {
    showPanel(c);
});
const PANEL = mPanel.done();

backend.render(PANEL, document.body);
```

A handler that sets `c.state.expanded` and runs `showPanel(c)` opens and closes it.

**Rule of thumb:** *remove* when the branch is heavy or must reset; *hide* when
it is light and should keep its state.

## Mixing static and dynamic — no fragments needed

A children port is a child, appended where it was declared, so it may stand
**between static siblings**. There is no wrapper element and no fragment host:

```ts
import { createExoMachineBuilder, createExoSchema } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoTextPort, TExoChildrenPort } from '@exodra/core';
import { ExoDomBackend, withExoChildList, withExoCompiler } from '@exodra/dom';
import type { TExoChildList, TExoDomNode } from '@exodra/dom';
import { reconcileExoOrder } from '@exodra/list-reconcile';

const backend = withExoChildList(withExoCompiler(new ExoDomBackend()));

function createStore<TValue>(value: TValue) {
    const listeners = new Set<() => void>();
    return {
        getValue: () => value,
        setValue(next: TValue) {
            value = next;
            for (const listener of Array.from(listeners)) listener();
        },
        onChange(listener: () => void): () => void {
            listeners.add(listener);
            return () => {
                listeners.delete(listener);
            };
        },
    };
}

type TTag = { readonly id: string; readonly label: string };

/** The row's own item, by index — the slot the build callback writes before building. */
const BUILDING: TTag[] = [];

const TAG_SCHEMA = createExoSchema((b) => {
    let label!: TExoTextPort;
    b.el('li', { class: 'tag' }, (li) => {
        label = li.textPort();
    });
    return { label };
});
const mTag = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoDomNode, unknown, TTag>(TAG_SCHEMA);
mTag.createInitialState((_c, index) => BUILDING[index]);
mTag.wire((c) => {
    c.text(TAG_SCHEMA.ports.label, c.state.label);
});
const TAG = mTag.done();

const tags = createStore<readonly TTag[]>([{ id: 'a', label: 'urgent' }]);

const TAG_BAR_SCHEMA = createExoSchema((b) => {
    let rows!: TExoChildrenPort;
    b.el('ul', { class: 'tags' }, (ul) => {
        // A pinned item, always first…
        ul.el('li', { class: 'tag tag--pinned' }, (li) => {
            li.text('Pinned');
        });
        // …the live rows, right here…
        rows = ul.childrenPort();
        // …and a static footer after them.
        ul.el('li', { class: 'tag tag--more' }, (li) => {
            li.text('More…');
        });
    });
    return { rows };
});
type TTagBarState = { rows: TExoChildList; shown: TTag[] };
const mTagBar = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoDomNode, unknown, TTagBarState>(TAG_BAR_SCHEMA);
mTagBar.createInitialState((c) => ({ rows: c.childList(TAG_BAR_SCHEMA.ports.rows), shown: [] }));
const showTags = mTagBar.transition((c) => {
    const want = tags.getValue();
    c.state.shown = reconcileExoOrder(c.state.rows, c.state.shown, want, want, (tag, i) => {
        BUILDING[i] = tag;
        return c.build(TAG, i);
    });
});
mTagBar.effect((c) => {
    showTags(c);
    return tags.onChange(() => showTags(c));
});
const TAG_BAR = mTagBar.done();

backend.render(TAG_BAR, document.body);
tags.setValue([...tags.getValue(), { id: 'b', label: 'blocked' }]);
```

The port's rows are inserted **before** the next static element, which the plan
records when the schema is compiled. Two children ports may also sit directly
next to each other — two conditionals in a row is an ordinary shape, and the
runtime resolves which region ends where, including when one of them is
currently empty.

:::caution Static *text* directly after a children port is refused
A region is anchored on the next static **element**, so text is not something it
can end at: the rows would land after that text on the client and before it on
the server. The schema compiler refuses this at module load, naming the text.
Wrap the text in an element, or make it part of what the wiring puts in the
region.
:::

## Raw markup

`c.unsafeHtml(port, html)` on a **children port** writes raw markup with `innerHTML` —
the `unsafeHtml` escape hatch. It is only allowed where the port is its
element's **only** child, because `innerHTML` takes the whole element and would
destroy any static siblings. Anywhere else the call is refused with a message
saying so. As everywhere, raw markup is your promise that the string is safe.

## The identity rule

Conditional children and lists are governed by one rule: children are
reconciled by **object identity**. No key is involved, and none is required.

- the **same item object** as last time → the same element, moved if its
  position changed, never rebuilt;
- a **new item object** → a child is built;
- an item that **disappeared** → its child is removed and its subscriptions end.

So whether a node survives an update is entirely about whether you hand back the
same object. See [Lists & Reconciliation](./lists.md) for what that means for a
list fed from a store, and [Core Concepts](../core/concepts.md#identity--reconciliation)
for why identity is first-class here rather than an escape hatch.

## The same patterns in JSX

In [Exodra JSX](./jsx.md) a children port is written where it stands, as
`<$.name />`, and the declaration says nothing about what fills it:

```tsx no-check
<ul><$.rows /></ul>
<div><h3>t</h3><$.details /><footer /></div>
<main><$.page /></main>
```

The machine makes the choice this page describes — `c.one`, `c.list`, or
`c.childList` reconciled with `reconcileExoOrder` — with the same consequences.
A component tag such as `<Row />` is a compile error: a schema has no notion of a
component.


==============================================================================
# Optimizations

Most of what an optimization guide usually contains — memoize this, hoist that,
add a key here — is not needed in Exodra, because the core does it
structurally rather than as an opt-in. (A key exists, but as a plugin for the case
where the data layer cannot supply identity — see below.) What is left is a short list of choices a
component author actually makes, and an explanation of what the core is already
doing so you can tell which of those choices matter.

For numbers, see [Benchmarks](../benchmarks.md). Nothing on this page restates
one — a figure kept in two places drifts.

## What the core does without being asked

### The schema is compiled once per process

A component's schema is built when its module loads, and the first render
compiles it — once, for the life of the process — into three things:

- **a prototype element**, parsed from the schema's markup inside an inert
  `<template>`, which every instance is a `cloneNode` of;
- **a walk plan**, a flat list of single hops (`firstChild` / `nextSibling`)
  reaching only the elements that carry a port. A subtree with no ports in it is
  emitted as markup and **never walked into** at render time;
- **a setter per port**, already bound to its attribute name and its element's
  namespace, so filling a port is two array loads and one indirect call with no
  branch on the port's kind.

A render is therefore: clone the prototype, replay the walk, run the wiring
function. There is no template parsing per render, no props object, no tree
diff and no per-node type dispatch.

Clone-and-patch is not an optimization applied to code that qualifies for it
here: it is what a component *is*, and there is no un-templated path to fall
back to. So there is no cache key to set, no heuristic to satisfy, and no
"this subtree was too dynamic to hoist" case to discover in production.

### Static costs nothing

Anything passed to `el()` is folded into the prototype's markup. It has no slot
in the instance's node array, no setter, no subscription and no work at update
time. That is the single biggest lever an author has, and it is the default: a
value only becomes a port when you declare one.

### The prototype is moved into the page's document

A `<template>`'s contents belong to a different document, `cloneNode` preserves
the owner, and inserting a foreign-owned subtree makes the DOM adopt it node by
node on **every** insertion. So the compiler imports the verified prototype into
the page's document once, and every instance skips that walk. It is skipped for
schemas containing elements whose adoption does work (`<img>` and friends),
because starting a fetch at module load would undo the inertness the
`<template>` parse exists for.

### Reconciliation is by identity, and there is a fast path per shape

`reconcileExoOrder`, called from a transition, reconciles a children port against
a list **by object identity** — the item reference is the key, and there is no `key` prop on this
path. (Where identity is unavailable, `EXO_KEYED_LIST_VOCABULARY` from
`@exodra/list-reconcile` is the opt-in pack, adding `c.keyedList`; it costs one
`keyOf` call per item and a key→item `Map` per update on top of what this list
pays.) The diff tries cheaper shapes first: the common head and tail by identity,
then a middle that is only inserted or only removed, done in place; only a middle
whose survivors changed order reaches the general case, which moves the minimum
number of nodes by keeping the longest increasing subsequence in place
(`packages/list-reconcile/src/reconcileExoOrder.ts`).

Per update the common paths allocate **nothing**. See
[Lists & Reconciliation](./lists.md) and
[Core Concepts → Identity & reconciliation](../core/concepts.md#identity--reconciliation).

### The trade behind "no scheduler"

Writing straight to the DOM is fast **precisely because** Exodra does **no
glitch-batching** — there is no scheduler coalescing writes
or topologically ordering a derived graph the way Solid's or Voby's (`oby`) do.
That is a deliberate design choice with two sides:

- **The common case pays nothing.** An effect following one value into one port,
  or a transition computing a value from a single read, has no deep dependency graph — so there is nothing to glitch
  and nothing to batch. You skip the per-write scheduler overhead entirely.
- **Heavy multi-source state delegates coherence upward.** If you build many
  interdependent values or computeds over collections, batching and glitch-free
  consistency are **not** the view layer's job — you hand them to the data layer.
  A reactive store like [`@oimdb/*`](https://oimdb.org/llms.txt)
  already owns a transactional queue: it coalesces writes, flushes a consistent
  snapshot, and feeds **already-settled** values into ports as plain direct
  writes. The batching did not disappear — it lives where a transaction model
  already exists, instead of being duplicated inside the renderer.

So the direct-write speed in the [benchmarks](../benchmarks.md) is one face of a
coin whose other face is "the renderer stays thin; the store owns coherence."
Most apps never touch that other face; data-dense ones get a clean division of
labour instead of two schedulers.

## The choices that are actually yours

### Declare it in `el()`, not as a port

A port costs a slot in the instance's node array and one call per instance; a
static attribute costs nothing at any point after module load. Anything that is
the same for every instance belongs in `el()`.

### `c.attr` in the wire when it cannot change, an effect when it can

`c.attr` is two array loads and a call, retaining nothing. An effect that follows a
value additionally subscribes, and its unsubscribe is held by the instance until it
goes. Following a value that never changes buys a subscription for nothing.

### `c.list` for a fixed run, `reconcileExoOrder` for a live one

A fixed list is rendered once: no row records, no shown order, no diff, no
teardown. It is not `reconcileExoOrder` over a constant array — the difference is
everything the reconciler exists for.

### Let the data layer hand you the delta

`reconcileExoOrder` takes the order shown and the order wanted and lets the diff
compute the delta (`packages/list-reconcile/src/reconcileExoOrder.ts`) — that path
is the one tuned for the shapes lists actually take. A producer that already knows
the exact mutation (a command stream, a drag-reorder) and wants it performed as-is
drives `c.childList(port)`'s `insert` / `move` / `remove` itself, from a
transition, in `O(1)` per operation.

### A shared handler instead of a closure for a repeated handler

`c.on(port, handler, subject)` takes either shape. A **closure** is the general
answer and costs one function per row. A **shared handler** — a module-level
function taking `(event, subject)`, see
[`@exodra/core`](../api/core.md#event-handlers) — holds nothing about any row, so
one function object serves every row of a template; which row it fired on
arrives as the third argument of the fill, which the wiring function already
holds and therefore does not allocate.

This is also what delegation is written against: `createExoDelegatedEvents(names)`
attaches one root listener per event name instead of one listener per element,
and it **refuses a fill with no subject** rather than leaving a handler that
cannot tell which row it is answering for. See
[Events as a plugin](../api/dom.md#events-as-a-plugin).

### Give hydration something it can adopt cheaply

A child list on a hydrating page adopts the rows the server printed rather than refusing
them, and it costs **no placeholder and no record**: opening the list collects the served
rows into a cursor, and `c.build` wires the instance straight onto the next one
(`packages/dom/src/dom/EXO_ADOPT_CURSOR.ts:16-21`). The initial state runs once, on the
server's element (`packages/dom/src/hydrate/buildAdoptedExoChild.ts:27-29`). When the data
wants more rows than the markup has, the cursor answers `null` and the rest are built the
client way.

How much the hydrating path costs on a real page is **unmeasured**.
See [SSR & Hydration](./ssr.md).

## Writing the schema in JSX

[`@exodra/babel-plugin-schema`](./jsx.md) compiles an `exoJsx(…)` schema
declaration — literal attributes as markup, every port named where it stands — into
a module-level `createExoNamedSchema()`. Hoisting the schema to module scope is not
a mode it offers — a rebuilt schema is a different program, because every backend
indexes its prepared plan by the schema's ports.

Hand-written components need no compiler at all — nothing on this page depends
on a build step.

## Measuring

Compare against Solid/Svelte/React with the suite in `packages/benchmarks` (the
exact commands are under [Benchmarks → Reproduce](../benchmarks.md#reproduce)),
and profile with
[`@exodra/dom-profiler`](../tooling/profiler.md) — `profileDom()` for a
per-method breakdown of the renderer, `profilePorts(component)` for where one
component's time goes port by port.


==============================================================================
# Plugins and the interfaces they implement

`@exodra/dom` is composed, not configured. A backend is `new ExoDomBackend()` — no
constructor arguments — and every capability an application adds is a decorator
wrapped around it. A few of the backend's members are **named plugin interfaces**:
fields that hold an implementation, which a composition replaces or wraps, while
everything it did not name stays what it ships. This page is the reference — what a
plugin is, which fields exist, which packs ship, and where the interfaces stop.

[Sugar, not restrictions](../why/sugar-not-restrictions.md) is the mechanism and its
rationale; this page does not restate it.

## What a plugin is

A plugin is a **bag of method factories** — an object whose every entry receives
whatever stands under that name right now and returns what stands there next
(`packages/core/src/plugins/types/TExoPlugin.ts`):

```ts no-check
export type TExoPlugin = {
    readonly [name: string]: (next: never) => unknown;
};
```

`new ExoDomBackend()` calls `composeExoPlugins(this, …)` once, in its constructor,
to put the **exonode surface** on itself — `attr`, `text`, `on`, `one`, `list`,
`build`, `childList` and the rest (`packages/dom/src/dom/ExoDomBackend.ts`,
`packages/core/src/plugins/composeExoPlugins.ts`). Every pack an application composes
is a unary decorator wrapped around that finished object:

```ts no-check
withExoHydration(withExoCompiler(withExoDefaults(new ExoDomBackend())));
```

Each one is `(base) => composeExoPlugins(base, ENTRIES)`, and `composeExoPlugins`
mutates the object it is handed and returns it, so the whole chain keeps **one
identity** — which the schema cache requires, because it keys the backend by
pointer. The class fields and the exonode surface are already written when a
decorator runs, so a pack's factory receives the **shipped value** as `next`. That
is what makes replacing and wrapping the same act: a pack that never calls `next`
has replaced; one that calls it has wrapped.

There is no registry, no namespace and no `needs` / `provides`. A merged method
exists only where it was merged.

**The capability check is the type of the composed object.** Nobody declares a
capability set. A decorator states its contribution in its return type —
`withExoCompiler(base)` answers `TBase & TExoCompilerApi`,
`composeExoPlugins(base, EXO_KEYED_LIST_VOCABULARY)` answers `typeof base &
TExoKeyedListApi` — and they compose by intersection. A backend composed without
`withExoHydration` has no `hydrate`, in the type as well as at runtime.

**Where that check lands.** A machine that calls `c.keyedList` needs an exonode type
that has it, and the compile error appears **on the line that calls it**. It comes
from `render` and `hydrate` as well: both declare their component against
`this & TExoDomInstanceRecord`, so a component demanding a pack the backend never
merged is refused in the file that built the backend. `TExoDomNode` itself names
no pack — it is the instance's record plus the shipped surface
(`packages/dom/src/dom/EXO_DOM_NODE_VOCABULARY.ts`). Following a source
needs no pack at all: it is an effect that runs a transition writing through the
fill doors every exonode has, then subscribes.

**There is no protection against two packs claiming one name.** They are resolved
by **nesting order** — the outermost decorator runs last and is therefore the
outermost wrapper — and two that both replace without calling `next` leave only the
outer one, with nothing thrown.

## The fields a composition can replace

A bare backend carries `events`, `writers`, `createInstance` and `createChild` as class
