field initialisers (`packages/dom/src/dom/ExoDomBackend.ts`). `withExoHydration`
adds two more. The API they make up is `TExoDomApi`
(`packages/dom/src/dom/types/TExoDomApi.ts`).

| Field | Interface | Shipped value | What replacing it decides |
|---|---|---|---|
| `events` | `TExoEventsApi` | `EXO_DIRECT_EVENTS` — one listener per element | how a listener reaches the DOM |
| `writers` | `TExoWritersApi` | `EXO_SHIPPED_WRITERS` | how a value reaches an element |
| `createInstance` / `createChild` | `TExoDomRecordFactories` | the two record factories built in the constructor | the shape of every record rendered |
| `hydrateSurface` *(optional)* | `TExoDomRecordFactories` | absent — `withExoHydration` installs it | whether this backend can adopt markup |
| `parserStability` *(optional)* | `TExoParserStability` | absent — `withExoHydration` installs it | the refusals for a schema the HTML parser would reshape |

`TExoEventsApi` has four members — `name`, `port(event)`, `attach`, and an optional
`install(root)` (`packages/dom/src/events/types/TExoEventsApi.ts`). `TExoWritersApi`
has four — `name`, `attr(name, proto, kind, at)`, `markupCarries(name, proto)` and
`text(proto)` (`packages/dom/src/backend/types/TExoWritersApi.ts`). Both are read
once per port while a schema compiles, never per write.

`createInstance` and `createChild` must be replaced **together**, or a module has made
a third record shape.

:::caution A wrapper is silent on an adopted page
**A pack that wraps an exonode method hydration also claims never runs on a
hydrated page.** `withExoHydration` builds its own adopting surface — an object
whose prototype is the composed backend — and merges the adopting bodies onto it
through `exoVocabulary`, whose factories are `() => method`: they **ignore `next`**,
so they replace rather than wrap (`packages/core/src/plugins/exoVocabulary.ts`). The
names it claims are `portNodeWriter`, `portNodeReader`, `on`, `one`, `list`,
`build` and `foreign`, the child-list seams `childListEndNode`, `childListStartNode` and
`openChildList`, and its own `publishChildListEnd`, `adoptFromNode` and `adoptStopNode`
(`packages/dom/src/hydrate/EXO_HYDRATE_NODE_VOCABULARY.ts`).

A name adoption does not claim falls through to the composed backend, so a wrapper
on it does run on an adopted page; one on a claimed name does not
(`packages/dom/src/hydrate/tests/exo-composed-hydrate.test.ts`).
:::

### What a replacement has to do

**`events`.** `port(event)` runs once per event port per schema, at compile time,
and is the only place a pack may refuse a name. `attach` is fixed per pack and runs
on every fill. Two rules the type cannot state, both because getting either wrong
double-dispatches silently: **namespace the event slots** — the property names a
pack writes on the element come from `exoEventSlotsFor(packId, event)` with a pack
id unique to the pack — and **build every port datum with
`createExoEventPortData`**, so every datum in the process shares one hidden class.
`install` is honoured by `render` and `hydrate` and by nothing else. `hydrate` reads
`this.events` off the backend it was composed onto, so a page hydrates with the
pack it renders with (`packages/dom/src/hydrate/withExoHydration.ts`).
`packages/dom/src/events/tests/third-pack.test.ts` is a third pack written from the
package barrel alone.

**`writers`.** `attr` and `text` are the two writers; `proto` is the prototype
element and must not be closed over. `markupCarries` answers "would a browser handed
this markup, and no fill, be in the state this value asks for?" — hydration reads it
to decide which ports it may silence and which keep their live writer. A text writer
is handed the element unless the function it returns sets `takesTextNode`. *Inert
case:* a pack whose `attr` and `text` return no-op setters renders an element with
neither the attribute nor the text
(`packages/dom/src/backend/tests/exo-composed-writers.test.ts`).

## Composing a backend

`new ExoDomBackend()` and a chain of `with*` decorators around it is the one
expression an application writes:

```ts
import { composeExoPlugins, createExoMachineBuilder, createExoSchema } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoTextPort } from '@exodra/core';
import {
    ExoDomBackend,
    createExoDelegatedEvents,
    withExoCompiler,
    withExoDefaults,
} from '@exodra/dom';
import type { TExoDomNode } from '@exodra/dom';

const GREETING_SCHEMA = createExoSchema((b) => {
    let label!: TExoTextPort;
    b.el('h1', null, (h1) => {
        label = h1.textPort();
    });
    return { label };
});
const mGreeting = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoDomNode>(GREETING_SCHEMA);
mGreeting.wire((c) => {
    c.text(GREETING_SCHEMA.ports.label, 'Hello');
});
const GREETING = mGreeting.done();

/** ONE pack per application, at module level: it keys the schema cache with the backend. */
const DELEGATED = createExoDelegatedEvents(['click', 'input']);

/** ONE backend, at module level. The chain reads inside-out. */
const backend = withExoCompiler(
    withExoDefaults(
        // A bare implementation is merged as the one-entry plugin it is.
        composeExoPlugins(new ExoDomBackend(), { events: () => DELEGATED })
    )
);

const dispose = backend.render(GREETING, document.getElementById('app') as Element);
```

`backend.render` mounts **one** instance and takes no count. A page of rows is a
children port filled by `c.list` or by `reconcileExoOrder` over `c.childList`
in some component's transition — see [Lists](./lists.md).

Three rules that decide whether this works at all:

- **Compose once, at module level.** Every backend object takes its own
  `backendType`, the index its schemas are cached at on `machine.forms`, so one built
  per render recompiles every schema, markup parse included, on every render.
  `warnExoFormGrowth` (`packages/core/src/machine/warnExoFormGrowth.ts`) says so out
  loud in a development build once a machine holds eight schemas.
- **Order is the caller's, and nothing refuses a collision.** Packs apply
  inside-out; the outermost decorator claims a name last and becomes the outermost
  wrapper. `withExoPropertyWriters` and `withExoReclaimingText` both claim `writers`
  and both delegate `text` to `next`, which is why either order keeps the reclaiming
  text writer.
- **A pack's factory cannot keep anything per-instance.** It runs **once**, at
  merge, and is handed `next` and nothing else. A method it returns must reach its
  siblings through `this` at call time, and must not be an arrow, or it has no
  `this` at all — a silent failure in both directions
  (`packages/core/src/plugins/types/TExoPlugin.ts`).

## The packs that ship

| Pack | Claims | Compose it when | Its cost | Its limitation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `withExoCompiler(base)` | `schema`, `render` | the page turns declarations into schemas | the compiler is in the bundle | a page whose schemas came off a build leaves it out and calls `mountExoSchema` instead |
| `withExoHydration(base)` | `hydrate`, `hydrateSurface`, `parserStability` | the page adopts markup `@exodra/string` printed | 3.2 kB gzipped that a client-only page never links | needs `withExoCompiler` beneath it; wrappers on the names it claims do not run while adopting |
| [`withExoChildList(base)`](../api/dom.md#withexochildlist) | `childList` on the exonode | a machine opens a child list — `reconcileExoOrder`, `c.keyedList`, the router's outlet, rows placed by hand | the commanded child list is in the bundle | without it the first `c.childList` throws [EXO0109](../errors.md#exo0109); `c.one` and a fixed `c.list` never need it |
| [`withExoForeignNamespaces(base)`](../api/dom.md#withexoforeignnamespaces) | `foreignNamespaces` | a schema contains `<svg>`, `<math>` or an SVG-only element | the SVG and MathML tables are in the bundle | without it such a schema is refused with [EXO0108](../errors.md#exo0108), or [EXO0110](../errors.md#exo0110) from a JSON declaration |
| `withExoDefaults(base)` | `writers` | an ordinary page — it is the safety bundle, holding `withExoReclaimingText` today | that of the pack inside it | none of its own |
| `withExoReclaimingText(base)` | `writers` (`text` only) | anything outside the renderer may rewrite visible text — a translator, an extension | one `firstChild` load and one `nodeType` test per text write | when the test fails it assigns `textContent`, which destroys everything inside the element |
| `withExoPropertyWriters(base, takesOver?)` | `writers` (`attr`, `markupCarries`) | a custom element takes an array, a `Date`, a `Map` or a callback | decided once per attribute port at compile time | the server is not composed, so byte parity is given up for taken-over ports |
| `createExoDelegatedEvents(names, options?)` | a value for `events` | many rows share the same handlers | one root listener per event name; dispatch walks from `e.target` to the root | a node moved out of its root stops responding; non-bubbling names are refused, high-frequency ones unless `allowHighFrequency` is set |
| `EXO_KEYED_LIST_VOCABULARY` (`@exodra/list-reconcile`) | `keyedList` on the exonode | rows arrive as fresh objects on every refetch, with no identity to reconcile by | one `keyOf` call per item and a key→item `Map` per update | it opens a child list, so the DOM backend needs `withExoChildList` beneath it; the row's data reaches it through the `update` argument, a transition the caller writes — there are no props |
| `EXO_DOM_FOREIGN_VOCABULARY` | `foreign` on the exonode | a children port must hold an element this renderer did not make | — | on an adopted page a foreign node is built fresh, never adopted, and the row the server printed for it is removed |

`createExoDelegatedEvents` returns a `TExoEventsApi` — a value for the `events`
field, not a decorator — so composing it is the one-entry factory
`() => DELEGATED`. `EXO_KEYED_LIST_VOCABULARY` and `EXO_DOM_FOREIGN_VOCABULARY` are
plugins merged with `composeExoPlugins(backend, VOCABULARY)`.

### `exo-reclaiming-text`

`withExoReclaimingText(base)` replaces `text` with `exoReclaimingText` and delegates
`attr` and `markupCarries` to `next` by call. `createExoReclaimingTextWriters(next)`
is the factory it is built on, for a caller filling the `writers` field itself
(`packages/dom/src/plugins/exo-reclaiming-text/index.ts`).

What it buys: the shipped writer stores into a Text node resolved at build time.
Anything rewriting visible text — a browser translator, an accessibility extension,
a userscript — replaces that node, and the store then lands on a node nobody
renders, with nothing thrown. `exoReclaimingText` re-reads `firstChild` on every
write and falls back to `textContent` when it is not a lone Text node.

Every text write reaches it, including the repeat writes a transition makes,
because those go through `c.text`. A wire that asked for `portNodeWriter()` is
the one route that bypasses it, because that closure loads the setter table once.

### `exo-property-writers`

The second implementation of `TExoWritersApi`. It turns a custom element's ports
into JavaScript property stores, so a component that accepts an array, a `Date`, a
`Map` or a callback can be reached from a schema at all
(`packages/dom/src/plugins/exo-property-writers/index.ts`).

Four exports:

- `withExoPropertyWriters(base, takesOver?)` — the decorator.
- `createExoPropertyWriters(next?, takesOver?)` — the factory it is built on, for a
  caller filling the `writers` field itself. Text is delegated to `next`; attribute
  ports the pack declines go to `EXO_SHIPPED_WRITERS`.
- `takesOverExoProperty(name, proto)` — the default predicate, exported so a
  narrower rule can be written as "the default, and also…". It takes a port only on
  a hyphenated tag, never for a name in `EXO_GLOBAL_ATTRIBUTES`, and never for a name
  containing `-` or `:`.
- `EXO_GLOBAL_ATTRIBUTES` — the set of global attribute names it leaves alone.

The predicate runs at compile time, once per attribute port, and must be pure in
its two arguments, because `attr` and `markupCarries` agree only by both asking it.
A taken-over port answers `markupCarries: false`, so hydration keeps its live writer
rather than silencing it. The one thing no member can fix is that **the server is
not composed for writers**: `@exodra/string` compiles through its own
`EXO_STR_WRITERS` (`packages/string/src/writers/EXO_STR_WRITERS.ts`), so it prints
the stringified attribute for the same port.

### Keys

The keyed pack is documented in full on [Lists](./lists.md#keys-when-identity-is-not-available).
It is `EXO_KEYED_LIST_VOCABULARY` from `@exodra/list-reconcile`, which puts
`c.keyedList(port, keyOf, build, update)` on the exonode over the free function
`createExoKeyedList(kids, keyOf, build, update)`. Both return a list whose
`reconcile(items)` a transition calls, and it runs the same `reconcileExoOrder` pass
the identity list runs, over `keyOf(item)` instead of the item.

## Keeping a subtree instead of recycling elements

There is no node source and no element pool. An element comes from one place,
`cloneExoNode(schema)` on the schema's prototype. What an application keeps instead
is **the whole exonode**: a child built once with `c.build` stays wired, subscribed
and filled for as long as the application holds it, and the child list moves it in
and out of the document without telling it.

```ts
import type { TExoChildrenPort } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoDomMachine, TExoDomNode } from '@exodra/dom';

export function keepPanel(c: TExoDomNode, port: TExoChildrenPort, panel: TExoDomMachine) {
    const kids = c.childList(port);
    const kept = c.build(panel);
    kids.insert(kept);
    return {
        hide: (): void => {
            kids.detach(0);
        },
        show: (): void => {
            kids.attach(kept, 0);
        },
    };
}
```

`detach(i)` takes the node out and runs **no** hook — nothing is unmounted or
disposed, so the exonode's subscriptions stay live and keep writing into a node that
is out of the document. `attach(child, i)` is `insert` without `mount`
(`packages/dom/src/dom/types/TExoChildList.ts`). A kept child is ended by putting it
back and calling `remove`, which runs its `unmount` and ends its subscriptions
(`packages/dom/src/dom/tests/make-exo-child-list.test.ts`). `detachAll()` takes every
child of the list in one call.

## A fourth backend

`@exodra/term` compiles the same schema into a **live plain-text tree** — elements
are lines, a text port is the line's content, a children port is an indented block,
and an event port is a listener a terminal input loop can fire by name
(`packages/term/src/index.ts`). It is in-repo and unpublished: its `package.json`
says `"private": true` and version `0.0.0`. The acceptance test is
`packages/term/src/doc/`: components copied character for character out of this
project's `README.md`, checked against it by a test, and run through this backend
(`packages/term/src/doc/tests/readme-verbatim.test.ts`).

It does not go through any of the fields above. `@exodra/term` is a separate
backend object written against the portable exonode surface:
`new ExoTermBackend(...plugins)` merges its surface onto itself and then the
plugins it is handed, and its entry point is `backend.renderScreen(component, n)`,
deliberately not named `render` (`packages/term/src/backend/ExoTermBackend.ts`).
Nothing hands the renderer itself to a composed name: an application chooses a
backend by importing it.

## What is not replaceable

**The renderer itself.** There is no plugin interface for a foreign backend, and
none for the element builder, the schema compiler, the child-list anchoring or
hydration's adoption pass. An element carries no pointer to its child, so there is
no element→child direction for a composition to take over; `exoNodeDom` takes a
child and refuses anything else (`packages/dom/src/dom/exoNodeDom.ts`).

**Where an element comes from.** `cloneExoNode` on the schema's prototype, with no
field to replace it. Keeping a subtree alive is the strategy that exists; recycling
an element under a different wiring is not.

**The children arm of the setter table.** `compileExoHydrateSchema` decides what an
adopting fill on a raw-markup port means by pointer-comparing its setter against
`setExoHtml`, so a replaceable children writer would turn a working adoption into a
refusal on every hydrated page
(`packages/dom/src/hydrate/compileExoHydrateSchema.ts`).

**The server's writers.** `@exodra/string` compiles through `EXO_STR_WRITERS` by
module import (`packages/string/src/schema/compileExoStrSchema.ts`), so replacing
what stands in `writers` is choosing a client-side behaviour the server does not
know about.

**The schema cache.** A machine carries one array, `forms`, and each backend stores
its schema at `machine.forms[backend.backendType]`
(`packages/core/src/machine/types/TExoMachine.ts`). A backend's own `backendType`
comes from `nextExoBackendType()` (`packages/core/src/backend/nextExoBackendType.ts`);
no name of any backend appears in core, so a backend written outside this
repository caches its schemas the same way. Hydration is not an index of its own:
its schema hangs off the DOM schema it derives from
(`packages/dom/src/hydrate/exoHydrateSchemaOf.ts`).


==============================================================================
# Server-Side Rendering & Hydration

Exodra renders to an HTML string on the server and **adopts** the existing DOM on
the client (no teardown, no flash).

What makes that safe here is that both sides run **the same component**: one
schema, compiled once for markup and once for nodes, and one wiring function
that neither backend can tell apart. The two agree because both index their
prepared plans by the port numbers the schema assigned — not because two code
paths were kept in step by hand.

That includes a reconciled list holding the **same item object at two positions**:
both backends print a row per position, and a test asserts the agreement
(`packages/dom/src/tests/duplicate-item-parity.test.ts`).
See [The same object twice in one list](../troubleshooting.md#the-same-object-twice-in-one-list).


Packages involved:

- [`@exodra/string`](../api/string.md) — `new ExoStrBackend().render(...)` turns a
  component into markup.
- [`@exodra/dom`](../api/dom.md) — `backend.hydrate(...)`, on a backend wrapped in
  `withExoHydration`, adopts that markup.
- [`@exodra/ssr`](#the-exodrassr-toolkit) — the rest of the response: head tags,
  status, headers, the embedded state script and its client-side reader, and the
  whole document.

## The two entry points are the same call, on two backends

```ts
import { createExoMachineBuilder, createExoSchema } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoMachineNode, TExoTextPort } from '@exodra/core';

const PAGE_SCHEMA = createExoSchema((b) => {
    let title!: TExoTextPort;
    b.el('main', { class: 'page' }, (main) => {
        main.el('h1', null, (h1) => {
            title = h1.textPort();
        });
    });
    return { title };
});
const mPage = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoMachineNode>(PAGE_SCHEMA);
mPage.wire((c) => {
    c.text(PAGE_SCHEMA.ports.title, 'Hello SSR');
});
export const PAGE = mPage.done();
```

On the server:

```ts
import { ExoStrBackend } from '@exodra/string';
import type { TExoStrMachine } from '@exodra/string';

declare const PAGE: TExoStrMachine;

/** ONE backend for the process, at module level — it is the plan cache key. */
const server = new ExoStrBackend();

const html = server.render(PAGE);
// → '<main class="page"><h1>Hello SSR</h1></main>'
```

On the client:

```ts
import { ExoDomBackend, withExoHydration, withExoCompiler } from '@exodra/dom';
import type { TExoDomMachine } from '@exodra/dom';

declare const PAGE: TExoDomMachine;

/** `hydrate` exists only on a backend composed with the hydration pack. */
const backend = withExoHydration(withExoCompiler(new ExoDomBackend()));

const root = document.getElementById('app') as HTMLElement;
const dispose = backend.hydrate(PAGE, root);
```

Same component, same argument order, same disposer. A page switches sides by
switching **which backend it holds** — not by learning a second calling
convention — and the return value is the difference: one hands back markup, the
other hands back a way to tear it down.

**Neither call takes an instance count.** `render` and `hydrate` each deal in
**one** instance, handed `0` as its index, because no library
asks an application how many copies of its root to make. Anything that repeats
inside the page is a **list** — a children port filled by `c.list` or by
`reconcileExoOrder` over `c.childList` — and that is true on both sides, which is exactly why the two agree
about how many rows there are without either being told.

**Type the machine against the shared exonode surface, or none of that is true.**
`TExoStrMachine` and `TExoDomMachine` are both `TExoMachine<C>`
with a backend's exonode type in `C`, and a machine's exonode parameter is
contravariant — so a component built with `createExoMachineBuilder<TExoDomNode>` is not a value
`@exodra/string` will accept, and no cast makes it one honestly. Say what the machine
actually needs instead:

```ts no-check
import { createExoMachineBuilder } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoMachineNode } from '@exodra/core';

// A machine that only fills values takes `TExoMachineNode`; one that also nests
// components takes `TExoChildrenWiring & TExoMachineNode`, which adds `one` / `list` / `build`.
// Following data adds nothing to this list: a transition writes through the fill doors and
// an effect subscribes to the data layer, so a machine that follows data still names the
// narrowest surface it actually uses.
const mPage = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoMachineNode>(PAGE_SCHEMA);
const showTitle = mPage.transition((c) => {
    c.text(PAGE_SCHEMA.ports.title, title.getValue());
});
mPage.effect((c) => {
    showTitle(c);
    return title.onChange(() => showTitle(c));
});
mPage.on(PAGE_SCHEMA.ports.click, onClick);
```

One value then satisfies `TExoStrMachine`, `TExoDomMachine`
and hydration's use of the same alias, with no cast anywhere — which is what
`packages/dom/src/tests/one-wire.test.ts` asserts by handing one component to all three
entry points.

For a page with **no** server render (a pure client app), call `backend.render`
instead of `backend.hydrate`, and drop `withExoHydration` from the
composition; nothing else changes. Dropping it is worth doing rather than
harmless: hydration is a pack precisely so a client-only bundle does not carry the
adopters, measured at 3.2 kB gzipped that such a page never runs. A backend
composed without it has no `hydrate` at all — in the type as well as at runtime —
so there is no way to call it by accident.

## What hydration actually does

It attaches listeners and takes subscriptions, and it **writes nothing where the
markup already agrees** — which is the whole reason it is cheaper than rendering.
It is *not* true that the served HTML is left byte-identical. Where the client's
data disagrees with what the server printed, hydration repairs it rather than
leaving the page wrong until something happens to fire:

- a **text** port fill is read and compared, and written only on a mismatch
  (`packages/dom/src/hydrate/factories/createExoRepairingFill.ts:29-38`);
- an **attribute** port fill is compared against `getAttribute` and repaired
  through the live setter (`packages/dom/src/hydrate/repairExoAttribute.ts:36-65`) —
  which is what makes a price rendered in the server's locale, or a flag that
  flipped while the bundle downloaded, come out right;
- **surplus rows** the server rendered that the client's data no longer has are removed
  (`packages/dom/src/hydrate/dropUnadoptedExoRows.ts:24-29`), because a list that
  inserts at the end would otherwise put every later row behind the dead ones;
- **unclaimed rows** of a child list are removed with no shape check at all, because the
  span the cursor collected was bounded by that list's own end, so everything left in it
  is a row of this list (`packages/dom/src/dom/EXO_ADOPT_CURSOR.ts:38-45`).

That holds for **every** fill — `c.attr` / `c.text` / `c.unsafeHtml`, whether a
wire, a transition or an effect's first draw makes it. The compare belongs to the
fill (`packages/dom/src/hydrate/factories/createExoRepairingFill.ts:13-15`,
`packages/dom/src/hydrate/compileExoHydrateSchema.ts:65-69`). What an effect adds on a
hydrated page is the subscription for later changes, not the first write's
correctness. An event port is a different branch: its entry is the real attachment,
which is the content of hydration.

Raw markup is repaired through its own compare, which normalises both sides through the
same parser so that markup the browser merely respelled (`<br/>` coming back `<br>`) does
not rebuild a correct subtree (`packages/dom/src/hydrate/repairExoHtml.ts:19-21`).

Two consequences:

- **Hydrate from the backend you rendered from.** Attaching listeners is not a
  detail of hydration, it is the content of it — so the event strategy is **not a
  parameter**: `hydrate` reads `this.events` off the backend it was composed onto,
  so composing the pack onto the same object makes a divergence unspellable rather
  than merely discouraged.

  ```ts
  import { composeExoPlugins } from '@exodra/core';
  import { ExoDomBackend, createExoDelegatedEvents, withExoHydration } from '@exodra/dom';
  import type { TExoDomMachine } from '@exodra/dom';

  declare const PAGE: TExoDomMachine;

  /** ONE pack and ONE backend for the application, both at module level. */
  const DELEGATED = createExoDelegatedEvents(['click', 'input']);
  const backend = withExoHydration(
      composeExoPlugins(new ExoDomBackend(), { events: () => DELEGATED })
  );

  const root = document.getElementById('app') as HTMLElement;

  // The same object serves both, so the two can never be composed differently:
  backend.hydrate(PAGE, root);
  ```

  `createExoDelegatedEvents` returns a `TExoEventsApi` — a value for the `events` field,
  not a plugin — which is why it is composed as the one-entry factory
  `() => DELEGATED`.

- **Hydration does not check every row.** It asks `findExoRowDisagreement` where the
  caller's component and the server's markup are two different moments, and not on
  a homogeneous reconciled list, where a mismatch is present on the first row or not at
  all. Call it yourself — in a test asserting the two backends agree, or in a bug
  report — as `findExoRowDisagreement(schema, root, backend)`; it returns a description of
  the first disagreement or `null`. The backend argument selects the same compiled
  plan the page renders through.

## Contexts across the two sides

`provide` / `inject` resolve identically on both backends, through the same
lookup function, because a component that resolved one value on the server and
another in the browser is a page that hydrates into different content than it
was served — and the divergence would be in the markup rather than in an error.

On the server the chain is a module-level frame, saved and restored around every
instance in a `finally`. In the browser the chain is a **value** and nothing is
written on any element: `provideExoContext` returns a new frame, the connector
stores it in `connector.context`, and every `one`, `list` and `build`
wired after it is handed that frame. A list captures the chain when it is wired, so
a row added an hour after hydration resolves what the page provided without reading
the document at all. Nothing is marked on an element, so a widget mounted by a
**separate** `render` call inherits nothing from the surrounding document and must
be handed the value.

## Moving state from the server to the client

The server and the client must draw the same instance from the same data, or
hydration repairs every port it disagrees with. The data travels in the response's
**state script**: the page puts it there with `setState` on `EXO_SSR_RESPONSE`, and
the client reads it back with `readExoStateScript()` before it adopts.

A page that takes its data as **params** has nothing else to do: the server renders
it with `renderExoPage(machine, { params })`, the wire records the params as state,
and the client hands the same object to `hydrate`.

```ts
import { createExoMachineBuilder, createExoSchema } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoMachineNode, TExoTextPort } from '@exodra/core';
import { EXO_SSR_RESPONSE, renderExoPage } from '@exodra/ssr';

type TGreeting = { readonly name: string };

const GREETING_SCHEMA = createExoSchema((b) => {
    let name!: TExoTextPort;
    b.el('h1', null, (h1) => {
        name = h1.textPort();
    });
    return { name };
});
const mGreeting = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoMachineNode, TGreeting>(GREETING_SCHEMA);
mGreeting.wire((c, greeting) => {
    c.inject(EXO_SSR_RESPONSE)?.setState('greeting', greeting);
    c.text(GREETING_SCHEMA.ports.name, greeting.name);
});
export const GREETING = mGreeting.done();

const page = renderExoPage(GREETING, { params: { name: 'Ada' } });
const documentHtml = page.renderDocument({ rootId: 'app' });
```

```ts
import { ExoDomBackend, withExoCompiler, withExoHydration } from '@exodra/dom';
import type { TExoDomNode } from '@exodra/dom';
import type { TExoMachine } from '@exodra/core';
import { readExoStateScript } from '@exodra/ssr';

type TGreeting = { readonly name: string };

declare const GREETING: TExoMachine<TExoDomNode, unknown, TGreeting>;

const backend = withExoHydration(withExoCompiler(new ExoDomBackend()));

const greeting = readExoStateScript()?.greeting as TGreeting;
backend.hydrate(GREETING, document.getElementById('app') as HTMLElement, greeting);
```

`c.inject(EXO_SSR_RESPONSE)` is `undefined` in the browser, so the same wire runs on
both sides and only the server records anything. State that is not a param — a
store the page reads from — is written the same way, from wherever the server
loaded it, and seeded into that store on the client from `readExoStateScript()`
**before** `hydrate`, so the effects' first draw sees the server's data.

## The `@exodra/ssr` toolkit

`ExoStrBackend.render` hands back the instance's markup and nothing else: no
doctype, no `<html>`, no `<head>`, no status, no headers, no state script.
`@exodra/ssr` is the rest of the response.

### `renderExoPage`

`renderExoPage(component, options?)` runs the same synchronous render with the
request installed as a context, and hands back the markup plus everything the
wiring said about the response:

```ts
import { renderExoPage } from '@exodra/ssr';
import type { TExoStrMachine } from '@exodra/string';

declare const PAGE: TExoStrMachine;

const page = renderExoPage(PAGE, { head: '<meta charset="utf-8">' });

page.html;                               // just the instances — what goes in the container
page.status;                             // what the page asked for, or 200
page.headers;                            // [{ name, value }, …]
page.head;                               // the seeded <head> markup, then what the page added
page.stateScript;                        // <script id="__EXODRA_STATE__">…</script>
page.state;                              // the same map, for a server that serialises it itself
page.renderDocument({ rootId: 'app' });  // the whole document
```

The ready-made strings sit beside the raw values on purpose: a server that owns
its own HTML shell splices `head`, `html` and `stateScript` into it, and a server
that does not calls `renderDocument()`.

`options` is what the server already knows before the page runs — `status`,
`headers`, `head` (markup, and the natural home for the charset, the viewport and
the stylesheet link), `state`, `backend`, and `params`, which is handed to the page
machine's `wire` exactly as `backend.render(machine, parent, params)` does. Entries the page adds are
concatenated after the seeded ones, so the fixed ones stay first.

`backend` is the `ExoStrBackend` this page renders from. Left out, the page runs
on a backend composed with nothing. Name it when the application composed plugins — and name the
**same object** every request, because a plan is cached per backend by pointer and
one built per request recompiles every schema, markup parse included, on every
request.

### How a page talks to the request

The request is an ordinary context, so there is nothing new to learn: any initial
state under `renderExoPage` injects `EXO_SSR_RESPONSE` and gets a `TExoSsrResponse`.

```ts
import { createExoMachineBuilder, createExoSchema } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoMachineNode, TExoTextPort } from '@exodra/core';
import { EXO_SSR_RESPONSE } from '@exodra/ssr';

declare const user: { readonly name: string };

const NOT_FOUND_SCHEMA = createExoSchema((b) => {
    let heading!: TExoTextPort;
    b.el('main', { class: 'page' }, (main) => {
        main.el('h1', null, (h1) => {
            heading = h1.textPort();
        });
    });
    return { heading };
});
const mNotFound = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoMachineNode>(NOT_FOUND_SCHEMA);
mNotFound.createInitialState((c) => {
    const ssr = c.inject(EXO_SSR_RESPONSE);
    ssr?.setStatus(404);
    ssr?.setHeader('cache-control', 'no-store');
    ssr?.addHead('<title>Not found</title>');
    ssr?.setState('user', user);
});
mNotFound.wire((c) => {
    c.text(NOT_FOUND_SCHEMA.ports.heading, 'Not found');
});
export const NOT_FOUND = mNotFound.done();
```

| Method | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `setStatus(code)` / `getStatus()` | the HTTP status; 200 unless something asks otherwise |
| `setHeader(name, value)` | replace every header with this name, then append it |
| `appendHeader(name, value)` | add another value under this name (`Set-Cookie`) |
| `getHeader` / `getHeaderValues` / `getHeaders` | read them back; `getHeaders()` is a copy |
| `addHead(entry)` | one `<head>` entry, **as markup** |
| `renderHead()` | everything `addHead` collected, in arrival order |
| `setState(key, value)` / `getState(key)` / `getStateSnapshot()` | the map that becomes the state script |
| `renderStateScript(options?)` | that map as a `<script type="application/json">`, or `''` |

Two things this type deliberately does **not** have are `renderBody()` and
`renderDocument()`: an initial state runs *during* the render, so the body does not exist
yet, and one that assembled the document would get one with an empty container
and no error. Saying things about the response is the machine's job; assembling it is
`renderExoPage`'s.

`addHead` takes **markup**, not a component — so a head entry is either a literal
(`'<title>Home</title>'`) or a component rendered on the spot with
`server.render(TITLE)`, on the same `ExoStrBackend` the page uses.

`c.inject(EXO_SSR_RESPONSE)` outside `renderExoPage` is `undefined`, which is the honest
answer: a component rendered in the browser has no request to talk to.

For a server driving the render by hand — installing `EXO_SSR_RESPONSE` around something
other than `renderExoPage` — `ExoSsrResponse` is exported so the collectors are not
reimplemented.

### Matching the two sides

**There is no count to keep in step.** `renderExoPage` renders one instance and
`hydrate` adopts one instance; how many rows appear inside it is decided by the
page's own `c.list` / `reconcileExoOrder`, from the same data on both sides.

What still has to match is the **element**. The one `hydrate` takes is the
**container** `renderDocument` emitted — `document.getElementById('app')`, not its
first child: it adopts out of that parent's first *element* child, so handing it
one level too deep puts every port on the wrong node and throws nothing.

Read the state back on the client with `readExoStateScript()` from the same package:

```ts
import { readExoStateScript } from '@exodra/ssr';

const state = readExoStateScript(); // undefined when the page transferred none
```

`readExoStateScript` lives in the server package because the protocol — the script's
id, its type, and how the JSON inside it is escaped — is decided there, and a
reader anywhere else is a second place that has to agree.

## Summary

1. Build a component, render it with `new ExoStrBackend().render(...)`, adopt it
   with `backend.hydrate(...)` on an `ExoDomBackend` wrapped in
   `withExoHydration` — same component, same arguments, and the event strategy
   travels with the backend rather than being passed again.
2. For head, status, headers and state, call `renderExoPage` from `@exodra/ssr` and
   let the page read the request through `c.inject(EXO_SSR_RESPONSE)`.
3. Put the data the client needs in the state script with `setState`, read it back
   with `readExoStateScript()`, and hand it to the page **before** you adopt.


==============================================================================
# Testing

A component is a **plain value** — no compiler, no transform, no runner plugin.
`createExoSchema(build)` and `createExoMachineBuilder(schema)` are function calls, so a test imports the
component and renders it, and the whole of this page up to the last section needs
nothing configured beyond a `document`.

Components written in [JSX](./jsx.md) do need the compiler in the transform
chain, because uncompiled JSX throws when it reaches the runtime — see
[Testing JSX components](#testing-jsx-components).

## Rendering into a DOM

Any runner that gives you a `document` works. Under Vitest that is
`environment: 'jsdom'` — [jsdom](https://github.com/jsdom/jsdom) is a DOM
implementation for Node, so `document` exists and you can assert against real
elements without a browser.

```ts
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
  test: { environment: 'jsdom' },
});
```

To scope jsdom to a single file instead of the whole config, put the pragma at
the top of that file:

```tsx
// @vitest-environment jsdom
```

Then render and assert:

```ts
import { createExoMachineBuilder, createExoSchema } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoTextPort } from '@exodra/core';
import { ExoDomBackend, withExoCompiler } from '@exodra/dom';
import type { TExoDomNode } from '@exodra/dom';
import { source } from '@exodra/test-utils';

declare const it: (name: string, fn: () => void) => void;
declare const expect: (value: unknown) => { toBe(other: unknown): void };

/** ONE backend for the suite, at module level — it is the plan cache key. */
const backend = withExoCompiler(new ExoDomBackend());

const label = source('a');

const LABEL_SCHEMA = createExoSchema((b) => {
    let text!: TExoTextPort;
    b.el('span', null, (span) => {
        text = span.textPort();
    });
    return { text };
});
const mLabel = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoDomNode>(LABEL_SCHEMA);
const showLabel = mLabel.transition((c) => {
    c.text(LABEL_SCHEMA.ports.text, label.getValue());
});
mLabel.effect((c) => {
    showLabel(c);
    return label.onChange(() => showLabel(c));
});
const LABEL = mLabel.done();

it('updates on setValue', () => {
    const host = document.createElement('div');
    const dispose = backend.render(LABEL, host);

    expect(host.querySelector('span')?.textContent).toBe('a');
    label.setValue('b');
    expect(host.querySelector('span')?.textContent).toBe('b');

    dispose();
});
```

`source(v)` from the private `@exodra/test-utils` package is a test double for
outside data: `getValue`, `setValue`, `onChange`, and `subscribers()` to assert
that a teardown left nothing behind. It is not published; outside this
repository any object with `getValue` and `onChange` plays the same part. The machine follows it with an **effect**
that draws first and then subscribes, returning the unsubscribe.

`backend.render` returns the disposer. Calling it in the test stops every
effect the render started — without that, a suite leaks a subscriber per test
and the leak only shows up as a later test seeing an unexpected update.

Build the backend **once**, at module level, in a test file as much as in an
application: it is the key a compiled schema plan is cached under and it is
compared by pointer, so one constructed inside each `it` recompiles every schema —
markup parse included — on every case.

## Asserting on markup instead

For a browser-free assertion, render the **same component** through
`@exodra/string` and assert on the string. This is faster than a DOM and it is
also the strongest check the codebase has, because the two backends only agree
while their port numbering agrees:

```ts
import { createExoMachineBuilder, createExoSchema } from '@exodra/core';
import type {
    TExoAttrPort,
    TExoChildrenPort,
    TExoChildrenWiring,
    TExoMachineNode,
} from '@exodra/core';
import { ExoStrBackend } from '@exodra/string';

declare const it: (name: string, fn: () => void) => void;
declare const expect: (value: unknown) => { toBe(other: unknown): void };

const server = new ExoStrBackend();

const ROW_SCHEMA = createExoSchema((b) => {
    let id!: TExoAttrPort;
    b.el('li', { class: 'row' }, (li) => {
        id = li.port('data-id');
    });
    return { id };
});
const mRow = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoMachineNode, unknown, number>(ROW_SCHEMA);
mRow.createInitialState((_c, i) => i);
mRow.wire((c) => {
    c.attr(ROW_SCHEMA.ports.id, c.state);
});
const ROW = mRow.done();

/**
 * TWO ROWS IS A LIST, NOT A COUNT ON THE ENTRY POINT. `render` mounts ONE instance
 * of its component; anything that repeats is a children port, and `c.list` is the
 * fixed form of one. Row `i` is handed the number `i` as its index, which is what
 * the initial state above reads.
 */
const LIST_SCHEMA = createExoSchema((b) => {
    let rows!: TExoChildrenPort;
    b.el('ul', null, (ul) => {
        rows = ul.childrenPort();
    });
    return { rows };
});
const mList = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoChildrenWiring & TExoMachineNode>(LIST_SCHEMA);
mList.createInitialState((c) => {
    c.list(LIST_SCHEMA.ports.rows, ROW, 2);
});
const LIST = mList.done();

it('renders one li per row', () => {
    expect(server.render(LIST)).toBe(
        '<ul><li class="row" data-id="0"></li><li class="row" data-id="1"></li></ul>'
    );
});
```

## Testing hydration

A hydration test is three lines, and it is the one that catches a port-numbering
drift before users do: serve the markup, adopt it, assert the markup did not
change and the listeners work.

```ts
import { ExoStrBackend } from '@exodra/string';
import { ExoDomBackend, withExoHydration, withExoCompiler } from '@exodra/dom';
import type { TExoMachine, TExoMachineNode } from '@exodra/core';

declare const it: (name: string, fn: () => void) => void;
declare const expect: (value: unknown) => { toBe(other: unknown): void };
// ONE type, not an intersection of two backends'. `TExoMachineNode` is the surface all
// three backends share; `TExoStrMachine` and `TExoDomMachine` are
// this same generic with a backend's node TYPE in it, and a transition's node
// parameter is contravariant, so this value satisfies both.
declare const APP: TExoMachine<TExoMachineNode>;


const server = new ExoStrBackend();
/** `hydrate` exists only on a backend composed with the hydration pack. */
const backend = withExoHydration(withExoCompiler(new ExoDomBackend()));

it('adopts its own server output without touching it', () => {
    const host = document.createElement('div');
    host.innerHTML = server.render(APP);
    const before = host.innerHTML;

    backend.hydrate(APP, host);

    expect(host.innerHTML).toBe(before);
});
```

Compose `withExoHydration` onto the **same** backend the test renders with.
That is not a formality: the composition decides how listeners attach and what
owns every adopted region, and hydrating under a different one is the failure the
one-object design exists to make unspellable — nothing throws, and the wrong
reconciler simply owns the tree from then on. A backend composed *without* the
pack has no `hydrate` at all, so getting this wrong is a compile error rather than
a call landing on `undefined`.

`findExoRowDisagreement(schema, root, backend)` from `@exodra/dom` is the explicit version
of that assertion: it returns a description of the first disagreement between an
element and a schema, or `null`. The backend argument is there to select the same
compiled plan the page renders through.

## Testing JSX components

`@exodra/babel-plugin-schema` replaces every `exoJsx(…)` with a module-level
schema declaration. So a test that runs uncompiled JSX does not render the wrong
thing, it throws — the JSX runtime exists precisely to fail with a sentence
naming the missing plugin.

Once the transform is in place, the machine built over a JSX schema **is** the
component value the rest of this page renders. Nothing about the assertions
changes.

### Vitest

Vitest uses Vite, so the [Vite plugin](../tooling/vite-plugin.md) already
compiles your components — add it to `vitest.config.ts` the same way you add it
to `vite.config.ts`:

```typescript
// vitest.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';
import exodra from '@exodra/vite-plugin';

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [exodra()],
  test: { environment: 'jsdom' },
});
```

Then render the machine and assert against the DOM:

```tsx
import { exoJsx } from '@exodra/jsx';
import { createExoMachineBuilder } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoAttrPort, TExoChildrenPort, TExoTextPort } from '@exodra/core';
import { ExoDomBackend, withExoCompiler } from '@exodra/dom';
import type { TExoDomNode } from '@exodra/dom';

declare const it: (name: string, fn: () => void) => void;
declare const expect: (value: unknown) => { toBe(other: unknown): void };

const backend = withExoCompiler(new ExoDomBackend());

const NAMES = ['Ada', 'Alan'];

const LABEL_SCHEMA = exoJsx<{ n: TExoAttrPort; name: TExoTextPort }>(($) => (
  <span data-n={$.n}>{$.name}</span>
));
const mLabel = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoDomNode, unknown, number>(LABEL_SCHEMA);
mLabel.createInitialState((_c, i) => i);
mLabel.wire((c) => {
  c.attr(LABEL_SCHEMA.ports.n, c.state);
  c.text(LABEL_SCHEMA.ports.name, `Hi ${NAMES[c.state]}!`);
});
const LABEL = mLabel.done();

const LABELS_SCHEMA = exoJsx<{ labels: TExoChildrenPort }>(($) => (
  <div>
    <$.labels />
  </div>
));
const mLabels = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoDomNode>(LABELS_SCHEMA);
mLabels.createInitialState((c) => {
  c.list(LABELS_SCHEMA.ports.labels, LABEL, NAMES.length);
  return null;
});
const LABELS = mLabels.done();

it('fills the text and attribute ports from the index', () => {
  const host = document.createElement('div');
  const dispose = backend.render(LABELS, host);

  const spans = host.querySelectorAll('span');
  expect(spans.length).toBe(2);
  expect(spans[1].textContent).toBe('Hi Alan!');
  expect(spans[1].getAttribute('data-n')).toBe('1');

  dispose();
});
```

### Jest

Jest compiles Exodra JSX through `babel-jest` (its default Babel transform),
which picks up `babel.config.js` automatically. Add the
[Babel preset](../tooling/babel-preset.md):

```javascript
// babel.config.js
module.exports = { presets: ['exodra'] };
```

Set the test environment in `jest.config.js`:

```javascript
// jest.config.js
module.exports = { testEnvironment: 'jsdom' };
```

:::warning ts-jest / @swc/jest do not work
`ts-jest` and `@swc/jest` do **not** run Babel plugins, so they cannot compile
Exodra JSX. If Jest reports an unexpected token on `<`, or *"namespace tags are
not supported"* on `on:click`, switch the transform to `babel-jest` and add the
preset above. (SWC users can instead use the [SWC plugin](../tooling/swc-plugin.md).)
:::


==============================================================================
# React Interop

Two packages, one for each direction. They are separate so a React app can adopt
Exodra — or an Exodra app can embed React — without installing the other
direction, and so both resolve the same `@exodra/*` instances through peer
dependencies instead of each pinning its own copy.

| Package | Direction |
| --- | --- |
| [`@exodra/react`](#react-inside-exodra) | a React component inside an Exodra component |
| [`@exodra/react-mount`](#exodra-inside-react) | an Exodra component inside a React tree |
| [`@exodra/react-compat`](./react-compat.md) | React code running on Exodra |
| [`@exodra/to-react`](./to-react.md) | Exodra code translated into plain React |

## React inside Exodra

```bash
npm install @exodra/react
# peers you already have in a React-interop app:
npm install react react-dom
```

`react` and `react-dom` are **peer dependencies** — Exodra never pulls in React;
you only pay for it where you use an island.

`reactIsland` is a **wiring helper**, in the shape `writeExoChoice` from
`@exodra/forms` has — a function of the exonode and ports your schema declared:
you declare the host element and its children port in the schema, call this
from the machine's initial state, and keep the handle it returns. `render(props)`
on that handle re-renders the island; a transition or an effect calls it.

```ts
import { createExoMachineBuilder, createExoSchema } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoChildrenPort, TExoMachineNode } from '@exodra/core';
import { reactIsland } from '@exodra/react';
import type { TExoReactIsland } from '@exodra/react';
import type { ComponentType } from 'react';

type TChartProps = { readonly series: readonly number[]; readonly theme: string };

declare const FancyChart: ComponentType<TChartProps>;

const chartProps = {
    value: { series: [], theme: 'dark' } as TChartProps,
    listeners: new Set<() => void>(),
    getValue(): TChartProps {
        return this.value;
    },
    setValue(next: TChartProps): void {
        this.value = next;
        for (const listener of Array.from(this.listeners)) listener();
    },
    onChange(listener: () => void): () => void {
        this.listeners.add(listener);
        return () => {
            this.listeners.delete(listener);
        };
    },
};

const CHART_SCHEMA = createExoSchema((b) => {
    let host!: TExoChildrenPort;
    b.el('div', { 'data-exo-react': '' }, (div) => {
        host = div.childrenPort();
    });
    return { host };
});
const mChart = createExoMachineBuilder<
    TExoMachineNode,
    unknown,
    { island: TExoReactIsland<TChartProps> }
>(CHART_SCHEMA);
mChart.createInitialState((c) => ({
    island: reactIsland(c, CHART_SCHEMA.ports.host, FancyChart, chartProps.getValue()),
}));
const showChart = mChart.transition((c) => {
    c.state.island.render(chartProps.getValue());
});
mChart.effect((c) => chartProps.onChange(() => showChart(c)));
const CHART = mChart.done();

// Later — one change re-renders the island with the latest props:
chartProps.setValue({ series: [1, 2, 3], theme: 'light' });
```

Exodra owns the host element; React owns everything inside it.

**The port must be its element's only child.** That restriction is the DOM
backend's rather than this package's: a children port that owns all of its
element's content is the one shape raw markup can be written into without
deleting a sibling — and a host element is that by construction.

### Props

Pass a plain props object for a static island, or anything with `getValue()` and
`onChange()` — which a bindable satisfies — for a reactive one. Every emit
re-renders the island with the latest value. Reactivity collapses to "re-render
this island" at the boundary, which is React's own model rather than a limitation
of the bridge.

### All three backends, from the one call

The helper asks the **connector** which backend is filling, not the environment —
`typeof document === 'undefined'` is wrong twice over, since a server suite under
jsdom has a `document` and no element to mount into.

- **Server:** the component is rendered to HTML and written into the port, so the
  island's content is in the initial payload (SEO, no layout shift).
- **Hydration:** the served markup is found in the host and handed to
  `hydrateRoot` — React taking over the server's DOM in place. Exodra writes
  nothing into the host itself.
- **Client render:** the host is empty, so the island mounts fresh with
  `createRoot`.

Which of the last two runs is decided by what is already in the host, and nothing
else can decide it: hydration and a client render run the **same** machine, so the
markup is the only evidence of which one produced this element.

`{ ssr: false }` makes an island client-only — an empty host on the server,
`createRoot` in the browser:

```ts
import type { TExoChildrenPort } from '@exodra/core';
import { reactIsland } from '@exodra/react';
import type { TExoDomNode } from '@exodra/dom';
import type { ComponentType } from 'react';

declare const c: TExoDomNode;
declare const host: TExoChildrenPort;
declare const Chart: ComponentType<Record<string, never>>;

reactIsland(c, host, Chart, {}, { ssr: false });
```

### Cleanup

The React root and the props subscription are registered against the child being
wired, so disposing the mount — or removing the list row the island sits in —
unmounts React and drops the subscription. Emits after that are ignored.

### Exports

- `reactIsland(connector, port, Component, props, options?)`
- Types: `TExoReactIslandOptions`, `TExoReactWiring`,
  `TExoReactDomWiring`, `TExoReadableSource`

### Notes & limits

- **Context does not cross the boundary.** Exodra `provide` / `inject` and React
  Context are separate — pass anything an island needs through its props.
- **One React root per island.** Prefer a few larger islands over many tiny ones.
- Server rendering pulls in `react-dom/server`. Use `{ ssr: false }` where you do
  not need it.

## Exodra inside React

```bash
npm install @exodra/react-mount
```

`useExoMount(component, options?)` returns `{ ref, node }`: `ref` goes on a
container element, and `node` holds the island's exonode once it is mounted.
React renders that element and never looks inside it again; Exodra builds,
updates and tears down everything below. The two never diff the same nodes, which
is what makes the boundary safe rather than a race.

<!-- no-check: React JSX, whose ref/prop types this repo's doc gate has not been pointed at. -->

```tsx no-check
/** @jsxImportSource react */
import { useExoMount } from '@exodra/react-mount';
import type { TExoDomMachine } from '@exodra/dom';

declare const CHART: TExoDomMachine;
declare const seriesId: string;

export function Chart() {
  const { ref } = useExoMount<HTMLElement>(CHART, { deps: [seriesId] });
  return <figure ref={ref} />;
}
```

`ExoMount` is the component form of the same thing:

<!-- no-check: React JSX, whose ref/prop types this repo's doc gate has not been pointed at. -->

```tsx no-check
/** @jsxImportSource react */
import { ExoMount } from '@exodra/react-mount';
import type { TExoDomMachine } from '@exodra/dom';

declare const CHART: TExoDomMachine;

export function Panel() {
  return <ExoMount component={CHART} className="chart" />;
}
```

### Options

| Option | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `hydrate` | adopt server markup already in the container instead of building; falls back to a fresh render when there is nothing to adopt |
| `params` | handed to the machine's `wire`. When they change — compared key by key, so a fresh object with the same values is no change — the wire re-runs on the same instance, without re-mounting |
| `deps` | re-mount when one of these changes, like a `useEffect` dependency array; defaults to "mount once" |
| `backend` | the backend this island renders from — the object your application composed. Left out, the island runs on this package's own, which composes `withExoHydration` because an island over server markup is what the package is for |

There is **no instance count**. `backend.render` mounts one instance, which is
exactly what an island is; rows that vary inside it are a list, filled by
`c.list` or by a transition calling `reconcileExoOrder` over `c.childList` in the component's own machine.

`ExoMount` takes those plus `html`, `className`, `id` and `style`. Passing `html`
(from `new ExoStrBackend().render(...)`) ships the markup inside the
server-rendered page and implies `hydrate`, so the first paint is the finished UI
and hydration only attaches behaviour.

:::caution A hydrating island needs the backend its markup was rendered from
Attaching listeners is the whole content of hydration, so the event strategy is
not a detail of it — and it is no longer a parameter that can disagree, because it
travels **with the backend**. Hand the island the same object the page rendered
from and the two cannot diverge; hand it a different one and every replaceable
decision inside the container changes with it.

`hydrate` is optional on that type because hydration is a **pack**: a backend
composed without `withExoHydration` genuinely has no `hydrate` method, and an
island given such a backend renders instead of adopting.

Pass the **same object** every time. A plan is cached per backend by pointer, so a
backend constructed in the component body is a new key on every render and
recompiles every schema in the island — markup parse included. Build it once, at
module level.
:::

### Params

A React parent passes values in through `params`; the machine reads them in its
`wire`, which runs once after `createInitialState` and again on every change:

<!-- no-check: React JSX, whose ref/prop types this repo's doc gate has not been pointed at. -->

```tsx no-check
/** @jsxImportSource react */
import { ExoMount } from '@exodra/react-mount';

export function Profile({ name }: { name: string }) {
  return <ExoMount component={GREETING} params={{ name }} />;
}
```

The instance is built with `backend.buildRoot` and placed with
`backend.mountRoot` (see [Build, then mount](../api/dom.md#build-then-mount));
a params change is `wireExoNode(node, GREETING, params)` on that same node, so
the elements, the machine state and the effects all stay.

Two limits come from the machine, not from this package:

- a machine with **no `wire`** has nothing to re-run, so a params change
  re-mounts it;
- a wire that **opens children** (`childList`, `one`, `list`) refuses a re-run
  with `EXO0103` — open them in `createInitialState`.

To reach the instance from React — to fire a transition from a React event
handler — read `node.current` from the hook:

<!-- no-check: React JSX, whose ref/prop types this repo's doc gate has not been pointed at. -->

```tsx no-check
/** @jsxImportSource react */
export function Greeting() {
  const { ref, node } = useExoMount<HTMLDivElement>(GREETING, { params: { name: 'Ann' } });
  return (
    <>
      <div ref={ref} />
      <button onClick={() => shout(node.current as never)}>shout</button>
    </>
  );
}
```

### What the component may be

`TExoMountSource` is a component **or a function returning one**. The plain value
is the normal thing to pass: `createExoSchema` builds the schema once at module

load, so there is nothing to rebuild per mount. The function form is how a
component gets *chosen* — `() => tab === 'chart' ? CHART : TABLE` — and it runs
once per mount, never per React render, with `deps` deciding when that choice is
made again.

### Cleanup

The effect's cleanup calls the disposer `backend.mountRoot` returned
and then empties the container. Emptying it is this package's job specifically because
its contract is that React owns the container and Exodra owns everything inside
it; without it, a `deps` change would append a second copy beside the first.

## Links

- npm: [`@exodra/react`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@exodra/react) ·
  [`@exodra/react-mount`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@exodra/react-mount)
- GitHub: [`packages/react`](https://github.com/abaikov/exodra/tree/master/packages/react) ·
  [`packages/react-mount`](https://github.com/abaikov/exodra/tree/master/packages/react-mount)


==============================================================================
# React Code on Exodra

`@exodra/react-compat` implements React's public API on Exodra machines. You alias
`react` and `react-dom` to it, and an existing React application — its components,
its hooks, the libraries it installs from npm — runs with Exodra as the renderer.
There is no virtual DOM: every host tag is an Exodra machine with a schema, and a
re-render writes into the same DOM nodes through that machine.

This is the third direction next to the two packages on the
[React Interop](./react.md) page. Those put an island of one framework inside the
other; this one replaces React underneath code that was written for React.

| What you install | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `@exodra/react-compat` | the runtime: `react`, `react-dom`, `react-dom/client`, `react-dom/server` and the JSX runtime, aliased to it |
| `@exodra/babel-plugin-schema/react` | optional compiler: host JSX in **your** files becomes a hoisted Exodra schema instead of a `jsx()` call per element |

## Install

```bash
npm install @exodra/react-compat
# peers:
npm install @exodra/core @exodra/dom @exodra/list-reconcile
```

`@exodra/core`, `@exodra/dom` and `@exodra/list-reconcile` are peer dependencies;
nothing is bundled into the package.

The package has these entry points:

| Entry | Stands in for |
| --- | --- |
| `@exodra/react-compat` | `react`, and also `react-dom` (it carries `createPortal`, `flushSync`, `findDOMNode`, `unstable_batchedUpdates` and the root functions too) |
| `@exodra/react-compat/client` | `react-dom/client` |
| `@exodra/react-compat/server` | `react-dom/server` |
| `@exodra/react-compat/jsx-runtime` | `react/jsx-runtime` |
| `@exodra/react-compat/jsx-dev-runtime` | `react/jsx-dev-runtime` (the same module as `jsx-runtime`) |

## Aliasing `react` to it

Every import of `react` and `react-dom` in your code **and in your dependencies**
has to land on the compat package, and on one copy of it: the runtime keeps its
render queue in module state, so two instances would be two renderers that do not
see each other's components. Alias to the package name, not to a file inside it,
so code compiled by the plugin below (which imports `@exodra/react-compat`
directly) and code that imports `react` reach the same module.

### Vitest

This is the configuration the repository runs fifteen React libraries under
(`packages/react-compat-libraries/vitest.config.ts`, which points the aliases at
the source files of the workspace packages instead of the package names):

```js
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';

export default defineConfig({
    oxc: { jsx: { runtime: 'automatic', importSource: 'react' } },
    resolve: {
        alias: [
            { find: /^react$/, replacement: '@exodra/react-compat' },
            { find: /^react\/jsx-runtime$/, replacement: '@exodra/react-compat/jsx-runtime' },
            { find: /^react\/jsx-dev-runtime$/, replacement: '@exodra/react-compat/jsx-dev-runtime' },
            { find: /^react-dom$/, replacement: '@exodra/react-compat' },
            { find: /^react-dom\/client$/, replacement: '@exodra/react-compat/client' },
            { find: /^react-dom\/server$/, replacement: '@exodra/react-compat/server' },
        ],
    },
    test: {
        environment: 'jsdom',
        server: { deps: { inline: true } },
        deps: {
            optimizer: {
                client: {
                    enabled: true,
                    // the React libraries your tests import, e.g. 'react-redux', 'swr'
                    include: ['react-redux', 'swr'],
                    exclude: ['react', 'react/jsx-runtime', 'react/jsx-dev-runtime', 'react-dom', 'react-dom/client'],
                },
            },
        },
    },
});
```

The optimizer settings are not decoration. Many libraries ship CommonJS that calls
`require('react')`; Node's native `require` does not go through Vite's aliases and
would load real React. Pre-bundling those libraries turns the `require` into an
import the alias can reach. The `react` ids themselves are excluded so that they
stay aliased instead of being bundled.

**styled-components needs two extra steps.** Pre-bundled, its default export
arrives wrapped in the module namespace, so it is left out of `include`, and it is
aliased to its browser ESM build, which imports `react` as ESM:

```js
import { fileURLToPath } from 'node:url';

const styledComponentsAlias = {
    find: /^styled-components$/,
    replacement: fileURLToPath(
        new URL(
            './node_modules/styled-components/dist/styled-components.browser.esm.js',
            import.meta.url
        )
    ),
};
```

Add `styledComponentsAlias` to `resolve.alias` above, and leave `styled-components`
out of `deps.optimizer.client.include`.

### Vite

The same alias list goes under `resolve.alias` in `vite.config.js`:

```js
import { defineConfig } from 'vite';

export default defineConfig({
    resolve: {
        alias: [
            { find: /^react$/, replacement: '@exodra/react-compat' },
            { find: /^react\/jsx-runtime$/, replacement: '@exodra/react-compat/jsx-runtime' },
            { find: /^react\/jsx-dev-runtime$/, replacement: '@exodra/react-compat/jsx-dev-runtime' },
            { find: /^react-dom$/, replacement: '@exodra/react-compat' },
            { find: /^react-dom\/client$/, replacement: '@exodra/react-compat/client' },
            { find: /^react-dom\/server$/, replacement: '@exodra/react-compat/server' },
        ],
    },
});
```

The repository's own Vite app (`packages/benchmarks`) does not use these aliases:
it rewrites the `react` imports of one React source file per row instead, because
the same file runs on several React implementations side by side. So the alias
form above is the Vitest list moved into a Vite config, not a configuration this
repository runs; a plain application has one implementation and wants the aliases.

### webpack

```js
module.exports = {
    resolve: {
        alias: {
            react$: '@exodra/react-compat',
            'react/jsx-runtime$': '@exodra/react-compat/jsx-runtime',
            'react/jsx-dev-runtime$': '@exodra/react-compat/jsx-dev-runtime',
            'react-dom$': '@exodra/react-compat',
            'react-dom/client$': '@exodra/react-compat/client',
            'react-dom/server$': '@exodra/react-compat/server',
        },
    },
};
```

The trailing `$` makes each key an exact match, so `react` does not also capture
`react/jsx-runtime`. Nothing in this repository builds with webpack; the shape is
webpack's standard alias form applied to the same six entries.

### Your code does not change

```tsx
/** @jsxImportSource react */
import { useState } from 'react';
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

function Counter() {
    const [n, setN] = useState(0);
    return <button onClick={() => setN(n + 1)}>clicked {n}</button>;
}

createRoot(document.getElementById('root')!).render(<Counter />);
```

With the aliases in place this file runs on Exodra as written, through the
automatic JSX runtime. The compiler below is optional.

## The compiler: `@exodra/babel-plugin-schema/react`

Without the compiler, every JSX element is a `jsx()` call at runtime, and each host
tag (`div`, `li`, …) is served by one generic machine per tag name, built on first
use and cached. With the compiler, a tree of host elements in your source becomes
**one schema per tree, hoisted to module scope** and built once per process, with
ports for exactly the parts that can change.

```bash
npm install -D @exodra/babel-plugin-schema @babel/core @babel/plugin-syntax-jsx
```

```js
// babel.config.js
module.exports = {
    plugins: ['@babel/plugin-syntax-jsx', '@exodra/babel-plugin-schema/react'],
};
```

The plugin replaces **every** JSX element and fragment in the files it transforms,
so those files need no other JSX transform. Babel runs plugins before presets, so
in a TypeScript project your TypeScript preset can stay where it is.

It takes two options, both with defaults:

| Option | Default | What it names |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `importSource` | `'@exodra/react-compat'` | where the compiled code imports the host runtime and `jsx` / `Fragment` (from `<importSource>/jsx-runtime`) |
| `schemaSource` | `'@exodra/core'` | where it imports `createExoSchema` |

### What gets compiled

A JSX element is compiled into a schema when its tag is a lowercase HTML or SVG
name (letters and digits only) and every attribute is a plain named attribute.
Nested elements that qualify join the same schema. Inside one:

- a literal attribute (`className="row"`, `width={10}`) is written into the schema
  once, as a static attribute;
- an expression attribute (`title={label}`) becomes an attribute port, written
  only when its value changed since the last render;
- an event handler (`onClick={…}`) becomes an event port whose handler is swapped
  on each render, with no listener re-attached;
- `style`, `value`, `checked`, `selected`, `defaultValue`, `defaultChecked`,
  `muted`, `indeterminate`, `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` and `ref`, and the handlers
  of a controlled `input` / `textarea` / `select` and every `…Capture` handler, go
  through the same props writer the runtime uses for uncompiled elements;
- literal text is written into the schema; an expression child becomes a children
  port reconciled at runtime, so components, lists and conditionals inside a
  compiled tree work as usual.

Everything else stays a runtime `jsx()` call: components (`<Badge />`), fragments,
member tags (`<Dialog.Root>`), custom elements (`<my-element>`), and a host element
with a spread (`{...props}`), a namespaced attribute or a `children` attribute. The
children of such an element are still visited, so a compilable tree below a spread
is compiled.

### Compiled elements are still elements

A compiled tree evaluates to an element object, not to a node. Its `type` is the
tag name and its `props` are built on first read, so the code that inspects
children keeps working:

```tsx
/** @jsxImportSource react */
import { Children, cloneElement, type ReactElement } from 'react';

type TTabsProps = { children: ReactElement<{ className: string }>[]; active: number };

function Tabs({ children, active }: TTabsProps) {
    return (
        <nav>
            {Children.map(children, (child, i) =>
                cloneElement(child, {
                    className: child.props.className + (i === active ? ' on' : ''),
                })
            )}
        </nav>
    );
}
```

Each `<a className="tab">` passed to `Tabs` is compiled, `child.props.className`
reads `'tab'`, and the clone renders with the merged class.

## How fast it is

On the benchmark application — an 80-card board written once as ordinary React and
run unchanged on React 19 and on this package, with byte-identical markup checked
before any timing — the compiled path mounts faster than React in every run that
measured both:

<!-- gate: unrecorded col=2 cmd="node scripts/run-one-axis.js initial-render 60 20 --only=exodra,react,reactCompat,reactCompatJsx,solid (narrowed; compat3/compat4 add reactCompatTemplates)" date=2026-10-31 -->
<!-- gate: unrecorded col=3 cmd="node scripts/run-one-axis.js initial-render 60 20 --only=exodra,react,reactCompat,reactCompatJsx,solid (narrowed; compat3/compat4 add reactCompatTemplates)" date=2026-10-31 -->
| run | compiled | React | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| `initial-render.compat1` | 1.065 ms | 1.225 ms | 1.15× faster |
| `initial-render.compat2` | 0.905 ms | 1.065 ms | 1.18× faster |
| `initial-render.compat3` | 0.850 ms | 0.995 ms | 1.17× faster |
| `initial-render.compat4` | 0.890 ms | 1.140 ms | 1.28× faster |

On updates it is ahead of React in all three runs that carried both
(`app-update.compat1`, `compat2`, `compat4`); that axis reports order only. The
runs are narrowed to the React family, Solid and Exodra, so only the ratios inside
a run are comparable. The plain runtime, without the compiler or host templates,
is behind React on both axes. The full account is the post
[Your React Code, Faster Than React](/blog/react-on-exodra-faster-than-react).

## Host templates, without the compiler

When the compiler is not in the build, the runtime can do the same job itself.
`enableExoReactHostTemplates()` turns it on for the whole application:

```ts
import { createElement, createRoot, enableExoReactHostTemplates } from '@exodra/react-compat';

enableExoReactHostTemplates();

function Card({ title }: { title: string }) {
    return createElement('article', null, createElement('h2', null, title), createElement('p', null, 'body'));
}

createRoot(document.getElementById('root')!).render(createElement(Card, { title: 'Hello' }));
```

The first time a component returns a tree of host elements, the runtime builds
one schema for that shape and caches it on the component. Every later instance
of the same shape is one machine with a port per prop and per text, instead of a
machine per DOM element. A list (an array of keyed elements of one type) and
anything that is not a host element stays a region the reconciler handles as
before.

Measured on the benchmark application (`initial-render.compat4`, narrowed run,
ratios only): mounting took 0.990 ms with templates, 1.330 without them and
1.140 in React. On `app-update` (`app-update.compat4`) the axis reports no
resolution, so only the order is known: templates ahead of React, the plain
runtime behind it.

**It is off by default because of one difference from React.** If a component
changes the shape of a tree it already rendered — a host element appears where
there was none, or a fixed-position key changes — the cached template no longer
fits. The runtime then builds a merged template that fits both shapes, and an
instance still on the old one is rebuilt once. React would keep the unchanged
siblings; here they are replaced, so focus or text typed into an uncontrolled
input inside that subtree is lost the one time it happens.

## What is supported

Everything below is exported and implemented; the names are the ones React uses.

**`react`**

| Area | Names |
| --- | --- |
| Elements | `createElement`, `cloneElement`, `isValidElement`, `Children` (`map`, `forEach`, `count`, `toArray`, `only`), `Fragment`, `StrictMode`, `createRef`, `version` |
| Components | `memo` (with an optional compare function), `forwardRef`, `lazy`, `Suspense`, `Profiler`, `Component`, `PureComponent` |
| Context | `createContext` with `Provider` and `Consumer`; the context object itself works as a provider (`<Theme value={…}>`) |
| State hooks | `useState`, `useReducer`, `useRef`, `useMemo`, `useCallback`, `useContext`, `useId`, `useSyncExternalStore`, `useImperativeHandle`, `useDebugValue` |
| Effect hooks | `useEffect`, `useLayoutEffect`, `useInsertionEffect` |
| Async | `use` (a promise or a context), `startTransition`, `useTransition`, `useDeferredValue`, `useOptimistic`, `useActionState` |
| Testing | `act` |

**`react-dom` / `react-dom/client`**: `createRoot`, `hydrateRoot`, `createPortal`,
`flushSync`, `findDOMNode`, `unstable_batchedUpdates`.

**`react-dom/server`**: `renderToString`, `renderToStaticMarkup`.

**`react/jsx-runtime`**: `jsx`, `jsxs`, `jsxDEV`, `Fragment`.

How the parts behave:

- **Rendering.** `root.render(…)` renders synchronously and runs layout effects
  before it returns; `useEffect` callbacks run after it, on a later task.
  `setState` calls made together are batched into one render on a microtask.
  `flushSync` applies its updates, and their effects, before it returns. Keyed
  children are moved, not rebuilt, and a re-render keeps the same DOM nodes.
- **Effects.** Insertion effects run before refs are attached, refs before layout
  effects, and a child's effects before its parent's. Cleanups run when deps
  change and on unmount.
- **Class components.** `setState` (object or updater, with a callback),
  `forceUpdate`, `getDerivedStateFromProps`, `shouldComponentUpdate`,
  `PureComponent`'s shallow comparison, `getSnapshotBeforeUpdate`,
  `componentDidMount`, `componentDidUpdate`, `componentWillUnmount` and
  `static contextType`.
- **Error boundaries.** A class with `static getDerivedStateFromError` or
  `componentDidCatch` catches an error thrown while it renders its children and
  renders its fallback state.
- **Suspense.** A component may throw a promise, or call `use(promise)`; the
  nearest `<Suspense>` shows its `fallback` and renders the content once the
  promise settles. `lazy` works through the same path. Content that was already
  shown and suspends again is hidden (`display: none`), not unmounted, so its state
  survives. A suspension with no `<Suspense>` above it is an error.
- **Transitions.** An update inside `startTransition` is applied on a later task
  than a plain update. `useTransition` reports pending until it lands;
  `useDeferredValue` shows the previous value first, then the new one.
- **Events.** Handlers receive an event object that is the native event plus
  `nativeEvent`, `currentTarget`, `persist`, `isPersistent`, `isDefaultPrevented`
  and `isPropagationStopped`. `onDoubleClick` listens to `dblclick`, `onFocus` /
  `onBlur` to `focusin` / `focusout`, and `onChange` on `input` and `textarea` to
  `input`. `…Capture` handlers listen in the capture phase.
- **Forms.** A controlled `input` / `textarea` is put back to its `value` /
  `checked` after a handler that did not accept the edit; a controlled `select`
  takes its `value` after its options are placed.
- **Server.** `renderToString` runs function components with their hooks, class
  components, context, `memo` and `forwardRef`; it escapes text and attributes,
  drops event handlers, prints `style` objects as CSS text, and writes
  `defaultValue` / `defaultChecked` as `value` / `checked`.

### Libraries run on it

`packages/react-compat-libraries` runs one test per library twice — once on
`@exodra/react-compat` and once on React itself — with the same assertions:

| Library | What its test exercises |
| --- | --- |
| `react-router` | the matching route renders, a `Link` click navigates, `useNavigate` goes back |
| `@tanstack/react-query` | a query resolves into the DOM and a refetch replaces it |
| `swr` | a key resolves into the DOM and `mutate()` revalidates it |
| `zustand` | a selecting consumer re-renders on a store update and an unrelated one does not |
| `jotai` | an atom write reaches a reader and a derived atom |
| `react-redux` + `@reduxjs/toolkit` | a `useSelector` consumer re-renders after a dispatch from inside and outside the tree |
| `react-hook-form` | a validation error shows, then the typed values submit |
| `formik` | a controlled `Field` stays in state and the typed value submits |
| `@radix-ui/react-dialog` | the trigger opens the dialog into a portal, Escape closes it |
| `@headlessui/react` | a `Disclosure` panel and its `aria-expanded` toggle through the button |
| `@emotion/react` | a `css` prop becomes a class backed by an inserted `<style>`, and changes with it |
| `styled-components` | a styled element's class maps to an inserted rule and restyles on a prop change |
| `framer-motion` | a `motion.div` mounts with its initial style and animates to a new target |
| `react-window` | only the rows in view render, and the window shifts on scroll |
| `react-i18next` | `t()` renders a key and re-renders on a language change |

## What differs, and what is not there

These come from the implementation, not from a list of intentions. If your code
depends on one of them, it will behave differently on compat than on React.

**Hydration.** `hydrateRoot(container, element)` is a client render: it empties
the container and builds the tree from scratch. Server markup is replaced, not
adopted, and nothing compares it with the client output.

**Server output.** `renderToString` does not insert the `<!-- -->` separators
React puts between adjacent text children: `text, ' ', value` prints as
`a b`, not `a<!-- --> <!-- -->b`. `renderToStaticMarkup` is the same function.
There are no streaming renderers (`renderToPipeableStream`,
`renderToReadableStream`). On the server, a component that suspends throws out of
