`renderToString` — no fallback is printed — and class components are not handed
their `contextType` context. A `value` on a `<select>` is printed as an attribute
of the `select`; no `<option>` is marked `selected`.

**Events.** Each handler is a native listener on its own element, not a listener
at the root. Two consequences:

- Events follow the **DOM** tree. A click inside a portal bubbles to the portal's
  container and its DOM ancestors, not to the React parent that rendered the
  portal, so an `onClick` on that parent does not see it.
- React handlers interleave with `addEventListener` listeners in plain DOM order,
  and `stopPropagation()` stops the native event.

**Errors.** An error boundary catches what is thrown while the boundary itself
renders its subtree. A descendant that re-renders on its own state update is
rendered outside that pass, so an error it throws is not caught by the boundary
above it; it is thrown out of the flush (`act`, `flushSync`, or the microtask that
applied the update). An uncaught error does not unmount the root — the rest of the
tree stays mounted and keeps updating. `componentDidCatch` receives an empty
`componentStack`. Errors in effects and event handlers are not caught by
boundaries.

**Concurrency.** Rendering is synchronous and never interrupted. A transition
defers its update to a later task; it does not render in the background, and an
urgent update does not abandon a transition's render half-way.

**APIs that are accepted but do nothing.** `StrictMode` is a `Fragment`: nothing
is rendered or run twice. `Profiler` renders its children and never calls
`onRender`. `useDebugValue` is a no-op. `unstable_batchedUpdates` calls its
function; batching happens anyway.

**Narrower signatures.** `createRoot`, `hydrateRoot` and `renderToString` take
one option, `identifierPrefix`, and no other. `useSyncExternalStore` takes no
`getServerSnapshot`.

**`useId`** counts through `nextExoId` from `@exodra/context`: every root and
every `renderToString` call starts its own count at `0`, so the server and
hydration hand out the same ids. The format is `:r-0`, `:r-1`, … — not React's
`:r0:` — and two roots on one page need different `identifierPrefix` values.

**Refs.** A function component does not receive `ref` among its props; use
`forwardRef`. A callback ref is called with `null` on removal; a cleanup function
it returns is not called. A compiled host element reports `element.ref` as
`null`, because its ref travels with its values; `cloneElement` reads the ref it
was written with and keeps it.

**Class lifecycles that are not called.** `componentWillMount`,
`componentWillReceiveProps`, `componentWillUpdate` and their `UNSAFE_` forms.

**`defaultProps`** is applied to every component type, function components
included.

**Not exported.** `useFormStatus`, `useEffectEvent`, `cache`, `Activity`,
`preload` / `preinit` and the legacy `render` / `hydrate` /
`unmountComponentAtNode`. A function passed as a form's `action` is not supported.

**Library code is not compiled.** The compiler only transforms files that go
through your Babel config. Libraries in `node_modules` arrive already built, so
their elements are `createElement` / `jsx()` calls served by the per-tag runtime
machines. They render correctly, without the per-tree schema the compiler gives
your own components.


==============================================================================
# Translating Exodra Code to React

`@exodra/to-react` reads Exodra source — `exoJsx` schemas and the machines built
on them — and writes plain React components that render the same DOM. Code
written on Exodra keeps running without it.

```bash
npm install --save-dev @exodra/to-react
```

```ts
import { translateExoToReact } from '@exodra/to-react';

declare const source: string;

const translation = translateExoToReact(source, 'Counter.tsx');
translation.code;        // the React module
translation.runtime;     // helper module source, or null when nothing needs it
translation.unsupported; // what could not be translated, one line each
```

`translateExoToReact(source, fileName?, runtimePath?)` returns:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `code` | the translated module. It imports from `react` and, when needed, from `runtimePath` (default `./exo-react-runtime`) |
| `runtime` | the source of that helper module — write it next to the translated file. `null` when the translation uses none of it |
| `unsupported` | every construct that has no React form, named with where it was found. An empty list is the only case where the output is complete |

The helpers are plain React and depend on nothing from Exodra: `buildExoChild`,
`wireExoChild`, `createExoChildren`, `reconcileExoOrder` and `exoStyleObject`.

## What a machine becomes

One machine — `createExoMachineBuilder(SCHEMA)` through `m.done()` — becomes one
function component, exported under a PascalCase name and under the machine's
original constant name:

```tsx no-check
export function Counter({ index = 0, params }: { index?: number; params?: unknown }) { … }
export const COUNTER = Counter;
```

| Exodra | React |
| --- | --- |
| every attribute, text, children and html port | a `useState` pair |
| a ref port | a `useRef` |
| the machine state | a `useRef` |
| `m.transition(fn)` | an inner function of the component |
| `m.on(port, fn)` | the handler prop on the element that declared the event port |
| `m.createInitialState(fn)` | a `useLayoutEffect` that runs once |
| `m.wire(fn)` | a `useLayoutEffect` that re-runs when `params` changes |
| `m.effect(fn)` | a `useEffect` that runs once |
| `c.onTeardown(off)` | collected and called on unmount |

Inside those functions:

| Exodra call | React form |
| --- | --- |
| `c.text`, `c.attr`, `c.unsafeHtml` | the port's state setter |
| `c.on(port, handler)` | stores the handler in state |
| `c.state`, `c.readState()` | the state ref's `current` |
| `c.childList(port)` | `createExoChildren(setter)` |
| `c.build(MACHINE, index, params)` | `buildExoChild(Component, index, params)` |
| `c.one`, `c.list` | the port's state setter with built children |
| `wireExoNode(node, MACHINE, params)` | `wireExoChild(child, Component, params)` — the row re-renders with the new `params` |
| `reconcileExoOrder(…)` from `@exodra/list-reconcile` | the helper of the same name and signature; a row that survives keeps its React key, so React keeps its DOM element |

In the schema, `class` becomes `className`, `on:event` and `onEvent` become
the React handler prop (`dblclick` → `onDoubleClick`, `focusout` → `onBlur`), a
static `value`/`checked` becomes `defaultValue`/`defaultChecked`, a static
`style` string becomes a style object, and `unsafeHtml` becomes
`dangerouslySetInnerHTML`.

## What it does not translate

Everything below lands in `unsupported` instead of in wrong code:

- a schema written with `createExoSchema` (the cursor form); only `exoJsx` is read;
- an `exoJsx` body that is not one returned element;
- any machine step other than `createInitialState`, `wire`, `effect`, `on`,
  `transition` and `done` — `transitionOverrides` among them;
- any connector call outside the tables above;
- an exonode passed around as a value, other than to the calls above;
- a machine whose schema is not declared in the same file.

## How it is checked

The package's tests compile one source both ways — the original through
`@exodra/babel-plugin-schema` onto the DOM backend, the translation through
React — and compare `innerHTML` after every click: a counter, and a list that
adds, reverses and re-wires a row through `wireExoNode`. A row that survives a
reorder is the same DOM element on both sides.


==============================================================================
# AI-Assisted Development

Exodra is unusually friendly to AI tools, and that's not an accident — it falls
out of the core design. This guide covers *why*, and the tooling built to lean
into it.

## Why Exodra is analyzable

A React component's behavior lives inside a function body that runs at runtime —
what's reactive, what re-renders, and why is opaque until it executes. Exodra is
the opposite:

- **The shape is separate from the behaviour.** A component is a **schema** built
  once and a **wiring function** run per instance. The schema is a straight-line
  builder — `el`, `text`, `port`, `eventPort`, `textPort`, `childrenPort` — so
  what markup a component produces is readable without running it.
- **How a value is filled is written, never inferred.** `c.attr` / `c.text` is a
  value written by the wire or a transition, an effect that runs a transition and
  then subscribes is one that keeps up with a source, `c.list` is a fixed run and
  `reconcileExoOrder` over `c.childList`, called from a transition, is a reconciled
  one. [JSX](./jsx.md) declares the schema only: a literal attribute is
  markup, and every port is named where it stands (`data-id={$.id}`, `{$.label}`,
  `onClick={$.toggle}`, `<$.rows />`) for the machine to fill. A tool sees exactly what can change and what can't — no dataflow
  guessing.
- **No virtual DOM, no hidden magic.** There's no diffing black box to model: a
  render is a clone, a walk plan and one call per port.

The practical upshot: static analysis (and an LLM) can answer "what does this
component render, what's reactive, where are the perf risks?" from the source
alone. That's what the tooling below is built on — `createExoSchema`,
`createExoNamedSchema`, `createExoStatic` and `exoJsx` are the schema calls its
analysis looks for, and `createExoMachineBuilder` / `createExoStatic` are what it
counts as components.

## `@exodra/introspect` — analyze the tree

```bash
npm install --save-dev @exodra/introspect
```

The package has no CLI. It exports two things, both reading only your source:

```ts
import { ExoIntrospectionEngine, eslintPlugin } from '@exodra/introspect';

const result = await new ExoIntrospectionEngine({
  projectRoot: '.',
  analysis: { schema: true, performance: true },
}).analyze();

// result carries: metrics, diagnostics, suggestions, summary
console.log(JSON.stringify(result, null, 2));
```

`ExoIntrospectionEngine` reports TypeScript diagnostics, schemas built inside a
function instead of at module scope, and per-file counts of components,
reactive sources and control-flow complexity. `eslintPlugin` reports the same
schema-scope mistake in the editor. The JSON result is structured enough to hand
to an assistant or gate in CI. See the [Introspect page](../tooling/introspect.md)
for the full list, and for what earlier versions invented and why it was removed.

## The canonical LLM reference

The single most useful thing to give any coding assistant is Exodra's LLM
reference — a compact, correct description of the schema/wiring split, the
JSX dialect, transitions and effects, list reconciliation, and the gotchas that trip up
React-trained models:

**[exodra.org/llms.txt](https://exodra.org/llms.txt)**

Paste it into your assistant's context (or your `.cursorrules` / project rules)
before asking it to write Exodra code. Most AI mistakes come from assuming React
semantics — flat props, `.value` signals, a virtual DOM keyed by `key` — and this
file corrects all of them up front.

There is a second failure mode, and the file ends with a section for it: **a model
whose training data contains an older Exodra.** The three-props renderer
(`h(type, attrs)`, the `static` / `bindable` / `bindableList` buckets,
`defineComponent`, `mount`/`hydrate`, `subscribe`, `@exodra/babel-plugin-jsx`) has
been **deleted** — `@exodra/core` and `@exodra/dom` both say so in their own
barrels. An assistant that produces any of it is not guessing at React, it is
recalling a program that no longer exists. The "What does NOT exist" section at the
bottom of `llms.txt` is written to be pasted for exactly that.

## A typical loop

1. Scaffold with `npm create exodra`.
2. Give the assistant **exodra.org/llms.txt** so it writes idiomatic Exodra
   (a schema plus a wiring function, `getValue`/`setValue`, identity-stable
   lists).
3. Run `ExoIntrospectionEngine` to get a structured report of TypeScript
   diagnostics, schemas built per call, and component / reactive-source counts.
4. Feed that report back to the assistant to review, refactor, or gate in CI.

Because the shape is declared once and every fill says how it fills, every step is
something a tool can read precisely — not something it has to guess by running
your app.


==============================================================================
# Troubleshooting

Symptoms that are hard to search for, each traced back to the decision that
produces it. Every entry is written in the same order — **what you see**, **why it
happens**, **what to do** — and every entry names the file the behaviour lives in,
so a claim here can be checked against the code rather than believed.

This page is for behaviour that is *working as designed and still surprising*.
Behaviour that is missing or planned is in
[Limits and plans](./limits-and-plans.md); behaviour that is simply how lists work
is in [Lists & Reconciliation](./guides/lists.md).

## The same object twice in one list

### What you see

A list holding the same item object at two positions renders **two rows**, on the
server and on the client alike, and the two rows share one identity.

### Why it happens

This is not a bug in the reconciler. It falls out of the rule the whole renderer
runs on, and the rule is documented before this page:
[children are reconciled by **object identity** rather than by keys](./core/concepts.md#identity--reconciliation).
A row's place in a region is decided by the **item object** it was built from.

So ask what a list means when it holds the same object at two positions. Two
entries in the array, and **one** identity between them — which makes "the second
one" a position with no owner. A key-based renderer never has to answer this: it
would either refuse a duplicate key or accept two distinct keys. Identity is the
engine here, so the question belongs to the engine.

**A POSITION is a row.** `reconcileExoOrder` hands out one row per position and
consults identity only to decide which row SURVIVES an update, never how many rows
there are (`packages/list-reconcile/src/reconcileExoOrder.ts`, "a repeated item is
one row per occurrence"). Three entries give three rows on the client, three on the
server, and the two agree.

### Three backends, one answer

A test asserts the agreement: it counts POSITIONS, including when every entry is the
same object, and it checks the served markup against the built tree
(`packages/dom/src/tests/duplicate-item-parity.test.ts`).

The rule underneath: **identity decides which row survives an update, not how many
rows exist.** A list holding one object twice gets two rows; when the data changes,
the row that keeps its item keeps its DOM element and its live subscriptions.

### `c.list` and `reconcileExoOrder` do not behave the same way here

This distinction is what tells you whether you are looking at this problem at all.

- **`c.list(port, ROW, count)`** — the fixed form. It has no reconcile at all; it builds
  `count` instances and each reads its datum by index, so a duplicated item renders twice
  and there is nothing here to diverge.
- **`reconcileExoOrder(c.childList(port), shown, items, items, build)`** — the reactive
  form, called from a transition. It reconciles, and reconciling is where identity is
  consulted — but it is consulted to decide which row SURVIVES, so the count still
  follows the positions.

So a duplicate is not a latent hydration bug in either form; what identity still
decides is which of the two rows survives an update.

### What to do

Give each row its own identity. Concretely: **one object per position**, never one
object referenced from two positions. The item object *is* the row's name, and two
rows cannot share a name.

```ts
import { createExoMachineBuilder, createExoSchema } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoTextPort, TExoChildrenPort } from '@exodra/core';
import { reconcileExoOrder } from '@exodra/list-reconcile';
import type { TExoChildList, TExoDomNode } from '@exodra/dom';

type TTag = { readonly label: string };

const TAG_SCHEMA = createExoSchema((b) => {
    let label!: TExoTextPort;
    b.el('li', null, (li) => {
        label = li.textPort();
    });
    return { label };
});
const mTag = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoDomNode>(TAG_SCHEMA);
const showTag = mTag.transition<TTag>((c, tag) => {
    c.text(TAG_SCHEMA.ports.label, tag.label);
});
const TAG = mTag.done();

const shared: TTag = { label: 'urgent' };

// ONE object, two positions: two rows, and one identity between them.
const ambiguous: readonly TTag[] = [shared, shared];

// One object PER position: two identities, two rows, on every backend.
const distinct: readonly TTag[] = [{ label: 'urgent' }, { label: 'urgent' }];

const TAGS_SCHEMA = createExoSchema((b) => {
    let rows!: TExoChildrenPort;
    b.el('ul', null, (ul) => {
        rows = ul.childrenPort();
    });
    return { rows };
});
const mTags = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoDomNode, unknown, { rows: TExoChildList; shown: TTag[] }>(
    TAGS_SCHEMA
);
mTags.createInitialState((c) => ({ rows: c.childList(TAGS_SCHEMA.ports.rows), shown: [] }));
const showTags = mTags.transition<readonly TTag[]>((c, tags) => {
    c.state.shown = reconcileExoOrder(c.state.rows, c.state.shown, tags, tags, (tag, i) => {
        const row = c.build(TAG, i);
        showTag(row, tag);
        return row;
    });
});
mTags.wire((c) => {
    showTags(c, distinct);
});
const TAGS = mTags.done();
```

Where duplicates usually come from, and what each one wants instead:

- **A shared constant used as a row** — a placeholder, an "empty" sentinel, a
  separator object hoisted to module scope and pushed into a list more than once.
  Build a fresh object at each position, as above.
- **A projection that returns the same cached object for two inputs** — a `map`
  over ids where two ids resolve to one entity. Two rows showing one entity are two
  rows, so the projection has to mint a wrapper per position; the entity can stay
  shared inside it.
- **A store handing back one permanent object per entity** — the shape Exodra is
  built for, and the shape that makes this impossible by construction: one entity,
  one slot, one row. If the same entity legitimately appears twice in one view,
  what varies between the two appearances (a role, a position, a context) belongs
  in the item object, which makes the two objects different objects.

If your rows genuinely have no stable identity — freshly parsed JSON on every
refetch — the keyed plugin is the documented alternative, with its own costs and
its own handling of duplicates:
[Keys, when identity is not available](./guides/lists.md#keys-when-identity-is-not-available).
It does not remove the question; it moves it from the object to the key: a
duplicate **key** is again one row per position, and identity of the key decides
which row survives.


==============================================================================
# Core API Reference

`@exodra/core` is the **backend-agnostic half** of the renderer: the shape of a
component, the numbering of its ports, the context tokens, the event-handler
signature, the escapers and the list-placement primitives. It renders nothing
by itself — [`@exodra/dom`](./dom.md) compiles a schema into nodes and
[`@exodra/string`](./string.md) compiles it into markup.

It does **not** contain reactivity: a schema's values are typed `unknown`, and a
machine follows outside data through an **effect** that draws first, subscribes
second and returns the unsubscribe — so core pairs with whatever data layer the
application already has.

## A component is one value

A component carries **two halves**:

-   a **schema** — the constant shape, built **once** when the module loads. It
    holds the static markup and declares the **ports**: the places a value may
    later be put.
-   a **wiring function** — run **once per instance**, against whichever backend's
    **connector** is filling. It puts values in the ports it names.

There is no per-render tree, no diff of props, and no walk: the walk happens
once, at definition time, so filling a port at render time is one array load and
one indirect call.

```ts
import { createExoMachineBuilder, createExoSchema } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoAttrPort, TExoMachineNode, TExoTextPort } from '@exodra/core';

type TRow = { readonly id: string; readonly title: string };

/** Where a row's item waits for it: a view is handed its INDEX and nothing else. */
const BUILDING: TRow[] = [];

// THE SCHEMA half. Runs once, at module load.
const ROW_SCHEMA = createExoSchema((b) => {
    // A port is minted inside a nested closure and escapes to the record below, so its
    // holder is declared first — and each port-declaring call has a named type to declare
    // it with.
    let id!: TExoAttrPort;
    let label!: TExoTextPort;
    b.el('li', { class: 'row' }, (li) => {
        id = li.port('data-id');
        li.el('span', { class: 'row__label' }, (span) => {
            label = span.textPort();
        });
    });
    // What the builder returns IS the component's API: the machine
    // names `ROW_SCHEMA.ports.id`, never "port 0".
    return { id, label };
});

// THE MACHINE half. `createInitialState` runs once per instance. `TExoMachineNode` is the
// surface ALL THREE backends share, so this one value is served, rendered and
// hydrated with no cast — see "The connector surface" below.
const mRow = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoMachineNode, unknown, TRow>(ROW_SCHEMA);
mRow.createInitialState((_c, index) => BUILDING[index]);
mRow.wire((c) => {
    const item = c.state;
    c.attr(ROW_SCHEMA.ports.id, item.id);
    c.text(ROW_SCHEMA.ports.label, item.title);
});
export const ROW = mRow.done();
```

Which produces, per item, `<li class="row" data-id="…"><span class="row__label">…</span></li>`
— identically on the server, on a client render and through hydration, because
all three index the same port numbers.

## createExoSchema()

```ts no-check
function createExoSchema<TPorts>(
    build: (builder: TExoSchemaCursor) => TPorts
): TExoCursorDeclaration<TPorts>;
```

The schema half. A component is made from it by handing it to
`createExoMachineBuilder` — see [Machines](#machines) — and the plan compilers,
which know nothing about filling, read it alone.

Call it **once, at module level**. It is not a render; it produces the thing
renders are made from.

It throws if the builder produced no element.

## TExoSchemaCursor

The definition-time cursor. It walks the shape once, when the module loads, and
records what it saw. Every port-declaring call hands back the port it created —
one object per template, shared by every row.

| Method                 | What it declares                                                                                                                                           | Hands back         |
| ---------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------ |
| `el(tag, attrs?, fn?)` | A child element with its **static** attributes, and optionally a body. Everything in `attrs` is folded into the prepared markup and costs nothing per row. | the builder        |
| `text(value)`          | Static text inside the current element.                                                                                                                    | the builder        |
| `port(name)`           | A port for **one attribute** of the current element.                                                                                                       | `TExoAttrPort`     |
| `eventPort(name)`      | A port for **one event listener**. It emits no markup and still takes a slot.                                                                              | `TExoEventPort`    |
| `textPort()`           | A port standing for the **whole text content** of the current element.                                                                                     | `TExoTextPort`     |
| `childrenPort()`       | A port holding a **variable-length sequence of children** — a list, or one nested instance.                                                                | `TExoChildrenPort` |
| `refPort()`            | A **reference to the current element** and no way to write to it.                                                                                          | `TExoRefPort`      |

Each of those five types pins its port's kind, so a holder declared for a text
port refuses an attribute port; the first four are `TExoPort`s, which is what
every writing signature takes, and `TExoRefPort` deliberately is not.

An attribute whose value varies is not an attribute here — it is a port.

A children port **is a child**: it is appended where it was declared, so it may
stand between static siblings.

```ts
import { createExoSchema } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoChildrenPort, TExoTextPort } from '@exodra/core';

export const PANEL = createExoSchema((b) => {
    let heading!: TExoTextPort;
    let body!: TExoChildrenPort;
    b.el('section', { class: 'panel' }, (section) => {
        section.el('h2', null, (h2) => {
            heading = h2.textPort();
        });
        // Declared between two static siblings — and that is where it renders.
        body = section.childrenPort();
        section.el('footer', { class: 'panel__foot' }, (foot) => {
            foot.text('—');
        });
    });
    return { heading, body };
});
```

### Document order

Ports are numbered **after** the whole shape is known, by walking it in document
order: for each element, its attribute and event ports in declaration order,
then its content port, then its static children recursively; a children port is
numbered where it stands among the static ones.

This ordering is the contract between the backends. They never speak to each
other; they agree because both index their prepared plans by these numbers. It
is not an implementation detail — a change to it shows up not as a crash but as
a page that hydrates into nonsense.

## createExoStatic()

A component with **nothing to fill**: a conditional block's body, an icon, a
separator, an empty state.

```ts
import { createExoStatic } from '@exodra/core';

export const SPINNER = createExoStatic((b) => {
    b.el('span', { class: 'spinner', role: 'status' }, (s) => {
        s.text('Loading…');
    });
});
```

It **throws at construction** if the builder declared any ports — a
component with ports and nothing to fill them is an attribute stuck empty, which
is a silent wrong page rather than an error.

The machine it returns has `createInitialState: null`, no `wire`, and the shared
`EXO_NO_EFFECTS` / `EXO_NO_HANDLERS`, so a backend arms nothing for an instance
of it.

## The initial state and the wire

```ts no-check
type TExoMachineInitialState<TWiring, TValue = unknown> = (
    enode: TWiring,
    index: number
) => TValue;
```

`m.createInitialState(make)` declares it: it runs once per instance, and what it returns is
what the instance keeps, read back with `c.readState()`. `m.wire((c, params) => …)` declares
the other half — a transition that writes ports only and may run again with new `params`.

**One declaration, three backends.** It is generic over the connector and
nothing else, which is what makes "the same hand-written wire runs on the
server, on a client render and through hydration" a fact about the type system
rather than a promise in two files.

**Fill `TWiring` with `TExoWiring` or `TExoChildrenWiring`, not with a
backend's own exonode type**, wherever the wire can be written against the
shared surface. Naming `TExoDomNode` or `TExoStrNode` names **one backend's
exonode**. (Neither names a class: an exonode is a plain object whose prototype
is the composed backend, and both are types.) A wire is a function, so its
exonode parameter is contravariant: a wire typed `TExoMachineInitialState<TExoDomNode>` can
only ever be run by something assignable to `TExoDomNode`, which carries
`nodes: Node[]` and the instance record's own fields — the server backend is
not, and never will be. Reach for it only when the wire genuinely touches those
members, as a plugin reading `c.nodes[c.schema.elem[port.index]]` does.

-   `index` is **the position at build time and nothing more**. A row keeps the
    number it was built with even after the rows around it move — the reconciler
    moves nodes, it does not re-run wiring. A component that needs a live position
    must bind one, not capture this.

## The shared surface

Two types say what a wire may assume about the exonode it is handed — the
calls `TExoStrNode`, `TExoDomNode` and `TExoHydrateNode` all carry with the same
signatures, and nothing else. Both are this package's.

```ts no-check
// `TEvent` / `TNode` are pass-through: this package hands both to a handler and
// reads neither, so naming the DOM's `Event` / `Element` here would bind every
// backend to a document. A DOM-facing surface narrows them.
interface TExoWiring<TEvent = unknown, TNode = unknown>
    extends TExoFillDoors,      // attr, text, unsafeHtml
        TExoBaseNodeMethods {   // onTeardown, provide, inject
    portTable(): TExoPortTable;
    portNodeWriter(): TExoPortNodeWriter;
    on(port: TExoEventPort, handler: TExoEventHandler<TEvent, TNode>, subject?: unknown): void;
}

interface TExoChildrenWiring<TEvent = unknown, TNode = unknown>
    extends TExoWiring<TEvent, TNode> {
    build(component: TExoMachine<this>, index?: number): TExoNode;
    one(port: TExoChildrenPort, component: TExoMachine<this>): void;
    list(port: TExoChildrenPort, component: TExoMachine<this>, count: number): void;
}
```

`childList(port)` is **not** in either: handing back a port's live children is a
backend's own door, so a wire that drives one names that backend's exonode —
`TExoMachineInitialState<TExoDomNode>` — and is browser-only by saying so.

**Two of them, and the line is drawn by what the call names.** Every call in
`TExoWiring` names a port and a plain value, so it can be spelled flatly and
a backend satisfies it by writing the methods out. Every call `TExoChildrenWiring`
adds takes another **component**, and a component is generic over the exonode
it is wired against — so those signatures name the exonode recursively. Said in
behaviour: the first is what a wire does to the instance it was handed, the
second is what it mounts below it.

**There is no third surface for watching data**, and the absence is the
design. A machine keeps ports in step with outside data through a **transition**
that writes them and an **effect** that runs the transition once and then
subscribes to the data layer; a reactive list is `reconcileExoOrder` from
`@exodra/list-reconcile`, called inside such a transition over
`childList(port)`. None of it is a door, so no backend declares it, no wire has
to name a wider surface to use it, and a page that watches nothing links none
of it.

Grading matters because a surface that forces a wire to declare capabilities it
does not use narrows what can **run** that wire: a leaf typed `TExoWiring` is
accepted by a backend, a test double or a plugin connector that fills values and
mounts nothing. A component typed against the minimal surface is nested happily
by a wire typed against the wider one — that direction is free, because
`TExoChildrenWiring` extends `TExoWiring` and the wire's parameter is
contravariant.

**During hydration every fill repairs.** The signature of `attr`, `text` and
`unsafeHtml` is the same on all three backends, and on an adopting pass each one
reads what the server printed, compares, and writes only on disagreement. A
value that differs between the server and the browser — a media query, a
locale, a clock — is therefore corrected by the same call that printed it:

```ts no-check
c.attr(P.cls, matchMedia('(hover: none)').matches ? 'touch' : 'mouse');
```

An **event** port is the exception in the other direction: its `set`-time
attachment is the whole content of hydration. See
[SSR & hydration](../guides/ssr.md#what-hydration-actually-does).

A hand-written surface narrower still is always allowed and sometimes better:
`@exodra/forms` asks `writeExoChoice` for `Pick<TExoFillDoors, 'attr'>` and
`readExoControlValues` for `portTable` plus `portNodeReader`, and `@exodra/router`
declares `TExoOutletWiring` as `TExoMachineNode` plus `build` and `childList`,
precisely so a helper can be run by anything that has those calls.

These types are erased: they emit no JavaScript and change nothing about the
connector object a wire receives at runtime.

## Ports

```ts no-check
type TExoPort = {
    index: number;             // where this port's value lands; -1 until the schema is closed
    readonly kind: TExoPortKind;
    readonly name: string | null;  // attribute/event name; null for text and children ports
};
```

The seven kinds are exported as plain constants — a plugin that compiles its own
plan switches on exactly these, and there is no enum object to load them from:

| Constant               | Value | Declared by                       |
| ---------------------- | ----- | --------------------------------- |
| `EXO_PORT_ATTR`        | `0`   | `port(name)` / `attrPort(name)`   |
| `EXO_PORT_TEXT`        | `1`   | `textPort()`                      |
| `EXO_PORT_CHILDREN`    | `2`   | `childrenPort()`                  |
| `EXO_PORT_EVENT`       | `3`   | `eventPort(name)`                 |
| `EXO_PORT_REF`         | `4`   | `refPort()`                       |
| `EXO_PORT_ATTR_STRING` | `5`   | `stringPort(name)`                |
| `EXO_PORT_ATTR_TOGGLE` | `6`   | `togglePort(name)`                |

`EXO_PORT_REF` is deliberately not in `TExoPortKind`: a ref port is read, never
written, so `c.set(refPort, …)` does not compile.

## Contexts

Every name in this section is exported by **`@exodra/context`**, not by this
package. It is a separate install because a backend needs the chain and does not
need the schema vocabulary — `@exodra/core` itself is one of its consumers.

A context token is an **identity**, not a string, so two packages cannot collide
on a name.

```ts no-check
function exoContextToken<TValue>(name?: string): TExoContextToken<TValue>;
```

`provide` and `inject` are **methods on the connector**, in the backends —
there is nothing to import to use them, and that is the point: a context exists
only while a wiring is running, and a method cannot be called without a
connector.

```ts
import { createExoMachineBuilder, createExoSchema } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoAttrPort, TExoMachineNode } from '@exodra/core';
import { exoContextToken } from '@exodra/context';

export const THEME = exoContextToken<string>('theme');

const BADGE_SCHEMA = createExoSchema((b) => {
    let cls!: TExoAttrPort;
    b.el('span', null, (span) => {
        cls = span.port('class');
    });
    return { cls };
});
const mBadge = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoMachineNode>(BADGE_SCHEMA);
mBadge.wire((c) => {
    // `undefined` when nobody above provided it — not a throw.
    c.attr(BADGE_SCHEMA.ports.cls, 'badge badge--' + (c.inject(THEME) ?? 'light'));
});
export const BADGE = mBadge.done();
```

:::caution Contexts are not reactive by themselves
What is provided is what a consumer holds forever: nothing watches the chain and
nothing re-runs a wire. Reactivity composes from **above** — provide a store
object, and have the consumer's effect draw from it and subscribe to it.
:::

`exoContextFrame(frame, key, value)` and `readExoContext(frame, key)` are the shared
half: a backend supplied from outside this repo builds its chain with the first
and reads it with the second, so "the nearest value wins" is one loop rather
than three. The types are `TExoContextToken<TValue>` and `TExoContextFrame`.

### Ids that survive hydration

`label for`, `aria-describedby` and `aria-controls` need an id that the server
prints and hydration finds again. `@exodra/context` counts them per render:

```ts
import { createExoMachineBuilder, createExoSchema } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoAttrPort, TExoMachineNode } from '@exodra/core';
import { nextExoId, provideExoIds } from '@exodra/context';

const FIELD_SCHEMA = createExoSchema((b) => {
    let labelFor!: TExoAttrPort;
    let inputId!: TExoAttrPort;
    b.el('p', null, (p) => {
        p.el('label', null, (label) => {
            labelFor = label.port('for');
        });
        p.el('input', null, (input) => {
            inputId = input.port('id');
        });
    });
    return { labelFor, inputId };
});
const mField = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoMachineNode, unknown, string>(FIELD_SCHEMA);
mField.createInitialState((c) => nextExoId(c)); // 'app-0', 'app-1', …
mField.wire((c) => {
    const id = c.state;
    c.attr(FIELD_SCHEMA.ports.labelFor, id);
    c.attr(FIELD_SCHEMA.ports.inputId, id);
});
export const FIELD = mField.done();

// in the root's createInitialState, on the server and in the browser:
// provideExoIds(c, 'app');
```

```ts no-check
function provideExoIds(c: { provide(...) }, prefix: string): TExoIdCounter;
function nextExoId(c: { inject(...) }): string; // `${prefix}-${n}`, n in base 36
```

**The counter lives in the render.** `provideExoIds` creates it, so every
render — every request on the server — starts at `0`. Call it in the root's
`createInitialState`, never at module level. With nothing provided above,
`nextExoId` throws [`EXO0104`](../errors.md#exo0104).

**Ids follow call order.** Exodra hydrates in one synchronous pass in document
order, so the server and the browser call `nextExoId` in the same order. The one
place they do not is an asynchronous boundary — a lazy page the browser builds
after the rest of the tree — and the router's outlet forks the count there: it
takes one id from the count above as its own prefix and starts its page at `0`,
so a page that arrives late takes the ids it would have taken at once, and what
follows the outlet does not move. Build your own asynchronous boundary the same
way: `provideExoIds(c, nextExoId(c))` before building what arrives later.

**Two roots on one page need two prefixes** — an island beside the page, a modal
rendered after hydration. The prefix is the only thing that keeps them apart.

A shifted id is not a broken page: hydration compares every attribute port with
what the server printed and writes the client's value where they differ, so both
ends of a `for`/`id` pair agree. What it costs is one write per port after the
point where the counts parted.

`EXO_ID_COUNTER` is the context token the counter is provided under, and
`TExoIdCounter` (`{ prefix, next }`) its type.

## Event handlers

An event port takes a **function**, and the third argument of
`on(port, handler, subject)` reaches it as the handler's **second parameter**:

```ts no-check
type TExoEventHandler<TEvent = unknown, TNode = unknown> = (
    this: TNode,
    event: TEvent,
    subject?: unknown
) => void;
```

Every backend calls it as `handler.call(node, event, subject)`, so `this` is the
node the port sits on. Two shapes fit that signature, and the difference between
them is what each one costs:

-   a **closure** — the general answer, one function per row, built knowing its
    row;
-   a **function that is told its row** — `(event, subject) => …`, a module-level
    constant holding nothing about any row, so **one function serves the whole
    template**. Which row a dispatch is about arrives as the subject. A handler
    declaring one parameter simply ignores it.

```ts
type TTodo = { readonly done: { setValue(next: boolean): void } };

/** ONE function for every row — the subject says which row fired. */
const REMOVE = (event: Event, subject?: unknown): void => {
    (subject as TTodo).done.setValue(true);
};
// in wire:  c.on(S.ports.click, REMOVE, todo);
```

A fill with no subject is allowed under the direct strategy and the handler
receives `undefined`. The **delegated** strategy refuses it: the subject is the
whole of what a shared handler is told about the position it fired on, so a fill
without one would be either a dead handler or a closure that carried its own row
— and a closure per row is the cost delegation exists to remove.

The handler type lives here rather than in `@exodra/dom` because a wiring
function that fills an event port is the same module on the server.

```ts
import { createExoMachineBuilder, createExoSchema } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoEventHandler, TExoEventPort, TExoMachineNode, TExoTextPort } from '@exodra/core';

type TCell<T> = { getValue(): T; setValue(next: T): void };
type TTodo = { readonly title: string; readonly done: TCell<boolean> };

/** ONE function for every row of this template. */
const toggleDone: TExoEventHandler = (_event, subject): void => {
    const cell = (subject as TTodo).done;
    cell.setValue(cell.getValue() === true ? false : true);
};

/** The row's own todo, by index — the build callback writes it, then builds. */
const BUILDING_TODO: TTodo[] = [];

const TODO_SCHEMA = createExoSchema((b) => {
    let click!: TExoEventPort;
    let label!: TExoTextPort;
    b.el('li', null, (li) => {
        li.el('button', { type: 'button' }, (btn) => {
            click = btn.eventPort('click');
            label = btn.textPort();
        });
    });
    return { click, label };
});
const mTodo = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoMachineNode, unknown, TTodo>(TODO_SCHEMA);
mTodo.createInitialState((_c, index) => BUILDING_TODO[index]);
mTodo.wire((c) => {
    const todo = c.state;
    c.text(TODO_SCHEMA.ports.label, todo.title);
    // THE SUBJECT is what makes one module-level handler serve every row: the
    // row hands its own datum to the fill, and the handler is told which.
    c.on(TODO_SCHEMA.ports.click, toggleDone, todo);
});
export const TODO = mTodo.done();
```

## Nodes

`TExoNode` is the value `c.build(machine, index, params)` hands back and the
only thing a `childList(port)` will insert — whatever the backend produced for
that position. It is nominal and opaque on purpose: what it
is made of is the backend's business (a DOM node on the client, a string on the
server), what it is to everyone else is an identity.

It lives in core for the same reason `TExoMachineInitialState` does — a wire that assembles
children is one function on all three backends. See
[the DOM renderer](./dom.md#children-as-values) for how a holder reaches the
element behind one.

## Machines

A component is a machine. `createExoMachineBuilder(schema)` hands you a
builder you declare against **once, at module load**, so a handler is one
function object for the whole component instead of one per row, and per-instance
state is a numbered slot rather than a captured variable.

```typescript
import { createExoMachineBuilder, createExoSchema } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoEventPort, TExoTextPort } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoDomNode } from '@exodra/dom';

const COUNTER = createExoSchema((b) => {
    let label!: TExoTextPort;
    let click!: TExoEventPort;
    b.el('button', { class: 'counter' }, (button) => {
        label = button.textPort();
        click = button.eventPort('click');
    });
    return { label, click };
});

const m = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoDomNode>(COUNTER);

// A slot, numbered here and seeded once per instance — never shared between two.
const COUNT = m.createInitialState(() => ({ n: 0 }));

// One handler object for the whole component; the instance arrives as an argument.
m.on(COUNTER.ports.click, (c) => {
    const state = c.readState(COUNT);
    state.n += 1;
    c.text(COUNTER.ports.label, `${state.n}`);
});

export const COUNTER_BUTTON = m.done();
```

| Method              | What it declares                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   | Hands back                       |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------- |
| `createInitialState(make)` | A numbered slot, seeded by `make(instance, index)` once per instance, taking its row in declaration order. `make` must be a **function**: a value handed here would be one object shared by every instance, each seeing every other's writes, so the builder refuses one. | `TExoMachineStateHandle<TValue>` |
| `effect(start)`     | An effect. `start(instance)` returns its own stop function or `null`, and the instance re-runs one through `restartEffect(handle)`.                                                                                                                                | `TExoMachineEffect<TWiring>`     |
| `on(port, handler)` | A listener on an event port. You write `handler(instance, event)`; the builder transposes it once per component into the `(event, subject)` shape a dispatcher calls, so nothing is allocated per row.                                                             | nothing                          |
| `done()`            | Compiles and seals the machine.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    | `TExoMachine<TWiring>`  |

`done()` may be called once and nothing may be declared after it. Both are
refusals carrying a named message rather than a silent no-op.

The object a seeder, a handler and an effect all receive is the **exonode** —
one per instance. `kept`, `onTeardown`, `inject`, `restartEffect` and `stopEffects` are
`EXO_BASE_NODE_VOCABULARY`'s bodies, merged onto every node; `set` and `on` are the
backend's.

A component that declares no slot gets `EXO_NO_STATE`, the shared empty table,
and no branch — so the machine form costs a component that keeps nothing
nothing.

A machine takes **no props and no seed**. Its declared start is
`m.createInitialState(make)`, which runs once per instance while the instance is
being armed and is the only thing that writes `state`; `c.readState(handle)`
reads it back.

Anything that belongs to ONE instance arrives instead as a **transition
argument**. `c.build(component)` arms the machine and hands back the exonode
with no element in the document, which is the moment a caller fires an init
transition at it before placing it — and an init transition is, in substance,
what `m.wire((c, params) => …)` declares once for the whole machine: a transition that writes
ports only and may run again with new `params`.

## Placement primitives — not here

`reconcileExoOrder`, `createExoKeyedList` and `TExoPlacedChildren` are
**`@exodra/list-reconcile`**, and this package exports none of them.

They move nodes: `parent.insertBefore(node, after)`, `parent.removeChild(out)`.
A base that the server renderer and `@exodra/term` both build on cannot be made
of calls that only a browser can answer — `Node` and `Element` do not exist
there — so the passes are a package of their own, which `@exodra/dom` declares
as a peer and nothing else links. Their interfaces, what the three uncalled ones
are for, and the withdrawn move counts are in
[`packages/list-reconcile/README.md`](https://github.com/abaikov/exodra/blob/master/packages/list-reconcile/README.md).

## The declarative machine — not here

`withExoComputedMachine`, `exoTransition`, `exoWiring`, `ExoWiringBlock`,
`EXO_HOLD_VOCABULARY`, `EXO_MOUNTED`, `exoMachineField`, `exoComputed`, `exoBody`,
`exoFieldBit`, `compileExoMachine`, `commitExoMachine`, `runExoMachineSlots`,
`fillExoMachineDerivations`, `chainExoMachineWakes`, `exoMachineSettle`,
`exoBoundTransition`, `bindExoMachineReads`, `EXO_MACHINE_LIMIT` and the
seventeen types that spell them are **`@exodra/computed`**, and this package
exports none of them.

What stays here is the **imperative** builder of
[the section above](#machines): `createExoMachineBuilder`,
`armExoNode`, `stopExoEffects`, `disconnectExoNode`,
`connectExoNode` (effects off and on again on a kept instance — see
`packages/core/README.md`), and `TExoMachineBuilder`,
`TExoMachine`, `TExoMachineEffect`, `TExoFillDoors`,
`TExoMachineStateHandle`, `TExoMachineNode`, `TExoMachineHandler`,
`TExoMachineInitialState`, `TExoTransitionOverrides` and `TExoWire`. A handler on one of those reads a slot
and writes a port; nothing is derived, so there is no field, no pending word
and no commit walk.

The split is the price, made choosable. Saying `m.derive(port, [field], by)`
instead of writing the port yourself buys the inversion table, the chain of
wakes and the commit — and a page that derives nothing must not pay for them.
`npm run check:computed-shake` is the gate that keeps that true, module by
module rather than by byte count.

The direction is one way and enforced: `@exodra/computed` names four types
from the list above, nothing here names anything of its, and the
`computed-names-only-core` rule in `.dependency-cruiser.cjs` fails the build if
that reverses. `TExoMachineStateHandle` and `TExoMachineEffect` in particular could
not follow — `kept()` and `restartEffect()` are methods on **every** node, merged
by `EXO_BASE_NODE_VOCABULARY`.

## Escaping and the shared tables

The escapers are an agreement **between** the backends: the markup the server
prints and the markup the DOM compiler parses its prototype from must be the
same bytes, so a copy made "for the DOM side" is not a duplicate helper — it is
the end of hydration.

| Export                           | Purpose                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| -------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `escapeExoText(value)`           | Escape a string for a text position.                                                                                                                                                                               |
| `escapeExoAttributeValue(value)` | Escape a string for inside a quoted attribute value — including `<` and `>`, which nothing but the quote could actually end a value with, but which a browser writes escaped and hydration therefore has to match. |
| `EXO_VOID_ELEMENTS`              | The `Set` of tags with no end tag.                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| `EXO_DOM_PROPERTIES`             | Which names are DOM properties rather than attributes.                                                                                                                                                             |
| `EXO_DOM_STRING_PROPERTIES`      | The DOM properties whose value is a string the browser keeps as live state (`value`).                                                                                                                             |
| `EXO_RAW_TEXT_ELEMENTS`          | The tags the HTML serialiser emits as raw text (`<script>`, `<style>`, `<noscript>` and five more), verbatim on both sides.                                                                                      |

## The shape rules the two compilers share

Both backends compile the same schema, so a shape one of them cannot build is
refused **where the schema is written** rather than on whichever side happened to
notice. These live here so the wording and the rule are one thing:

| Export                                     | Refuses                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| ------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `assertExoChildrenPort(port, method, who)` | a nested instance placed anywhere but a children port.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| `assertExoNoTextAfterChildrenPort(…)`      | static text **after** a children port. The region anchors on the next static element, so its rows would land after that text in the browser and before it on the server.                                                                                                                |
| `assertExoIntactRawTextBoundary(…)`        | a static inside `<script>` / `<style>` (see `EXO_RAW_TEXT_ELEMENTS`) that carries the element's own closing sequence. Text in there is emitted verbatim by both compilers, so escaping it produced the same broken bytes on both sides — which is exactly why no parity test caught it. |

`exoDomPropertyKind(tag, name)` answers, of an _element_, the question
`EXO_DOM_PROPERTIES` answers of a name alone: `value` is live state on an `<input>`,
a plain reflected attribute on an `<option>`, and nothing at all on a `<div>`.
The browser could always ask the element and the server could not, so the server
used to apply the `<input>` rule everywhere and the two printed different
controls. Both compilers read this now.

## Plugins

A **plugin** is a bag of **method factories**, and that is the whole of it. Each
entry receives whatever stands under that name right now — `next` — and returns
what will stand there instead.

```ts no-check
export type TExoPlugin = {
    readonly [name: string]: (next: never) => unknown;
};
```

| Export                              | Purpose                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| ----------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `composeExoPlugins(base, ...plugins)` | Write every plugin's names onto `base`, left to right, once. Returns `base` typed as itself intersected with everything the plugins added. A backend calls it in its own constructor, so an application never calls it directly. |
| `TExoPlugin`                        | The shape above — what an author annotates a pack with.                                                                                                                                                                          |
| `TExoPluginMethods<TPack>`          | What one pack contributes, read off its factories' return types.                                                                                                                                                                 |
| `TExoMergedPluginMethods<TPacks>`                | Everything a list of packs adds, intersected in order — the whole of the capability check.                                                                                                                                       |

There is **no** namespace, no slot registry, no `needs` / `provides` and no
resolution pass. Four properties are worth stating because they are structural
rather than requested:

-   **Replacing and wrapping are one act.** A plugin that never calls `next` has
    replaced; one that calls it has wrapped. That is what `super` gave a prototype
    chain, and it is the only reason this is not `Object.assign`.
-   **Order is the caller's**, left to right, so the last plugin to claim a name is
    the outermost wrapper. Two plugins that both replace one name without calling
    `next` leave only the second, with nothing thrown.
-   **The capability check is the type of the composed object.** Nobody declares a
    capability set: `TExoMergedPluginMethods` computes it from the constructor arguments, so a
    wire that touches `c.keyedList` infers a connector that has it, and handing that
    component to a backend composed without that plugin fails to compile — at the line
    that composed it, rather than as a call landing on `undefined` inside a render.
-   **A plugin cannot resolve on a hot path**, because it is never on one. A factory
    runs **once**, at merge, before the first render; it is handed no connector, no
    plan and no child, so there is nothing per-row it could reach for. At call time
    a merged name is an own property on one flat object — no chain is walked and no
    map is consulted.

Two rules a pack must obey, both silent if broken: the returned function must not
be an **arrow** (an arrow has no `this`, so it can reach neither the connector it
was called on nor `next.call(this, …)`), and a method must reach its siblings
through `this` rather than through a captured connector (a connector is pooled —
one object serves every instance of its plan in turn).

The replaceable pieces themselves are a backend's, not core's. See
[`@exodra/dom`](./dom.md#composing-plugins) for its replaceable fields —
`events`, `writers`, `createInstance` and `createChild` — and for the packs that ship —
`withExoCompiler`, `withExoHydration`, `withExoPropertyWriters`,
`withExoReclaimingText` and the `withExoDefaults` bundle; the keyed list is
`EXO_KEYED_LIST_VOCABULARY`, in `@exodra/list-reconcile`.
`new ExoDomBackend()` — which takes **no** arguments at all — is a complete working
composition; customisation is wrapping it in a decorator, or merging one plugin
that claims one name.


==============================================================================
# DOM Renderer

`@exodra/dom` is the **browser backend** of the schema core. It takes the
component values [`@exodra/core`](./core.md) describes and turns them into live
DOM — and it can adopt markup [`@exodra/string`](./string.md) already printed,
with the same component.

Nothing here parses a template per render. A schema is compiled **once** into a
prototype element, a walk plan and a setter per port; an instance is a clone
plus one indirect call per port.

```bash
npm install @exodra/dom @exodra/core @exodra/context
```

## ExoDomBackend

The client entry point is an **object you construct and render from**, not a free
function. A backend is the composition — the event strategy, the value writers,
and the two record factories — and `render` arrives with `withExoCompiler`.

```ts no-check
class ExoDomBackend {
    constructor();

    events: TExoEventsApi;
    writers: TExoWritersApi;
    createInstance: TExoDomApi['createInstance'];
    createChild: TExoDomApi['createChild'];

    // NO `render`. It is composed in — see `withExoCompiler` below.
}
```

The constructor takes **nothing**, and packs are applied by **wrapping** the
object. There is no runtime object, no slot registry and no `needs` / `provides`
declaration: a plugin is a bag of factories that write names onto the backend, so
composing nothing costs nothing and a capability nobody composed does not exist —
in the type as well as at runtime.

The backend also carries every **exonode method** as an own property, merged in
the constructor before anything an application composes, so a pack naming `attr`,
`text` or `list` receives the shipped body as its `next` and may wrap it rather
than only replace it — **on a client render**. A wrapper is silent on an adopted
page for every name hydration claims: `withExoHydration`'s bodies ignore `next` and
replace. See [Plugins](../guides/plugins.md#the-fields-a-composition-can-replace).

```ts
import { createExoMachineBuilder, createExoSchema } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoTextPort } from '@exodra/core';
import { ExoDomBackend, withExoCompiler } from '@exodra/dom';
import type { TExoDomNode } from '@exodra/dom';

const GREETING_SCHEMA = createExoSchema((b) => {
    let label!: TExoTextPort;
    b.el('h1', { class: 'title' }, (h1) => {
        label = h1.textPort();
    });
    return { label };
});
const mGreeting = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoDomNode>(GREETING_SCHEMA);
mGreeting.wire((c) => {
    c.text(GREETING_SCHEMA.ports.label, 'Hello');
});
const GREETING = mGreeting.done();

/** ONE backend for the application, at module level — it is the schema cache key. */
const backend = withExoCompiler(new ExoDomBackend());

const root = document.getElementById('root') as HTMLElement;
const dispose = backend.render(GREETING, root);

// later…
dispose();
```

Four things about it are deliberate:

- **It takes a machine, not a schema and a wiring side by side.** The schema is
  inside the machine, so a schema can never be paired with somebody else's wiring,
  compiled against one numbering and filled against another.
- **It mounts one instance, and takes no count.** The instance is handed `0` as
  its index, and there are no props — a lone root has nothing else to be about.
- **It is not a list.** There is no reconciler and no diff: this renders and
  stops. Rows that vary over time are a **list** — a children port filled by
  `reconcileExoOrder` over `c.childList`, below — and keeping the two
  apart is what stops a static mount from paying for a diff it will never run.
- **It returns the disposer**, because the instance may subscribe. Disposing tears
  the instance down and ends every subscription it made.

:::caution Build the backend once
The backend is the key a compiled schema is cached under: each backend object takes
its own `backendType`, the index its schemas are stored at on `machine.forms`. One
constructed inside a component, a route handler or a render loop is a fresh index
every time and recompiles every schema it touches — markup parse included. Build it
at module level. `warnExoFormGrowth` says so out loud in development once a machine
holds eight schemas.
:::

### Composing plugins

A plugin is an object whose entries are factories receiving what already stands
under that name. The constructor takes **no arguments** — composition is a chain
of unary `with*` decorators, each of which merges its own entries onto the object
it is handed and returns that same object, so the whole chain is one identity:

```ts
import { composeExoPlugins } from '@exodra/core';
import {
    ExoDomBackend,
    createExoDelegatedEvents,
    withExoCompiler,
    withExoDefaults,
} from '@exodra/dom';

/** ONE pack for the application, at module level. */
const DELEGATED = createExoDelegatedEvents(['click']);

const backend = withExoCompiler(
    withExoDefaults(
        // …a bare implementation, written as the one-entry plugin it is:
        composeExoPlugins(new ExoDomBackend(), { events: () => DELEGATED })
    )
);
```

`composeExoPlugins` comes from `@exodra/core`, and every shipped decorator is built
on it. The order reads **inside-out** where a variadic
constructor read left to right — that is the price of the decorator form, and it
is not papered over with a second spelling.

**A bare backend carries four replaceable fields and that is the whole of it** —
`events`, `writers`, `createInstance`, `createChild`
(`packages/dom/src/dom/ExoDomBackend.ts:16-22`):

| Field | Interface | Default | What replacing it buys |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `events` | `TExoEventsApi` | `EXO_DIRECT_EVENTS` | how a listener reaches the DOM — one per element, or one per root |
| `writers` | `TExoWritersApi` | `EXO_SHIPPED_WRITERS` | how a value reaches an element — `setAttribute`, or a property |
| `createInstance` | — | `createExoDomInstanceFactory(this)` | where the record of an instance placed by `c.one` or a fixed `c.list` comes from |
| `createChild` | — | `createExoDomChildFactory(this)` | the same for a child — a root, a built child and a reconciled row — and it is why every child's leading fields share offsets |

A plugin may also **introduce a name that was never there**:

| Decorator | What it adds or replaces |
| --- | --- |
| `withExoCompiler` | adds `schema`, `buildRoot`, `mountRoot` and `render` — a bare backend has none, so it cannot turn a declaration into a schema and has no entry point |
| `withExoHydration` | adds `adoptRoot`, `hydrate`, `hydrateSurface`, `parserStability` |
| [`withExoChildList`](#withexochildlist) | adds `c.childList(port)` to every exonode — the commanded child list every reconciled list, the keyed list and the router outlet open. Without it the call throws [EXO0109](../errors.md#exo0109) |
| [`withExoForeignNamespaces`](#withexoforeignnamespaces) | adds `foreignNamespaces`, the SVG and MathML tables. Without it a schema with `<svg>`, `<math>` or an SVG-only element is refused with [EXO0108](../errors.md#exo0108) ([EXO0110](../errors.md#exo0110) from a JSON declaration) |
| `withExoDefaults` | the safety bundle; today it is `withExoReclaimingText` and nothing else |
| `withExoReclaimingText` | replaces `writers.text` with `exoReclaimingText`, and **delegates** the rest to what was composed under it |
| `withExoPropertyWriters` | replaces `writers` for custom-element properties, and **delegates** text to what was composed under it through `next` |

Each decorator declares its own contribution in its return type, and they
compose by intersection. What each costs and refuses is on
[Plugins](../guides/plugins.md#the-packs-that-ship).

## Following data is an effect

A machine keeps its ports in step with outside data the same way everywhere: a
**transition** writes the ports from the data, and an **effect** runs that
transition once and then subscribes, returning the unsubscribe. A reactive list
is the same shape with `reconcileExoOrder` from `@exodra/list-reconcile` inside
the transition, over the child-list door:

```ts no-check
const show = m.transition((c) => {
    c.text(P.label, store.getValue().label);
});
m.effect((c) => {
    show(c);
    return store.onChange(() => show(c));
});
```

**Why this shape rather than a door.** A backend carrying a `bind` would make
every page link subscription machinery it may never use, and would decide for
the application what a data source is. A backend carrying a list reconciler would
be a backend with one list strategy welded in, and a second strategy could no
longer be a second FUNCTION. The effect subscribes to whatever the application
already has — a store object, an `oimdb` collection — and names no Exodra package
for it.

`TExoDomNode` is the type a machine names — the instance's record plus the shipped
surface. A machine that must stay portable across backends names only the methods
it calls, as a local type; that is structural, so one component drives the
DOM, the server and the terminal with no cast.

:::caution Where the refusal lands
`render` and `hydrate` declare their component against `this`, so a machine naming
a capability the composition does not have is refused **at the entry point**, in
the file that built the backend — most commonly `render` itself on a backend
built without `withExoCompiler`. The same demand is checked again at every
`one`, `list` and `build` that places a child, because those name `this` too.
:::

## The exonode

A machine's initial state and transitions are handed a `TExoDomNode` — the
instance's own record. It is **not a cursor**: nothing walks, nothing descends, and
no method depends on the order the others were called in. A port names itself, so
the last port may be filled first.

| Method | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `attr(port, value)` / `text(port, value)` / `unsafeHtml(port, markup)` | Fill a port. One method per port KIND, so the write is one indirect call with its data already resolved — no runtime test of what sort of port this is. |
| `on(port, handler, subject?)` | Put a [handler](./core.md#event-handlers) in an event port — a closure, or a module-level function plus the subject it is told its position by. |
| `provide(token, value)` | Put a value where everything below this instance can reach it. |
| `inject(token)` | The nearest value for a token, or `undefined`. |
| `one(port, component)` | One nested instance of another component, in a children port. Hands back the child's exonode. |
| `list(port, component, count)` | A **fixed** list of instances — one row per POSITION, rendered once, never reconciled, nothing subscribed. |
| `build(component, index?)` | Build one child and put it nowhere — hands back the child's exonode. |
| `childList(port)` | The child-list door for a children port: it holds whatever is put in it. This is the half a reconciler stands on — see below. |
| `onTeardown(off)` | Hand the instance a disposer to run when it goes. |
| `foreign(t)` | A child this renderer did not make. A pack: compose `EXO_DOM_FOREIGN_VOCABULARY` first. |
| `portTable()` / `portNodeReader()` / `portNodeWriter()` | The instance's node table, and readers and writers over it. |

There is no `bind` method on this list. Keeping a port in step with data is a
transition plus an effect; a reactive list is `reconcileExoOrder` from
`@exodra/list-reconcile` inside a transition, over `childList(port)`. Both stand
on doors every backend answers, so one body serves the DOM, the server and the
terminal — and a page that uses neither links neither.

An exonode is **one instance's own record**, so capturing it in a callback is safe,
and is exactly what an effect's subscription does. `build` may legally be called
after the initial state returned, because it reads per-schema state only — which
is what lets a reconciler keep calling it on every later update.

### Reactive attributes and text

The data can live anywhere that offers a read and a change notification. Here it
is a store object of a dozen lines; in an application it is the data layer.

```ts
import { createExoMachineBuilder, createExoSchema } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoAttrPort, TExoEventPort, TExoTextPort } from '@exodra/core';
import { ExoDomBackend, withExoCompiler } from '@exodra/dom';
import type { TExoDomNode } from '@exodra/dom';

const backend = withExoCompiler(new ExoDomBackend());

function createStore<TValue>(value: TValue) {
    const listeners = new Set<() => void>();
    return {
        getValue: (): TValue => value,
        setValue(next: TValue): void {
            value = next;
            listeners.forEach((listener) => listener());
        },
        onChange(listener: () => void): () => void {
            listeners.add(listener);
            return () => listeners.delete(listener);
        },
    };
}

const active = createStore(false);

const PANEL_SCHEMA = createExoSchema((b) => {
    let panelClass!: TExoAttrPort;
    let buttonText!: TExoTextPort;
    let click!: TExoEventPort;
    b.el('div', null, (div) => {
        panelClass = div.port('class');
        div.el('button', { type: 'button' }, (btn) => {
            click = btn.eventPort('click');
            buttonText = btn.textPort();
        });
    });
    return { panelClass, buttonText, click };
});
const P = PANEL_SCHEMA.ports;

const mPanel = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoDomNode>(PANEL_SCHEMA);
const showActive = mPanel.transition((c) => {
    const on = active.getValue();
    c.attr(P.panelClass, on ? 'panel panel--open' : 'panel');
    c.text(P.buttonText, on ? 'Close' : 'Open');
});
mPanel.effect((c) => {
    showActive(c);
    return active.onChange(() => showActive(c));
});
mPanel.on(P.click, () => active.setValue(!active.getValue()));
const PANEL = mPanel.done();

backend.render(PANEL, document.body);
```

The first `showActive(c)` runs synchronously inside the effect, so the instance
is drawn before anything subscribes. On the server the same effect runs too: it
draws, subscribes, and the render stops it as soon as the markup is taken.
Through **hydration** every value port is filled through a repairing fill: the
served bytes are read and overwritten only where they disagree. See
[SSR & hydration](../guides/ssr.md#what-hydration-actually-does).

### withExoChildList

```ts no-check
function withExoChildList<TBase extends TExoDomApi>(base: TBase): TBase;
```

Adds `c.childList(port)` — the commanded child list, with its `insert`, `move`,
`remove`, `removeAll`, `detach` and `attach` — to every exonode the backend
builds. Everything that places children one at a time opens one: `reconcileExoOrder`
over `c.childList`, the keyed list (`c.keyedList` calls `childList`), the router's
`ExoOutlet` / `exoOutlet`, and any machine that places `c.build` children by hand.
On a backend composed without it the call throws [EXO0109](../errors.md#exo0109).

A page that fills its children ports only with `c.one` and a fixed `c.list` links
none of it. Compose it once, at module level, on the backend that renders a machine
which opens a child list:

```ts no-check
const backend = withExoChildList(withExoCompiler(new ExoDomBackend()));
```

### withExoForeignNamespaces

```ts no-check
function withExoForeignNamespaces<TBase extends TExoDomApi>(
    base: TBase
): TBase & { readonly foreignNamespaces: TExoForeignNamespaces };
```

Adds `foreignNamespaces`: the SVG and MathML tables — the namespace an element is
created in, tag and attribute case adjustment (`viewBox`, `foreignObject`),
namespaced attributes (`xlink:href`) and the HTML integration points. A schema
containing `<svg>`, `<math>` or an SVG-only element (`circle`, `path`, `g`, …)
compiled on a backend without it is refused with [EXO0108](../errors.md#exo0108),
naming the tag, rather than built in the HTML namespace where it would not draw. A
JSON declaration with an attribute on such an element is refused with
[EXO0110](../errors.md#exo0110).

A page with no SVG or MathML links none of those tables. Compose it once, at module
level, on the backend that renders a schema with SVG or MathML in it:

```ts no-check
const backend = withExoForeignNamespaces(withExoCompiler(new ExoDomBackend()));
```

The packs are independent, so the order among them does not matter:
`withExoChildList(withExoForeignNamespaces(withExoCompiler(new ExoDomBackend())))`.

### Nesting and lists

```ts
import { createExoMachineBuilder, createExoSchema } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoAttrPort, TExoChildrenPort, TExoTextPort } from '@exodra/core';
import { ExoDomBackend, withExoChildList, withExoCompiler } from '@exodra/dom';
import type { TExoChildList, TExoDomNode } from '@exodra/dom';
import { reconcileExoOrder } from '@exodra/list-reconcile';

const backend = withExoChildList(withExoCompiler(new ExoDomBackend()));

type TTask = { readonly id: string; readonly title: string };

const TASK_SCHEMA = createExoSchema((b) => {
    let id!: TExoAttrPort;
    let title!: TExoTextPort;
    b.el('li', null, (li) => {
        id = li.port('data-id');
        title = li.textPort();
    });
    return { id, title };
});
const mTask = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoDomNode>(TASK_SCHEMA);
const showTask = mTask.transition((row: TExoDomNode, task: TTask) => {
    row.attr(TASK_SCHEMA.ports.id, task.id);
    row.text(TASK_SCHEMA.ports.title, task.title);
});
const TASK = mTask.done();

let tasks: readonly TTask[] = [
    { id: 'a', title: 'First' },
    { id: 'b', title: 'Second' },
];
const taskListeners = new Set<() => void>();
function setTasks(next: readonly TTask[]): void {
    tasks = next;
    taskListeners.forEach((listener) => listener());
}

const BOARD_SCHEMA = createExoSchema((b) => {
    let rows!: TExoChildrenPort;
    b.el('ul', { class: 'board' }, (ul) => {
        rows = ul.childrenPort();
    });
    return { rows };
});

type TBoardState = { rows: TExoChildList; shown: TTask[] };

const mBoard = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoDomNode, unknown, TBoardState>(BOARD_SCHEMA);
mBoard.createInitialState((c) => ({ rows: c.childList(BOARD_SCHEMA.ports.rows), shown: [] }));
const showTasks = mBoard.transition((c) => {
    c.state.shown = reconcileExoOrder(c.state.rows, c.state.shown, tasks, tasks, (task, at) => {
        const row = c.build(TASK, at);
        showTask(row, task);
        return row;
    });
});
mBoard.effect((c) => {
    showTasks(c);
    const listener = (): void => showTasks(c);
    taskListeners.add(listener);
    return () => {
        taskListeners.delete(listener);
    };
});
const BOARD = mBoard.done();

backend.render(BOARD, document.body);

setTasks([...tasks, { id: 'c', title: 'Third' }]);
```

`reconcileExoOrder(kids, shown, keys, want, build)` reconciles **by object
identity** when `keys` is the item array itself — a row that survives an update
is the same element it was, and a row that leaves is disposed. It returns the new
shown order, which the machine keeps in its state for the next pass. No keys are
involved; keys are the opt-in `EXO_KEYED_LIST_VOCABULARY` pack. See the
[Lists guide](../guides/lists.md).

Use `c.list(port, component, count)` instead when the contents cannot change: a
fixed list pays for no row records, no diff and no teardown.

### Children as values

A reconciler is a function over two doors, and both are public:

- `c.build(component, index?)` returns a child — a complete, wired, detached
  instance, placed nowhere.
- `c.childList(port)` returns the port's `TExoChildList`: `insert` (places and
  mounts), `move`, `remove` (unmounts and disposes), `removeAll`, and the placement
  pair `detach` / `attach`, which take a child out and put it back **without** any
  hook — nothing unmounted, nothing disposed, subscriptions left live
  (`packages/dom/src/dom/types/TExoChildList.ts`). `detachAll` is `detach` at every
  index.

Whoever drives those doors decides everything else — which item reuses which
child, whether a child that leaves is disposed or kept, what a key would mean.
Keeping a whole exonode across a hide and a show is `detach` then `attach` on a
child you hold; there is no element pool, and an element only ever comes from
`cloneExoNode` on the schema's prototype.

`exoNodeDom(child).node` is the documented way a holder reaches the element
behind a child. `exoNodeDom` takes a **child** — an element carries no pointer back
to its child, so there is no element→child direction — and a hand-made element is
refused by name (`assertBuiltExoChild`), because it carries no lifecycle and could
never be unmounted.

Related exports: `createExoChildList`, `TExoChildList`, `TExoDomChild`,
`dropExoChild`, `clearOwnedExoChildList`, `assertBuiltExoChild`.

### Contexts

`provide` and `inject` are methods on the exonode — there is nothing to import,
because a context exists only while an instance is being built.

`provide` extends the chain **on the exonode**. A list captures that chain when it
is wired and holds it for its whole life, so a row added an hour later, from inside
a subscriber with no render on the stack, resolves off the captured chain and walks
nothing.

**A context does not travel through the document.** A separate `render()` into an
element that some other render provided into starts from nothing — it does not
