# Router API Reference

`@exodra/router` is a renderer-neutral core plus the handful of pieces that draw
a route.

| Half | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **The renderer-neutral half** — `createExoRouter`, the histories, `matchExoRoutes`, `parseExoPath`, the guards, `exoLazy` / `fetchExoRouteChunk`, and the query helpers | A plain service: it knows about URLs, route tables and matches, calls `onChange` subscribers after every commit, and knows nothing about how anything is drawn. |
| **The components** — `ExoOutlet`, `exoOutlet`, `ExoLink`, `provideExoRouter`, `injectExoRouter`, `preloadExoPage` | A page is a machine, a route boundary is a machine whose one child is the page the URL selects, and the router reaches components through `provide` / `inject`. |

Matching, chaining, guards and `handle` read `path`, `children`, `catchAll` and
`handle`, and never read `component` — so a route's component is carried, not
interpreted.

## How the names are spelt

Two name shapes, and the shape tells you the layer:

| Shape | What it is | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ExoThing` | A **value you pass**, never a call — a ready-made machine | `ExoOutlet`, `ExoLink` |
| `exoThing(…)` | A **factory you call** (at module level) that returns one | `exoOutlet('main')`, `exoLazy(() => import(…))` |

And two pairs of words that are not interchangeable:

- **Route** vs **page.** A *route* is a table entry — a path, its children, its
  guards, and a `component` this half of the package never looks inside. A *page*
  is that component once it is a real machine the renderer can draw.
  So `matchExoRoutes`, `collectExoRouteGuards` and `fetchExoRouteChunk` are about
  the table; `isExoPageMachine` and `preloadExoPage` are about the thing that gets
  drawn.
- **Query** vs **search.** A *query* is the parsed record (`{ page: 2 }`);
  *search* is only the raw `?page=2` text, spelt that way because
  `Location.search` is. Everything that parses, builds, merges or validates one
  says *query*.

Exports: `createExoRouter`, `createExoBrowserHistory`, `createExoMemoryHistory`,
`matchExoRoutes`, `matchExoRouteChain`, `parseExoPath`, `collectExoRouteGuards`,
`executeExoGuards`, `exoLazy`, `isExoLazyLoader`, `loadExoLazyMachine`,
`fetchExoRouteChunk`, `resolveExoRouteMachine`, the query helpers (`exoQuery`,
`parseExoQuery`, `stringifyExoQuery`, `mergeExoQuery`,
`ExoQueryValidationError`), the components (`ExoOutlet`, `exoOutlet`, `ExoLink`,
`shouldIgnoreExoLinkClick`, `provideExoRouter`, `injectExoRouter`, `EXO_ROUTER`,
`preloadExoPage`, `isExoPageMachine`), and the package's types.

---

# The renderer-neutral half

The router is read with getters and followed with `onChange`; a component that
follows it subscribes from a machine effect
([Following the router](#following-the-router)).

## createExoRouter()

Creates a router instance. **`routes` is the first positional argument**, and
options are a second optional argument.

```typescript signature
function createExoRouter(
  routes: readonly TExoRoute[],
  options?: {
    history?: TExoHistory;
    beforeEach?: TExoRouteGuard;
    afterEach?: (to: TExoRouteMatch | undefined, from?: TExoRouteMatch) => void;
  }
): TExoRouter;

type TExoRoute = {
  id?: string;
  path: string;
  component: TExoRouteMachine;
  children?: readonly TExoRoute[];
  beforeEnter?: TExoRouteGuard;
  beforeLeave?: TExoRouteGuard;
  catchAll?: string;          // parameter name for [...params]
  optionalCatchAll?: string;  // parameter name for [[...params]]
  handle?: unknown;
};
```

There is **no** `mode`, `base`, or `options.routes` — the base path is configured
on the history (`basePath`), and there is no hash mode toggle.

### Example

```javascript
import { createExoRouter, createExoBrowserHistory } from '@exodra/router';
import Home from './pages/home';
import About from './pages/about';

const routes = [
  { path: '/', component: Home },
  { path: '/about', component: About },
  { path: '/users/:id', component: UserDetail },
];

const router = createExoRouter(routes, {
  history: createExoBrowserHistory(),
  beforeEach: (to, from) => {
    // return true to allow, false to block, or a string path to redirect.
    return true;
  },
});
```

If you omit `history`, the router uses an in-memory history.

## History

```typescript signature
function createExoBrowserHistory(options?: { window?: Window; basePath?: string }): TExoHistory;
function createExoMemoryHistory(initialPathOrOptions?: string | { initialPath?: string; basePath?: string }): TExoHistory;
```

- `createExoBrowserHistory()` drives the browser URL via the History API and
  `popstate`.
- `createExoMemoryHistory('/start')` is for SSR and tests — seed it with the
  initial path.

```javascript
import { createExoRouter, createExoMemoryHistory } from '@exodra/router';

// On the server, seed the location from the request URL.
const router = createExoRouter(routes, { history: createExoMemoryHistory(url) });
```

## Router instance

A `TExoRouter` is a plain service — getters, navigation methods and one
subscription:

| Member | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `routes` | The route table. |
| `getLocation()` | The current `{ pathname, search, hash, href, state? }`. |
| `getMatch()` | The current leaf match, or `undefined` when nothing matched. |
| `getMatches()` | The full matched branch, root → leaf. An entry a navigation did not change is the **same object** as before. |
| `getNavigationState()` | `'idle' \| 'loading'` — `'loading'` only while an async guard decides. |
| `getQuery(options?)` | The current query, parsed from `location.search`. |
| `navigate(to, options?)` | Navigate; returns `Promise<TExoLocation>`. |
| `setPathname(pathname, options?)` | Navigate keeping the current search/hash. |
| `setSearch(search, options?)` | Replace the whole `?…` string. Handed an object instead, it does exactly what `setQuery` does. |
| `setQuery(query, options?)` | Replace the whole query from a record. |
| `patchQuery(query, options?)` | Merge a query patch into the URL (`undefined` clears a key). |
| `onChange(update)` | Call `update` after every commit and every navigation-state change; returns `off`. |
| `createHref(to)` | Resolve a path to an href (applies base path). |
| `dispose()` | Tear down the router — and its history. |

Every navigation method returns `Promise<TExoLocation>`.

### navigate()

```typescript signature
router.navigate(
  to: string,
  options?: { replace?: boolean; state?: unknown }
): Promise<TExoLocation>;
```

```javascript
await router.navigate('/users/123');
await router.navigate('/login', { replace: true });
await router.navigate('/checkout', { state: { from: 'cart' } }); // see "Location state"
```

`navigate()` runs the guards **before** it writes history, so a refused
navigation writes nothing, needs no rollback and does not fire `afterEach`. A
change the router did not write — back/forward, or someone else's
`history.push` — is put back with `history.replace` when it is refused, silently:
no guard runs again and `afterEach` does not fire.

Only the **latest** navigation may commit: an older one whose guard answers late
does nothing. A branch with no guard, or only synchronous guards, commits
**synchronously inside** `navigate()`. The returned promise resolves after a
redirect chain has landed, with the location it landed on.

### Route `handle` and the match chain

Attach arbitrary static metadata to a route with `handle` — the equivalent of
React Router's route `handle`. It surfaces on **every** entry of the matched
branch, so `getMatches()` (root → leaf) is your breadcrumb / title / layout-flag
source. `getMatch()` returns just the leaf.

```javascript
const routes = [
  { path: '/', component: Root, handle: { crumb: 'Home' }, children: [
    { path: 'users', component: Users, handle: { crumb: 'Users' }, children: [
      { path: ':id', component: User, handle: { crumb: 'Profile' } },
    ]},
  ]},
];

const crumbs = router.getMatches().map(m => ({ label: m.handle.crumb, href: m.pathname }));
// at /users/42 → [{Home, /}, {Users, /users}, {Profile, /users/42}]
```

Each entry also carries its own resolved `pathname` (params substituted) and only
the params named in **its own** full path, root through itself; the leaf carries
all of them. `handle` is typed `unknown` — cast it to your own metadata shape at
the read site.

### Which route wins

Matching ranks the routes; it does not take the first one declared. Position by
position, a **static** segment beats a `:param`, a `:param` beats a pattern that
has **ended** there, and an ended pattern beats a `*` **catch-all**. Between equal
patterns the **deeper** route wins — so an index child (`path: ''`) is reached
inside its layout — and after that, declaration order. `/users/new` beats
`/users/:id` whichever is declared first.

### Location state

Carry per-navigation data that should **not** live in the URL — a "came from"
hint, a scroll target, a small object you don't want to serialize into query
params. It's stored in the History API, so it survives back/forward, and is read
back on `location.state`:

```javascript
await router.navigate('/checkout', { state: { from: 'cart' } });
router.getLocation().state; // { from: 'cart' }
```

> Location `state` is lost on a hard reload and is not shareable (not in the
> URL). If you need state that survives reloads or is linkable, use query params
> (`setQuery` / `patchQuery`) instead. `state` is typed `unknown`.

### Following the router

A component that follows the URL subscribes with `onChange` from a machine
**effect**. `onChange` returns its `off`, which is what an effect returns, so
`disconnectExoNode` / `connectExoNode` switch the subscription off and on and
teardown ends it:

```ts
import { createExoMachineBuilder, createExoSchema } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoMachineNode, TExoTextPort } from '@exodra/core';
import { injectExoRouter } from '@exodra/router';

const WHERE_SCHEMA = createExoSchema((b) => {
    let path!: TExoTextPort;
    b.el('p', null, (p) => {
        path = p.textPort();
    });
    return { path };
});
const mWhere = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoMachineNode>(WHERE_SCHEMA);
const showPath = mWhere.transition((c) => {
    c.text(WHERE_SCHEMA.ports.path, injectExoRouter(c).getLocation().pathname);
});
mWhere.wire((c) => showPath(c));
mWhere.effect((c) => {
    showPath(c);
    return injectExoRouter(c).onChange(() => showPath(c));
});
const WHERE = mWhere.done();
```

`onChange` runs after every commit and every navigation-state change, and only
after every route boundary has redrawn. A subscriber added while a notification is
running is first called on the next one. For the current link in a nav bar, use
`ExoLink`'s `currentWhen` instead of writing this by hand.

### Navigation state

`getNavigationState()` is `'idle'` or `'loading'`. It is `'loading'` only while an
**asynchronous** guard decides; a branch with no guard or only synchronous guards
never leaves `'idle'`, and a refused navigation returns to `'idle'` as well as a
committed one. Each change notifies `onChange`.

## Lazy routes

`exoLazy()` wraps a dynamic import into a loader the router resolves on match;
`fetchExoRouteChunk()` makes that chunk arrive ahead of time. `isExoLazyLoader`,
`loadExoLazyMachine` and `resolveExoRouteMachine` are the same machinery,
exported for a renderer that resolves a route's component itself.

```javascript
import { exoLazy, fetchExoRouteChunk } from '@exodra/router';

const routes = [
  { path: '/settings', component: exoLazy(() => import('./pages/settings')) },
];

// Start the download early — on hover, on idle, on a hunch about what is next.
fetchExoRouteChunk(routes[0].component);
```

To *render* a lazy route rather than merely fetch it, use
[`preloadExoPage`](#lazy-pages-preloadexopage) instead. The two differ in what
they leave behind, which is why one is spelt **route** and the other **page**:

| | `fetchExoRouteChunk(component)` | `preloadExoPage(loader)` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Takes | a route's `component` — a page already here is a no-op | the loader itself |
| Checks the module is a page | no | yes, and rejects if it is not |
| Leaves behind | the in-flight *promise*, which no synchronous render can read | the resolved *component*, where the outlet looks for it |
| Makes a lazy route server-renderable | no | yes |

## Guards

`beforeEach` (router-wide) and `beforeEnter` / `beforeLeave` (per route) each
return `true` to allow, `false` to block, or a string path to redirect — and may
return a promise of any of those. A guard that throws or rejects counts as
`false`. `collectExoRouteGuards` and `executeExoGuards` are exported for a
renderer that runs the chain itself; `executeExoGuards` stays synchronous until a
guard returns a promise, and returns a `TExoRouteGuardResult`.

## Query helpers

A **query** is the parsed record; **search** is only the raw `?page=2` string.
None of these read a URL by themselves — hand them
`router.getLocation().search`, or use `router.getQuery()`, which does that for
you.

| Helper | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `parseExoQuery(search, options?)` | A `?…` string in, a query record out (optionally typed and validated by a schema). The leading `?` is optional; a repeated key becomes an array. **The record has a NULL PROTOTYPE** — see below. |
| `stringifyExoQuery(query)` | A query record in, a `?…` string out. Empty gives `''`, not `'?'`; `undefined` / `null` drop their key. |
| `mergeExoQuery(current, patch)` | Lay a patch over a parsed query. |
| `exoQuery` | Typed field builders (`exoQuery.string()`, `exoQuery.number()`, `exoQuery.boolean()`, `exoQuery.array()`, `exoQuery.optional()`) for schema parsing. |
| `ExoQueryValidationError` | Thrown when a schema field rejects a value. |

### The parsed record has a null prototype, and that is deliberate

`parseExoQuery` builds its record with `Object.create(null)`, so it inherits nothing. Read a key,
spread it, `Object.entries` it, hand it to `stringifyExoQuery` — all unchanged. What stops working is
anything reached through `Object.prototype`:

```ts
import { parseExoQuery } from '@exodra/router';

const query = parseExoQuery('?page=2');

// `query.hasOwnProperty('page')` throws: the record inherits nothing, so there is no such method.
const present = 'page' in query;
const alsoPresent = Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(query, 'page');
// `Object.hasOwn(query, 'page')` is the modern spelling and needs an ES2022 lib; this package
// targets ES2020, which is why the call above is written the long way.
```

**Why.** A URL supplies the KEYS as well as the values, and an ordinary `{}` already answers to
twelve of them. `?__proto__=x` invoked the prototype setter and the parameter vanished — no own key,
nothing in `Object.entries`, and the record silently reparented. `?constructor=1` was worse in a
quieter way: the assignment created a real own property whose value contained the `Object`
constructor **function**, and that survived every check downstream to reach the caller as a query
value. Neither wrote into anything shared, so neither was prototype pollution — they were a dropped
parameter and a returned object nobody chose the shape of.

`Object.create(null)` closes all twelve at once, at the accumulator, which is why the fix is one line
per accumulator rather than a list of names to keep up to date.

Route **params** are a different case and stay an ordinary object: their keys come from the route
table the application wrote (`:id`, a catch-all), and the URL supplies only values.

```javascript
import { parseExoQuery, stringifyExoQuery, exoQuery } from '@exodra/router';

parseExoQuery('?page=2', { parseNumbers: true }); // { page: 2 }
stringifyExoQuery({ page: 2, tags: ['a', 'b'] }); // '?page=2&tags=a&tags=b'

// Typed schema parsing:
const result = parseExoQuery('?page=3', {
  schema: { page: exoQuery.number({ default: 1 }) },
}); // { page: 3 }
```

Earlier versions also exported `readExoSearch` and `createExoSearch`, aliases of
exactly these two functions. They are gone: two exported names for one function
is a guess at the autocomplete, and `read` suggested a difference (reading the
live URL?) that never existed. Rename `readExoSearch` → `parseExoQuery` and
`createExoSearch` → `stringifyExoQuery`; the signatures are unchanged.

---

# The components

Three things make a routed page, and none of them is a JSX element:

- **A page is a machine**, and the match that selected it arrives as the
  **params of its wire**: `createExoMachineBuilder<TExoMachineNode, TExoRouteMatch>(SCHEMA)`,
  then `mPage.wire((c, match) => …)`.
- **A route boundary is a machine.** `ExoOutlet` (a `<div>`) or `exoOutlet(tag, attrs)`,
  placed with `c.one(port, ExoOutlet)`; its one child is the page the URL selects.
- **The router travels in the context.** `provideExoRouter(c, router)` above,
  `injectExoRouter(c)` below — boundaries and links do the injecting themselves.

A routed page renders on the server (`ExoStrBackend`), in the browser
(`ExoDomBackend`), and hydrates: `withExoHydration` adopts the server's markup by
identity, nested layouts included. A boundary opens a child list for its page, so the
DOM backend that renders one is composed with
[`withExoChildList`](./dom.md#withexochildlist); without it the first outlet throws
[EXO0109](../errors.md#exo0109).

The route table itself is **data**, not markup: a plain array of objects. A
schema is a tag with numbered ports, built once at module load, and there is
nowhere in it to put a component reference or a guard function — which is exactly
what a route entry is made of.

```ts no-check  // `./pages` stands for your own page components
import type { TExoRoute } from '@exodra/router';
import { ABOUT_PAGE, HOME_PAGE, USER_PAGE } from './pages';

const ROUTES: readonly TExoRoute[] = [
  { path: '/', component: HOME_PAGE },
  { path: '/about', component: ABOUT_PAGE, handle: { crumb: 'About' } },
  { path: '/users/:id', component: USER_PAGE },
];
```

## A routed page, end to end

```ts
import { createExoMachineBuilder, createExoSchema } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoChildrenPort, TExoMachineNode, TExoTextPort } from '@exodra/core';
import { ExoDomBackend, withExoChildList, withExoCompiler } from '@exodra/dom';
import type { TExoDomNode } from '@exodra/dom';
import {
  ExoLink,
  ExoOutlet,
  createExoBrowserHistory,
  createExoRouter,
  provideExoRouter,
} from '@exodra/router';
import type { TExoRoute, TExoRouteMatch } from '@exodra/router';

const USER_PAGE_SCHEMA = createExoSchema(b => {
  let name!: TExoTextPort;
  b.el('h1', null, h => {
    name = h.textPort();
  });
  return { name };
});
const mUserPage = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoMachineNode, TExoRouteMatch>(USER_PAGE_SCHEMA);
mUserPage.wire((c, match) => {
  c.text(USER_PAGE_SCHEMA.ports.name, match.params.id);
});
const USER_PAGE = mUserPage.done();

const ROUTES: readonly TExoRoute[] = [{ path: '/users/:id', component: USER_PAGE }];

const router = createExoRouter(ROUTES, { history: createExoBrowserHistory() });

const APP_SCHEMA = createExoSchema(b => {
  let nav!: TExoChildrenPort;
  let page!: TExoChildrenPort;
  b.el('div', { class: 'app' }, d => {
    d.el('nav', null, n => {
      nav = n.childrenPort();
    });
    d.el('main', null, m => {
      page = m.childrenPort();
    });
  });
  return { nav, page };
});
const mApp = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoDomNode>(APP_SCHEMA);
mApp.createInitialState(c => {
  provideExoRouter(c, router);
  c.one(APP_SCHEMA.ports.nav, ExoLink, { to: '/users/1', label: 'First user' });
  c.one(APP_SCHEMA.ports.page, ExoOutlet);
});
const APP = mApp.done();

const backend = withExoChildList(withExoCompiler(new ExoDomBackend()));
backend.render(APP, document.getElementById('root') as HTMLElement);
```

`TExoDomNode` types the app against the browser. A machine that has to run on the
server too names only what it uses — for placing a boundary, an interface with
`one(port: TExoChildrenPort, machine: TExoMachine<never>): void` over
`TExoMachineNode` (see [Nested routes](#nested-routes)).

## provideExoRouter()

```typescript signature
function provideExoRouter(connector: TExoProvideWiring, router: TExoRouter): void;
```

Puts the router where every boundary and every link below can find it. It is a
**call inside a machine**, not a component: `provide` is a method on the exonode,
and a component on this core is exactly one element — so a provider component
would have to invent a wrapper node to carry a value that needs no node.

It does **not** create a router and does **not** dispose one. An initial state
runs once per instance on *both* backends, so a router created inside one would be
created twice on a page that is rendered and then hydrated. `createExoRouter()`
and `router.dispose()` belong beside the mount that owns them.

`injectExoRouter(c)` is the other side — `useRouter` asked of an exonode. It
**throws** when nothing above provided a router, because a boundary with no
router shows nothing and a link with no router cannot resolve an href, and both of
those otherwise fail much later with nothing pointing at the missing
`provideExoRouter`.

## ExoOutlet and exoOutlet()

Two spellings of one route boundary — a machine **value** you pass, and a
**factory** you call to get one around another tag. `ExoOutlet` *is*
`exoOutlet('div')`.

```typescript signature
const ExoOutlet: TExoMachine<TExoOutletWiring, { page: TExoChildrenPort }>;
function exoOutlet(tag?: string, attrs?: Readonly<Record<string, unknown>> | null):
  TExoMachine<TExoOutletWiring, { page: TExoChildrenPort }>;
```

| Form | Use it when |
| --- | --- |
| `c.one(port, ExoOutlet)` | You just want a boundary; it is a `<div>`. |
| `c.one(port, ROUTED)`, with `const ROUTED = exoOutlet('main')` at module level | The boundary should be the tag the layout was going to write anyway — the node then costs nothing. |
| `c.childList(port).insert(c.build(ExoOutlet))` | The boundary goes into a child list the layout already manages. |

`exoOutlet()` builds a schema, so **call it at module level** — per render it
would rebuild and re-plan a shape that has not changed.

### Nested routes

A layout is a route with `children`, and its page places its own `ExoOutlet`:

```ts
import { createExoMachineBuilder, createExoSchema } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoChildrenPort, TExoMachine, TExoMachineNode } from '@exodra/core';
import { ExoOutlet } from '@exodra/router';

interface TNestingNode extends TExoMachineNode {
  one(port: TExoChildrenPort, machine: TExoMachine<never>): void;
}

const LAYOUT_SCHEMA = createExoSchema(b => {
  let page!: TExoChildrenPort;
  b.el('section', { class: 'layout' }, s => {
    page = s.childrenPort();
  });
  return { page };
});
const mLayout = createExoMachineBuilder<TNestingNode>(LAYOUT_SCHEMA);
mLayout.createInitialState(c => {
  c.one(LAYOUT_SCHEMA.ports.page, ExoOutlet);
});
const LAYOUT = mLayout.done();
```

Depth is automatic: the nested boundary finds its parent boundary through the
context and draws the next entry of the matched branch. Two outlets in one page
both stand for the same depth and draw the same page.

Only the **outermost** boundary listens to the router. Nested ones are reached
top-down, through their parent, after the parent's level is settled — so on a
navigation across two layouts the arriving page is built once, inside the
arriving layout, and never into the layout that is leaving.

### When a page is rebuilt

- **A different route component** at a depth: the old page is removed (its
  teardown runs) and the new one is built.
- **The same component, a different match** — `/users/1` → `/users/2`: a page
  **with a wire** is **re-wired in place** — same DOM nodes, same listeners. A
  page **without a wire** is rebuilt.
- **The same match**: that level is kept, and the boundary goes on to the levels
  below it. Entries of `getMatches()` a navigation did not change are the same
  objects, so a query-only change keeps every page.

A page's wire may only **write ports**. Placing children (`childList`, `one`,
`list`) in a wire throws `EXO0103` when the wire is re-run. Place children in
`createInitialState`, which can read its match with
`injectExoRouter(c).getMatches()[index]` — `index` is the boundary depth it was
built at.

## ExoLink

A machine around a real `<a href>` the router takes over on a plain left click.
Its values are the **params of its wire**, `TExoLinkParams`:

```typescript
type TExoLinkParams = {
  readonly to: string;         // resolved through router.createHref
  readonly label?: string;     // the anchor's text
  readonly replace?: boolean;  // replace the history entry instead of pushing
  readonly state?: unknown;    // per-entry location state
  readonly target?: string;    // anything but _self is left to the browser
  readonly download?: string;
  readonly onClick?: (event: MouseEvent) => void;  // preventDefault() calls the click off
  readonly currentWhen?: 'exact' | 'prefix';       // writes aria-current="page"
};
```

```ts
import { createExoMachineBuilder, createExoSchema } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoChildrenPort } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoDomNode } from '@exodra/dom';
import { ExoLink } from '@exodra/router';

const NAV_SCHEMA = createExoSchema(b => {
  let items!: TExoChildrenPort;
  b.el('nav', null, n => {
    items = n.childrenPort();
  });
  return { items };
});
const mNav = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoDomNode>(NAV_SCHEMA);
mNav.createInitialState(c => {
  const items = c.childList(NAV_SCHEMA.ports.items);
  items.insert(c.build(ExoLink, 0, { to: '/', label: 'Home', currentWhen: 'exact' }));
  items.insert(c.build(ExoLink, 1, { to: '/about', label: 'About', currentWhen: 'prefix' }));
});
const NAV = mNav.done();
```

`ExoLink` injects the router itself, and it renders on the **server** too — the
string backend prints the same anchor the browser draws.

**`currentWhen`** writes `aria-current="page"` while the location is current for
the link: `'exact'` when the pathname equals `to`, `'prefix'` also for any path
below it. Only a link with `currentWhen` subscribes to the router.

The interesting half is the clicks it does **not** take — a middle click, a
⌘/Ctrl/Shift/Alt click, a `download`, a `target` other than `_self`, another
origin, or a click something upstream already called off. That policy is exported
on its own as `shouldIgnoreExoLinkClick(event, href, target?, download?)` for a
hand-written anchor that wants to behave identically. A destination that carries
its own scheme or authority (`https://…`, `mailto:…`, `//host/x`) is used as the
href verbatim; everything else goes through `router.createHref`.

There is **no** `activeClass` param — `currentWhen` writes `aria-current`, and
`a[aria-current="page"]` is the selector.

## Lazy pages: preloadExoPage()

```typescript signature
function preloadExoPage(loader: TExoLazyRouteLoader): Promise<void>;
```

A render is one synchronous call on all three backends, so a route whose
component is still a `() => import(…)` prints **nothing**: the boundary is an
empty region and the browser fills it once the chunk lands. `preloadExoPage` fetches
the chunk **and remembers the resolved component**, so a synchronous render
afterwards can print it — which is what makes a lazy route server-renderable.

```ts no-check  // `./shell` and `./pages/dashboard` stand for your own modules
import { ExoStrBackend } from '@exodra/string';
import { createExoMemoryHistory, createExoRouter, exoLazy, preloadExoPage } from '@exodra/router';
import { SHELL } from './shell';

const DASHBOARD = exoLazy(() => import('./pages/dashboard'));

const router = createExoRouter([{ path: '/dashboard', component: DASHBOARD }], {
  history: createExoMemoryHistory('/dashboard'),   // seeded from the request URL
});

await preloadExoPage(DASHBOARD);                        // before the server render
const html = new ExoStrBackend().render(SHELL);         // the dashboard is in the markup
```

`fetchExoRouteChunk` is **not** this: it only makes the chunk arrive, which stops
a second fetch but hands a synchronous render nothing it can read
([the full comparison](#lazy-routes)).
A loader that resolves to something that is not a page is refused by
`preloadExoPage`, where the caller is awaiting and can see it — rather than inside a
subscriber an hour later, with no call stack pointing at the table.

`isExoPageMachine(component)` is the test underneath: a page is a machine — an
object carrying `declaration` and `handlers`, which `createExoMachineBuilder(…).done()`
returns — and a loader or a plain function is not one.

## Context tokens

`EXO_ROUTER` is the token `provideExoRouter` and `injectExoRouter` use, exported
for a component that wants `c.inject(EXO_ROUTER)` without the throw.

## Names this router does not have

> There is **no** `useRoute`, `useParams`, `useLocation`, or `useQuery`. A page
> receives its match as the params of its wire; anything else reads
> `router.getMatch()` (its `.params` holds path params) and `router.getQuery()`.

> Nonexistent APIs: `createBrowserRouter`, `createMemoryRouter`,
> `RouterView`, `useRoute`, `useParams`, `useLocation`, `useQuery`,
> `router.beforeEach()` (it's the `beforeEach` **option**), and the
> `activeClass` param.


==============================================================================
# String Renderer

`@exodra/string` is the **server backend** of the schema core. It runs the same
component values [`@exodra/core`](./core.md) describes and the **same wiring
function** [`@exodra/dom`](./dom.md) runs, and hands back markup instead of
nodes.

A schema is cut **once** into the fewest strings a render can be, so an instance
is a handful of concatenations. No tree is ever built to be serialised.

```bash
npm install @exodra/string @exodra/core
```

## ExoStrBackend

```ts no-check
class ExoStrBackend {
    constructor(...plugins: readonly TExoPlugin[]);
    schema(component: TExoMachine<never>): TExoStrSchema;
    render(component: TExoStrMachine, context?: TExoContextFrame | null, params?: unknown): string;
}
```

The server entry point is an **object you construct and render from**, exactly as
[`ExoDomBackend`](./dom.md#exodombackend) is, and `render` is the same method name
taking the component as one value — a page switches sides by switching which
backend it holds, not by learning a second calling convention, and the return value
*is* the difference.

The **constructors differ**, and it is worth stating rather than discovering:
`ExoDomBackend` takes nothing and is composed by wrapping it in `with*` decorators;
this one still accepts a variadic list of plugins, merged after the connector
surface.

```ts
import { createExoMachineBuilder, createExoSchema } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoTextPort } from '@exodra/core';
import { ExoStrBackend } from '@exodra/string';
import type { TExoStrNode } from '@exodra/string';

const CARD_SCHEMA = createExoSchema((b) => {
    let title!: TExoTextPort;
    let body!: TExoTextPort;
    b.el('article', { class: 'card' }, (card) => {
        card.el('h2', null, (h2) => {
            title = h2.textPort();
        });
        card.el('p', null, (p) => {
            body = p.textPort();
        });
    });
    return { title, body };
});
const mCard = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoStrNode>(CARD_SCHEMA);
mCard.wire((c) => {
    c.text(CARD_SCHEMA.ports.title, 'Card');
    c.text(CARD_SCHEMA.ports.body, 'Welcome to Exodra');
});
const CARD = mCard.done();

const backend = new ExoStrBackend();

const html = backend.render(CARD);
// <article class="card"><h2>Card</h2><p>Welcome to Exodra</p></article>
```

`render` prints **one** instance and takes **no count**, exactly as the browser
backend mounts one. `createInitialState` receives `0` as its index, because a
lone root has nothing else to be about. Rows that vary are a **list** — `list` /
`one` on the exonode, which hand each row its own position as its index through
the same signature.

### What it does not have, stated rather than discovered

`ExoDomBackend` carries two replaceable implementation fields — `events` and
`writers` — beside its record factories, and **neither has a field here**. A string
has no listeners to attach; escaping and attribute form are decided by
`compileExoStrSchema` through `EXO_STR_WRITERS`, which the two backends must agree
on byte for byte or hydration is wrong; and there is nothing on this side to adopt.
So this backend's composable surface is its **methods**: `new ExoStrBackend(...plugins)`
merges its exonode surface onto itself first, so a pack naming `attr`, `text` or
`list` receives the shipped body as `next` and may wrap it, and a pack naming
something new adds it to `c.` for every component this backend runs.

That asymmetry is a bound on what a pack can promise. A pack that replaces
`writers` composes into a DOM backend and is silently inert here, because
nothing on this side reads that name. Composing it is not refused — the merge
writes any name — so a pack that means to serve both sides has to say what it
does on each.

## The exonode

`TExoStrNode` is shaped **exactly** like `TExoDomNode`, method for
method — both are **types** rather than classes, and both name an object whose
prototype is its backend — because a component's wiring function is the one piece written by hand
and it must not be able to tell which backend it is filling.

| Method | On the server |
| --- | --- |
| `attr(port, value)` | Escape for an attribute position, and store. |
| `text(port, value)` | Escape for a text position, and store. |
| `unsafeHtml(port, markup)` | Store the markup as given, escaping nothing. |
| `on(port, handler, subject?)` | Accepted in **both** forms and printed as nothing. The slot is still written. |
| `onTeardown(off)` | Filed, and run at the end of the render — after the markup has been taken. |
| `provide(token, value)` / `inject(token)` | The same chain and the same lookup rule the browser uses. |
| `one(port, component)` | Render one nested instance into the port. |
| `list(port, component, count)` | `count` instances, concatenated. |
| `build(component, index?)` | Render one child and hand it back as a value. |
| `childList(port)` | The port's children, for a caller to place into. |

Two of those are worth spelling out, because they look like omissions:

- **`on` must accept both forms or the design breaks in half.** A component's
  wiring function is written once and run by three backends; the moment
  `c.on(H.click, TOGGLE_DONE, subject)` is a call the server does not have, every
  component with a declarative handler needs a second wiring function.
- **There is no `bind` here, and none is missing.** Following data is a
  machine's effect: it draws through a transition, then subscribes. On this
  backend the effect runs once while the instance is armed, the draw is the only
  write that reaches the markup, and the render stops the effect as soon as the
  markup is taken — so a server render reads the data once and leaves no
  subscription behind the response.

A **node** on this backend is a string of markup — the type it comes back
as (`TExoNode`) is opaque, which is what lets one wiring function assemble
children on all three backends without learning that the server's are strings
and the browser's are DOM nodes.

## Contexts on the server

`provide` and `inject` are methods on the connector, as in the browser. What
this backend threads is a **frame on the connector** rather than a mark on
anything: there are no nodes, and the server builds strictly depth-first, once, so
the chain in force is exactly the one the current call stack passed down.

There is no module-level slot. The chain lives on the exonode
(`TExoStrNode.context`) and is threaded downwards, so `provide` and `inject` touch
no module state and no `finally` puts anything back. A caller with an OUTER frame
of its own passes it as `render`'s second argument, or as `renderExoStrInstance`'s
`context` when driving instances by hand (`packages/string/src/node/ExoStrBackend.ts`).
`@exodra/ssr`'s `renderExoPage` is what uses it: it hands `render` an
`exoContextFrame` carrying the request's response object, so a page can
`c.inject(EXO_SSR_RESPONSE)` and two requests rendering at once cannot see each
other's.

## Escaping

Text and attribute values are escaped through `escapeExoText` and
`escapeExoAttributeValue`, which live in [`@exodra/core`](./core.md#escaping-and-the-shared-tables)
so that the markup this package prints and the markup `@exodra/dom` parses its
prototype from are **the same bytes**. That identity is what hydration rests on.

## Compiled plans

Exported for the same reason `@exodra/dom`'s are: a caller that renders
instances itself — a compiler's output, a custom entry point, a streaming shell —
needs **the plan the entry point would have built**. Without them it either
re-exports blind or writes a second compiler, and the first thing a second
compiler disagrees about is port numbering, which is shared with `@exodra/dom`
and is the reason one wiring function can fill both backends. Every name here has
a counterpart in the DOM package.

| Export | Counterpart in `@exodra/dom` |
| --- | --- |
| `exoStrSchemaOf(machine, backend)` | `exoDomSchemaOf` |
| `compileExoStrSchema(declaration, backend)` | `compileExoDomSchema` |
| `renderExoStrInstance(schema, machine, index, context?, params?)` | `mountExoInstance` |
| `EXO_STR_WRITERS` | *(none in the barrel — see below)* |

The `backend` parameter is **not optional and not defaulted**: it is the plan cache
key as well as the argument the compiler needs, and defaulting it would mean naming
a composed backend from a module the connector imports, which closes a module
cycle. `ExoStrBackend.render` passes `this`, and every nested call passes
`connector.backend`. `renderExoStrInstance`'s `context` defaults to `null` — a caller
driving this function by hand inherits no context, because nothing is read off an
ambient any more.

`EXO_STR_WRITERS` has no DOM counterpart and is exported anyway: its writers are
what decide an attribute's **absence** — `disabled` for `false` is no attribute at
all, not `disabled=""` — and a caller building writers by hand without them is the
shape that produces a hydration mismatch on every conditional attribute.

| Type | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `TExoStrSchema` | A schema compiled for this backend: cut into prepared strings, with a writer per port. |
| `TExoStrWriter` | The per-port function that escapes a value for its position. |
| `TExoStrMarkupFiller` | The prepared markup with a hole per port — hand it an instance's values, get the instance's markup. |
| `TExoStrMachine` | `TExoMachine` with this backend's exonode in it — what `createExoMachineBuilder<TExoStrNode>(schema).done()` returns. |

There is **no** `renderToStream`.

## API Reference

| Export | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `ExoStrBackend` / `TExoStrBackend` / `TExoStrBackendConstructor` | The server backend: `new ExoStrBackend(...plugins)`, then `backend.render(component)`, which prints one instance as markup. The connector's methods are merged onto it first, so a pack naming one receives the shipped body as its `next`. |
| `TExoStrNode` / `TExoStrNodeApi` / `TExoStrNodeFields` / `TExoStrSurface` | What a wiring function is handed on the server — **types**, not a class. An exonode is a plain object whose prototype is the composed backend. |
| `createExoStrInstanceFactory` / `EXO_STR_NODE_VOCABULARY` | The factory that builds one of those objects — call it once per composed backend — and the exonode surface as the pack the backend merges onto itself. Exported for a custom entry point and for a tool that needs the list of method names. |
| `exoStrSchemaOf` / `compileExoStrSchema` / `renderExoStrInstance` / `EXO_STR_WRITERS` | Plans, for custom entry points. Both plan functions take the **backend**. |
| `exoForeignMarkup` / `TExoStrMark` / `EXO_STR_FOREIGN_VOCABULARY` / `TExoStrForeignApi` | Markup this backend did not print, placed like markup it did. |
| `TExoStrApi` / `TExoStrMachine` / `TExoStrSchema` / `TExoStrWriter` / `TExoStrMarkupFiller` | Types. |

## Links

- npm: [`@exodra/string`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@exodra/string)
- GitHub: [exodra/packages/string](https://github.com/abaikov/exodra/tree/master/packages/string)


==============================================================================
# Forms

`@exodra/forms` reads form controls and writes the mark of a choice. It holds no model and
imports nothing at runtime: the field keeps its own value, a [machine](./core.md#machines)
listens where it chooses, and a transition writes only what depends on that value.

```bash
npm install @exodra/forms @exodra/core
```

Exports: `readExoControlValue`, `readExoControlValues`, `writeExoChoice`,
`checkExoControlValues`, `setExoControlErrors`, and the `TExoControlValue` and
`TExoControlRule` types.

## Signatures

```ts no-check
type TExoControlValue = string | number | boolean | readonly string[] | FileList;

function readExoControlValue(
    target: EventTarget | null | undefined
): TExoControlValue | undefined;

function readExoControlValues(
    c: { portTable(): TExoPortTable; portNodeReader(): TExoPortNodeReader<EventTarget | undefined> },
    ports: readonly TExoRefPort[]
): (TExoControlValue | undefined)[];

function writeExoChoice<TValue>(
    c: Pick<TExoFillDoors, 'attr'>,
    ports: readonly TExoAttrPort[],
    values: readonly TValue[],
    chosen: TValue
): void;

type TExoControlRule = (
    value: TExoControlValue | undefined,
    values: readonly (TExoControlValue | undefined)[]
) => string | null;

function checkExoControlValues(
    values: readonly (TExoControlValue | undefined)[],
    rules: readonly (TExoControlRule | null)[]
): (string | null)[];

function setExoControlErrors(
    c: { portTable(): TExoPortTable; portNodeReader(): TExoPortNodeReader<EventTarget | undefined> },
    ports: readonly TExoRefPort[],
    errors: readonly (string | null)[]
): void;
```

| Function | Call it | It does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `readExoControlValue` | in an event handler, on `event.target` | reads the control as the value its type means |
| `readExoControlValues` | on submit, on validate | reads the live controls behind ref ports, in port order |
| `writeExoChoice` | in `createInitialState`, a wire, or a transition | writes `true` on the port at `values.indexOf(chosen)`, or `false` on every port when `chosen` is not in `values` |
| `checkExoControlValues` | anywhere — it touches no document | runs `rules[i]` on `values[i]` and answers its error, or `null`; a `null` rule checks nothing |
| `setExoControlErrors` | on submit, on input, after an async check | hands each error to its control's `setCustomValidity` (`null` clears it); nothing on a backend with no document |

## readExoControlValue()

Reads by the element's `localName` and, for an `<input>`, its `type`:

| Control | Reads | As |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `<input type="checkbox">` | `checked` | `boolean` |
| `<input type="number">`, `<input type="range">` | `valueAsNumber` | `number` |
| `<input type="radio">` | `value` while checked, else nothing | `string` or `undefined` |
| `<input type="file">` | `files` | `FileList` |
| any other `<input>` (text, email, date, …) | `value` | `string` |
| `<select>` | `value` | `string` |
| `<select multiple>` | the `value` of every selected option | `string[]` |
| `<textarea>` | `value` | `string` |
| anything else — including a form-associated custom element and a `contenteditable` element — and `null`, `undefined` | — | `undefined` |

A number field reads **`NaN`** when it is empty or half-typed (`1e`), not `0`. Whether an
empty field is invalid, means "unset", or keeps the last good number is the form's
decision, so `NaN` is handed to it rather than replaced.

It checks `localName` rather than `instanceof`, so it touches no DOM global, is safe to
import in a server bundle, and reads a control from another realm (an iframe).

### The pattern: one listener on a container

`input` and `change` bubble, so **one** event port on an element that contains the fields
hears all of them. The container can be a `<form>`, a `<fieldset>` or a plain `<div>` —
fields do not need a `<form>` — and a single field can carry its own event port.

```ts
import { createExoMachineBuilder, createExoSchema } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoAttrPort, TExoEventPort, TExoTextPort } from '@exodra/core';
import { ExoDomBackend, withExoCompiler } from '@exodra/dom';
import type { TExoDomNode } from '@exodra/dom';
import { readExoControlValue } from '@exodra/forms';

const SIGNUP_SCHEMA = createExoSchema((b) => {
    let input!: TExoEventPort;
    let greeting!: TExoTextPort;
    let error!: TExoTextPort;
    let send!: TExoAttrPort;
    b.el('div', { class: 'signup' }, (d) => {
        input = d.eventPort('input');
        d.el('input', { type: 'text', name: 'name' });
        d.el('input', { type: 'number', name: 'age' });
        d.el('p', null, (p) => {
            greeting = p.textPort();
        });
        d.el('p', { class: 'error' }, (p) => {
            error = p.textPort();
        });
        d.el('button', { type: 'button' }, (button) => {
            send = button.port('disabled');
            button.text('Send');
        });
    });
    return { input, greeting, error, send };
});

type TSignup = { name: string; age: number };

const mSignup = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoDomNode, unknown, TSignup>(SIGNUP_SCHEMA);
mSignup.createInitialState(() => ({ name: '', age: Number.NaN }));
mSignup.wire((c) => {
    c.attr(SIGNUP_SCHEMA.ports.send, true);
});
const takeName = mSignup.transition<string>((c, name) => {
    c.state.name = name;
    c.text(SIGNUP_SCHEMA.ports.greeting, name === '' ? '' : `Hello, ${name}`);
    c.attr(SIGNUP_SCHEMA.ports.send, name === '' || Number.isNaN(c.state.age));
});
const takeAge = mSignup.transition<number>((c, age) => {
    c.state.age = age;
    c.text(SIGNUP_SCHEMA.ports.error, Number.isNaN(age) ? 'Age has to be a number' : '');
    c.attr(SIGNUP_SCHEMA.ports.send, c.state.name === '' || Number.isNaN(age));
});
mSignup.on(SIGNUP_SCHEMA.ports.input, (c, event) => {
    const field = event.target as HTMLInputElement;
    if (field.name === 'name') takeName(c, readExoControlValue(field) as string);
    else if (field.name === 'age') takeAge(c, readExoControlValue(field) as number);
});

const backend = withExoCompiler(new ExoDomBackend());
backend.render(mSignup.done(), document.getElementById('root') as HTMLElement);
```

The rules this follows:

- **The field's own `value` is not written back on user input.** The browser already holds
  it. Transitions write only what depends on it — a read-out, an error text, a `disabled`
  flag. A `value` port is for a **programmatic** set (a "clear" button, a loaded record),
  in a transition of its own.
- **Identify the field** by `event.target.name`, as above, or by comparing `event.target`
  with the element behind a ref port, read once in `createInitialState` and kept in the
  state: `c.portNodeReader()(c.portTable(), P.email)`.
- **State lives in `c.state`**, typed by the builder's third type argument,
  `createExoMachineBuilder<TExoDomNode, unknown, TState>`. On a builder typed with
  `TExoDomNode` the handler's `event` is an `Event`.
- **A transition with an argument names its type**: `m.transition<number>((c, to) => …)`.
  Writing `(c, to: number) => …` without the explicit type argument leaves `c` implicitly
  `any`.
- **`focus` and `blur` do not bubble.** Validate-on-leave listens for `focusout` on the
  container.

## readExoControlValues()

A form that needs its values only when it is sent registers nothing per field: a ref port
on each control, one read in the submit handler.

```ts
import { createExoMachineBuilder, createExoSchema } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoEventPort, TExoRefPort } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoDomNode } from '@exodra/dom';
import { readExoControlValues } from '@exodra/forms';

const CONTACT_SCHEMA = createExoSchema((b) => {
    let submit!: TExoEventPort;
    let name!: TExoRefPort;
    let age!: TExoRefPort;
    b.el('form', null, (f) => {
        submit = f.eventPort('submit');
        f.el('input', { type: 'text' }, (i) => {
            name = i.refPort();
        });
        f.el('input', { type: 'number' }, (i) => {
            age = i.refPort();
        });
        f.el('button', { type: 'submit' }, (button) => button.text('Send'));
    });
    return { submit, name, age };
});
const CONTACT_FIELDS = [CONTACT_SCHEMA.ports.name, CONTACT_SCHEMA.ports.age];

const mContact = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoDomNode>(CONTACT_SCHEMA);
mContact.on(CONTACT_SCHEMA.ports.submit, (c, event) => {
    event.preventDefault();
    const [name, age] = readExoControlValues(c, CONTACT_FIELDS);
    console.log({ name, age });
});
export const CONTACT = mContact.done();
```

It reads the controls that are on the page **when it is called**. On a served page, what a
person typed before the bundle arrived is what comes back. On `@exodra/string` there is no
document, and every entry is `undefined`. A radio reads as its `value` only while checked,
so ref ports on a whole radio group come back as, for example, `[undefined, 'm', undefined]`.

## writeExoChoice()

A choice is a mark on one member of a group — `checked` on a radio, `selected` on an
`<option>`. Give each member an attribute port for its mark; `writeExoChoice` finds `chosen`
in `values` and writes `true` to that one port. The browser clears the rest of a same-`name`
radio group or a single `<select>` itself, so nothing remembers the previous member, and a
mark the person moved by hand is simply overridden. A `chosen` that is not in `values`
writes `false` to every port.

- **In `createInitialState`** it sets the starting mark, and the server prints it
  (`checked=""`, `selected`).
- **In a transition** it sets the mark when the application decides. A person's own click
  moves it natively, with nothing to write.
- **In a wire**, for a group whose value belongs to a parent: the group machine's
  `wire((c, chosen) => writeExoChoice(c, P.radios, VALUES, chosen))`, built by the parent with
  `c.build(GROUP, i, chosen)` and re-run with `wireExoNode(node, GROUP, next)`. The package
  README has the complete sample.

```ts
import { createExoMachineBuilder, createExoSchema } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoAttrPort, TExoEventPort } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoDomNode } from '@exodra/dom';
import { writeExoChoice } from '@exodra/forms';

const PLANS = ['free', 'team', 'business'];

const PLAN_SCHEMA = createExoSchema((b) => {
    let reset!: TExoEventPort;
    const options: TExoAttrPort[] = [];
    b.el('div', null, (d) => {
        d.el('select', null, (s) => {
            for (const plan of PLANS) {
                s.el('option', { value: plan }, (o) => {
                    options.push(o.port('selected'));
                    o.text(plan);
                });
            }
        });
        d.el('button', { type: 'button' }, (button) => {
            reset = button.eventPort('click');
            button.text('Back to free');
        });
    });
    return { reset, options };
});

const mPlan = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoDomNode>(PLAN_SCHEMA);
mPlan.createInitialState((c) => {
    writeExoChoice(c, PLAN_SCHEMA.ports.options, PLANS, 'team');
});
const backToFree = mPlan.transition((c) => {
    writeExoChoice(c, PLAN_SCHEMA.ports.options, PLANS, 'free');
});
mPlan.on(PLAN_SCHEMA.ports.reset, (c) => backToFree(c));
export const PLAN = mPlan.done();
```

A radio group is the same code with `port('checked')` on each `<input type="radio">` sharing
one `name`. It is **not** for a group of checkboxes or a `<select multiple>`: neither clears
its other members, so write each member's port yourself there.

## Validation

Rules are plain functions; the result reaches the browser as the controls' own
validity. The field keeps its value **and** its error, so `:invalid`,
`:user-invalid`, `form.checkValidity()` and `reportValidity()` all see what the
machine decided, and nothing is stored beside the field.

```ts no-check
import { checkExoControlValues, readExoControlValues, setExoControlErrors } from '@exodra/forms';
import type { TExoControlRule } from '@exodra/forms';

const requiredName: TExoControlRule = (value) => (value === '' ? 'Name is required' : null);
const adultAge: TExoControlRule = (value) =>
    typeof value === 'number' && value >= 18 ? null : 'Must be 18 or older';
const RULES = [requiredName, adultAge];

mSignup.on(SIGNUP_SCHEMA.ports.submit, (c, event) => {
    event.preventDefault();
    const values = readExoControlValues(c, FIELDS);
    const errors = checkExoControlValues(values, RULES);
    setExoControlErrors(c, FIELDS, errors);
    if (errors.every((error) => error === null)) send(c, values);
});
```

A rule gets every value as its second argument, so one field can be checked
against another (`value === values[0] ? null : 'Passwords differ'`). The same
rule functions import into an API server unchanged: they read values, not
elements.

**Put `novalidate` on the form.** Without it the browser refuses to fire
`submit` while a field is invalid and shows its own bubble, so the machine never
sees the attempt. With it, `submit` always arrives and the machine decides.

**Write the whole array every time.** `setCustomValidity` keeps a message until
it is set back to `''`; `setExoControlErrors` sets every port it is given,
clearing where the error is `null`, so a field that was fixed stops being
invalid on the next check.

**Touched needs no state.** `:user-invalid` matches only after the person has
interacted with the field or tried to submit, so an error element next to it can
be shown with CSS alone:

```css
.error { display: none; }
input:user-invalid + .error { display: block; }
```

**Submitting.** A pending flag is machine state, and the button's `disabled` is
an attr port written by the transition that starts and the one that ends the
request.

**`invalid` does not bubble**, and event ports listen on their own element, so a
container listener does not hear it; give each control its own
`eventPort('invalid')` if you need it.

## Fields in the rows of a list

When something outside a row needs the values of fields inside the rows, the **parent**
holds the state, listens once on the container, and passes values down as the params of the
row's wire: `c.build(ROW, i, params)` builds the row, and `wireExoNode(node, ROW, params)`
from `@exodra/core` re-runs its wire on the live row. A row's wire may only write ports.

```ts no-check
const setQuantity = mCart.transition<number, number>((c, at, quantity) => {
    c.state.quantities[at] = quantity;
    wireExoNode(c.state.rows[at], ROW, { price: PRICES[at], quantity });
    c.text(CART_SCHEMA.ports.sum, sumOf(c.state.quantities));
});
mCart.on(CART_SCHEMA.ports.input, (c, event) => {
    const field = event.target as HTMLInputElement;
    setQuantity(c, Number(field.dataset.row), readExoControlValue(field) as number);
});
```

The complete cart, with the row machine and the parent that builds the rows, is in the
[package README](https://github.com/abaikov/exodra/tree/master/packages/forms#fields-in-the-rows-of-a-list).

## Where it runs

| Backend | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| `@exodra/dom` | everything above |
| `@exodra/string` | `writeExoChoice` in `createInitialState` or a wire prints the starting mark; handlers never run; `readExoControlValues` answers `undefined` for every port; `setExoControlErrors` does nothing; `checkExoControlValues` runs as anywhere |
| hydration | adopts the served controls with whatever was typed into them; `readExoControlValues` reads it |

Pinned in `packages/forms/src/controls/tests/controls.test.ts` and `packages/forms/src/controls/tests/validation.test.ts`.

## Known limits

- **A `<select>` has no `value` port the server can print.** `port('value')` on a `<select>`
  is refused when the schema is built ([`EXO0015`](../errors.md#exo0015)): the markup for the chosen
  option is `selected` on the `<option>`. Use `port('selected')` on each option and
  `writeExoChoice`. `port('value')` on an `<output>` is refused for the same reason; its value
  is its text, so use a `textPort()`.
- **`form.reset()` empties a client-rendered field.** The DOM backend writes a `value` port
  as the `value` property, not the attribute, so a field rendered in the browser has no
  default to reset to; a served field resets to what the server printed. `checked` and
  `selected` write the attribute too and reset the same on both. See the header of
  `packages/dom/src/tests/property-parity.test.ts`.
- **A container outside a shadow root does not read the controls inside it.** The event is
  retargeted, so the handler sees the **host** as `event.target`; and `change` is not
  composed, so it does not leave the shadow root at all. Read `event.composedPath()[0]`
  yourself, or listen inside the component.
- **Form-associated custom elements and `contenteditable` read as `undefined`.**

## Links

- npm: [`@exodra/forms`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@exodra/forms)
- GitHub: [exodra/packages/forms](https://github.com/abaikov/exodra/tree/master/packages/forms)


==============================================================================
# Style

`exoStyle` from `@exodra/core/style` turns a plain object into a valid CSS `style`
string, so you don't hand-write `"color:red;font-size:12px"`. It is pure and
dependency-free — the output is just a string, so it goes into a schema's static
attributes, into a `style` port a transition fills with `c.attr`, or anywhere else
a `style` attribute is accepted, and works identically in the DOM and in SSR.

It is a separate entry of `@exodra/core`, so neither a bundle nor the CDN build of
the core carries it unless something imports `@exodra/core/style`.

Exports from `@exodra/core/style`: `exoStyle`, and the `TExoStyleInput`, `TExoStyleObject`,
`TExoStyleScalar` types.

## `exoStyle(...args)`

```typescript signature
type TExoStyleScalar = string | number | null | undefined | false;
type TExoStyleObject = Record<string, TExoStyleScalar | readonly (string | number)[]>;
type TExoStyleInput = TExoStyleObject | string | null | undefined | false;

function exoStyle(...args: TExoStyleInput[]): string;
```

Each argument is either a style object, a raw CSS string (appended verbatim), or
a falsy value (skipped — handy for conditionals). The results are joined with
`;`; later arguments come after earlier ones, so they win in the browser.

```javascript
import { exoStyle } from '@exodra/core/style';

exoStyle({ color: 'red', fontSize: 12, '--gap': 8 });
// "color:red;font-size:12px;--gap:8"
```

### Normalization rules

| Input | Output | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `backgroundColor: 'red'` | `background-color:red` | camelCase → kebab-case |
| `fontSize: 12` | `font-size:12px` | numbers get `px`… |
| `margin: 0` | `margin:0` | …except `0` |
| `opacity: 0.5`, `zIndex: 10` | `opacity:0.5;z-index:10` | …and unitless props (`opacity`, `zIndex`, `lineHeight`, `fontWeight`, `flexGrow`, grid spans, …) |
| `'--gap': 8` | `--gap:8` | custom properties pass through untouched (no kebab, no `px`) |
| `padding: [4, 8]` | `padding:4px 8px` | arrays expand with per-item formatting |
| `color: null` / `undefined` / `false` | *(omitted)* | falsy values are dropped |
| `WebkitTransform: 'scale(2)'` | `-webkit-transform:scale(2)` | explicit vendor prefixes serialize correctly (`msFlexAlign` → `-ms-flex-align`) |

There is **no autoprefixing** — `exoStyle` serializes what you write, it
doesn't invent prefixes. Modern targets rarely need them; when you do need one,
write it explicitly (`WebkitBackdropFilter`, `msFlexAlign`, …) and it is emitted
verbatim.

### Conditionals and merging

Falsy arguments and falsy values are skipped, so conditional styles read
cleanly:

```javascript
exoStyle(
  base,                          // an object of shared declarations
  isActive && { color: 'blue' }, // dropped entirely when isActive is false
  { opacity: hidden ? 0 : 1 }
);
```

## Usage

A style that never changes is a **static attribute** on the schema, so call
`exoStyle()` once at module load and let the compiled markup carry the result:

```ts
import { createExoStatic } from '@exodra/core';
import { exoStyle } from '@exodra/core/style';

export const TOOLBAR = createExoStatic((b) => {
    b.el('div', { style: exoStyle({ display: 'flex', gap: 8 }) }, (div) => {
        div.text('—');
    });
});
```

A style that changes is a **port**. A transition builds the string from state
and writes it — the value that reaches the DOM is still a plain string, so
nothing about the renderer knows the style was an object:

```ts
import { createExoMachineBuilder, createExoSchema } from '@exodra/core';
import { exoStyle } from '@exodra/core/style';
import type { TExoAttrPort, TExoEventPort, TExoMachineNode } from '@exodra/core';
import { ExoDomBackend, withExoCompiler } from '@exodra/dom';

const backend = withExoCompiler(new ExoDomBackend());

const CARD_SCHEMA = createExoSchema((b) => {
    let boxStyle!: TExoAttrPort;
    let toggle!: TExoEventPort;
    b.el('div', null, (div) => {
        boxStyle = div.port('style');
        toggle = div.eventPort('click');
    });
    return { boxStyle, toggle };
});
const mCard = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoMachineNode, unknown, { active: boolean }>(CARD_SCHEMA);
mCard.createInitialState(() => ({ active: false }));
const show = mCard.transition((c) => {
    c.attr(
        CARD_SCHEMA.ports.boxStyle,
        exoStyle({ padding: 16, borderRadius: 8, background: c.state.active ? '#eef' : '#fff' })
    );
});
mCard.wire((c) => show(c));
mCard.on(CARD_SCHEMA.ports.toggle, (c) => {
    c.state.active = !c.state.active;
    show(c);
});
const CARD = mCard.done();

backend.render(CARD, document.body);
```

In the [JSX dialect](../guides/jsx.md) a string literal (`style="padding:16px"`)
is markup baked into the schema, and `style={$.css}` declares an attribute port
that the machine fills with `c.attr` — a constant from `exoStyle()` declared at
module scope, or a string a transition builds from state, like the one above.

There is **no compile-time folding of style objects.** The one compiler,
`@exodra/babel-plugin-schema`, has no style pass; calling `exoStyle()` at module
scope does that work once per process, exactly where a constant belongs.

## Links

- source: [exodra/packages/core/src/style](https://github.com/abaikov/exodra/tree/master/packages/core/src/style)


==============================================================================
# create-exodra

`create-exodra` scaffolds a new Exodra application. The CLI asks at a prompt
(Next.js style): run it and answer a few questions, or pass flags to skip the
prompts. It also installs an `exodra` binary for generating components, pages,
and API routes inside an existing project.

## Quick start

```bash
# Using npm
npm create exodra@latest my-app

# Or directly
npx create-exodra my-app
```

If you omit a project name you'll be prompted for one. Without flags, the CLI
prompts for TypeScript, ESLint, Tailwind CSS, a `src/` directory, SSR, App
Router, and the import alias.

After scaffolding:

```bash
cd my-app
npm install
npm run dev
```

## CLI usage

```bash
npx create-exodra [project-name] [options]
```

Any option you don't pass is asked interactively. Passing a flag skips that
prompt.

### Options

- `--ts`, `--typescript` — use TypeScript
- `--js`, `--javascript` — use JavaScript
- `--tailwind` — set up Tailwind CSS
- `--eslint` — set up ESLint
- `--src-dir` — use a `src/` directory
- `--ssr` — scaffold a server-side-rendered app
- `--app` — use the App Router (`@exodra/router`)
- `--import-alias <alias>` — import alias to use (default `@/*`)
- `--use-npm` / `--use-yarn` / `--use-pnpm` / `--use-bun` — choose the package
  manager

### Examples

```bash
# TypeScript app with the App Router and Tailwind, no prompts
npx create-exodra my-app --typescript --app --tailwind

# JavaScript app, no App Router
npx create-exodra simple-app --javascript

# Server-side-rendered app
npx create-exodra my-ssr-app --ssr
```

## What gets generated

**Every scaffold writes plain modules — there is no JSX in any of them.** A
component is one value: a schema that declares the shape once when the module
loads, and a machine whose `wire` fills its ports per instance. The generated
project therefore compiles with nothing but Vite and TypeScript; the
[Babel preset](./babel-preset.md) is what you add the day you want to write schemas
as [JSX](../guides/jsx.md) instead.

A standard (non-SSR) app uses Vite with `@exodra/vite-plugin` and depends on
`@exodra/core` and `@exodra/dom` — plus `@exodra/router`
when the App Router is enabled, which also gets `src/pages`, a generated route
table from `virtual:exodra-routes`, and a `main` that provides the router inside
a machine (`provideExoRouter(c, router)`), places the boundary with
`c.one(port, ExoOutlet)` and inserts the nav's `ExoLink`s into `c.childList(port)`. The outlet
and the nav both open a child list, so that `main` renders through
`withExoChildList(withExoCompiler(new ExoDomBackend()))`; a backend without
[`withExoChildList`](../api/dom.md#withexochildlist) refuses with
[EXO0109](../errors.md#exo0109). Without the App Router, `main` opens no child list and composes
`withExoCompiler` alone.

An SSR app (`--ssr`) instead depends on `@exodra/string` alongside `@exodra/core`
and `@exodra/dom`, with an Express dev/prod server. **One** component module is
shared by both halves: `new ExoStrBackend().render(APP)` prints it on the server,
and a `@exodra/dom` backend composed with `withExoHydration` adopts exactly
those nodes on the client through `backend.hydrate(APP, root)`, so only listeners
and subscriptions are added. See the
[SSR guide](../guides/ssr.md).

## The `exodra` CLI

The package also installs an `exodra` binary for scaffolding inside an existing
project:

```bash
npx exodra component Button      # create a component (alias: c)
npx exodra page Home             # create a page (alias: p)
npx exodra api hello             # create an API route (alias: a)
npx exodra config                # create exodra.config.js
```

Common options for `component` / `page`: `-d, --dir <path>`,
`-t, --typescript`, and `--naming <PascalCase|kebab-case|snake_case>`.

A page is a machine **default-exported** from its module (the route table
imports it that way), and it takes no props — the match that selected it is read
from the router, `router.getMatch()`, whose `params` and `pathname` are what a page
needs. The outlet mounts a machine and nothing else. A component is a named machine
export, filled from its parent with `c.one(port, Name)` or repeated with
`c.list(port, Name, count)`. With `-t` the files carry type annotations; without
it they are the same code with the types dropped.

```tsx
// src/pages/Home.tsx, from `npx exodra page Home -t`
import { createExoMachineBuilder, createExoSchema } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoMachineNode, TExoTextPort } from '@exodra/core';

// A page takes no props — the match that selected it is read from the router the app created,
// `router.getMatch()`, whose `params` and `pathname` are what a page needs. It is
// default-exported because the route table imports it that way.
const PAGE_SCHEMA = createExoSchema(b => {
  let heading!: TExoTextPort;
  b.el('div', { class: 'page' }, d => {
    d.el('h1', null, h => {
      heading = h.textPort();
    });
    d.el('p', null, p => p.text('Welcome to the Home page.'));
  });
  return { heading };
});
const mPage = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoMachineNode>(PAGE_SCHEMA);
mPage.wire(c => {
  c.text(PAGE_SCHEMA.ports.heading, 'Home');
});
export default mPage.done();
```

`api` emits a module with `GET` and `POST` handlers: request/response code that
touches no renderer.

## Writing Exodra components

State lives in the machine. `createInitialState` runs once per instance and returns
it; a **transition** is the one place that turns that state into port writes; the
wire and the handlers call the transition. A port written with `c.text` / `c.attr`
holds that value until the next write — there is no source attached to it.

```ts
import { createExoMachineBuilder, createExoSchema } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoEventPort, TExoTextPort } from '@exodra/core';
import { ExoDomBackend, withExoCompiler } from '@exodra/dom';
import type { TExoDomNode } from '@exodra/dom';

const backend = withExoCompiler(new ExoDomBackend());

const COUNTER_SCHEMA = createExoSchema(b => {
  let text!: TExoTextPort;
  let click!: TExoEventPort;
  b.el('div', { class: 'counter' }, div => {
    div.el('span', null, span => {
      text = span.textPort();
    });
    div.el('button', { class: 'btn', type: 'button' }, btn => {
      click = btn.eventPort('click');
      btn.text('+1');
    });
  });
  return { text, click };
});
const mCounter = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoDomNode, unknown, { count: number }>(COUNTER_SCHEMA);
mCounter.createInitialState(() => ({ count: 0 }));
const showCount = mCounter.transition(c => {
  c.text(COUNTER_SCHEMA.ports.text, `Count: ${c.state.count}`);
});
mCounter.wire(c => showCount(c));
mCounter.on(COUNTER_SCHEMA.ports.click, c => {
  c.state.count++;
  showCount(c);
});
const COUNTER = mCounter.done();

backend.render(COUNTER, document.getElementById('app') as HTMLElement);
```

Data that lives **outside** the instance — a store several components follow — is
read the same way, from an effect that draws first and then subscribes:

```ts no-check
const showTotal = mCounter.transition(c => {
  c.text(COUNTER_SCHEMA.ports.text, `Total: ${store.getValue()}`);
});
mCounter.effect(c => {
  showTotal(c);
  return store.onChange(() => showTotal(c));
});
```

The [Components guide](../guides/components.md) covers the builder and the
connector in full; the [JSX guide](../guides/jsx.md) covers the compiled dialect
that produces the same pair from markup.

## Links

- npm: [create-exodra](https://www.npmjs.com/package/create-exodra)
- GitHub:
  [packages/create-exodra](https://github.com/abaikov/exodra/tree/master/packages/create-exodra)
