# Vite Plugin

`@exodra/vite-plugin` wires Exodra into Vite: it compiles Exodra JSX through the
[Babel preset](./babel-preset.md) and generates file-based routes and API endpoints from your directory
structure.

## Installation

```bash
npm install --save-dev @exodra/vite-plugin
```

## Configuration

Add the plugin to your Vite config. It runs with `enforce: 'pre'` so it owns the
JSX pipeline before Vite's esbuild, and it sets esbuild's `jsx: 'preserve'` so
no foreign JSX runtime is injected.

```typescript
// vite.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vite';
import exodra from '@exodra/vite-plugin';

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [
    exodra({
      pagesDir: 'src/pages',  // Default: src/pages
      apiDir: 'src/api',      // Default: src/api
    }),
  ],
});
```

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `pagesDir` | string | `'src/pages'` | Directory for page components. |
| `apiDir` | string | `'src/api'` | Directory for API routes. |
| `schemaSource` | string | `'@exodra/core'` | Where the compiled output imports `createExoSchema` from. |

`ssr` and `alias` are still declared on the options type but nothing in the
plugin reads them — passing either changes no behaviour. For server rendering,
see the section at the bottom of this page.

## JSX transform

The plugin transforms every `.tsx` / `.jsx` file (outside `node_modules`) through
`babel-preset-exodra`, which is the same single pipeline Jest, esbuild, Rollup
and Bun use. Each `exoJsx(…)` declaration becomes a module-level
`createExoNamedSchema()` — the shape, built once when the module loads — whose
ports the machine fills per instance. Because the plugin runs before esbuild, the output is plain JS by the
time Vite sees it.

esbuild's own JSX handling would be wrong here twice over: it lowers JSX to a
call per element at runtime, and it throws on the namespaced `on:` listeners the
dialect uses. See the
[JSX guide](../guides/jsx.md) for the dialect itself.

## File-based routing

Routes are generated automatically from your `pagesDir`:

```
src/pages/
├── index.tsx             → /
├── about.tsx             → /about
├── _shared.tsx           → ignored (starts with `_`)
├── blog/
│   ├── index.tsx         → /blog
│   ├── [id].tsx          → /blog/:id
│   └── [...slug].tsx     → /blog/* (catch-all)
├── shop/
│   ├── [[...path]].tsx   → /shop (optional catch-all)
│   └── checkout.tsx      → /shop/checkout
└── admin/
    └── dashboard.tsx     → /admin/dashboard
```

### Special files

- `index.tsx` — default route for a directory.
- A file whose name starts with `_` is ignored by the generator: it produces no
  route and nothing else.

### Layouts

The generated table is **flat** — one entry per page file, no `children` — and
`_layout.tsx` has no meaning to the generator. In `@exodra/router` a layout is a
**route with `children`**, and its page places its own `ExoOutlet`: the nested
boundary finds its parent boundary through the context and draws the next entry
of the matched branch. Such a table is written by hand; see
[Nested routes](../api/router.md#nested-routes). The router has no error
boundary, so catching a throwing page is the application's job.

### Dynamic routes

- `[param].tsx` — single dynamic segment (`:param`).
- `[...params].tsx` — catch-all route.
- `[[...params]].tsx` — optional catch-all route.

### Using generated routes

Import the routes from the `virtual:exodra-routes` module. Each entry is
`{ path, component: exoLazy(() => import(…)) }`, and `exoLazy` resolves the page
module's **default export** — so a page is a machine default-exported from its
file, and it receives the match that selected it as the **params of its wire**:
`createExoMachineBuilder<TExoMachineNode, TExoRouteMatch>(SCHEMA)`, then
`mPage.wire((c, match) => …)`.

There is no provider component and no `<Outlet />` element: the router is
provided by a call inside a machine, and the route boundary is the `ExoOutlet`
machine, or `exoOutlet(tag)` for another element.

```ts no-check  // `virtual:exodra-routes` is generated by the plugin at build time
// main.ts
import { createExoMachineBuilder, createExoSchema } from '@exodra/core';
import type { TExoChildrenWiring, TExoChildrenPort, TExoMachineNode } from '@exodra/core';
import { ExoDomBackend, withExoChildList, withExoCompiler } from '@exodra/dom';
import {
  createExoBrowserHistory,
  createExoRouter,
  exoOutlet,
  provideExoRouter,
} from '@exodra/router';
import type { TExoOutletWiring } from '@exodra/router';
import { routes } from 'virtual:exodra-routes';

const router = createExoRouter(routes, { history: createExoBrowserHistory() });
const ROUTED = exoOutlet('main');

const APP_SCHEMA = createExoSchema(b => {
  let body!: TExoChildrenPort;
  b.el('div', { class: 'app' }, d => {
    body = d.childrenPort();
  });
  return { body };
});
const mApp = createExoMachineBuilder<TExoChildrenWiring & TExoMachineNode & TExoOutletWiring>(
  APP_SCHEMA
);
mApp.createInitialState(c => {
  provideExoRouter(c, router);
  c.one(APP_SCHEMA.ports.body, ROUTED);
});
const APP = mApp.done();

const backend = withExoChildList(withExoCompiler(new ExoDomBackend()));
backend.render(APP, document.getElementById('app') as HTMLElement);
```

For TypeScript, declare the virtual module:

```typescript no-check
// env.d.ts
/// <reference types="vite/client" />

declare module 'virtual:exodra-routes' {
  import type { TExoRoute } from '@exodra/router';
  export const routes: TExoRoute[];
}
```

## API routes

Files in `apiDir` become API endpoints. Export functions named after the HTTP
method; they are served during development at `/api/<file>`:

```typescript
// src/api/users.ts
declare function fetchUsers(): Promise<unknown[]>;
declare function createUser(data: unknown): Promise<unknown>;

export async function GET(request: Request) {
  const users = await fetchUsers();
  return new Response(JSON.stringify(users), {
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
  });
}

export async function POST(request: Request) {
  const data = await request.json();
  const user = await createUser(data);
  return new Response(JSON.stringify(user), {
    status: 201,
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
  });
}
```

If no matching method (or `default`) export is found, the request returns
`405 Method not allowed`.

## Hot Module Replacement

**The plugin appends no HMR glue, and a changed component is a full reload.**
A module that accepts a hot update stops Vite propagating it to its importer, so
glue that accepted the update without applying it would suppress the reload that
shows the change.

The plugin has no `handleHotUpdate` hook, so what applies is Vite's own
propagation: a changed page or component that nothing accepts reloads the page.

The route table is built once, in `buildStart`, and `virtual:exodra-routes` is
generated from it; nothing re-scans `pagesDir` while the dev server runs. A page
added, removed or renamed mid-session appears in `routes` only after the dev
server is restarted.

## SSR

Server rendering is a Vite concern rather than a plugin option — mark the Exodra
packages as non-external for the SSR build so they are compiled rather than
required from `node_modules`:

```typescript
// vite.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vite';
import exodra from '@exodra/vite-plugin';

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [exodra()],
  ssr: {
    noExternal: ['@exodra/core', '@exodra/string'],
  },
});
```

The same component renders to markup with `ExoStrBackend.render` and is adopted
by `backend.hydrate` on a `@exodra/dom` backend composed with
`withExoHydration`. See the [SSR guide](../guides/ssr.md).

## Links

- npm:
  [@exodra/vite-plugin](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@exodra/vite-plugin)
- GitHub:
  [packages/vite-plugin-exodra](https://github.com/abaikov/exodra/tree/master/packages/vite-plugin-exodra)


==============================================================================
# Babel Preset

`babel-preset-exodra` is the one-line way to compile Exodra JSX with Babel. It
bundles the whole pipeline — JSX syntax parsed with `throwIfNamespace: false` so
namespaced `on:event` listeners survive parsing, the JSX compiler
`@exodra/babel-plugin-schema`, and `@babel/preset-typescript` for `.ts` / `.tsx` — so you don't assemble those three
by hand.

It is the integration hub: [Jest](../guides/testing.md), webpack, Parcel, the
[Vite plugin](./vite-plugin.md) and the [bundler plugins](./bundlers.md) for
esbuild / Rollup / Bun all run through it, so every toolchain compiles Exodra JSX
**identically**.

## Installation

```bash
npm install --save-dev babel-preset-exodra
```

## Usage

```javascript
// babel.config.js
module.exports = {
  presets: ['exodra'],
};
```

Babel resolves the `exodra` shorthand to `babel-preset-exodra`.

## What comes out

The compiler turns an `exoJsx(…)` call into a **schema declaration** built once
when the module loads, with every port created under the name written after `$.`.
The machine that fills those ports is written in TypeScript around it.

```tsx no-check
import { exoJsx } from '@exodra/jsx';

const ROW_SCHEMA = exoJsx<TRowPorts>(($) => (
  <li class="row" data-id={$.id}>
    <span class="row__label">{$.label}</span>
    <button class="row__btn" onClick={$.toggle} />
  </li>
));
```

becomes:

```javascript no-check
import { createExoNamedSchema } from '@exodra/core';

const _s0 = createExoNamedSchema((_b0) => {
  _b0.el('li', { class: 'row' }, (_b1) => {
    _b1.port('data-id', 'id');
    _b1.el('span', { class: 'row__label' }, (_b2) => { _b2.textPort('label'); });
    _b1.el('button', { class: 'row__btn' }, (_b2) => { _b2.eventPort('click', 'toggle'); });
  });
});

const ROW_SCHEMA = _s0;
```

The declaration left the expression it was written in and landed at module
scope. That is not an optimisation with a switch behind it — every backend
indexes its prepared plan by the schema's ports, so a schema rebuilt per render
would be a different program, not a slower one. The compiled module imports
nothing but `@exodra/core`. The full dialect, with every refusal and a machine
for each sample, is in the [JSX guide](../guides/jsx.md).

For TypeScript, point JSX at the dialect's types:

```json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "jsx": "react-jsx",
    "jsxImportSource": "@exodra/jsx/schema"
  }
}
```

### Options

```javascript
// babel.config.js
module.exports = {
  presets: [
    ['exodra', {
      typescript: true,             // include preset-typescript (off if TS is handled elsewhere)
      schemaSource: '@exodra/core', // where the schema factory is imported from
      schemaImport: 'createExoNamedSchema', // its exported name
      markerName: 'exoJsx',         // the marker call the compiler compiles away
    }],
  ],
};
```

| option | default | what it is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `typescript` | `true` | include `@babel/preset-typescript` |
| `schemaSource` | `'@exodra/core'` | where the schema factory is imported from |
| `schemaImport` | `'createExoNamedSchema'` | the exported name of the schema factory |
| `markerName` | `'exoJsx'` | the marker call the compiler compiles away |
| `mode` | `'schema'` | which compiler runs — and there is only one, so this names it rather than choosing it |

`'schema'` is the only legal value of `mode`. Any other value — `'legacy'`,
`'dom'` and `'ssr'` included — makes the preset **throw** by name rather than
compile the file and fail later and further away.

## Programmatic runner

The preset also exports the single function every bundler plugin calls, so there
is one copy of the pipeline **and** its invocation:

```javascript
import { transformExodraJsx } from 'babel-preset-exodra';

const result = await transformExodraJsx(sourceCode, '/abs/path/File.tsx');
// -> { code, map } | null   (typescript defaults on for .tsx, off otherwise)
```

It takes the preset's options as a third argument, so anything in the table above
reaches a bundler plugin without a second list of field names to keep in step.

## Not with ts-jest / @swc/jest

`ts-jest` and `@swc/jest` do **not** run Babel plugins, so they cannot compile
Exodra JSX. Use `babel-jest` with this preset (see [Testing](../guides/testing.md)),
or the native [SWC plugin](./swc-plugin.md).


==============================================================================
# Bundlers & build tools

Exodra JSX is compiled by a **Babel** plugin, so any tool that can run Babel can
compile it — through the [Babel preset](./babel-preset.md). Tools that do **not**
run Babel plugins (esbuild, SWC, Bun's native transpiler) each have a dedicated
plugin that hands the file to Babel; those wrap the same preset, so every path
compiles identically.

| Tool | How | Package |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Vite / Vitest | plugin | [`@exodra/vite-plugin`](./vite-plugin.md) |
| Jest | `babel-jest` + preset | [`babel-preset-exodra`](./babel-preset.md) |
| esbuild / tsup | plugin | `esbuild-plugin-exodra` |
| Rollup | plugin | `rollup-plugin-exodra` |
| Bun | plugin | `bun-plugin-exodra` |
| webpack | `babel-loader` + preset | *(no package — see below)* |
| Parcel | `.babelrc` + preset | *(no package — see below)* |
| SWC / Next.js | native Wasm plugin | [`swc-plugin-exodra`](./swc-plugin.md) |

Every one of these plugins intercepts `.jsx` / `.tsx` **before** the bundler's own
JSX handling. That is not a preference: esbuild, Bun and friends lower JSX to a
call per element at runtime, where the point of this dialect is that the shape is
built once at module load — and they throw on the namespaced `on:` listeners
outright.

## Vite

See [Vite Plugin](./vite-plugin.md). It also adds HMR and file-based routing.

## esbuild / tsup

```javascript
import * as esbuild from 'esbuild';
import { exodra } from 'esbuild-plugin-exodra';

await esbuild.build({
  entryPoints: ['src/main.tsx'],
  bundle: true,
  outfile: 'dist/main.js',
  plugins: [exodra()],
});
```

With tsup:

```javascript
// tsup.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'tsup';
import { exodra } from 'esbuild-plugin-exodra';

export default defineConfig({
  entry: ['src/main.tsx'],
  esbuildPlugins: [exodra()],
});
```

## Rollup

```javascript
// rollup.config.js
import { exodra } from 'rollup-plugin-exodra';

export default {
  input: 'src/main.tsx',
  output: { dir: 'dist', format: 'esm' },
  plugins: [exodra()],
};
```

## Bun

```javascript
import { exodra } from 'bun-plugin-exodra';

await Bun.build({
  entrypoints: ['./src/main.tsx'],
  outdir: './dist',
  plugins: [exodra()],
});
```

## Options

Each plugin accepts two:

| option | default | what it is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `filter` (`include` for Rollup) | `/\.[jt]sx$/` | which files to compile |
| `schemaSource` | `'@exodra/core'` | where the compiled output imports `createExoSchema` from |

Both are forwarded to `babel-preset-exodra`'s runner unchanged — there is no
per-bundler behaviour to configure, because there is no per-bundler pipeline.

## webpack

No package needed — `babel-loader` runs the preset:

```javascript
// webpack.config.js
module.exports = {
  module: {
    rules: [
      {
        test: /\.[jt]sx$/,
        use: { loader: 'babel-loader', options: { presets: ['exodra'] } },
      },
    ],
  },
  resolve: { extensions: ['.js', '.jsx', '.ts', '.tsx'] },
};
```

## Parcel

Parcel reads Babel config automatically:

```json
// .babelrc
{ "presets": ["exodra"] }
```

## SWC / Next.js

SWC does not run Babel plugins. Use the native [SWC plugin](./swc-plugin.md),
configured with `{ "mode": "schema" }`.


==============================================================================
# Using Exodra from a CDN

:::danger `0.3.0` is not on npm yet — every URL on this page 404s today

This page is written for the release that is being prepared, and its version pins
say `0.3.0` because that is the version in this repository. **Nothing of the
current library has been published.** The newest thing on npm under these names is
the `0.2.0` line, which is the DELETED three-props renderer — it exports `h`,
`text`, `defineComponent`, `walkSchema` and `createContextKey`, and not one call
on this page exists in it. So there is no URL that works right now: `@0.3.0` is a
404 and `@0.2.0` is a different program that happens to share a name.

Two consequences while this box is here. Every code sample below is **correct
against the source in this repository** and can be run today against the
repository's own `dist/` — `packages/examples/no-build/` does exactly that. And
`npm run check:docs` cannot catch this class of error: it checks each pin against
the version in the repository, never against the registry.

**Delete this box the moment `0.3.0` of the five packages is published.** Nothing
else on the page needs to change.

:::

Every runtime package publishes to npm, and npm is mirrored by the public CDNs
(jsDelivr, unpkg, esm.sh), so you can use Exodra in a plain HTML file with **no
build step**. There are two ways in, depending on whether you want ES modules or a
classic `<script>`.

Both ways in are demonstrated by a runnable pair of pages in the repository —
`packages/examples/no-build/` (`esm.html` and `global.html`, one application,
identical below the import block). Serve that folder over HTTP and open them; its
README says why a local server is needed and what each page proves.

The browser-relevant packages are `@exodra/core`, `@exodra/list-reconcile`,
`@exodra/dom`, `@exodra/router`, `@exodra/forms` — and those five are exactly the
ones that ship the two browser builds below. (`@exodra/ssr` and `@exodra/string`
are server-side.)

Each of the five publishes **three** files a browser can load (`dist/index.cjs` is
the fourth and is for Node), and picking the right one is the whole of this page:

| file | for | minified |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `dist/index.js` | anyone with a bundler — this is what `import '@exodra/dom'` resolves to | no, deliberately: your bundler minifies it and decides your own `NODE_ENV` |
| `dist/exodra.esm.js` | `<script type="module">` on a page with no build step | yes, and `NODE_ENV` is baked to `production` |
| `dist/exodra.global.js` | classic `<script src>`, no modules | yes, and `NODE_ENV` is baked to `production` |

**Do not import `dist/index.js` from a CDN.** It is the readable, un-minified
copy, and for `@exodra/dom` that is 55.7 KB gzip against `exodra.global.js`'s
17.2 KB (measured 2026-08-16 with `gzip -9` on the built files; the figures
here were 47.6 and 14.6 until then, understating both by about 17%). The two `exodra.*` files exist so that the no-build path is not the
slowest way to load this library.

**There is no JSX without a build step, and that is not a limitation of the CDN.**
`@exodra/jsx` is a types package: its `jsx` / `jsxs` / `jsxDEV` exports are one
function that throws, because an element in that dialect is compiled away into a
`b.el(…)` line inside a schema and a `c.text(…)` / `c.attr(…)` line inside a
machine's `wire`, and no runtime can interpret one. On a page with no
compiler you write those two halves yourself — `createExoSchema(build)` and
`createExoMachineBuilder(schema)` — which is what every example below does.

## ES modules (recommended)

The module build is `dist/exodra.esm.js`, named outright in the URL:

```
https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@exodra/dom@0.3.0/dist/exodra.esm.js
https://unpkg.com/@exodra/dom@0.3.0/dist/exodra.esm.js
```

**Use an import map.** `@exodra/dom` and `@exodra/router` do not re-bundle the
runtime — `@exodra/dom`'s module leaves `import … from '@exodra/core'` as a bare
specifier, exactly as the source wrote it, so a page that loads both ships **one**
core rather than two. Nothing rewrites that specifier for you; the import map is
what resolves it, and it pins every version in one place as a bonus:

```html
<script type="importmap">
{ "imports": {
  "@exodra/core":       "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@exodra/core@0.3.0/dist/exodra.esm.js",
  "@exodra/context":    "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@exodra/context@0.3.0/dist/index.js",
  "@exodra/dom":        "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@exodra/dom@0.3.0/dist/exodra.esm.js",
  "@exodra/router":     "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@exodra/router@0.3.0/dist/exodra.esm.js",
  "@exodra/forms":      "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@exodra/forms@0.3.0/dist/exodra.esm.js",
  "@exodra/list-reconcile": "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@exodra/list-reconcile@0.3.0/dist/exodra.esm.js"
}}
</script>
<script type="module">
  import { createExoMachineBuilder, createExoSchema } from '@exodra/core';
  import { ExoDomBackend, withExoCompiler } from '@exodra/dom';

  const backend = withExoCompiler(new ExoDomBackend());

  const COUNTER_SCHEMA = createExoSchema(b => {
    let click, text;
    b.el('div', null, div => {
      div.el('button', { type: 'button' }, btn => {
        click = btn.eventPort('click');
        btn.text('+');
      });
      div.el('span', null, span => { text = span.textPort(); });
    });
    return { click, text };
  });
  const mCounter = createExoMachineBuilder(COUNTER_SCHEMA);
  mCounter.createInitialState(() => ({ count: 0 }));
  const showCount = mCounter.transition(c => {
    c.text(COUNTER_SCHEMA.ports.text, `Count: ${c.state.count}`);
  });
  mCounter.wire(c => showCount(c));
  mCounter.on(COUNTER_SCHEMA.ports.click, c => {
    c.state.count++;
    showCount(c);
  });
  const COUNTER = mCounter.done();

  backend.render(COUNTER, document.body);
</script>
```

The import map is a browser feature, not a build step — it needs no tooling and
works in every browser that supports modules at all.

### Without an import map

`@exodra/core`, `@exodra/forms` and `@exodra/list-reconcile` reference nothing, so
their `exodra.esm.js` loads straight from a URL:

```html
<script type="module">
  import { reconcileExoOrder } from 'https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@exodra/list-reconcile@0.3.0/dist/exodra.esm.js';
</script>
```

`@exodra/dom` and `@exodra/router` will not: without a map the browser stops at
`Failed to resolve module specifier "@exodra/core"`. That is the deliberate cost
of not shipping a second core — add the map above, or use the `<script>` globals
further down.

### The subpath name

The same file is reachable by name rather than by path, which is what to write if
some tool is resolving package exports for you: `@exodra/dom/browser`. Do **not**
reach for it from an application you bundle — it is a pre-minified copy with
`NODE_ENV` already baked, and a bundler that sees both `@exodra/dom` and
`@exodra/dom/browser` puts two copies of the package in your output.

### `/+esm` is jsDelivr's file, not this repository's

jsDelivr also answers `…/@exodra/dom@0.3.0/+esm`. That is jsDelivr's own transform
of `dist/index.js`, produced on their servers — it resolves the internal
`@exodra/*` imports for you, so it needs no import map, but it is not a file this
repository publishes, measures or can promise anything about. `dist/exodra.esm.js`
is. Prefer it.

### Routing

```html
<script type="module">
  // A page is a machine, the router is provided by a call inside a
  // machine, and the route boundary is the `ExoOutlet` machine.
  // `@exodra/router` references core, so it needs the import map above.
  // The outlet opens a child list, so the backend composes withExoChildList.
  import { ExoDomBackend, withExoChildList, withExoCompiler } from '@exodra/dom';
  import {
    createExoRouter,
    createExoBrowserHistory,
    exoOutlet,
    provideExoRouter,
    ExoLink,
  } from '@exodra/router';

  const backend = withExoChildList(withExoCompiler(new ExoDomBackend()));
  // ...
</script>
```

## Classic `<script>` globals

For no-module pages, each of those five packages also ships a minified IIFE that
attaches to a single `window.Exodra` namespace. jsDelivr serves it from the bare
package URL (via the package's `jsdelivr` / `unpkg` field, which points at
`./dist/exodra.global.js`); naming that path outright —
`…/@exodra/core@0.3.0/dist/exodra.global.js` — works too and does not depend on
the CDN resolving the field.

Those two manifest fields keep pointing at the IIFE now that there is a module
build beside it, and on purpose: a bare package URL is the URL a `<script src>`
has no way to make more specific, while a module URL is written out in an import
map anyway. Pointing them at ESM would turn every existing `<script src>` on the
internet into `Uncaught SyntaxError: Unexpected token 'export'`.

```html
<!-- load the shared runtime FIRST, then the pieces that use it -->
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@exodra/core@0.3"></script>
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@exodra/dom@0.3"></script>
<script>
  const { createExoMachineBuilder, createExoSchema } = Exodra.core;
  const { ExoDomBackend, withExoCompiler } = Exodra.dom;

  const backend = withExoCompiler(new ExoDomBackend());

  const COUNTER_SCHEMA = createExoSchema(b => {
    let click, text;
    b.el('div', null, div => {
      div.el('button', { type: 'button' }, btn => {
        click = btn.eventPort('click');
        btn.text('+');
      });
      div.el('span', null, span => { text = span.textPort(); });
    });
    return { click, text };
  });
  const mCounter = createExoMachineBuilder(COUNTER_SCHEMA);
  mCounter.createInitialState(() => ({ count: 0 }));
  const showCount = mCounter.transition(c => {
    c.text(COUNTER_SCHEMA.ports.text, `Count: ${c.state.count}`);
  });
  mCounter.wire(c => showCount(c));
  mCounter.on(COUNTER_SCHEMA.ports.click, c => {
    c.state.count++;
    showCount(c);
  });
  const COUNTER = mCounter.done();

  backend.render(COUNTER, document.body);
</script>
```

These globals do **not** re-bundle the runtime — they reference it, so one
instance is shared no matter how many packages a page loads. Both browser builds
draw the same lines, in the two dialects; each package's `tsup.config.ts` is where
they are declared:

| package | `exodra.global.js` references | `exodra.esm.js` imports |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `@exodra/dom` | `Exodra.core` | `@exodra/core` |
| `@exodra/router` | `Exodra.core` | `@exodra/core` |
| `@exodra/core`, `@exodra/forms`, `@exodra/list-reconcile` | nothing — self-contained | nothing — self-contained |

**Load order matters** for the two that reference something: put `core` on the
page before `dom` / `router`. Loading all of
them with `core` first and the rest after it is always safe. The module
build has no such rule — the browser resolves the import graph itself — which is
the one thing it is strictly easier about than the globals.

What each namespace holds:

| package | global |
| --- | --- |
| `@exodra/core` | `Exodra.core` — `createExoSchema`, `createExoMachineBuilder`, `createExoNamedSchema`, `createExoStatic`, `exoPorts`, `withExoSchemaAsserts`, `composeExoPlugins` |
| `@exodra/dom` | `Exodra.dom` — `ExoDomBackend`, `withExoCompiler`, `withExoHydration`, `exoForeignNode` |
| `@exodra/router` | `Exodra.router` — `createExoRouter`, `createExoBrowserHistory`, `provideExoRouter`, `injectExoRouter`, `ExoOutlet`, `exoOutlet`, `ExoLink` |
| `@exodra/list-reconcile` | `Exodra.listReconcile` — `reconcileExoOrder`, `createExoKeyedList`, `EXO_KEYED_LIST_VOCABULARY` |
| `@exodra/forms` | `Exodra.forms` — `readExoControlValue`, `readExoControlValues`, `writeExoChoice` |

## Versions

CDNs serve exactly what's **published to npm**. Pin an exact version (`@exodra/core@0.3.0`)
for production so a future release can't shift under you; use a range (`@0.3`) to
follow patch/minor. Whatever code is on the CDN is the last published version — to
get a change onto the CDN, publish a new version to npm.

The five browser packages are at `0.3.0` in this repository, which is the version
every pin above names.

`packages/examples/no-build/` does **not** use a CDN URL, and that is deliberate
rather than an oversight: it maps the four bare specifiers to this repository's
own `/packages/*/dist/` builds (and loads the same files by path in the
`<script>` page), so the two pages run the code in the working tree and need no
network at all. The moment `0.3.0` is published, swapping those four paths for
the jsDelivr URLs above is the whole change — nothing else in either page moves.


==============================================================================
# SWC Plugin

`swc-plugin-exodra` is a native Rust/Wasm SWC plugin that compiles Exodra JSX for
SWC-based toolchains — Next.js's default compiler, `@swc/jest`, `swc-loader` —
which cannot run Babel plugins. It is a port of `@exodra/babel-plugin-schema`,
the same dialect in Rust.

:::note `"mode"` is optional, and `"schema"` is the only value
An omitted key selects `"schema"`, and writing `"mode": "schema"` is what the
samples below do. Any other value — `"legacy"` included — is a compile error
naming the value.
:::

## Installation

```bash
npm install --save-dev swc-plugin-exodra
```

The published package ships a prebuilt `.wasm`. To build from source you need the
Rust toolchain and the `wasm32-wasip1` target:

```bash
rustup target add wasm32-wasip1
npm run build
```

## Usage

### .swcrc / @swc/core

```jsonc
{
  "jsc": {
    "parser": { "syntax": "typescript", "tsx": true },
    "experimental": {
      "plugins": [["swc-plugin-exodra", { "mode": "schema" }]]
    }
  }
}
```

### Next.js

```javascript
// next.config.js
module.exports = {
  experimental: {
    swcPlugins: [['swc-plugin-exodra', { mode: 'schema' }]],
  },
};
```

### Options

```jsonc
{
  "mode": "schema",                     // optional — the only value, and the default
  "schemaSource": "@exodra/core",       // where the schema factory is imported from
  "schemaImport": "createExoNamedSchema", // its exported name
  "markerName": "exoJsx"                // the marker call the plugin compiles away
}
```

An unreadable config is treated as an empty one **with a diagnostic**, rather than
in silence: the keys below `"mode"` decide what the emitted imports name, and a
config that was quietly dropped compiles to a module whose imports resolve to
nothing.

## What it emits

An `exoJsx(…)` call in; a module-level schema declaration out, built once for the
process, with every port created under the name written after `$.`. The machine
that fills the ports is written in TypeScript around it and is not touched.

```tsx no-check
import { exoJsx } from '@exodra/jsx';

const ROW_SCHEMA = exoJsx<TRowPorts>(($) => (
  <li class="row" data-id={$.id}>
    <span class="row__label">{$.label}</span>
    <button class="row__btn" onClick={$.toggle} />
  </li>
));
```

```javascript no-check
import { createExoNamedSchema } from '@exodra/core';

const _s0 = createExoNamedSchema((_b0) => {
  _b0.el('li', { class: 'row' }, (_b1) => {
    _b1.port('data-id', 'id');
    _b1.el('span', { class: 'row__label' }, (_b2) => { _b2.textPort('label'); });
    _b1.el('button', { class: 'row__btn' }, (_b2) => { _b2.eventPort('click', 'toggle'); });
  });
});

const ROW_SCHEMA = _s0;
```

There is no hoisting switch: every backend indexes its prepared plan by the
schema's ports, so a schema rebuilt per render is a different program, not a
slower one.

## Parity with the Babel plugin

`@exodra/babel-plugin-schema` is the specification, and this plugin compiles the
same dialect to the same output, up to SWC's own codegen formatting (arrow
spacing, quote style).

| written | schema call | filled by the machine with |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `class="row"`, `tabindex={0}`, `disabled` | folded into the markup | — |
| `data-id={$.id}` | `port("data-id", "id")` | `c.attr(P.id, value)` |
| `<span>{$.label}</span>` | `textPort("label")` | `c.text(P.label, value)` |
| `onClick={$.toggle}` | `eventPort("click", "toggle")` | `m.on(P.toggle, handler)` |
| `on:dblclick={$.edit}` | `eventPort("dblclick", "edit")` | `m.on(P.edit, handler)` |
| `ref={$.box}` | `refPort("box")` | — |
| `unsafeHtml={$.body}` | `childrenPort("body")` | `c.unsafeHtml(P.body, markup)` |
| `<$.rows />` | `childrenPort("rows")` | `c.one`, `c.list`, or `c.childList` + `reconcileExoOrder` |

Everything else is a compile error naming the spelling that would have worked —
there is no runtime under this JSX to defer a decision to. The full dialect,
including every refusal, is in the [JSX guide](../guides/jsx.md).

## Version compatibility

An SWC Wasm plugin is tied to the `swc_core` version it was built against, which
must be compatible with your `@swc/core` / Next.js version. A mismatch fails to
load with *"ensure the version of `swc_core` … is compatible with the host
runtime"*. Rebuild (or upgrade) the plugin against a matching `swc_core` when you
upgrade SWC.

If you would rather not manage that, use the [Babel pipeline](./babel-preset.md):
under Next.js, adding a `babel.config.js` with `presets: ['exodra']` opts the
project into Babel and disables the SWC transform.


==============================================================================
# Introspect

[`@exodra/introspect`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@exodra/introspect) is
static analysis for Exodra projects: an ESLint plugin, and a ts-morph engine
(`ExoIntrospectionEngine`) that reads a project's TypeScript source and reports what
is in it. There is no CLI.

:::danger Versions 0.1.0, 0.1.1 and 0.2.0 reported findings that were not about
your code

`CodeAnalyzer.analyzeCode` returned the same three "security vulnerabilities" for
every project: a `CWE-79` at `src/components/UserContent.tsx:25`, a
high-severity `CWE-521` "No password complexity requirements enforced" at
`src/auth/validation.ts:10`, and a `CWE-200` at `src/utils/logger.ts:8` — files
that need not exist in the project being analysed. Quality scores, a
maintainability index, 30-day "trends", design-pattern locations, component
lists, performance hotspots and route analytics (`frequency: 1500`,
`bounceRate: 25`) were fixed values too, and the `ai.ts` providers returned
canned strings such as `'Code explanation from Claude'` without contacting a
model.

Nothing from those versions was a measurement. If you acted on a finding from
them, discard it. All of it has been removed — and so have the
`exo-introspect` CLI, the AI-provider registry, the plugin system, the Cursor
integration, the browser explorer and the four analyzers that had no discovery
pass behind them.
:::

## Installation

```bash
npm install --save-dev @exodra/introspect
```

## `ExoIntrospectionEngine`

```typescript
import { ExoIntrospectionEngine } from '@exodra/introspect';

const engine = new ExoIntrospectionEngine({
  projectRoot: './',
  analysis: { schema: true, performance: true },
});

const result = await engine.analyze();
// result.diagnostics, result.suggestions, result.metrics, result.summary
```

What it reports, per file:

- **TypeScript diagnostics** — every error and warning the compiler produces.
- **Schema scope** (`analysis.schema`) — a `schema-built-per-call` suggestion
  wherever `createExoSchema`, `createExoNamedSchema` or `createExoStatic` is
  called inside a function. A schema numbers its ports when it is closed and
  every backend indexes its prepared plan by those numbers, so a schema built
  inside a function is not a slower program but a different one. `exoJsx` is
  exempt, because the compiler hoists it to module scope wherever it was written.
- **Counts** (`analysis.performance`):
  - `components` — calls to `createExoMachineBuilder` and `createExoStatic`;
  - `complexity` — control-flow statements plus one, with a `high-complexity`
    warning above 20.

Per project it adds `total_files` and `total_lines`. `analyzeFilePath(path)`
runs the same pass over a single file, and a folder without a `tsconfig.json`
is analysed as plain TypeScript.

Callees are matched by their text rather than by resolving the import, so an
aliased import (`createExoSchema as build`) is missed — the direction that
reports nothing rather than something wrong.

## `eslintPlugin`

```js
import { eslintPlugin } from '@exodra/introspect';

export default [
  {
    plugins: { exodra: eslintPlugin },
    rules: eslintPlugin.configs.recommended.rules,
  },
];
```

| rule | recommended | what it reports |
|---|---|---|
| `exodra/no-schema-in-function` | warn | a schema builder called inside a function (`exoJsx` exempt) |
| `exodra/schema-validation` | error | `exoJsx()` given anything but a function literal |
| `exodra/no-inline-objects` | warn | an object literal inside a JSX expression or a schema builder call |

`configs.strict` makes every rule an error.

## Links

- npm: [`@exodra/introspect`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@exodra/introspect)
- GitHub: [`packages/introspect`](https://github.com/abaikov/exodra/tree/master/packages/introspect)


==============================================================================
# Profiler

[`@exodra/dom-profiler`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@exodra/dom-profiler)
times Exodra's DOM renderer. There is no profiling built into the core — it is
added at runtime when you import this package, and removed again when you
`stop()`.

It works **wherever the renderer runs** — the browser, [jsdom](../guides/testing.md),
or plain Node with a DOM shim — because timing uses `performance.now()` with a
`Date.now()` fallback and it needs no browser-only APIs.

## What can be measured, and what cannot

A render in the schema core is a **clone**, a **replay of a walk**, and one
indirect call per **port**. Neither the clone nor the walk is a method with a
name, so there is nothing there to patch. Two things do have names:

| instrument | patches | answers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `profileDom(backend)` | the **composed backend** you hand it | which **calls your wiring makes** cost — `attr`, `text`, `list`, `one` |
| `profilePorts(C)` | one schema's **setter table** | which **place in your template** costs — `attr:style`, `text` |

:::caution Wrapping the hot path measures a different program
A setter's body is often a single `setAttribute`; the wrapper around it — two
clock reads, a `try`/`finally`, a map lookup — costs several times that, and it
defeats the inlining the unwrapped table relies on. Read the **ratios** inside
one report. The absolute numbers are the profiler's, not the renderer's, and a
benchmark run with a profiler active is not measuring Exodra.
:::

## Installation

```bash
npm install --save-dev @exodra/dom-profiler
```

## Per-method: `profileDom(backend)`

```ts setup
import type { TExoCompilerApi, TExoDomBackend, TExoDomMachine } from '@exodra/dom';

declare const APP: TExoDomMachine;
declare const container: Element;
declare const backend: TExoDomBackend & TExoCompilerApi;
declare const theme: { setValue(value: string): void };
```

```ts
import { profileDom } from '@exodra/dom-profiler';

// Patch the backend the application already built — reversible.
const profiler = profileDom(backend);

backend.render(APP, container);     // exercise the renderer

console.table(profiler.stop());     // per-method report; also restores the backend
```

**It takes the backend**, and that is the whole of what changed when a connector
stopped being a class. A connector is a plain object whose prototype is the
composed backend, and the connector methods are own properties of that backend, so
there is no shared prototype to reach: the object an application constructed and
named is the target. Pass the one the page renders through — profiling a second
backend built for the purpose would be a second plan-cache key, a recompile of
every schema, and a report about a composition nobody renders with.

The names it wraps are the keys of `EXO_DOM_NODE_VOCABULARY` — `attr`, `text`,
`html`, `on`, `one`, `list`, `onTeardown` and the rest of the exonode
surface, which is exactly what a wiring function calls. Patching covers every
exonode on every plan's stack **of that backend** and is **reversible**.

The six plugin-interface fields are deliberately **not** wrapped, and the reason is
not tidiness: each is spent into a plan when that plan compiles, so wrapping one
would do nothing for a schema already compiled and would bake the wrapper
permanently into any schema first rendered while profiling was on — surviving
`stop()`. `render` and `hydrate` are excluded too, as entry points rather than
things a wiring function calls.

- `getReport()` — aggregated timings so far, heaviest first.
- `reset()` — clear collected samples, keep profiling active.
- `stop()` — put the backend's own methods back and return the final report.

An update is timed too: a transition writes through `c.attr` / `c.text`, which are
the wrapped names, so every write an effect or a handler makes while profiling is
on lands in the report.

Two things it will not show you:

- **A static component's instances.** They never touch a connector.
- **Hydration.** The adopting surface is a separate object — its prototype is the
  backend, but its own methods shadow the ones this patched — so an adopted page is
  not profiled by this.

## Per-port: `profilePorts(component)`

```ts
import { profilePorts } from '@exodra/dom-profiler';

const profiler = profilePorts(APP, backend);   // BEFORE the render
const dispose = backend.render(APP, container);
theme.setValue('dark');                        // updates go through the wrapped setters

console.table(profiler.stop());
// port  label        count  totalMs  avgMs  maxMs
//    2  attr:style      41    3.902  0.095  0.31
//    5  text            41    0.284  0.007  0.02
```

It takes a **component** (or a bare schema) and wraps the entries of its compiled
plan's setter table, so a report names the template position to look at rather
than the method that was called. It is **opt-in and per schema**: a setter table
belongs to one plan, and there is no registry of plans to walk.

Two rules, both structural:

- **Start it before the render to see the render.** Every fill indexes
  `schema.setters[port.index]` afresh — `attr`, `text` and `html` all do, and so
  does the shared writer `portNodeWriter()` hands out — so a profiler started
  after the render still times every later update; what it loses is the initial
  fills, which is most of the mount.
- **An event port and a ref port are invisible, and they always will be.** `on`
  reads the event pack's body off the schema rather than the setter table, and a
  ref port has no writer at all; the table's entries for both are
  `exoUnsettableEvent` and `exoUnsettableRef`, which exist to throw. A **text**
  port, by contrast, *is* timed: the Text node it writes is a slot in the walk,
  so the write goes through the table like any attribute.

**Pass it the backend the page renders from.** The second parameter is
**required** and it must be the **same object**:

```ts
import { composeExoPlugins } from '@exodra/core';
import { ExoDomBackend, createExoDelegatedEvents, withExoCompiler } from '@exodra/dom';
import { profilePorts } from '@exodra/dom-profiler';

// once, at module level
const delegatedBackend = composeExoPlugins(withExoCompiler(new ExoDomBackend()), {
  events: () => createExoDelegatedEvents(['click']),
});

const profiler = profilePorts(APP, delegatedBackend);
delegatedBackend.render(APP, container);
```

A plan is compiled per **(schema, backend)** and the backend is compared by
pointer, so profiling under one backend while the page renders under another
compiles a second plan under a key no render ever uses: the profiler then wraps a
setter table nothing calls, nothing throws, and the report comes back **empty**.
`new ExoDomBackend()` returns a fresh object per call — and a `with*` decorator
mutates and returns whatever it was handed, so the identity that matters is the one
the outermost call produced. Construct the chain once and pass that value to both.

The parameter has no default for exactly that reason. A default would have to name
a shipped composition here, and every application that composed anything at all
would then be profiled under a key it never rendered through.

### Focusing on specific methods

```ts
import { profileDom } from '@exodra/dom-profiler';

const profiler = profileDom(backend, {
  methods: ['attr', 'text', 'list'],      // allow-list
  // excludeMethods: ['onTeardown'],      // or deny-list
});
```

An allow-list **narrows** the connector set rather than replacing it: naming a
method the connector does not have profiles nothing, and naming none profiles the
whole surface.

### Under jsdom

Since it only uses `performance.now()`/`Date.now()`, it profiles the renderer the
same way inside a jsdom test (or any Node DOM environment):

```ts
// @vitest-environment jsdom
import { profileDom } from '@exodra/dom-profiler';

const profiler = profileDom(backend);
const root = document.createElement('div');
document.body.appendChild(root);
backend.render(APP, root);
console.table(profiler.stop());
```

## Report format

`getReport()` / `stop()` return one entry per profiled method, sorted by total
time:

```ts
interface TExoDomProfileEntry {
  method: string;   // e.g. 'attr'
  count: number;    // how many times it ran
  totalMs: number;  // total wall time
  avgMs: number;    // totalMs / count
  maxMs: number;    // slowest single call
}
```

## Profiling any class, or any object

`profileClass` patches the prototype methods of **any** class and returns a
`restore()` — use it to profile your own services. Its twin,
`profileMethods(target, label, callback, options?)`, does the same for
the **own** properties of a plain object, and is what `profileDom` is built on now
that a backend is an object rather than a class:

```ts
import { profileClass } from '@exodra/dom-profiler';

declare class MyService { load(): Promise<void>; save(): Promise<void>; }

const restore = profileClass(MyService, (sample) => {
  console.log(`${sample.className}.${sample.method}: ${sample.durationMs}ms`);
}, {
  methods: ['load', 'save'],    // optional allow-list
  excludeMethods: ['toString'], // optional deny-list
});

// ...exercise MyService...
restore(); // put the original methods back
```

## Links

- npm: [`@exodra/dom-profiler`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@exodra/dom-profiler)
- GitHub: [`packages/dom-profiler`](https://github.com/abaikov/exodra/tree/master/packages/dom-profiler)
